    # only wait for exactly that number.
    if self.fast and cmd.fast and (cmd in self.__frame_counts):
        cmd_string += str(self.__frame_counts[cmd]).encode()
    # if we sent this last time, just send a CR
    if self.fast and (cmd_string == self.__last_command):
        cmd_string = b""
    return cmd_string
```
This is a genuinely good idea for your dashboard: **the first time a command is sent, it doesn't know the frame count, so it waits for the ELM's full timeout; it then remembers "this PID returns N frames" and appends that digit to every subsequent request** (e.g. `010C1` tells the ELM327 "stop listening after 1 response"), which lets the adapter return the instant it hears one frame instead of waiting out its internal ~200ms timeout. This is the biggest lever for polling speed and it's ECU/car-specific, learned at runtime.

Sources: obd.py (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/obd.py), elm327.py (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/elm327.py), OBDCommand.py (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/OBDCommand.py), protocols/protocol.py (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/protocols/protocol.py).

### `ELM327` class responsibilities (the AT-command layer)

From `obd/elm327.py`. Connection sequence on `__init__`: open serial port -> (`start_low_power` wake, optional) -> `set_baudrate()` (auto-detect by trying `_TRY_BAUDS = [38400, 9600, 230400, 115200, 57600, 19200]` and writing junk bytes `\x7F\x7F\r` looking for a `>` prompt) -> `ATZ` (reset, 1s delay) -> `ATE0` (echo off) -> `ATH1` (headers **on**, hardcoded — see §10/§12 implications) -> `ATL0` (linefeeds off) -> status becomes `ELM_CONNECTED` -> optional `AT RV` voltage check (must read >6V or it aborts) -> status becomes `OBD_CONNECTED` -> `set_protocol()` (manual `ATTP<id>` or `auto_protocol()` which does `ATSP0`, sends `0100`, reads back the chosen protocol via `ATDPN`, and if that comes back unrecognized, falls back to manually trying protocols in `_TRY_PROTOCOL_ORDER`) -> status becomes `CAR_CONNECTED`.

Low-level read/write (`__write`/`__read`) accumulate bytes until the `>` prompt byte is seen, strip null bytes, decode UTF-8 with `errors="ignore"`, split into lines on `\r`/`\n`. `__send()` has a retry loop: if nothing came back within the delay, it polls every 0.1s up to 1.0s total before giving up (this is the "1 second read-retry loop for unresponsive dongles" added in v0.7.2, see §12).

## 2. `obd.Async` — exact API, thread model, callback dispatch

Source of truth: `obd/asynchronous.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/asynchronous.py) + docs page https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Async%20Connections/ (raw markdown: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/docs/Async%20Connections.md).

`Async` is a subclass of `OBD` (single-inheritance, not a wrapper), so it inherits `query()`'s signature but **overrides** it non-blockingly.

**Constructor** (adds one param over `OBD`):
```python
Async(portstr=None, baudrate=None, protocol=None, fast=True,
      timeout=0.1, check_voltage=True, start_low_power=False,
      delay_cmds=0.25)
```
`delay_cmds` (default 0.25s): sleep duration after each full pass over all watched commands. Setting it to `0` makes the background thread hammer the adapter continuously with no delay between polling cycles.

**Watch/callback model** — exact source:
```python
def watch(self, c, callback=None, force=False):
    # the dict shouldn't be changed while the daemon thread is iterating
    if self.__running:
        logger.warning("Can't watch() while running, please use stop()")
    else:
        if not force and not self.test_cmd(c):
            return  # test_cmd() prints its own warning
        if c not in self.__commands:
            self.__commands[c] = OBDResponse()   # give it an initial (null) value
            self.__callbacks[c] = []
        if hasattr(callback, "__call__") and (callback not in self.__callbacks[c]):
            self.__callbacks[c].append(callback)
```
Key facts:
- **`watch()`/`unwatch()`/`unwatch_all()` all hard-refuse to run while the thread is active** — they just log a warning and no-op. You must `stop()` first (or use the `paused()` context manager). This is enforced because `self.__commands` is a plain `dict` iterated by the daemon thread — no lock is used; the mutual exclusion is achieved purely by "don't touch it while running," not real thread-safety primitives.
- `force=False` (default): `watch()` calls `self.test_cmd(c)` — same support-check `query()` uses — and silently refuses to add the command if unsupported (with a logged warning). `force=True` skips that check.
- Callbacks are a list per command — you can register multiple callbacks for the same command (confirmed by `test_async_unwatch_callback` in the test suite, which registers two independent callbacks and unwatches only one).
- `unwatch(c, callback=None)`: if `callback` given, removes only that one; **if that empties the callback list, it also pops the command entirely** from `self.__commands`. If `callback` is omitted, drops the command and all its callbacks.

**Thread/loop implementation** — exact `run()`:
```python
def run(self):
    while self.__running:
        if len(self.__commands) > 0:
            for c in self.__commands:
                if not self.is_connected():
                    logger.info("Async thread terminated because device disconnected")
                    self.__running = False
                    self.__thread = None
                    return
                r = super(Async, self).query(c, force=True)   # force=True: already checked in watch()
                self.__commands[c] = r
                for callback in self.__callbacks[c]:
                    callback(r)
            time.sleep(self.__delay_cmds)
        else:
            time.sleep(0.25)  # idle
```
- **One daemon thread total** (`threading.Thread(target=self.run); self.__thread.daemon = True`), not one thread per command. It round-robins through every watched command **sequentially and synchronously** in a single pass, then sleeps `delay_cmds`. There is no per-command rate/priority control — every watched PID gets polled at the same cadence, gated only by how long the serial round-trips for all of them take plus the flat `delay_cmds` sleep. If you watch 20 PIDs and each round-trip takes 50ms, your true refresh rate per PID is ~(20×50ms + delay_cmds), not "delay_cmds per PID." **There is no priority/rate-per-command system in this library** — if you want RPM at 50ms and VIN at 1x/connection, you'd have to build that yourself (e.g., separate `Async` instances, or your own scheduler on top of `query()`).
- Callbacks are invoked **synchronously, on the polling thread itself**, in the order registered, before moving to the next command. A slow callback blocks the whole polling loop — worth avoiding heavy work (UI redraw, disk I/O) directly in a callback; hand off to a queue instead.
- If the device disconnects mid-loop, the thread quietly sets `__running = False` and returns (no exception raised) — this was an explicit v0.7.1 change: *"Async connections will no longer throw exceptions when the underlying transport is disconnected. They will instead terminate gracefully. Async status is observable via the `Async.running` parameter."*
- `query()` on `Async` is fully non-blocking and never touches serial:
```python
def query(self, c, force=False):
    if c in self.__commands:
        return self.__commands[c]
    else:
        return OBDResponse()
```
So an unwatched command always returns a fresh null `OBDResponse()`.

**`paused()` context manager** — literally a self-return stub; the real logic is in `__enter__`/`__exit__`:
```python
def paused(self):
    """ enables: with connection.paused() as was_running: ... """
    return self

def __enter__(self):
    self.__was_running = self.__running
    self.stop()
    return self.__was_running

def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
    if not self.__running and self.__was_running:
        self.start()
    return False
```
Docs example (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/docs/Async%20Connections.md):
```python
with connection.paused() as was_running:
    # connection is stopped within this block
    ...
```

**Full watch+callback usage example straight from the docs:**
```python
import obd, time
connection = obd.Async()

def new_rpm(r):
    print(r.value)

connection.watch(obd.commands.RPM, callback=new_rpm)
connection.start()
# callback fires on every new value now
time.sleep(60)
connection.stop()
```

**`start()`/`stop()`**: `start()` no-ops (with a log message) if not connected or if zero commands are watched. `stop()` sets the flag and calls `self.__thread.join()` — i.e. it blocks the caller until the in-flight poll finishes, so `stop()` can take up to one full round of all watched commands to return.

The real integration-test suite in `tests/test_obdsim.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/tests/test_obdsim.py) is a good API confirmation/usage reference — it exercises `watch()`, `start()`, `paused()`, `unwatch()`, `unwatch_all()`, and multi-callback unwatch, against a real simulated adapter (`obdsim`, see §9/§12).

## 3. Command tables: `obd.commands`, `OBDCommand` constructor, `ECU`, `fast`

Full source: `obd/commands.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/commands.py), `obd/OBDCommand.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/OBDCommand.py). Docs: https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Command%20Lookup/ and https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Command%20Tables/.

**The `Commands` class** (instantiated once at import as the module-level `commands` object):
```python
class Commands():
    def __init__(self):
        self.modes = [
            [], __mode1__, __mode2__, __mode3__, __mode4__,
            [], __mode6__, __mode7__, [], __mode9__,
        ]  # index 0,5,8 are empty placeholders — modes are 1,2,3,4,6,7,9
        for m in self.modes:
            for c in m:
                if c is not None:
                    self.__dict__[c.name] = c   # <-- attribute access, e.g. commands.RPM
        for c in __misc__:
            self.__dict__[c.name] = c

    def __getitem__(self, key):
        # obd.commands.RPM / obd.commands["RPM"] / obd.commands[1][12]
        if isinstance(key, int):
            return self.modes[key]
        elif isinstance(key, basestring):
            return self.__dict__[key]

    def base_commands(self):
        """ commands that should always be supported by the ELM327 """
        return [self.PIDS_A, self.PIDS_9A, self.MIDS_A,
                self.GET_DTC, self.CLEAR_DTC, self.GET_CURRENT_DTC,
                self.ELM_VERSION, self.ELM_VOLTAGE]

    def pid_getters(self):
        """ returns list of PID-listing GET commands (the 'PIDS_A' style bitmask probes) """
        getters = []
        for mode in self.modes:
            getters += [cmd for cmd in mode if (cmd and cmd.decode == pid)]
        return getters

    def has_command(self, c):
        return c in self.__dict__.values()

    def has_name(self, name):
        return name.isupper() and name in self.__dict__

    def has_pid(self, mode, pid):
        if (mode < 0) or (pid < 0): return False
        if mode >= len(self.modes): return False
        if pid >= len(self.modes[mode]): return False
        return self.modes[mode][pid] is not None
```
So `obd.commands.RPM`, `obd.commands['RPM']`, and `obd.commands[1][12]` are **three different lookup paths converging on the same object**: attribute/dict access by uppercase name vs. list-indexing by `[mode][pid]` where the mode-1 list is literally built PID-ordered so that `list[pid]` works directly. `'RPM' in obd.commands` also works because `Commands.__contains__` delegates to `has_name`.

**How mode 2 is generated**: it's *not* hand-written — it's mechanically cloned from mode 1 at import time:
```python
__mode2__ = []
for c in __mode1__:
    c = c.clone()
    c.command = b"02" + c.command[2:]        # 0100 -> 0200
    c.name = "DTC_" + c.name                 # RPM -> DTC_RPM
    c.desc = "DTC " + c.desc
    if c.decode == pid:
        c.decode = drop  # never send mode 02 PID-listing requests
    __mode2__.append(c)
```
So `obd.commands.DTC_RPM` is mode 2's freeze-frame RPM, auto-derived. `OBDCommand.clone()` exists specifically to support this pattern — a nice, cheap way to derive command families without hand-duplicating 100+ definitions.

**`OBDCommand.__init__` — exact constructor signature** (this answers your Q3 directly):
```python
def __init__(self, name, desc, command, _bytes, decoder,
             ecu=ECU.ALL, fast=False, header=ECU_HEADER.ENGINE):
    self.name = name        # human readable name (also the dict key)
    self.desc = desc        # human readable description
    self.command = command  # command bytes, e.g. b"010C"
    self.bytes = _bytes     # expected response byte length (0 = unknown/variable)
    self.decode = decoder   # decoding function
    self.ecu = ecu          # ECU filter bitmask
    self.fast = fast        # allow the "01"-style response-count optimization
    self.header = header    # AT SH header to use for this query (default b'7E0')
```
Derived properties: `.mode` and `.pid` parse the hex `command` bytes (`int(self.command[:2], 16)` / `int(self.command[2:], 16)`), returning `None` if the command isn't cleanly hex (e.g. AT-commands like `ATRV`).

**Equality/hashing is by `(header, command)`, not by name** — important if you're rolling your own custom commands:
```python
def __hash__(self):
    return hash(self.header + self.command)
def __eq__(self, other):
    if isinstance(other, OBDCommand):
        return self.command == other.command and self.header == other.header
    return False
```
This is how the command tables (and `supported_commands`, which is a `set`) dedupe — two `OBDCommand` instances with the same header+command bytes are the *same key* even if you gave them different names/decoders. Watch for this if you define multiple BMW custom commands with the same raw PID under different names.

**`ECU` flags** (from `obd/protocols/protocol.py`) — bit flags, ORable, used both to tag which module a `Message` came from and to filter which messages a command will accept:
```python
class ECU:
    ALL        = 0b11111111  # accept messages from any ECU
    ALL_KNOWN  = 0b11111110  # ignore genuinely-unknown ECUs
    UNKNOWN    = 0b00000001
    ENGINE     = 0b00000010
    TRANSMISSION = 0b00000100
```
python-OBD currently only auto-identifies **Engine** and (in principle) **Transmission** — the docs are explicit that "python-OBD can currently only distinguish the engine, but this list may be expanded over time." `OBDCommand.__call__` filters incoming messages with `messages = [m for m in messages if (self.ecu & m.ecu) > 0]` — a bitwise AND test.

**`fast` flag** — from `docs/Custom Commands.md`: *"tells python-OBD whether it is safe to append a `"01"` [style digit] to the end of the command. This will instruct the adapter to return the first response it receives, rather than waiting for more... enabled for most of python-OBD's internal commands. However, for unusual commands, it is safest to leave this disabled."* Combined with `OBD.fast` (a global on/off on the connection) — both must be true, and the frame count must already be known, for the optimization to actually apply (see the `__build_command_string` code in §1).

**`header`** default is `ECU_HEADER.ENGINE = b'7E0'` (from `obd/protocols/protocol.py`). `OBD.__set_header()` only issues `AT SH <header>` when the header differs from the last one used, to minimize AT-command chatter:
```python
def __set_header(self, header):
    if header == self.__last_header:
        return
    r = self.interface.send_and_parse(b'AT SH ' + header + b' ')
    ...
    self.__last_header = header
```
This is your hook for **manufacturer-specific / BMW-specific requests** — see §11.

**Mode-1 table snippet** (illustrating the declarative style, from `commands.py`):
```python
__mode1__ = [
    OBDCommand("PIDS_A" , "Supported PIDs [01-20]" , b"0100", 6, pid,     ECU.ENGINE, True),
    OBDCommand("STATUS" , "Status since DTCs cleared", b"0101", 6, status, ECU.ENGINE, True),
    ...
    OBDCommand("RPM"    , "Engine RPM"              , b"010C", 4, uas(0x07), ECU.ENGINE, True),
    OBDCommand("SPEED"  , "Vehicle Speed"           , b"010D", 3, uas(0x09), ECU.ENGINE, True),
    ...
]
```
Note commands must be **in strict PID order, one per PID slot**, specifically so `self.modes[mode][pid]` is an O(1) list index — reserved/unimplemented PIDs are filled with literal `None` placeholders (see the mode-6 table using `+ ([None] * 15) + [...]` to skip reserved MID ranges). If you copy this pattern for a BMW-specific table, keep that PID-ordering invariant if you want `[mode][pid]` indexing to work; otherwise just use a plain dict for your custom table.

## 4. Pint units: `Unit`, `Quantity`, migration history, gotchas

Source: `obd/UnitsAndScaling.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/UnitsAndScaling.py), docs page https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Responses/ (raw: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/docs/Responses.md), and the GitHub Releases changelog (https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/releases).

**Setup:**
```python
import pint
Unit = pint.UnitRegistry()
Unit.define("ratio = []")
Unit.define("percent = 1e-2 ratio = %")
Unit.define("gps = gram / second = GPS = grams_per_second")
Unit.define("lph = liter / hour = LPH = liters_per_hour")
Unit.define("ppm = count / 1000000 = PPM = parts_per_million")
```
`obd.Unit` **is literally the process-wide Pint `UnitRegistry` instance** — every response value that's a `Quantity` is stamped from this exact registry (Pint requires quantities to share a registry to interoperate in arithmetic; mixing quantities from two different `UnitRegistry()` instances raises errors — good to know if you build your own units module alongside `obd.Unit`, you should probably reuse `obd.Unit` rather than creating a second registry).

**`UAS` (Units-And-Scaling) table** — this is the reusable scale/offset/unit lookup Mode 06 (and many Mode 01 PIDs) use, keyed by a byte ID defined in the J1979 standard:
```python
class UAS:
    def __init__(self, signed, scale, unit, offset=0.0):
        self.signed = signed; self.scale = scale; self.unit = unit; self.offset = offset
    def __call__(self, _bytes):
        value = bytes_to_int(_bytes)
        if self.signed:
            value = twos_comp(value, len(_bytes) * 8)
        value *= self.scale
        value += self.offset
        return Unit.Quantity(value, self.unit)

UAS_IDS = {
    0x07: UAS(False, 0.25, Unit.rpm),
    0x09: UAS(False, 1,    Unit.kph),
    0x16: UAS(False, 0.1,  Unit.celsius, offset=-40.0),
    ... # ~65 entries, unsigned 0x01-0x41 and signed 0x81-0xFE
}
```
and in `decoders.py`, `uas(id_)` is just `functools.partial(decode_uas, id_=id_)` — a slick way to turn "give me the decoder for UAS ID 0x07" into a zero-boilerplate decoder function reference used directly in the command tables (`OBDCommand("RPM", ..., uas(0x07), ...)`).

**Response value access** (verbatim from docs/Responses.md):
```python
>>> response.value
<Quantity(100, 'kph')>
>>> response.value.magnitude          # raw python float/int
100
>>> str(response.value)
'100 kph'
>>> obd.Unit("100 kph")               # parse a string into a Quantity
<Quantity(100, 'kph')>
>>> response.value.to('mph')          # conversion
<Quantity(62.13711922373341, 'mph')>
>>> response.value / 2                # scalar math preserves units
<Quantity(50.0, 'kph')>
>>> response.value + (20 * obd.Unit.kph)   # non-scalar math needs explicit units
<Quantity(120, 'kph')>
>>> response.value + (20 * obd.Unit.mph)   # Pint auto-converts mismatched units
<Quantity(132.18688, 'kph')>
```
The docs explicitly flag: *"NOTE: for backwards compatibility with previous versions of python-OBD, use `response.value.magnitude` in place of `response.value`"* — i.e. `.magnitude` is your escape hatch to a plain float whenever you don't want to carry Pint objects through your own code (e.g. into a plotting library or a struct you're serializing over MQTT/websocket for your dashboard).

**Migration history (verified against the actual GitHub Releases, not v0.7 as guessed — it was v0.6.0):**

| Version | Date | Relevant change |
|---|---|---|
| v0.5.0 | 2016-06-14 | Decoders changed to `def name(messages): return (<value>, <unit>)` tuple format (pre-Pint) |
| **v0.6.0** | **2016-07-27** | **"using Pint for values and units. `OBDResponse.value` now holds Pint Quantities... for backwards compatibility, use `response.value.magnitude`... obd.Unit is now a Pint unit registry. All unit names have changed"** — this is the actual Pint migration |

Full changelog source: https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/releases (fetched via GitHub API, all 13 tags v0.1.0→v0.7.3).

**Pint gotchas actually reported by users (GitHub Issues, not speculation):**
- **`import obd` is slow** — issue #136 ("import obd very slow", https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/136): *"On my raspberry pi 'import obd' takes more than 10 seconds to complete."* A maintainer/community reply diagnoses it precisely: *"my hunch would be the massive DTC and command tables that get instantiated upon import. Would probably be best to move these to a file that is searched/accessed at runtime."* This is **not actually Pint's fault** so much as: (a) constructing a `pint.UnitRegistry()` has nontrivial import-time cost, and (b) `codes.py` is a ~130KB Python module-level dict literal (thousands of `"P0001": "description"` DTC entries) that gets fully parsed and built into a dict at import, plus the entire `commands.py` table (hundreds of `OBDCommand` objects) is constructed eagerly. **If you're building your own dashboard and care about cold-start latency on an embedded board, lazy-load your DTC description table and avoid constructing a `pint.UnitRegistry()` (or any large tables) at module import time — construct once, cache, or defer.**
- **Pint version pinning has bitten packaging** — issues #285 ("Upgrade dependency 'pint' from pint==0.20.* to pint==0.24.4") and #269 ("new 0.7.2 does not install due to pint version bug") — python-OBD pins Pint tightly (`pint==0.24.*` in the current `pyproject.toml`) and has repeatedly needed point releases just to bump that pin for new Python versions. If you depend on Pint directly in your own dashboard, don't assume the version python-OBD wants is the one you want; check for conflicts.
- **Dependencies today** (from `pyproject.toml`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/pyproject.toml): `pyserial==3.*`, `pint==0.24.*`, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`.

## 5. "Supported commands" probing: `supported_commands`, `print_commands()`, `supports()`, PID bitmask scanning, `check_voltage`

Source: `obd/obd.py` and https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Connections/ (raw: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/docs/Connections.md).

**On every connect**, `OBD.__load_commands()` runs automatically:
```python
def __load_commands(self):
    if self.status() != OBDStatus.CAR_CONNECTED:
        logger.warning("Cannot load commands: No connection to car")
        return

    pid_getters = commands.pid_getters()   # PIDS_A (0100), PIDS_B (0120), PIDS_C (0140), PIDS_9A (0900), MIDS_A (0600), etc.
    for get in pid_getters:
        if not self.test_cmd(get, warn=False):
            continue   # e.g. PIDS_B only becomes testable once PIDS_A said bit-0x20 is set

        response = OBD.query(self, get)   # explicit OBD.query(self,...) — bypasses Async override!
        if response.is_null():
            continue

        for i, bit in enumerate(response.value):     # response.value is a BitArray, iterable of booleans
            if bit:
                mode = get.mode
                pid = get.pid + i + 1
                if commands.has_pid(mode, pid):
                    self.supported_commands.add(commands[mode][pid])
                if mode == 1 and commands.has_pid(2, pid):
                    self.supported_commands.add(commands[2][pid])   # mode 2 (freeze frame) mirrors mode 1 support
```
This is exactly your Q5 "how it queries PIDs 0x00/0x20/0x40 bitmask PIDs" — `PIDS_A` (`0100`) returns a 32-bit mask covering PIDs 01-20 including a top bit that says "PIDS_B (0120) is supported"; walking that chain (`PIDS_A` -> `PIDS_B` -> `PIDS_C` ...) is what `pid_getters()` + the `test_cmd(get, warn=False)` gate implements. The bitmask decoder itself (`pid` in decoders.py) is trivial: `BitArray(messages[0].data[2:])` — just wraps the raw bytes after the mode/PID header in the hand-rolled `BitArray` class (`obd/utils.py`), which supports `[i]` indexing, slicing, `.num_set()`, `.value(start, stop)`.

Note the explicit comment `# when querying, only use the blocking OBD.query() / prevents problems when query is redefined in a subclass (like Async)` — a deliberate defensive pattern: calling `OBD.query(self, get)` (unbound-style) rather than `self.query(get)` specifically to dodge `Async`'s overridden non-blocking `query()`. Worth remembering if you build your own subclass hierarchy with an overridden core method — internal bootstrapping code needs to pin down *which* implementation it calls.

**Base/always-supported commands** — `commands.base_commands()` returns `[PIDS_A, PIDS_9A, MIDS_A, GET_DTC, CLEAR_DTC, GET_CURRENT_DTC, ELM_VERSION, ELM_VOLTAGE]`, and `OBD.__init__` seeds `self.supported_commands = set(commands.base_commands())` *before* any car probing happens — these are assumed always safe to send.

**`supports()` / `test_cmd()` / `print_commands()`** — exact source:
```python
def supports(self, cmd):
    return cmd in self.supported_commands

def test_cmd(self, cmd, warn=True):
    if not self.supports(cmd):
        if warn: logger.warning("'%s' is not supported" % str(cmd))
        return False
    if cmd.mode == 6 and self.interface.protocol_id() not in ["6", "7", "8", "9"]:
        if warn: logger.warning("Mode 06 commands are only supported over CAN protocols")
        return False
    return True

def print_commands(self):
    """ Utility function meant for working in interactive mode. """
    for c in self.supported_commands:
        print(str(c))
```
So `supports()` is a plain set-membership test; `test_cmd()` layers on a hardcoded rule that **Mode 06 monitor commands are CAN-only** (checked against `protocol_id()` being one of the four ISO-15765-4 CAN IDs) — this rule is baked into core `obd.py`, not just docs. `print_commands()` is genuinely just a `for`/`print` loop, meant for REPL exploration (`str(OBDCommand)` renders as `"010C: Engine RPM"`).

**`fast` and `protocol` on `obd.OBD()`** — full constructor documented at https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Connections/:
```python
OBD(portstr=None, baudrate=None, protocol=None, fast=True,
    timeout=0.1, check_voltage=True, start_low_power=False)
```
- `protocol`: forces a specific ELM protocol ID string (`"1"`.."9","A"`, see table in §10) instead of auto-detecting; `None` = auto.
- `fast`: global on/off for the two "fast mode" optimizations described in §1/§3 (CR-repeat + frame-count truncation). Docs: *"Disabling fast mode will guarantee that python-OBD outputs the unaltered command for every request."*
- `check_voltage` (added v0.7.1, default `True`): sends `AT RV` and requires >6V readback or it aborts and treats the port as unusable; this is what unlocks the `OBD_CONNECTED` state distinct from `ELM_CONNECTED`. Docs explain the nuance in detail: *"If the OBDII socket does not support the unswitched battery positive supply, or the OBDII adapter cannot detect it, then the `check_voltage` option should be set to `False`."*
- `start_low_power` (added v0.7.1): if `True`, sends a leading space and sleeps 1s *before* baud-rate detection, to wake an ELM327 that's in low-power sleep.

`supported_commands` is a public, mutable `set` attribute — the docs explicitly tell you to add to it directly for custom commands (see §11) rather than treating it as read-only: `connection.supported_commands.add(<OBDCommand>)`.

## 6. Response validity: `is_null()`, `.time`, `.messages`, null-response causes

Full source of `OBDResponse` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/OBDResponse.py):
```python
class OBDResponse:
    def __init__(self, command=None, messages=None):
        self.command = command
        self.messages = messages if messages else []
        self.value = None
        self.time = time.time()

    def is_null(self):
        return (not self.messages) or (self.value == None)

    def __str__(self):
        return str(self.value)
```
So a response is "null" under exactly two conditions: **no messages at all** (nothing came back / wasn't sent) **or the decoder itself returned `None`** (e.g. a value out of a lookup table's range, or your ECU didn't reply with data for that ECU filter). Concretely, `OBDResponse()` (no args) is returned by `OBD.query()` in every early-exit branch: not connected, unsupported command without `force`, or empty `messages` list back from the adapter — each of these constructs a fresh, blank, `is_null()==True` response rather than raising an exception. **This is a deliberate "never throw, always return a typed null" API design** — worth adopting: your dashboard code can always safely do `r = conn.query(cmd); if not r.is_null(): use(r.value)` without try/except scaffolding.

`.time` is a plain `time.time()` float epoch timestamp captured **when the `OBDResponse` object is constructed** (i.e., right after the round-trip completes, not when the query was issued) — useful for your dashboard to detect stale/cached values (e.g., an `Async` connection returning "last known" for a still-being-polled command).

`.messages` (plural; the property is named `message` singular in the class-level docstring table in the docs but the actual attribute is `messages`, holding a `list[Message]`) — the docs table itself even lists it as "message: The internal Message object" but the constructor and code consistently use `self.messages` as a list; treat that docs table entry as slightly imprecise phrasing, the real attribute is a list.

The `.unit` property is a backward-compat shim:
```python
@property
def unit(self):
    from obd import Unit  # local import to avoid cyclic-dependency
    if isinstance(self.value, Unit.Quantity):
        return str(self.value.u)
    elif self.value is None:
        return None
    else:
        return str(type(self.value))
```
Note the explicit comment about avoiding a circular import — `OBDResponse.py` can't import `Unit` at module scope because `obd/__init__.py` imports `OBDResponse` before `Unit` is defined; it does the import lazily inside the property instead. (You didn't ask about `Unit.NONE` specifically — there is no `Unit.NONE` constant in the source; responses that carry no meaningful unit (strings, tuples, booleans, DTC lists, `Status`/`Monitor` objects) simply hold non-`Quantity` Python values in `.value`, and `.unit` degrades to `None` or `str(type(...))` as shown above.)

## 7. `OBDStatus` — exact states

Source (`obd/utils.py`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/utils.py) — this is a plain class with string class-attributes, **not** a Python `enum.Enum`:
```python
class OBDStatus:
    """ Values for the connection status flags """
    NOT_CONNECTED = "Not Connected"
    ELM_CONNECTED = "ELM Connected"
    OBD_CONNECTED = "OBD Connected"
    CAR_CONNECTED = "Car Connected"
```
Confirmed exact strings — your Q7 guess was right on all four names and I can confirm the literal string values too. `connection.status()` returns one of these four sentinel strings (comparison is by string equality/identity, e.g. `status() == OBDStatus.CAR_CONNECTED`).

Full semantics, quoted from https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Connections/ (raw: docs/Connections.md), because the ordering/meaning nuance matters:
- `NOT_CONNECTED` ("Not Connected"): no connection attempted or the attempt failed before even reaching the ELM chip.
- `ELM_CONNECTED` ("ELM Connected"): successful AT-command handshake with the ELM327 chip itself, but the OBD-II socket isn't necessarily plugged into a car (or `check_voltage=False`, in which case this state absorbs what would otherwise be `OBD_CONNECTED`).
- `OBD_CONNECTED` ("OBD Connected"): *"successful communication with the ELM327 adapter, OBD port connected to the car, ignition off (not available with argument check_voltage=False)"* — i.e. plugged into the car's port (battery voltage detected, >6V) but the ignition/ECU isn't answering yet.
- `CAR_CONNECTED` ("Car Connected"): *"successful communication with the ELM327 and the vehicle; ignition on"* — full protocol handshake succeeded (a real `0100` response came back).

Direct quote worth keeping verbatim because it's a subtle footgun: *"`status()` shall not be checked after the queries to verify that the connection is kept active."* — i.e. `status()` is a **snapshot set once during connect and never updated afterward**; it does NOT reflect a mid-session disconnect. (`Async` handles mid-session disconnects itself by checking `is_connected()` every poll loop iteration and shutting itself down — see §2 — but a plain `OBD` connection will happily let you call `query()` after the adapter has vanished; you'd get null responses / IO errors surfacing through `elm327.py`'s exception handling, which force status to `NOT_CONNECTED` internally on write/read failure, rather than through a live `status()` check pattern.)

`is_connected()` is literally `return self.status() == OBDStatus.CAR_CONNECTED`.

## 10. Protocol support — full table + auto-detect mechanics

Source: `obd/protocols/protocol_legacy.py`, `obd/protocols/protocol_can.py`, `obd/elm327.py` (all at https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/tree/master/obd/protocols), and https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Connections/.

**Full ELM protocol ID table** (exact `ELM_ID`/`ELM_NAME` class attributes from source, cross-checked against the docs table — they match exactly):

| ID | `ELM_NAME` | Implementing class | Framing family |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"1"` | SAE J1850 PWM | `SAE_J1850_PWM` | Legacy |
| `"2"` | SAE J1850 VPW | `SAE_J1850_VPW` | Legacy |
| `"3"` | ISO 9141-2 | `ISO_9141_2` | Legacy |
| `"4"` | ISO 14230-4 (KWP 5BAUD) | `ISO_14230_4_5baud` | Legacy |
| `"5"` | ISO 14230-4 (KWP FAST) | `ISO_14230_4_fast` | Legacy |
| `"6"` | ISO 15765-4 (CAN 11/500) | `ISO_15765_4_11bit_500k` | CAN |
| `"7"` | ISO 15765-4 (CAN 29/500) | `ISO_15765_4_29bit_500k` | CAN |
| `"8"` | ISO 15765-4 (CAN 11/250) | `ISO_15765_4_11bit_250k` | CAN |
| `"9"` | ISO 15765-4 (CAN 29/250) | `ISO_15765_4_29bit_250k` | CAN |
| `"A"` | SAE J1939 (CAN 29/250) | `SAE_J1939` | CAN |

(Your task description's example "6 = ISO 15765-4 CAN 11/500" is exactly right.) These IDs are what `protocol_id()` returns and what you'd pass as the `protocol=` kwarg to `obd.OBD()` to force a choice instead of auto-detecting.

**Auto-detect algorithm** (`ELM327.auto_protocol()`, exact logic):
1. `ATSP0` (tell the ELM to auto-search) + delay.
2. Send `0100`; if the reply contains `"UNABLE TO CONNECT"`, fail immediately (`return False`) — no point continuing.
3. `ATDPN` to ask the ELM which protocol it landed on; strip a leading `"A"` (which the ELM prefixes to mean "automatically found") from the returned ID.
4. If that ID is one of the 10 known IDs above, instantiate the matching protocol class and succeed.
5. **If the ELM reports something unrecognized** (commonly `"0"` on cheap ELM clones), fall back to **manually trying protocols one-by-one** in this hardcoded priority order — `_TRY_PROTOCOL_ORDER = ["6","8","1","7","9","2","3","4","5","A"]` — i.e., CAN 11-bit/500k and CAN 11-bit/250k first (statistically most common on modern-ish cars), then legacy J1850, then the rest. For **each** candidate it does `ATTP<id>` then a fresh `0100` and checks for `"UNABLE TO CONNECT"` again.

**Protocol class hierarchy**: `Protocol` (base, in `protocol.py`) defines the whole frame->message->ECU pipeline generically; `LegacyProtocol` and `CANProtocol` subclass it and implement the two abstract hooks, `parse_frame()` and `parse_message()`, differently per framing style; then each of the 10 concrete classes above is just a 2-line stub setting `ELM_NAME`/`ELM_ID` (and, for CAN, `id_bits=11` or `29`).

**CAN multi-frame reassembly** (`CANProtocol.parse_frame`/`parse_message`, `obd/protocols/protocol_can.py`) — this is a real, working ISO-TP-lite implementation, useful if you ever bypass the ELM327's own reassembly and talk to a raw CAN bus/MCP2515 directly for your E36:
- PCI (Protocol Control Information) byte in the first data byte's high nibble distinguishes **SF** (single frame, `0x00`, 4-bit length in the low nibble), **FF** (first frame of multi-frame, `0x10`, 12-bit length across the low nibble + next byte), and **CF** (consecutive frame, `0x20`, 4-bit rolling sequence index in the low nibble).
- For multi-frame: it collects all `FF`+`CF` frames, **reconstructs full sequence numbers from the 4-bit rolling counter** by comparing against the previous frame's index and adding `0x10` on wraparound (`if seq < prev.seq_index - 7: seq += 0x10`), sorts by that reconstructed index, verifies contiguity via a `contiguous()` helper (`obd/utils.py`), then concatenates payload bytes and truncates to the length declared in the FF header.
- 11-bit CAN headers are **manually padded to look like 29-bit ones** (`"00000" + raw`) purely so the rest of the byte-offset parsing logic can be shared between 11-bit and 29-bit implementations — a small but instructive normalization trick.
- ECU identification for CAN: `TX_ID_ENGINE = 0`, `TX_ID_TRANSMISSION = 1` (as offsets into the low nibble of the response arbitration ID, e.g. response ID `7E8` = request `7E0` + engine offset 8... actually stored as `raw_bytes[3] & 0x07` for 11-bit), later mapped through `ecu_map` built by `populate_ecu_map()` in the base `Protocol` class (§below).

**Legacy (K-line/J1850) reassembly** (`LegacyProtocol`, `obd/protocols/protocol_legacy.py`) — relevant if your E36 (see caveat below) turns out to be ISO 9141-2 or ISO 14230 (KWP) rather than CAN: frames carry a 3-byte header (`priority`, `rx_id`, `tx_id`) plus a trailing checksum byte that the ELM already validates/strips; multi-line responses use an explicit **order byte** (not a rolling counter) at a fixed offset, and DTC (mode `0x43`) responses get a synthetic CAN-style `DTC_count` byte spliced in (`bytearray([0x43, 0x00])`) purely so the shared `dtc()` decoder in `decoders.py` can treat legacy and CAN DTC responses identically — a good example of normalizing protocol differences at the parsing boundary so your decoder layer stays protocol-agnostic.

**ECU auto-mapping** (`Protocol.populate_ecu_map`, in the shared base class): sent once, right after connecting, using the very first `0100` response. If exactly one ECU replies, it's assumed to be the engine. If multiple reply, it prefers an exact match against the protocol's hardcoded `TX_ID_ENGINE`/`TX_ID_TRANSMISSION`; failing that, it falls back to **"whichever ECU's PID-support bitmask has the most bits set wins the Engine label"** (`BitArray(message.data).num_set()`) — a pragmatic heuristic for cars with multiple modules answering `0100`.

**A practical flag for your specific car**: python-OBD's Mode 06 (test monitors) is hard-gated to CAN protocols only (`test_cmd()` in §5 checks `protocol_id() in ["6","7","8","9"]`), and the docs mark Mode 06 and Mode 09 as *"experimental... has not been tested on a real vehicle"* / *"only a subset... has been tested"*. Worth independently verifying with `connection.protocol_id()` / `protocol_name()` once you're wired into your E36, rather than assuming CAN: US-market E36s from the OBD-II-compliant model years (roughly 1996-1999, M50TU/M52-era) predate BMW's broad adoption of a CAN backbone and commonly speak the legacy **ISO 9141-2** (`"3"`) diagnostic protocol rather than ISO 15765-4 CAN — I'd flag this as something to confirm empirically (e.g. log what `auto_protocol()` picks) rather than assume, since it directly determines whether you get Mode 06 monitors, how fast polling can go, and which reassembly code path (`LegacyProtocol` vs `CANProtocol`) actually runs.

## 11. DTCs, freeze frame, and custom/manufacturer-specific commands (BMW-relevant)

This is the section most directly load-bearing for your project, so I'm keeping full exact code.

### Built-in DTC / freeze-frame commands (`obd/commands.py`)
```python
__mode3__ = [ OBDCommand("GET_DTC", "Get DTCs", b"03", 0, dtc, ECU.ALL, False) ]
__mode4__ = [ OBDCommand("CLEAR_DTC", "Clear DTCs and Freeze data", b"04", 0, drop, ECU.ALL, False) ]
__mode7__ = [ OBDCommand("GET_CURRENT_DTC", "Get DTCs from the current/last driving cycle", b"07", 0, dtc, ECU.ALL, False) ]
```
And Mode 02 (freeze frame) is the mechanically-cloned mirror of every Mode 01 command (`DTC_RPM`, `DTC_SPEED`, etc. — see §3), plus a dedicated `FREEZE_DTC` (PID `02`) that returns the single DTC that triggered the freeze frame.

**DTC decoding** (`decoders.py`), the actual bit-twiddling to turn 2 raw bytes into a `"P0104"`-style code:
```python
def parse_dtc(_bytes):
    if (len(_bytes) != 2) or (_bytes == (0, 0)):
        return None
    dtc = ['P', 'C', 'B', 'U'][_bytes[0] >> 6]           # top 2 bits -> system letter
    dtc += str((_bytes[0] >> 4) & 0b0011)                # next 2 bits -> first digit
    dtc += bytes_to_hex(_bytes)[1:4]                      # remaining nibbles -> rest of code
    return (dtc, DTC.get(dtc, ""))                        # (code, description-or-empty-string)

def dtc(messages):
    """ Mode 03/07: converts a frame of 2-byte DTCs into a list of DTCs """
    codes = []
    d = []
    for message in messages:
        d += message.data[2:]  # strip mode + DTC_count bytes
    for n in range(1, len(d), 2):
        c = parse_dtc((d[n-1], d[n]))
        if c is not None:
            codes.append(c)
    return codes

def single_dtc(messages):
    """ Mode 01 PID 02 (FREEZE_DTC): parses exactly one DTC """
    d = messages[0].data[2:]
    return parse_dtc(d)
```
`DTC` is a giant `{code: description}` dict in `obd/codes.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/codes.py) — confirmed ~130KB of generic-code descriptions (e.g. `"P0001": "Fuel Volume Regulator Control Circuit/Open"`). **Manufacturer-specific/BMW codes are not in this table** — `DTC.get(dtc, "")` falls back to an empty description string for any code it doesn't recognize, so BMW-proprietary DTCs will still decode to a correct `Pxxxx`/`Bxxxx`/`Cxxxx`/`Uxxxx` code string, just with a blank description — you'd maintain your own BMW code->description table and look it up yourself alongside `response.value`.

Response shapes, straight from docs/Responses.md:
```python
# obd.commands.GET_DTC
response.value = [
    ("P0104", "Mass or Volume Air Flow Circuit Intermittent"),
    ("B0003", ""),   # unknown/manufacturer-specific code -> empty description
    ("C0123", "")
]
# obd.commands.FREEZE_DTC
response.value = ("P0104", "Mass or Volume Air Flow Circuit Intermittent")
```

### Defining a custom `OBDCommand` — exact, complete pattern

Full worked example straight from https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Custom%20Commands/ (raw: docs/Custom Commands.md):
```python
from obd import OBDCommand, Unit
from obd.protocols import ECU
from obd.utils import bytes_to_int

def rpm(messages):
    """ decoder for RPM messages """
    d = messages[0].data   # only operate on a single message
    d = d[2:]               # chop off mode and PID bytes
    v = bytes_to_int(d) / 4.0
    return v * Unit.RPM     # construct a Pint Quantity

c = OBDCommand("RPM",        # name
               "Engine RPM", # description
               b"010C",      # command (raw hex bytes)
               4,             # number of return bytes to expect
               rpm,           # decoding function
               ECU.ENGINE,    # (optional) ECU filter
               True)          # (optional) allow a "01" to be added for speed
```
(Note: the docs example writes `Unit.RPM`, but the library's own internal decoders use lowercase `Unit.rpm` — e.g. `UAS_IDS[0x07] = UAS(False, 0.25, Unit.rpm)`. Pint unit-name lookup is generally case-sensitive for user-defined vs. base units, so treat `Unit.rpm` as the verified-working attribute and the docs' `Unit.RPM` as a possible doc inconsistency — test it in a REPL before relying on it.)

**Getting an unsupported/custom command to actually query** — two documented ways (verbatim):
```python
o = obd.OBD()
# option 1: force it every time
o.query(c, force=True)
# option 2: mark it permanently supported
o.supported_commands.add(c)
o.query(c)
```
This matters because `OBDCommand.__eq__`/`__hash__` key off `(header, command)` (see §3) — as long as your custom command's header+command-bytes pair is unique, adding it to `supported_commands` is safe and persists for the life of the connection.

**Manufacturer-specific header** — the whole reason `header` exists as a constructor field:
```python
c = OBDCommand(name, desc, command, n_bytes, decoder, ecu=ECU.ALL, fast=False, header=b'<your BMW module ID>')
```
Per docs: *"The optional `header` argument tells python-OBD to use a custom header when querying the command. If not set, python-OBD assumes that the default 7E0 header is needed... The switch between default and custom header (and vice versa) is automatically done by python-OBD."* — meaning `OBD.__set_header()` (see §1/§3) transparently issues `AT SH <header>` right before it sends your command, and swaps back to `7E0` automatically the next time you query a standard PID; you don't have to manage that yourself. This is your primary hook for BMW-specific requests: if BMW's DME/other module needs a non-standard CAN arbitration ID (or, if it's KWP2000-era, a non-standard functional address) for a proprietary PID, set it as `header=` on your custom command and let python-OBD do the AT SH juggling.

**Decoder contract, in full** (from Custom Commands.md, verbatim, because it's exactly your interface spec):
```python
def <name>(<list_of_messages>):
    ...
    return <value>
```
Guarantees given to you: the `messages` list is guaranteed non-empty when your decoder is invoked (`OBDCommand.__call__` only calls `.decode()` if `messages` is truthy after ECU filtering); each `Message.data` is guaranteed padded/truncated to exactly the `bytes` you declared in the constructor (via `__constrain_message_data`, see the exact code quoted in §1's OBDCommand section — zero-pads on the right if short, truncates on the right if long, both cases logged at `DEBUG`); `data` **includes the mode+PID header bytes** in front (an explicit v0.7.0 breaking change — decoders must skip `data[2:]` themselves, as literally every stock decoder does). You also get `Message.hex()` and `Message.raw()` as escape hatches to the pre-parsed hex string / literal ELM output line, if your BMW-specific decoding logic wants to work from the wire format directly instead of the parsed `bytearray`.

### Freeze frame (Mode 02) recap
Not a separate mechanism — it's the exact same command table as Mode 01, mechanically re-keyed to mode byte `02` and name-prefixed `DTC_`. `obd.commands.DTC_RPM` gets you "RPM at the moment the freeze-triggering DTC was set," using the identical decoder as `obd.commands.RPM`. This is a nice pattern if you want your own BMW custom PIDs to also have a "freeze frame" variant — just run the same `clone()` + rename + remap-mode trick over your own custom command list.

## 12. Known limitations / gotchas (sourced from real GitHub Issues, not speculation)

I pulled these directly from the issue tracker rather than guessing, since your prompt specifically wanted real-world pain points:

- **`fast=True`'s CR-repeat trick is not universal across ELM327 clones** — issue #131 ("Multiple queries of same command fail to send data", https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/131): a user on a "v1.5" clone chip got `None` after the first two identical queries. A collaborator's diagnosis, confirmed by the reporter: *"Adding `fast=False` worked perfectly... Notice that the behavior of python-OBD reflects [ELM327 documentation] page 9/94"* — plus the pointed aside *"You are anyway not using an original ELM327 chipset."* **This is exactly the README's documented Bluetooth-adapter fix (`fast=False, timeout=30`) — confirmed as a real, reproducible clone-chip incompatibility, not just a defensive default.** If you're sourcing a cheap ELM327 clone for your E36 rig, budget time to test with `fast=False` if you see queries silently going null after the first one or two.
- **Cheap post-2022 clones can send non-UTF-8 garbage that breaks the read loop** — issue #282 ("Make elm327.py able to talk to ELM327 clones", https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/282, open, unmerged as of this research): a submitted patch wraps `buffer.decode("utf-8", "ignore")` in a `try/except`, claiming *"this increases compatibility by 5-10x with post elm327 made after 2022 (I've tested this)."* Since it's unmerged, current released python-OBD (v0.7.3) does **not** have this guard — worth patching locally if you hit silent hangs/crashes with a newer clone adapter.
- **Cold `import obd` latency on Raspberry Pi-class hardware** (~10 seconds) — issue #136, see §4 above; root-caused by eager construction of the full DTC table + command tables + Pint registry at import time, not fixed as of v0.7.3.
- **Baud-rate auto-detection and general responsiveness can be materially worse than a competing product on the same hardware** — issue #232 ("Slower response vs Torque - any ideas?", https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/232): direct BT-capture analysis in the comments found Torque Pro's "faster responses" mode sets **`ATAT2`** (aggressive ELM adaptive-timing mode) which python-OBD never sets, and also toggles `ATH0` (headers off) / `ATS0` (spaces off) — python-OBD hardcodes `ATH1` (headers **on**, needed for its ECU-tagging logic) and never touches adaptive timing at all. **If polling latency matters for your dashboard's refresh rate, sending `AT AT2` yourself (via `interface.send_and_parse` or a raw AT passthrough) after connecting is a documented, real lever python-OBD doesn't pull for you.**
- **Flaky/inconsistent behavior across "the same" BT clone adapters and Pi models** — issue #161 ("First value gets read out the following don't, also really slow", open, https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/161) and issue #177 ("Data does not update on Async connection", https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/177): both report a counterfeit "v1.5" ELM327 that intermittently works, and in #177 the reporter found that **merely enabling debug logging (`obd.logger.setLevel(obd.logging.DEBUG)`) changed the connection's success/failure** — a strong signal of a timing-sensitive race (the extra I/O from logging perturbs the serial timing enough to matter). If you hit unreliable connects on cheap hardware, trying `timeout=` increases and/or inserting small deliberate delays is a more productive debugging path than assuming it's a code bug.
- **KWP/legacy timing vs. CAN timing are genuinely different code paths with different guarantees** (see §10) — `LegacyProtocol` relies on an explicit order byte for multi-frame reassembly and a trailing checksum the ELM strips, versus `CANProtocol`'s ISO-TP-style rolling sequence counter; Mode 06 is unconditionally refused outside the four CAN protocol IDs (enforced in `test_cmd()`, §5); and the "fast mode" frame-count-learning optimization (§1) only pays off once the *first* full-timeout round-trip has happened for a given command, which matters more on protocols/adapters with slower default timeouts.
- **The Bluetooth guidance in the README is still the load-bearing top-level advice**: *"There are sometimes connection issues when using a Bluetooth OBD-II adapter... This can be fixed by setting... `fast=False, timeout=30`."* (https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/blob/master/README.md) — given everything above, treat this less as boilerplate and more as "if you're on BT and anything is flaky, this is priority-one to try."

## Design ideas worth borrowing for your E36 dashboard (synthesis)

Since the point of this research was to inform your own build, here's the short list of transferable architectural decisions, distilled from everything above:

1. **Separate the pipeline into exactly these layers, each independently testable**: transport (serial) -> adapter/AT-command shim -> protocol frame/message parser -> per-PID decoder function -> typed response object. python-OBD's `tests/` directory (unit tests per-layer: `test_protocol.py`, `test_protocol_can.py`, `test_decoders.py`, `test_uas.py`, plus `test_obdsim.py` for full end-to-end against a simulated port) shows this pays off — you can unit-test your BMW decoders against synthetic byte arrays without any hardware.
2. **A command is a self-contained, callable "recipe" object** (`OBDCommand.__call__(messages) -> OBDResponse`) that bundles the request bytes, expected length, ECU filter, and decoder together — not a loose dict of configs interpreted elsewhere. Makes custom/BMW-specific PIDs trivially pluggable (one object per PID, same interface as built-ins).
3. **Never raise on missing data — always return a typed "null" object** (`is_null()` pattern) so UI code doesn't need try/except scaffolding on every read.
4. **Learn per-PID frame counts at runtime and use them to truncate adapter timeouts** — the single biggest, car-specific latency win in the whole codebase, and it's genuinely simple to implement (a dict cache keyed by command).
5. **One background thread, round-robin, with a flat inter-cycle delay** is a fine baseline for `Async`-style polling — but note its explicit limitation (no per-command rate/priority) and design in that control yourself from day one if your E36 dashboard wants RPM at high rate and VIN at connection-time-only.
6. **Ship a units abstraction (Pint or otherwise) from the start**, but be conscious of its import/construction cost on constrained hardware (Raspberry Pi-class), and give yourself a `.magnitude`-style raw-value escape hatch for hot paths (rendering, serialization).
7. **Design your "supported commands" probing as its own bootstrap phase**, separate from steady-state polling, using the manufacturer's PID-support bitmask convention if BMW exposes one, or your own hardcoded list if you're going straight at proprietary PIDs.
8. **Treat "header" (arbitration ID / functional address) as a first-class, per-command field**, with automatic switch-back-to-default bookkeeping in the connection layer — exactly the `__set_header`/`__last_header` pattern — so callers never manage AT SH state manually.

from .obd import OBD
from .asynchronous import Async
from .commands import commands
from .OBDCommand import OBDCommand
from .OBDResponse import OBDResponse
from .protocols import ECU

import logging

This is also documented as the "Module Layout" on the docs home page (https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/):
```python

obd.Async          # asynchronous OBD connection class
obd.commands       # command tables
obd.Unit           # unit tables (a Pint UnitRegistry)
obd.OBDStatus      # enum for connection status
obd.scan_serial    # util function for manually scanning for OBD adapters
obd.OBDCommand     # class for making your own OBD Commands
obd.ECU            # enum for marking which ECU a command should listen to
obd.logger         # the OBD module's root logger (for debug)
```

**Layering, concretely, from a `connection.query(cmd)` call:**

1. **`OBD.query()`** (obd/obd.py) — checks `status()`/`supports()`, calls `self.__set_header(cmd.header)` (sends `AT SH <header>` only if it differs from the last header used — avoids redundant AT commands), builds the command string via `__build_command_string()`, and calls `self.interface.send_and_parse(cmd_string)`.
2. **`ELM327.send_and_parse()`** (obd/elm327.py) — wakes from low-power if needed, calls private `__send()`/`__write()`/`__read()` against the raw `pyserial` port, gets back a list of raw string lines, then feeds them to `self.__protocol(lines)`.
3. **`Protocol.__call__()`** (obd/protocols/protocol.py) — splits lines into hex-OBD lines vs. non-OBD lines (e.g. `"NO DATA"`), parses each hex line into a `Frame` via the protocol subclass's `parse_frame()`, groups frames by transmitting ECU (`tx_id`), and reassembles each ECU's frames into a `Message` via `parse_message()` (this is where multi-frame ISO-TP-style reassembly happens for CAN, see §10). Each `Message` gets tagged with an `ecu` flag from `self.ecu_map`.
4. **`OBDCommand.__call__(messages)`** (obd/OBDCommand.py) — filters messages to only those from the command's target ECU (`self.ecu & m.ecu`), pads/truncates each message's `data` to the expected byte length, and calls `self.decode(messages)`.
5. The **decoder function** (obd/decoders.py) — a plain function `def name(messages): ... return value` — turns the raw bytearray into a Python value, usually a Pint `Quantity`.
6. Result is wrapped in an **`OBDResponse`** (obd/OBDResponse.py) with `.value`, `.command`, `.messages`, `.time`.

Source for step 1 (`OBD.query`, exact code, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/obd.py):
```python
def query(self, cmd, force=False):
    if self.status() == OBDStatus.NOT_CONNECTED:
        logger.warning("Query failed, no connection available")
        return OBDResponse()

    if not force and not self.test_cmd(cmd):
        return OBDResponse()

    self.__set_header(cmd.header)

    logger.info("Sending command: %s" % str(cmd))
    cmd_string = self.__build_command_string(cmd)
    messages = self.interface.send_and_parse(cmd_string)

    if cmd_string:
        self.__last_command = cmd_string

    if cmd not in self.__frame_counts:
        self.__frame_counts[cmd] = sum([len(m.frames) for m in messages])

    if not messages:
        logger.info("No valid OBD Messages returned")
        return OBDResponse()

    return cmd(messages)  # compute a response object
```
Note `cmd(messages)` — `OBDCommand` implements `__call__`, so the command object itself is the thing that turns raw messages into a response (nice pattern: the "recipe" object also knows how to execute itself against raw data).

`__build_command_string` (the "fast mode" optimizer, worth stealing — see §12 for why it also causes bugs on ELM clones):
```python
def __build_command_string(self, cmd):
    cmd_string = cmd.command
    # if we know the number of frames that this command returns,
    # only wait for exactly that number.
    if self.fast and cmd.fast and (cmd in self.__frame_counts):
        cmd_string += str(self.__frame_counts[cmd]).encode()
    # if we sent this last time, just send a CR
    if self.fast and (cmd_string == self.__last_command):
        cmd_string = b""
    return cmd_string
```
This is a genuinely good idea for your dashboard: **the first time a command is sent, it doesn't know the frame count, so it waits for the ELM's full timeout; it then remembers "this PID returns N frames" and appends that digit to every subsequent request** (e.g. `010C1` tells the ELM327 "stop listening after 1 response"), which lets the adapter return the instant it hears one frame instead of waiting out its internal ~200ms timeout. This is the biggest lever for polling speed and it's ECU/car-specific, learned at runtime.

### `ELM327` class responsibilities (the AT-command layer)

From `obd/elm327.py`. Connection sequence on `__init__`: open serial port -> (`start_low_power` wake, optional) -> `set_baudrate()` (auto-detect by trying `_TRY_BAUDS = [38400, 9600, 230400, 115200, 57600, 19200]` and writing junk bytes `\x7F\x7F\r` looking for a `>` prompt) -> `ATZ` (reset, 1s delay) -> `ATE0` (echo off) -> `ATH1` (headers **on**, hardcoded — see §10/§12 implications) -> `ATL0` (linefeeds off) -> status becomes `ELM_CONNECTED` -> optional `AT RV` voltage check (must read >6V or it aborts) -> status becomes `OBD_CONNECTED` -> `set_protocol()` (manual `ATTP<id>` or `auto_protocol()` which does `ATSP0`, sends `0100`, reads back the chosen protocol via `ATDPN`, and if that comes back unrecognized, falls back to manually trying protocols in `_TRY_PROTOCOL_ORDER`) -> status becomes `CAR_CONNECTED`.

Low-level read/write (`__write`/`__read`) accumulate bytes until the `>` prompt byte is seen, strip null bytes, decode UTF-8 with `errors="ignore"`, split into lines on `\r`/`\n`. `__send()` has a retry loop: if nothing came back within the delay, it polls every 0.1s up to 1.0s total before giving up (this is the "1 second read-retry loop for unresponsive dongles" added in v0.7.2, see §12).

## 2. `obd.Async` — exact API, thread model, callback dispatch

Source of truth: `obd/asynchronous.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/asynchronous.py) + docs page https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Async%20Connections/ (raw markdown: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/docs/Async%20Connections.md).

`Async` is a subclass of `OBD` (single-inheritance, not a wrapper), so it inherits `query()`'s signature but **overrides** it non-blockingly.

**Constructor** (adds one param over `OBD`):
```python
Async(portstr=None, baudrate=None, protocol=None, fast=True,
      timeout=0.1, check_voltage=True, start_low_power=False,
      delay_cmds=0.25)
```
`delay_cmds` (default 0.25s): sleep duration after each full pass over all watched commands. Setting it to `0` makes the background thread hammer the adapter continuously with no delay between polling cycles.

**Watch/callback model** — exact source:
```python
def watch(self, c, callback=None, force=False):
    # the dict shouldn't be changed while the daemon thread is iterating
    if self.__running:
        logger.warning("Can't watch() while running, please use stop()")
    else:
        if not force and not self.test_cmd(c):
            return  # test_cmd() prints its own warning
        if c not in self.__commands:
            self.__commands[c] = OBDResponse()   # give it an initial (null) value
            self.__callbacks[c] = []
        if hasattr(callback, "__call__") and (callback not in self.__callbacks[c]):
            self.__callbacks[c].append(callback)
```
Key facts:
- **`watch()`/`unwatch()`/`unwatch_all()` all hard-refuse to run while the thread is active** — they just log a warning and no-op. You must `stop()` first (or use the `paused()` context manager). This is enforced because `self.__commands` is a plain `dict` iterated by the daemon thread — no lock is used; the mutual exclusion is achieved purely by "don't touch it while running," not real thread-safety primitives.
- `force=False` (default): `watch()` calls `self.test_cmd(c)` — same support-check `query()` uses — and silently refuses to add the command if unsupported (with a logged warning). `force=True` skips that check.
- Callbacks are a list per command — you can register multiple callbacks for the same command (confirmed by `test_async_unwatch_callback` in the test suite, which registers two independent callbacks and unwatches only one).
- `unwatch(c, callback=None)`: if `callback` given, removes only that one; **if that empties the callback list, it also pops the command entirely** from `self.__commands`. If `callback` is omitted, drops the command and all its callbacks.

**Thread/loop implementation** — exact `run()`:
```python
def run(self):
    while self.__running:
        if len(self.__commands) > 0:
            for c in self.__commands:
                if not self.is_connected():
                    logger.info("Async thread terminated because device disconnected")
                    self.__running = False
                    self.__thread = None
                    return
                r = super(Async, self).query(c, force=True)   # force=True: already checked in watch()
                self.__commands[c] = r
                for callback in self.__callbacks[c]:
                    callback(r)
            time.sleep(self.__delay_cmds)
        else:
            time.sleep(0.25)  # idle
```
- **One daemon thread total** (`threading.Thread(target=self.run); self.__thread.daemon = True`), not one thread per command. It round-robins through every watched command **sequentially and synchronously** in a single pass, then sleeps `delay_cmds`. There is no per-command rate/priority control — every watched PID gets polled at the same cadence, gated only by how long the serial round-trips for all of them take plus the flat `delay_cmds` sleep. If you watch 20 PIDs and each round-trip takes 50ms, your true refresh rate per PID is ~(20×50ms + delay_cmds), not "delay_cmds per PID." **There is no priority/rate-per-command system in this library** — if you want RPM at 50ms and VIN at 1x/connection, you'd have to build that yourself (e.g., separate `Async` instances, or your own scheduler on top of `query()`).
- Callbacks are invoked **synchronously, on the polling thread itself**, in the order registered, before moving to the next command. A slow callback blocks the whole polling loop — worth avoiding heavy work (UI redraw, disk I/O) directly in a callback; hand off to a queue instead.
- If the device disconnects mid-loop, the thread quietly sets `__running = False` and returns (no exception raised) — this was an explicit v0.7.1 change: *"Async connections will no longer throw exceptions when the underlying transport is disconnected. They will instead terminate gracefully. Async status is observable via the `Async.running` parameter."*
- `query()` on `Async` is fully non-blocking and never touches serial:
```python
def query(self, c, force=False):
    if c in self.__commands:
        return self.__commands[c]
    else:
        return OBDResponse()
```
So an unwatched command always returns a fresh null `OBDResponse()`.

**`paused()` context manager** — literally a self-return stub; the real logic is in `__enter__`/`__exit__`:
```python
def paused(self):
    """ enables: with connection.paused() as was_running: ... """
    return self

def __enter__(self):
    self.__was_running = self.__running
    self.stop()
    return self.__was_running

def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
    if not self.__running and self.__was_running:
        self.start()
    return False
```
Docs example (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/docs/Async%20Connections.md):
```python
with connection.paused() as was_running:
    # connection is stopped within this block
    ...
```

**Full watch+callback usage example straight from the docs:**
```python
import obd, time
connection = obd.Async()

def new_rpm(r):
    print(r.value)

connection.watch(obd.commands.RPM, callback=new_rpm)
connection.start()
# callback fires on every new value now
time.sleep(60)
connection.stop()
```

**`start()`/`stop()`**: `start()` no-ops (with a log message) if not connected or if zero commands are watched. `stop()` sets the flag and calls `self.__thread.join()` — i.e. it blocks the caller until the in-flight poll finishes, so `stop()` can take up to one full round of all watched commands to return.

The real integration-test suite in `tests/test_obdsim.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/tests/test_obdsim.py) is a good API confirmation/usage reference — it exercises `watch()`, `start()`, `paused()`, `unwatch()`, `unwatch_all()`, and multi-callback unwatch, against a real simulated adapter (`obdsim`, see §9/§12).

## 3. Command tables: `obd.commands`, `OBDCommand` constructor, `ECU`, `fast`

Full source: `obd/commands.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/commands.py), `obd/OBDCommand.py` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/master/obd/OBDCommand.py). Docs: https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Command%20Lookup/ and https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Command%20Tables/.

**The `Commands` class** (instantiated once at import as the module-level `commands` object):
```python
class Commands():
    def __init__(self):
        self.modes = [
            [], __mode1__, __mode2__, __mode3__, __mode4__,
            [], __mode6__, __mode7__, [], __mode9__,
        ]  # index 0,5,8 are empty placeholders — modes are 1,2,3,4,6,7,9
        for m in self.modes:
            for c in m:
                if c is not None:
                    self.__dict__[c.name] = c   # <-- attribute access, e.g. commands.RPM
        for c in __misc__:
            self.__dict__[c.name] = c

    def __getitem__(self, key):
        # obd.commands.RPM / obd.commands["RPM"] / obd.commands[1][12]
        if isinstance(key, int):
            return self.modes[key]
        elif isinstance(key, basestring):
            return self.__dict__[key]

    def base_commands(self):
        """ commands that should always be supported by the ELM327 """
        return [self.PIDS_A, self.PIDS_9A, self.MIDS_A,
                self.GET_DTC, self.CLEAR_DTC, self.GET_CURRENT_DTC,
                self.ELM_VERSION, self.ELM_VOLTAGE]

    def pid_getters(self):
        """ returns list of PID-listing GET commands (the 'PIDS_A' style bitmask probes) """
        getters = []
        for mode in self.modes:
            getters += [cmd for cmd in mode if (cmd and cmd.decode == pid)]
        return getters

    def has_command(self, c):
        return c in self.__dict__.values()

    def has_name(self, name):
        return name.isupper() and name in self.__dict__

    def has_pid(self, mode, pid):
        if (mode < 0) or (pid < 0): return False
        if mode >= len(self.modes): return False
        if pid >= len(self.modes[mode]): return False
        return self.modes[mode][pid] is not None
```
So `obd.commands.RPM`, `obd.commands['RPM']`, and `obd.commands[1][12]` are **three different lookup paths converging on the same object**: attribute/dict access by uppercase name vs. list-indexing by `[mode][pid]` where the mode-1 list is literally built PID-ordered so that `list[pid]` works directly. `'RPM' in obd.commands` also works because `Commands.__contains__` delegates to `has_name`.

**How mode 2 is generated**: it's *not* hand-written — it's mechanically cloned from mode 1 at import time:
```python
__mode2__ = []
for c in __mode1__:
    c = c.clone()
    c.command = b"02" + c.command[2:]        # 0100 -> 0200
    c.name = "DTC_" + c.name                 # RPM -> DTC_RPM
    c.desc = "DTC " + c.desc
    if c.decode == pid:
        c.decode = drop  # never send mode 02 PID-listing requests
    __mode2__.append(c)
```
So `obd.commands.DTC_RPM` is mode 2's freeze-frame RPM, auto-derived. `OBDCommand.clone()` exists specifically to support this pattern — a nice, cheap way to derive command families without hand-duplicating 100+ definitions.

**`OBDCommand.__init__` — exact constructor signature** (this answers your Q3 directly):
```python
def __init__(self, name, desc, command, _bytes, decoder,
             ecu=ECU.ALL, fast=False, header=ECU_HEADER.ENGINE):
    self.name = name        # human readable name (also the dict key)
    self.desc = desc        # human readable description
    self.command = command  # command bytes, e.g. b"010C"
    self.bytes = _bytes     # expected response byte length (0 = unknown/variable)
    self.decode = decoder   # decoding function
    self.ecu = ecu          # ECU filter bitmask
    self.fast = fast        # allow the "01"-style response-count optimization
    self.header = header    # AT SH header to use for this query (default b'7E0')
```
Derived properties: `.mode` and `.pid` parse the hex `command` bytes (`int(self.command[:2], 16)` / `int(self.command[2:], 16)`), returning `None` if the command isn't cleanly hex (e.g. AT-commands like `ATRV`).

**Equality/hashing is by `(header, command)`, not by name** — important if you're rolling your own custom commands:
```python
def __hash__(self):
    return hash(self.header + self.command)
def __eq__(self, other):
    if isinstance(other, OBDCommand):
        return self.command == other.command and self.header == other.header
    return False
```
This is how the command tables (and `supported_commands`, which is a `set`) dedupe — two `OBDCommand` instances with the same header+command bytes are the *same key* even if you gave them different names/decoders. Watch for this if you define multiple BMW custom commands with the same raw PID under different names.

**`ECU` flags** (from `obd/protocols/protocol.py`) — bit flags, ORable, used both to tag which module a `Message` came from and to filter which messages a command will accept:
```python
class ECU:
    ALL        = 0b11111111  # accept messages from any ECU
    ALL_KNOWN  = 0b11111110  # ignore genuinely-unknown ECUs
    UNKNOWN    = 0b00000001
    ENGINE     = 0b00000010
    TRANSMISSION = 0b00000100
```
python-OBD currently only auto-identifies **Engine** and (in principle) **Transmission** — the docs are explicit that "python-OBD can currently only distinguish the engine, but this list may be expanded over time." `OBDCommand.__call__` filters incoming messages with `messages = [m for m in messages if (self.ecu & m.ecu) > 0]` — a bitwise AND test.

**`fast` flag** — from `docs/Custom Commands.md`: *"tells python-OBD whether it is safe to append a `"01"` [style digit] to the end of the command. This will instruct the adapter to return the first response it receives, rather than waiting for more... enabled for most of python-OBD's internal commands. However, for unusual commands, it is safest to leave this disabled."* Combined with `OBD.fast` (a global on/off on the connection) — both must be true, and the frame count must already be known, for the optimization to actually apply (see the `__build_command_string` code in §1).

**`header`** default is `ECU_HEADER.ENGINE = b'7E0'` (from `obd/protocols/protocol.py`). `OBD.__set_header()` only issues `AT SH <header>` when the header differs from the last one used, to minimize AT-command chatter:
```python
def __set_header(self, header):
    if header == self.__last_header:
        return
    r = self.interface.send_and_parse(b'AT SH ' + header + b' ')
    ...
    self.__last_header = header
```
This is your hook for **manufacturer-specific / BMW-specific requests** — see §11.

**Mode-1 table snippet** (illustrating the declarative style, from `commands.py`):
```python
__mode1__ = [
    OBDCommand("PIDS_A" , "Supported PIDs [01-20]" , b"0100", 6, pid,     ECU.ENGINE, True),
    OBDCommand("STATUS" , "Status since DTCs cleared", b"0101", 6, status, ECU.ENGINE, True),
    ...
    OBDCommand("RPM"    , "Engine RPM"              , b"010C", 4, uas(0x07), ECU.ENGINE, True),
    OBDCommand("SPEED"  , "Vehicle Speed"           , b"010D", 3, uas(0x09), ECU.ENGINE, True),
    ...
]
```
Note commands must be **in strict PID order, one per PID slot**, specifically so `self.modes[mode][pid]` is an O(1) list index — reserved/unimplemented PIDs are filled with literal `None` placeholders (see the mode-6 table using `+ ([None] * 15) + [...]` to skip reserved MID ranges). If you copy this pattern for a BMW-specific table, keep that PID-ordering invariant if you want `[mode][pid]` indexing to work; otherwise just use a plain dict for your custom table.
