## 7. Multi-ECU / headers / UDS / ISO-TP multi-frame

**Yes**, and the exact gating mechanism is in `elm/elm.py::handle_request`:

Setting the header (client sends `ATSH7E2`):
```python
'AT_SET_HEADER': {
    'Request': '^ATSH[0-9A-F]+$',
    'Exec': 'self.counters["cmd_set_header"] = re.sub(r"^0*([0-9A-F]+)$", r"\1", cmd[4:])',
    'Response': '<writeln>OK</writeln>'
}
```
Matching a PID entry against the currently active header:
```python
if 'REQUEST' in uc_val and re.match(uc_val['REQUEST'], cmd):
    if ('HEADER' in uc_val and header and
            uc_val['HEADER'].upper() != self.counters["cmd_set_header"]):
        continue   # this ECU doesn't answer — wrong header selected
    ...
```
So a PID entry with `'Header': ECU_ADDR_H` (`"7E2"`, HV ECU) only answers while the client has done `ATSH7E2`; a PID with `'Header': ECU_ADDR_E` (`"7E0"`, engine) only answers under `ATSH7E0` (the default, per `reset()`: `self.counters['cmd_set_header'] = ECU_ADDR_E.upper()`); entries with **no** `Header` field answer regardless. This is exactly how the `'car'` scenario fans a single serial/pty/TCP stream out to multiple simulated ECUs (`7E0`/`7E8` engine, `7E5` Continental powertrain, and constants exist in source for `7E1/7E9` transmission, `7E2/7EA` HV, `7E3/7EB` battery, `7C0/7C8` ICE, `7C4/7CC` A/C, `7B0/7B8` skid control, `747/74F` and `7D2/7DA`).

**ISO-TP multi-frame / KWP2000** answer construction is real, in `uds_answer()`:
```python
if length > 7:  # multiframe output
    answer = answer_header + sp + "10" + sp + "%02X" % length + sp   # First Frame
    ...
    while remaining_length > 0:
        answer += answer_header + sp + "%02X" % (frame_count + 0x20) + sp   # Consecutive Frames (0x21, 0x22, ...)
        ...
```
and flow-control frames are auto-emitted by `IsoTpMultiframe` as shown in §6. The `mt05` scenario is the concrete manufacturer-specific UDS demo: `UDS_RMBA` (Mode 23, Read Memory By Address) and `UDS_WRITE_MEM_ADDR` (Mode 0x3D) are backed by `task_mt05_read_mem_addr.py`/`task_mt05_write_mem_addr.py`, which read/write a byte range out of a `mmap`-backed file (`mmap-input.bin` / `mmap-output.bin`, per `task_ecu_11F1.py`'s ECU-task setup, `MEM_RANGE = 0x3fffff`) — i.e. it can genuinely simulate a flashable ECU memory image, not just canned answers.

## For your BMW E36 specifically

One thing worth flagging that isn't in the brief but matters a lot for you: the built-in `'car'` scenario is explicitly a **Toyota Auris Hybrid on ISO 15765‑4 CAN, 500 kbps** — a much newer electrical architecture than an E36. Depending on your car's actual model year:

- **US OBD‑II E36s (roughly 1996–1999)** talk standard SAE J1979 Mode‑01 PIDs, but over **ISO 9141‑2 / KWP2000 K‑line**, not CAN. The good news: OBD‑II *PID request/response byte semantics* (`010C` → RPM, etc.) are the same regardless of the underlying wire protocol, so python-OBD + ELM327-emulator's `'default'` scenario (which has no CAN-specific header requirements) is a reasonable generic starting point, and the emulator does implement the `ATSP`/K‑line-family AT commands (`AT_PROTO`, `^ATSP[0-9A-C]$`) if any client software inspects the reported protocol number.
- **Pre‑1996 E36s are OBD1, not OBD‑II at all** — no standard PIDs, no ELM327 compatibility, a completely different (largely undocumented/proprietary BMW) diagnostic protocol. ELM327-emulator/python-OBD won't help there regardless of scenario.
- Either way, the `'car'` scenario's specific CUSTOM_ Toyota-hybrid PIDs (battery SOC, inverter temps, etc.) are meaningless for your car — don't use it as a template for realism, just as a *syntax* reference.
- Given all this, your highest-leverage path is almost certainly: get an ELM327/OBDLink dongle on your actual E36 once (even briefly), run `obd_dictionary -i <port> -p 20 -n e36 -o e36_scenario.py` while idling/revving so RPM/SPEED/COOLANT_TEMP actually vary across probes, then develop your dashboard forever after against `merge e36_scenario` / `scenario e36` with zero car dependency — which is precisely the workflow this whole project was built for.

# ECU tuning / RAM-watch tool conventions: interaction models & definition schemas

**Bonus finding first, because it may short-circuit your whole project:** RomRaider ships a **BMW DS2 logger definition for MS41/MS42/MS43** with real RAM addresses. If your E36 is an M52 on MS41.1, TPS and road speed are already published. See §6.

---

## 1. RomRaider

### 1.1 The Logger definition DTD (verbatim, authoritative)

Source: `https://github.com/RomRaider/RomRaider/blob/master/definitions/logger.dtd`

```dtd
<!ELEMENT address ( #PCDATA ) >
<!ATTLIST address length CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST address bit ( 0 | 1 | ... | 31 ) #IMPLIED >

<!ELEMENT conversion ( replace* ) >
<!ATTLIST conversion expr        CDATA #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST conversion format      ( 0 | 0.0 | 0.00 | 0.000 | 0.0000 | 0.00000 | 0.000000) #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST conversion storagetype ( int8 | int16 | uint8 | uint16 | int32 | uint32 | float ) #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion endian      CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion units       CDATA #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST conversion gauge_min   CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion gauge_max   CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion gauge_step  CDATA #IMPLIED >

<!ELEMENT parameter ( ( address+, conversions?) | (depends, conversions?) ) >
<!ATTLIST parameter target CDATA #REQUIRED >      <!-- 1=ECU 2=TCU 3=both -->
<!ATTLIST parameter ecubit ( 0..7 ) #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST parameter ecubyteindex CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST parameter desc CDATA #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST parameter name CDATA #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST parameter id ID #REQUIRED >

<!ELEMENT ecuparam ( ecu+, conversions? ) >
<!ATTLIST ecuparam groupsize CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST ecuparam subgroup  CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST ecuparam group     CDATA #IMPLIED >
...
<!ELEMENT replace EMPTY >
<!ATTLIST replace value CDATA #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST replace with  CDATA #REQUIRED >

<!ELEMENT switch EMPTY >
<!ATTLIST switch bit ( 0..7 ) #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST switch byte CDATA #REQUIRED >
```

**Critical: one parameter can have N conversions.** The unit is not a label — it's a selector. The user picks °C vs °F vs raw at runtime and each carries its *own* expression, format, and gauge range. This is the single most important convention to steal.

### 1.2 Parser defaults (from `LoggerDefinitionHandler.java`)

`https://github.com/RomRaider/RomRaider/blob/master/src/main/java/com/romraider/logger/ecu/definition/xml/LoggerDefinitionHandler.java`

| Attribute | Default when absent |
|---|---|
| `address@length` | `1` (byte) |
| `address@bit` | `-1` (no bit extraction) |
| `conversion@endian` | **BIG** |
| `conversion@storagetype` | unsigned int of `length*8` |
| `gauge_min/max/step` | looked up **by units string** |

### 1.3 Default gauge ranges keyed on the units string

`ConverterMaxMinDefaults.java` — steal this table wholesale; it makes a new parameter render sensibly with zero configuration:

```java
add("%",       0.0, 100.0,  10.0);   add("f",     0.0, 400.0, 40.0);
add("c",     -20.0, 200.0,  20.0);   add("psi",  -20.0,  40.0,  5.0);
add("bar",    -1.5,   3.0,   0.5);   add("rpm",      0,  8000, 1000.0);
add("mph",     0.0, 200.0,  20.0);   add("km/h",   0.0, 300.0, 20.0);
add("degrees",-15.0, 60.0,   5.0);   add("g/s",    0.0, 400.0, 20.0);
add("v",       0.0,   5.0,   0.5);   add("ms",     0.0, 100.0, 10.0);
add("afr",    10.0,  20.0,   1.0);   add("lambda", 0.5,   1.5,  0.1);
add("gear",    0.0,   6.0,   1.0);   add("mmHg",   0.0,2000.0,100.0);
// fallback: min 0.0, max 100.0, step 10.0
```

### 1.4 `parameter` vs `ecuparam` — the actual distinction

From the official Logger XML Reference Guide (`https://www.romraider.com/RomRaider/LoggerXMLReferenceGuide`):

- **`<parameter>`** = a *well-known, manufacturer-documented* PID. One address, valid across all ECUs on that protocol. Availability is gated by **capability bits**: `ecubyteindex` + `ecubit` index into a bitmask the ECU returns at init. If the bit is 0, RomRaider **hides the parameter from the list entirely**. This is a great UI convention: don't show what this ECU can't produce.
- **`<ecuparam>`** = an *extended / reverse-engineered* RAM address that differs per ECU calibration ID. It carries `<ecu id="...">` children, each with its own `<address>`. RomRaider matches the connected ECU's ID and picks the right address. Conventionally named with a `*` suffix in the UI.

```xml
<ecuparam id="E2" name="Engine Load*" desc="">
    <ecu id="1B04400405"><address length="2">0x21847</address></ecu>
    <ecu id="4304594005"><address length="2">0x200F2</address></ecu>
    <conversions>
        <conversion units="g/rev" expr="x*.00006103515625" format="0.00"/>
    </conversions>
</ecuparam>
```

`group` / `subgroup` / `groupsize` batch several ecuparams into **one** memory read — the release notes say *"Group individual DS2 ECU queries into a single memory read start address"*. Exactly your 252-byte block problem.

### 1.5 Derived parameters — `<depends>` / `<ref>`

Computed channels with no address of their own. This is how you build "is this byte × RPM = something meaningful?" experiments:

```xml
<parameter id="P200" name="Engine Load (Calculated)" desc="...">
    <depends>
        <ref parameter="P8"/>   <!-- Engine Speed -->
        <ref parameter="P12"/>  <!-- MAF -->
    </depends>
    <conversions>
        <conversion units="g/rev" expr="(P12*60)/P8" format="0.00"/>
    </conversions>
</parameter>

<parameter id="P202" name="Manifold Rel. Pressure (Corrected)">
    <depends><ref parameter="P7"/><ref parameter="P24"/></depends>
    <conversions>
        <conversion units="psi" expr="[P7:psi]-[P24:psi]" format="0.00"/>
    </conversions>
</parameter>
```

Note `[P7:psi]` — reference another parameter **in a specific unit**. Cyclic dependencies are the author's problem ("Be careful of cyclic dependencies!" is a literal comment in the file).

### 1.6 Expression language

`JEPUtil.java` uses **JEP** (Java Expression Parser) with `addStandardFunctions()` + one custom function:

```
BitWise(Number mask, Number variable, Number operation)
  operation: 1=AND, 2=OR, ...   mask must be DECIMAL (0x18 fails to parse)
  e.g. BitWise(24, x, 1)
```

Real usage from the MS41 def: `BitWise(8,x,1)/8` → extract bit 3 as 0/1. `!BitWise(32,x,1)/32` → inverted bit 5. Variable is always `x`.

### 1.7 `<replace>` — the discrete lookup escape hatch

```xml
<conversion units="status" expr="x" format="0">
    <replace value="8"  with="Closed Loop"/>
    <replace value="10" with="Open Loop"/>
</conversion>
```

Parsed into a `Map<String,String>` applied *after* conversion. For enum-ish bytes (gear, fuel system status) this beats a formula.

### 1.8 ROM-side definition (`ecu_defs.dtd`)

`https://github.com/RomRaider/RomRaider/blob/master/definitions/ecu_defs.dtd`

```dtd
<!ELEMENT scale ( unit+ ) >
<!ATTLIST scale storagetype (uint8|int8|uint16|int16|float|hex|char) "uint8" >
<!ATTLIST scale endian (big|little) "big" >
<!ATTLIST scale logparam IDREF #IMPLIED >     <!-- links a ROM table to a live logger param! -->

<!ELEMENT unit EMPTY >
<!ATTLIST unit to_real CDATA #REQUIRED >      <!-- raw -> human -->
<!ATTLIST unit to_byte CDATA #REQUIRED >      <!-- human -> raw (inverse!) -->
<!ATTLIST unit format CDATA "0.00" >
<!ATTLIST unit coarseincrement CDATA "1" >
<!ATTLIST unit fineincrement CDATA "0.1" >
```

**Two formulas, forward and inverse** (`to_real` / `to_byte`, or `expression` / `to_byte` in `<scalingbase>`). Any editable field needs both. Also `fineincrement` should equal "the smallest change the raw value will accept" — i.e. one LSB expressed in engineering units.

`<scalingbase>` defaults (from the Editor XML Reference Guide, `https://www.romraider.com/RomRaider/EditorXMLReferenceGuide`): `expression="x"`, `to_byte="x"`, `format="#.##"`, `coarseincrement=2`, `fineincrement=1`, `min=0.0`, `max=0.0`.

```xml
<scalingbase name="engineSpeedRpm" units="RPM" expression="x*.1953125" to_byte="x/.1953125"
             format="#" fineincrement="50" coarseincrement="100" />
```

### 1.9 Logger UI, profiles, learning tables

Live data table columns (`LiveDataTableModel.properties`): **`Logger Data | Min Value | Current Value | Max Value | Units`**. Min/max are session-accumulated — free "what range does this byte actually cover?" instrumentation. Steal this.

Gauge labels (`PlainGaugeStyle.properties`): `min`, `max`, `Warn`, `above`/`below`.

**Profiles** (`profile.dtd`) — the logging profile is just a per-parameter set of three independent checkboxes:

```dtd
<!ATTLIST parameter livedata ( selected ) #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST parameter graph    ( selected ) #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST parameter dash     ( selected ) #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST parameter units    CDATA #IMPLIED >   <!-- remembers unit choice -->
```

Tabs: Data / Graph / Dashboard, plus tool tabs (Dyno, Injector, MAF). Menu: `Load Profile / Save Profile As`, `Tools → Learning Table Values`.

**Learning tables** are *not* a definition-file feature — they're hardcoded readers (`DS2FlkcTableQueryBuilder.java`) that generate one query per cell over a contiguous RAM block:

```java
final String addrStr = String.format("0x%06X", flkcAddr + (i * dataSize));
```

and split queries per row "to avoid maxing out the ECU send/receive buffer". Results render as a labelled grid (`Adaptation Table Values`, axes = Engine Load mg/stroke × Engine Speed RPM) with `Save to File` / `Save as Image`.

## 2. TunerPro RT

Help system root: `http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/` (individual pages under `/WebHelp/source/`).

### 2.1 XDF item General tab — the canonical field set

`http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/XDFConstantEditor.htm`

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Title / Description / Units | display |
| **Address** | hex, offset by XDF header `Base Offset` |
| **Size** | **in bits** (8/16/32) — not bytes |
| **Signed** | checkbox |
| **LSB First** | checkbox — "checked for Intel, unchecked for Motorola" |
| **Output Type** | Floating Point / Integer / Hex Digits / String |
| **Significant Digits** | decimals for float; zero-padding width for int |
| Category A/B | two-axis tagging, used for filtering |
| **Use Low/High Range** | if enabled, input is *truncated* to range |
| **Visibility Level** | progressive disclosure by "knowledge level" |

Flags (`XDFFlagEditor.htm`): Address + **Bit Number, zero-based (0..7)**. That's it.

Tables (`XDFTableEditor.htm`) add: **Cell Data Size (bits)**, **Populate By** (row-major vs column-major), rows/cols counts, per-axis Units + Label Type + explicit label lists.

### 2.2 The conversion engine — genuinely worth stealing

`http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/genconv.htm`

Operators: `* / + - %` and bitwise `| & ^`, plus parentheses. Any alpha character is an **argument**, and each argument is independently bound to one of **three source types**:

1. **This Item's Raw Data** (default)
2. **Other XDF Item Output** — the *converted* output of another item
3. **Raw Value at Address** — arbitrary address + **size in bits** + **endianness (1 = LSB first, 0 = MSB first)**

Worked examples straight from the docs:

```
(1.35 * X) - 40                 ; temperature, X = this item's raw data
0.351567 * (X - Y)              ; X = raw data, Y = raw value at bias address
(0.351567 * X) - Y              ; X = raw data, Y = another XDF item's output
```

Note `X * X` is legal and the two X's are *not* necessarily the same value — argument identity is positional, not by name.

### 2.3 Real XDF XML (v1.60)

Verified against `https://github.com/saildot4k/MSS54-XDFs` (BMW MSS54) and `https://github.com/jaytektas/PIS/blob/master/delco.xdf`.

```xml
<XDFFORMAT version="1.60">
  <XDFHEADER>
    <flags>0x1</flags>
    <deftitle>MSS54 v2801 E30 Swap Items</deftitle>
    <author>Justin Ooms</author>
    <BASEOFFSET offset="0" subtract="0" />
    <DEFAULTS datasizeinbits="8" sigdigits="2" outputtype="1"
              signed="0" lsbfirst="0" float="0" />
    <REGION type="0xFFFFFFFF" startaddress="0x0" size="0x8000"
            regionflags="0x0" name="Binary File" desc="..." />
    <CATEGORY index="0x13" name="Contains Alpha-N map (DKBA)" />
  </XDFHEADER>

  <XDFCONSTANT uniqueid="0x1D4C" vislevel="1">
    <title>Sport Mode_MEMORY</title>
    <description>...</description>
    <CATEGORYMEM index="2" category="66" />
    <EMBEDDEDDATA mmedaddress="0x4024" mmedelementsizebits="8"
                  mmedmajorstridebits="0" mmedminorstridebits="0" />
    <units>"-"</units>
    <outputtype>2</outputtype>
    <datatype>0</datatype>
    <DALINK index="0" />
    <MATH equation="x"><VAR id="x" /></MATH>
  </XDFCONSTANT>

  <XDFFLAG uniqueid="0x7C09">
    <title>Two Stroke</title>
    <EMBEDDEDDATA mmedaddress="0xF004" mmedelementsizebits="16" />
    <mask>0x1</mask>
  </XDFFLAG>

  <XDFPATCH uniqueid="0x544A">
    <title>Disable SAP/CAT Heating/DTC</title>
    <XDFPATCHENTRY name="SAP" address="0x75D4" datasize="0x6" patchdata="00FF04B0B9B9" />
    <XDFPATCHENTRY name="DTC" address="0x7BBE" datasize="0xE" patchdata="AA010101010101000102032800FF" />
  </XDFPATCH>
</XDFFORMAT>
```

A table is `<XDFTABLE>` containing three `<XDFAXIS id="x|y|z">`, each with its own `EMBEDDEDDATA`, `indexcount`, `<MATH>`, and optional static `<LABEL index= value=/>`. `<min>`, `<max>`, `<decimalpl>`, `<rangehigh>` sit on the axis.

**`mmedtypeflags` bitfield decode** — authoritative, from RomRaider's `XDFConversionLayer.java` (`src/main/java/com/romraider/xml/ConversionLayer/XDFConversionLayer.java`):

```
0x01  signed
0x02  LSB first (little-endian);  clear => big-endian
0x04  swap X/Y (row/column-major flip)
```

`mmedmajorstridebits` / `mmedminorstridebits` are the row/column strides **in bits** — negative values are legal (see the `-32` in the MSS54 y-axis above), which lets you walk a table backwards. That's a nice trick if your byte layout is reversed.

**There is no published XDF spec document.** The format is only documented through the WebHelp UI descriptions above; everyone else reverse-engineers it. Best executable references: `RomRaider/XDFConversionLayer.java`, `https://github.com/bri3d/a2l2xdf` (A2L→XDF generator), `https://github.com/willemml/xdftuneparser-rs`, `https://github.com/whalenlg/xdf_parser`.

### 2.4 ADX — the live-datastream format (this is your actual analogue)

TunerPro splits *bin definition* (XDF) from *datastream definition* (ADX/ADS). ADX is what you want to copy.

**ADX Value** (`http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DADefValue.htm`):

| Field | Note |
|---|---|
| Title, **Unique ID** (max 15 chars, referenced by lists/dashes/histograms) | |
| Data Type + Stock Units | *optional*, used only to auto-link to XDF items |
| **Units Override** | what's actually displayed |
| **Packet Offset (H \| D)** | zero-based byte index into the packet — **dual hex/decimal input fields side by side** |
| **Data Source Size** | bits |
| **Signed**, **LSB First** | |
| **Range Low / Range High** | raw limits, used by "Percentage of defined range" output |
| **Alarm High / Low + enables** | value renders red bold when breached |
| Command Association | which request this value arrives in |

Conversion tab: same equation engine, but argument types are only **Native** (raw at this offset) or **Linked Output** (another ADX Value). Then optionally **"Send converted data to lookup table"**.

Output formats: Hex, Integer, Unsigned Integer, Floating Point, **Percentage of Defined Range** (`[current - min] / [max - min]`). Truncation, never rounding.

**ADX Lookup Tables** (`DADefLookup.htm`) — a first-class calibration primitive, list of (input, output) pairs with four **Lookup Modes**:

| Mode | Given entries `[2.0→4.0]`, `[4.0→8.0]`, input 2.5/3.0/3.5 |
|---|---|
| **Interpolate** | 5.0 / 6.0 / 7.0 |
| **Closest** | 4.0 / 8.0 / 8.0 |
| **Previous** | 4.0 / 4.0 / 4.0 |
| **Next** | 8.0 / 8.0 / 8.0 |

Clamps at both ends; exact input matches always bypass the mode. There's a **Table Graph tab where you drag points with the mouse**. This is exactly the right UI for "I have 40 samples of raw byte vs. known ground truth, fit me a curve."

**ADX Bitmask** (`DADefBitmask.htm`): offset, size, LSB First, **Operation = bitwise AND or XOR** against an operand, then **Display on TRUE** / **Display on FALSE** strings + alarm-on-true/false. Not a bit *index* — a mask plus an operator.

**ADX Header** (`DADefHeader.htm`): Baud (1200–921600), **RS232 Echo** (discard local echo — matters on K-line), and three command slots: **Connection Command**, **Monitor Command** (sent in a loop), **Disconnect Command**. Commands are Send / Listen / **Macro** (an ordered group, typically send+listen).

Packets are modelled as **fixed-size header + body + footer**; the payload lives in the body, and packet offsets are relative to it.

**Data Acquisition Tracing** (`DATracing.htm`) is the killer feature: link the XDF to the ADX, then while streaming, **the live value lights up the currently-active cell in the ROM table**. Axis labels must be numeric, not strings, for this to resolve.

## 3. WinOLS

Vendor: `https://www.evc.de/en/product/ols/software/`

### 3.1 Automatic map detection — the heuristics

Vendor claims: *"Automatic processor recognition to distinguish between program and data area"*; *"Program code, empty areas, maps etc. are automatically detected. An overview window shows what can be found where in the file. Program code and empty areas are automatically displayed in pale."*

Reported detection criteria (`https://ecufiles.io/technik/winols-map-erkennung`):

1. **Statistical distribution analysis** to separate code from data (machine code has a distinct byte histogram).
2. **Axis monotonicity** — runs of *strictly monotonically increasing* values, ~8–32 elements, in plausible numeric ranges, flag a candidate axis.
3. **Smoothness / second derivative** — maps have low second derivatives; noise has high ones throughout.
4. **Value-range plausibility** per candidate data type (uint8/int16/…); reject regions of all-`0xFF` or all-`0x00`.
5. **Known-ECU database matching** for recognised binaries.
6. **Cross-version differencing** — the most reliable method: two calibrations of the same ECU *"differ almost exclusively in the map regions"* because code is identical.

Corroborating visual description (`https://www.fileservice24.at/en/blog/winols-guide-finding-maps`): code is *"chaotic, high-frequency noise with no discernible pattern"*; maps are *"smooth, structured shapes: gentle curves, clean staircases, ramps that rise and plateau, or flat lines."*

### 3.2 Visual conventions

- Raw data shown as **2D graphic OR hex/decimal dump**, switchable, plus **3D chart**, **table**, and (5.46+) **"Slices"** — all lines drawn at the same height so shapes can be compared.
- **Overview window**: whole-file map, code and empty regions greyed pale.
- **Preview window**: free-floating, resizable, renders the *current selection* as a live 3D map. This is the key interaction — the 3D preview updates as you drag the selection, and a coherent shape is the confirmation signal.
- Four preset colour schemes, user-configurable.

### 3.3 Manual map definition — actual keystrokes

From the HP Academy WinOLS course (`https://www.hpacademy.com/courses/winols-mastery-map-identification-and-editing/`):

| Action | Input |
|---|---|
| Increase / decrease display width (columns) | **M** / **W** |
| Shift alignment by one byte (remove the green vertical guide line) | **Ctrl + arrow keys** |
| Select the map region | click-drag from left of the data; drag edges to fine-tune |
| **Convert selection into a defined map** | **K** |
| Open properties | double-click the map |
| Reuse scaling | right-click → **"copy map properties"**, untick *"data source plus address"*, **Ctrl+V** onto the next map |

Properties dialog fields: Name/Description, Units, **Data Type** (e.g. *"16 bit high low"* — endianness is part of the type name), **Factor** and **Offset**.

Axis linking for 3D maps is done from the hex view, *before* creating the map:
- right-click the first Y value → **"address as Y axis of the next map"**
- right-click the first X value → **"address as X axis of the next map"**

Axes can differ in width from the Z data (16-bit axis + 8-bit map data is common); switching the view between 8/16-bit is how you tell whether an axis is real — *"the second axis just becomes complete garbage"* in the wrong width.

Typical factors seen in the wild: `/4096` for relative fill %, `/327.68` for throttle % (16-bit full-scale 0–100), `×40` for RPM, `/128` for lambda.

Also relevant: **`File → Import → Map Pack / Damos / A2L`** (import known definitions), **`File → Compare with File`**, an **XDF importer plugin** (`https://www.evc.de/en/product/ols/xdf_importer.asp`), and a **LUA scripting** plugin.

## 4. ECUFlash

XML format, real example (`https://github.com/Crowley2012/SubaruTuning/blob/master/Definitions/ECUFlash/subaru/Forester%202.5/EP5D201D.xml`):

```xml
<rom>
  <romid>
    <xmlid>EP5D201D</xmlid>
    <internalidaddress>2004</internalidaddress>
    <internalidstring>EP5D201D</internalidstring>
    <ecuid>7112346007</ecuid>
    <year>2011</year> <market>USDM</market> <make>Subaru</make>
    <memmodel>SH7058</memmodel>
    <checksummodule>subarudbw</checksummodule>
    <flashmethod>subarucan</flashmethod>
  </romid>
  <include>32BITBASE</include>

  <scaling name="Advance(degrees)2" units="Advance (degrees)"
           toexpr="(x*.001525879)-40" frexpr="(x+40)/.001525879"
           format="%.2f" min="0" max="50.00" inc=".5"
           storagetype="uint16" endian="big" />

  <table name="Primary Open Loop Fueling Cruise" address="cd35c">
    <table name="X" address="cd308" elements="13" />
    <table name="Y" address="cd33c" elements="8" />
  </table>
</rom>
```

Full table forms (from `https://github.com/dparrish/ecurom/tree/master/xml/ecuflash`):

```xml
<table name="ALS minimum vehicle speed to trigger" category="Turbo"
       address="1e12" type="1D" level="1" scaling="VehicleSpeed"/>

<table name="ALS Air injection time" category="Turbo" address="4e3a"
       type="2D" level="1" scaling="Timesecbyte">
    <table name="RPM" address="7792" type="X Axis" elements="9" scaling="RPM"/>
</table>

<table name="Fuel Map 1 - HI OCTANE" category="Fuel and Ignition Maps"
       address="118A3" type="3D" swapxy="true" scaling="AFR">
    <table name="Load" address="2eb42" type="X Axis" elements="10" scaling="Load"/>
    <table name="RPM"  address="2ec62" type="Y Axis" elements="15" scaling="RPM"/>
</table>
```

Table `type` values observed: `1D`, `2D`, `3D`, `X Axis`, `Y Axis`, `Static X Axis`, `Static Y Axis`. `storagetype` values: `uint8`, `int8`, `uint16`, `int16`, plus **`bloblist`** — the enum/selection editor:

```xml
<scaling name="blobbits" storagetype="bloblist" storagebits="1">
    <data name="0" value="00"/>
    <data name="1" value="01"/>
</scaling>
```

**Relationship to RomRaider — they are near-isomorphic, and converted in both directions in production:**
- The Subaru file above is literally stamped *"This file was generated by RR2EcuFlash version: 1.0.0.33977"* (RomRaider → EcuFlash).
- `<include>32BITBASE</include>` is EcuFlash's inheritance; RomRaider uses `<rom base="32BITBASE">`.
- Attribute mapping: EcuFlash `toexpr`/`frexpr` ⇄ RomRaider `expression`(`to_real`)/`to_byte`; `inc` ⇄ `fineincrement`; `format="%.2f"` (printf) ⇄ `format="0.00"` (DecimalFormat). `storagetype`, `endian`, `address`, `elements`/`size` are identical in spirit.
- Converters in the wild: `https://github.com/Switchleg1/xdf2xml`, `https://gist.github.com/guicho271828/dbb4195df9316fd37e333eb9b828fde3`, and RomRaider's own `XDFConversionLayer.java` / `VDFConversionLayer.java` / `BMWCodingConversionLayer.java`.

Discovery methodology on the EcuFlash side is *disassembly*-driven, not statistical (`https://evoecu.logic.net/wiki/Locating_Tables`): find calls to the shared axis-lookup routine `sub_CC6`, read the axis header (result pointer, input-value pointer, length word, then data), then the table header carries a **dimension marker (0x2 = 2D, 0x3 = 3D)** plus a global offset. Different problem from yours, but the *header-describes-shape* idea is worth noting.

### Domain-specific

| Tool | What it gives you | URL |
|---|---|---|
| **TunerPro Comparison Tool** | Best-documented model. Pick 2 of 5 loaded bins (1 editable + 4 compare buffers), enter **start/end address range**, checkbox **"limit to items defined in the XDF"**. Output = one row per differing byte; **undefined bytes rendered in blue**; click → locate in list, double-click → open editor. Explicitly notes a 2-byte item shows as 2 rows. | `http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DiffTool.htm` |
| **WinOLS** | `File → Compare with File`; differing ranges highlighted in the 2D/hex view. Vendor treats cross-version diff as the primary map-finding method. | `https://www.evc.de/en/product/ols/software/` |
| **OpenRemap** | Python lib + CLI. `identify` / `scan` / `cook` / `tune`. Diffs two binaries into a portable **`.remap` recipe** capturing every changed byte **plus 32 bytes of context anchors** so the patch survives firmware revisions. Confidence-scored ECU identification (30 extractors, Bosch/Siemens/Delphi/Marelli). | `https://github.com/v-arapidis/openremap-core` |
| **romHEX14** | A2L-aware ROM-to-ROM comparison, **map-by-map in physical units** rather than raw bytes. | `https://romhex14.com` |
| **ECU-Mod Pro / Softechpro / BinUnlock BinCompare** | Free browser-based "upload original + modified, get changed offsets". | `https://ecu-modpro.com/static/en/bin-compare`, `https://softechpro-solutions.com/bin-compare.html` |
| **EcuTek ProECU ROM Compare** | Commercial multi-ROM compare. | `https://ecutek.atlassian.net` |

### General-purpose (better UI ideas)

- **ImHex** (`https://imhex.werwolv.net/`) — pattern language, data inspector, **file diffing**, and visualizers: **entropy, digram, byte distribution**. The digram/entropy plots are the closest open-source analogue to WinOLS's code-vs-data overview.
- **radare2 `radiff2`** — `-c` byte count, `-s` similarity/distance, `-x` hex-column diff.
- **VBinDiff** (`https://www.cjmweb.net/vbindiff/`) — two-pane synchronised scrolling hex with differences highlighted; tiny and the interaction model is trivially copyable.
- **binvis.io / Veles** — space-filling-curve and trigram binary visualisation; good for "where is the structured region".
- **bsdiff / xdelta / Kaitai Struct / 010 Editor binary templates** — for the record.

### Also worth stealing from an adjacent field

Your actual problem — *N unknown bytes streaming at low rate, find which one is TPS* — is the **CAN signal-identification** problem, which has better-published algorithms than the ECU-tuning world. Relevant prior art: **READ** (Reverse Engineering of Automotive Data frames), **LibreCAN**, **CAN-D**, and **SavvyCAN**'s sniffer view, which highlights *changed bytes since last frame* with per-byte colour decay and offers a "signal finder" that correlates candidate bit-ranges against a reference channel. That colour-decay-on-change hex grid is probably the single highest-value widget for your UI.

## 6. Direct hit for your E36 — RomRaider's BMW MS41 DS2 logger definition

RomRaider release notes: *"BMW DS2 protocol implementation for MS41, MS42 and MS43 DME"*, *"DS2 protocol now supports 'Telegram', logging arbitrary addresses, requires a new logger definition v352 or later"*.

Definition file (v354, DS2-only, 89 `ecuparam`s, covering ECU IDs `1405854, 1406464, SHINDE1, 1429373, 1429861, 1432401, 1437806, 1440176`):
`https://github.com/0x000NULL/tuning/blob/main/BMW/MS41%20Logger%20Definitions.xml`

**The two you're looking for:**

```xml
<ecuparam id="P13" name="..TPS" desc="Throttle Position (STATUS_DROSSELKLAPPEN)"
          group="0x0B" subgroup="0x01" target="1">
    <ecu id="1405854,1429373,1429861,1432401,1437806,1440176">
        <address>0x0000E8D7</address>
    </ecu>
    <ecu id="1406464,SHINDE1">
        <address>0x0000E8D0</address>   <!-- TPS Post Adaptation -->
    </ecu>
    <conversions>
        <conversion units="%" expr="x*100/255" format="0.0"
                    gauge_min="0" gauge_max="100" gauge_step="10" />
    </conversions>
</ecuparam>

<ecuparam id="P9" name="/VS" desc="Vehicle Speed (STATUS_GESCHWINDIGKEIT)"
          group="0x0B" subgroup="0x01" target="1">
    <ecu id="1405854,1406464,SHINDE1,1429373,1429861,1432401,1437806,1440176">
        <address>0x0000DA63</address>
    </ecu>
    <conversions>
        <conversion units="km/h" expr="x" format="0" gauge_min="0" gauge_max="300" gauge_step="30" />
        <conversion units="mph"  expr="x*0.621371192" format="0.0" gauge_min="0" gauge_max="250" gauge_step="25" />
    </conversions>
</ecuparam>
```

So: **TPS = `0xE8D7`, uint8, `x*100/255` %** and **road speed = `0xDA63`, uint8, `x` km/h (raw = km/h, 1:1)**.

Cross-check against your five knowns — these are the same file:

| Addr | Name | Type | Expr | Units |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0xDA2A` | RPM | uint16 | `x` | RPM |
| `0xDA34` | MAF | uint16 | `x*0.25` | kg/h |
| `0xDA50` | IAT | uint8 | `x*0.747-48` | °C |
| `0xDA5A` | ECT (coolant) | uint8 | `x*0.747-48` | °C |
| **`0xDA63`** | **Vehicle Speed** | **uint8** | **`x`** | **km/h** |
| `0xDAA5` | Atmospheric Pressure | uint8 | `101.325*37/255` | psi |
| **`0xE8D7`** | **TPS** | **uint8** | **`x*100/255`** | **%** |
| `0xE8DE` | TPS Adaptation | int16 | `x*1.526E-3` | % |
| `0xE989` | Ignition | uint8 | `0.373*x-23.6` | °BTDC |
| `0xE98D` | Knock | uint8 | `(x-128)*0.375` | ° corr |
| `0xE9E6` | VANOS | uint8 | `x*0.3745` | KW° |
| `0xEF7E` | IPW (injection pulse width) | uint16 | `x*0.00534` | ms |
| `0xF01E`/`0xF030` | STFT1 / LTFT1 | uint16 | `(x-32768)*100/65535` | % |
| **`0xFAFC`** | **Load** | **uint16** | **`x*0.0212`** | **mg/stroke** |
| `0xF141` | Compressor relay | uint8 | `!BitWise(32,x,1)/32` | On/Off |

Battery voltage appears as an **ADC pseudo-channel** (`V_Batt`, `x*0.102` VDC) rather than a RAM address, so if your battery-volts byte is in the 252-byte window, your window may be a different block than these — but note **coolant, IAT and RPM all live in `0xDA2A–0xDA5A`**, a ~50-byte span. A 252-byte window starting near `0xDA00` would contain RPM, MAF, IACV, IAT, ECT, **vehicle speed (`0xDA63`)**, knock sensors and atmospheric pressure — but **not TPS**, which is 3.6 kB higher at `0xE8D7`, and not Load at `0xFAFC`. If your window does contain injection load, it isn't the `0xDA00` block. Worth resolving before you build anything: dump your window's base address and check it against this table.

Companion definitions for the other Siemens BMW DMEs: `https://github.com/Rustle333/Siemens-MS43`, `https://github.com/Rustle333/MSS52`, `https://github.com/Rustle333/M5.2`.

## 7. What to actually steal for your UI

**Data model** — one `Parameter` with N `Conversion` children:

```
Parameter { id, name, desc, address, length=1, bit=-1, group/subgroup }
Conversion { units*, expr*, format*, storagetype?, endian?=big,
             gauge_min?, gauge_max?, gauge_step?, replace[] }
```

Everything else is optional with a defaulting rule. RomRaider's exact set, and it's the smallest schema that covers all five known-good channels above.

**Nine conventions, ranked by value to your discovery problem:**

1. **Min / Current / Max columns, session-accumulated** (RomRaider live data table). Free range discovery on every unknown byte at once — a byte that has covered 0–255 is not coolant temp.
2. **Default gauge ranges keyed on the units string** (§1.3). Type "km/h", get a 0–300 axis. Zero-config plausibility checking.
3. **Change-highlighted hex grid with colour decay** (SavvyCAN sniffer / WinOLS 2D view). At 1 Hz over 252 bytes this is the primary instrument: idle the engine, blip the throttle, watch which cell flashes.
4. **A live 3D/2D preview slaved to the current selection** (WinOLS preview window). Shape coherence is the confirmation signal — a monotone ramp when you sweep the throttle *is* the proof.
5. **Adjustable display width + one-byte alignment nudge** (WinOLS `M`/`W` and `Ctrl+arrow`). You don't know the stride; make it a slider, not a config field.
6. **Interactive lookup table with 4 modes and a draggable graph** (TunerPro ADX). Plot raw byte vs. ground truth from a scan tool, drag points, get a conversion. Far better than making the user guess `a*x+b`.
7. **Derived/computed channels via `depends`+`ref`** (RomRaider). Lets the user test hypotheses — "byte 47 × 0.5 minus byte 12" — without touching code. Reference other params *in a chosen unit*: `[P7:psi]`.
8. **Bit-level items as first-class citizens**, both styles: TunerPro's `mask` + AND/XOR + TRUE/FALSE labels, and RomRaider's `bit` index + `BitWise(mask, x, op)`. Road speed on some ECUs is packed; switches definitely are.
9. **Capability gating and visibility levels** — hide what this ECU can't produce (RomRaider `ecubyteindex`/`ecubit`), and tier by confidence (TunerPro `vislevel`, RomRaider `userlevel 1–5`). For a discovery tool, repurpose this as a **confidence field**: `confirmed / probable / guess / unknown`, and colour the hex grid by it.

**Two more, specific to your workflow:** adopt RomRaider's `*`-suffix convention to mark reverse-engineered vs. documented parameters, and store the unit selection in the saved profile (`profile.dtd` `parameter@units`) so a session reload doesn't lose the user's calibration choices.

## 0. CRITICAL CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF — Stack does NOT have a curved/arc LED-segment tachometer on the ST8100/ST700/ST8130/ST8150 family

I read the **official Stack ST8100 "Display System Users Guide" (Part No. ST542030-006, © 2004 Stack Limited, 54 pages, full text+diagrams extracted)** and cross-checked it against Stack's own 2011 product catalog and current stackltd.com listings. All primary sources agree: **ST700, ST8100, ST8130, ST8150 (and the ST8916S/ST800 family) are hybrid units — a real needle-type analogue tachometer combined with a small 2‑line dot‑matrix LCD panel.** There is no curved/arc LED-segment rev counter on any of these. This is stated explicitly in Stack's own marketing: *"ANALOGUE TACHOMETER — the preferred choice of most racers"* (2011 catalog, Integrated Dash Display Systems page).

What Stack *does* make with an LED-segment/bar rev indicator is a **different, later product line**: the **ST8956SWD (steering-wheel-integrated) / ST8956SD (satellite dash)**, introduced "NEW for 2013." That unit has a straight (not curved) row of small round LEDs across the top described as a **"9 Stage Sequential Shift Light/Tachometer,"** plus genuine 7/14-segment-style red and green LED numeric digit clusters for gear/lap time/speed. This is a distinct product from the ST8100/ST700/ST8130 dash family and should not be conflated with it.

**Recommendation for the design guide:** treat "Stack ST8100 family" as an analogue-needle-tach + LCD hybrid, and treat "Stack ST8956SWD/SD" separately if a straight-LED-bar reference is wanted.

## 1. Stack ST8100/ST700/ST8130 — actual verified screen layout

Confirmed via the 2004 manual's own diagrams (reproduced faithfully across every ST8100/ST8130 unit still sold) and current photography in Stack's 2011 catalog:

- **Housing shape:** a single molded carbon-composite panel, asymmetric rounded "shield/wedge" silhouette (not a rectangle or circle) — wider at the bottom-left, tapering to a curved top edge.
- **Overall module size:** **190mm × 97mm (7.48 in × 3.82 in)** — confirmed both in the manual's dashboard cut-out template and by Summit Racing/Pegasus/Demon Tweeks listings.
- **Top ⅔ of the panel:** analogue needle tachometer, semicircular scale (~230–270°), numerals 1–8, 1–10, etc. depending on RPM range variant (7 dial-face range options are sold), major tick at each numeral with several minor ticks between.
- **Two built-in warning lights** flank the tachometer near its upper corners (confirmed explicitly in the manual text: *"The Display Module has two built-in warning lights"*): one is the **amber Alarm light** (shown "lit" as a sun-burst icon in the manual, left side), the other is the **Gear-shift warning light** (right side). Both are simple round telltale lamps set into the black fascia, not a bar or arc.
- **Bottom ⅓ of the panel:** a rectangular **2-line, ~20-character dot-matrix LCD** (transflective, backlit — Stack's copy: *"Contrast improves when under bright illumination — clearly visible in bright sunlight"*). It is a genuine character/segment LCD, not a bitmap graphic panel — **no pixel "resolution" spec exists for it** because it isn't a raster display (this is a real difference vs. the Bosch DDU family below).
- **LCD backlight color:** yellow-green/amber (confirmed in multiple official product photos), with dark segmented-look digits.
- **Right of the LCD:** the "STACK / STACK / STACK" triple-stacked wordmark logo (echo/perspective effect), rendered in red on the physical product and in black/grey on print collateral.

## 2. Classic analogue gauge face conventions — Stack (52mm/80mm aux gauges, ST200, ST700 tach) vs VDO (Cockpit/Vision/Viewline)

I obtained and visually inspected actual product photography for both brands (not just marketing copy).

### Stack

- **Tick treatment:** major tick at every numeral, ~1 minor tick between majors on 52mm gauges (e.g., 0–7 Oil Pressure); ~4–5 minor ticks per major on the larger 80mm ST700 tachometer.
- **Numeral placement:** inside the tick ring (numerals sit inboard, ticks radiate outward to the rim) — upright, not rotated to follow the arc.
- **Face color:** black is standard across all ranges; **white and silver are optional** dial-face finishes on "selected gauges" (2011 catalog: *"White & Silver dial face options on selected gauges"*).
- **Needle color pairing:** **white needle on black face; orange needle on white/silver face** — confirmed both in text and in photos.
- **Needle shape:** thin, tapering to a point at the tip; no visible counterweight tail extending past the pivot in any Stack photo I inspected.
- **Hub/pivot cap:** small dark circular cap, unobtrusive (much smaller than VDO's, see below).
- **Bezel:** **plain black** ring on the 52mm/small auxiliary gauges (confirmed across Pro-Control, Electric, and Mechanical ranges — all listed only in "BLACK"). The larger 80mm ST700 tachometer's official hero photo shows a **bright/reflective chrome-look bezel** — but catalog thumbnails of what appears to be the same model show a plain black bezel. **I could not fully resolve this discrepancy** — it may be gloss-black plastic photographed under specular studio lighting rather than true chrome plate. Flagged as unverified.
- **Sweep angle:** explicitly stated — **270° sweep** for Pro-Control/stepper-motor and mechanical (Bourdon-tube) gauges; **90° sweep** for the cheaper "Electric Analogue" air-core range.
- **Alarm rendering (Pro-Control series):** a genuinely distinctive Stack feature — **the entire dial face backlight changes color** when a min/max alarm threshold is exceeded (7 selectable colors: white, red, yellow, green, blue, purple, turquoise), rather than a separate warning lamp.
- **Brand mark:** small "STACK/STACK/STACK" triple-stack logo printed near the 6 o'clock position on most dial faces.
- Numbers on ST200 specifically (from spec/retail pages, not photographed directly): 80mm diameter, IP67 sealed, stepper-motor movement; I could **not** obtain a clean, high-resolution photo of the ST200 dial itself (only the 52mm Pro-Control and 80mm ST700 families) — its tick/numeral geometry is presumed similar to the ST700 family shown above based on shared design language, but this is an **inference, not a direct observation, and should be flagged as such**.

### VDO

I inspected four real product photos directly (VDO Cockpit/Vision 80mm tachometer; two VDO Viewline units).

**VDO Cockpit / Vision (classic, e.g. 80mm tachometer, RPM×1000 0–10):**
- Face: matte **black**.
- Bezel: **plain, thin, flat black** ring (Vehiclecontrols.com's own copy calls it a **"peaked black" bezel** — no chrome option in this classic line).
- Numerals: **white**, bold condensed sans-serif, placed **inside** the tick ring, upright.
- Ticks: bold major tick at each numeral (0–10), with what appears to be **4 minor ticks per major interval** (i.e., graduated every ~200 rpm on the example photographed) — counted directly from product photography.
- Needle: **red**, thin, slight taper to a point, no counterweight tail past the pivot; VDO's own retailer copy independently confirms **"fire red/orange" pointers** on Cockpit-series gauges.
- Hub/pivot cap: a comparatively **large, glossy black domed cap** at the center — proportionally bigger than Stack's equivalent, and a recurring VDO signature.
- "RPM x 1000" and "VDO" wordmark printed in white in the same condensed font family, "VDO" logotype at the 6 o'clock position.
- Lighting: VDO's own copy distinguishes **Vision as "backlit with light coming through the numbers, fiber-optic needle"** vs **Cockpit as "side-lit"** — I could not independently visually verify this lighting-method distinction, only relay the manufacturer/retailer claim (flagged as sourced-but-unverified by direct inspection).

**VDO Viewline (modern):**
- Bezel: markedly **thicker, rounded/domed black bezel** with a soft "donut" cross-section — a visibly chunkier, more three-dimensional profile than the flat Cockpit/Vision bezel. A composite catalog thumbnail also shows **chrome/silver-bezel Viewline variants** alongside black-bezel ones, matching VDO's own marketing copy: *"three attractive designs in black, white, and chrome."*
- Two color schemes confirmed directly from product photos:
  - **"Onyx"** = black face + **white** needle + white numerals/ticks.
  - **"Ivory"** = white/cream face + **red** needle + black numerals/ticks.
  (Needle color pairs with face color, same pattern logic as Stack, but the specific colors used differ.)
- Hub/pivot cap: **very large, glossy, domed black cap** with a visible specular highlight — an even more pronounced version of the Cockpit/Vision hub, and the strongest single "VDO-look" identifier across both sub-lines.
- **Distinctive Viewline-only features not present on classic Cockpit/Vision:** an integrated **amber/yellow LCD sub-display window** (small rounded-rectangle segment-LCD, e.g. a 6-digit odometer) set into the lower half of the dial face, and a **red warning-triangle icon** printed directly on the face below the hub that illuminates for alarms.
- Ticks: major tick at each numeral, ~1 minor tick between majors (half-graduations) on the units photographed.
- "VDO" wordmark at 6 o'clock, same condensed white/black lettering depending on face color.

**Typeface:** No official VDO typeface name could be confirmed from any source. The one concrete data point I found is a **VW/Porsche forum consensus (914World.com, VWVortex.com) that "Arial Black" is the closest common font match**, specifically citing the shape of VDO's numeral "1" (a small flag/tail at the top-left) as the distinguishing tell. This is a **community approximation, not a manufacturer-confirmed fact** — flagged accordingly. Visually (from the photos I inspected) the numerals are a bold, geometric, condensed grotesque sans-serif with tabular (uniform-width) figures and minimal stroke contrast — consistent with, but not proof of, the Arial-Black-family claim.

## 3. Bosch Motorsport DDU — display layout, alarms, shift lights (verified via official manuals, not marketing pages)

I obtained and fully extracted (text + rendered screenshot images) the **official DDU8 manual (162 pp.)** and **DDU11 manual (204 pp.)**, plus official datasheets for DDU7, DDU9, DDU10, DDU11.

### Hardware specs (all confirmed from primary datasheets)

| Model | Screen | Resolution | Shift/warning LEDs | Size (mm) | Weight | IP rating |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DDU 7 | 5.7" trans-reflective color | 640×480 | 10 RGB (top row) | 148×126×32 | 440g | IP54 |
| DDU 8 | 5" full-color TFT | 800×480 | 10 RGB (top row) | 161×111×31(49) | 675g | (not stated) |
| DDU 9 | 5.7" trans-reflective color | 640×480 | 10 RGB (top row) | 151×126×33.5 | 540g | IP54 |
| DDU 10 | 7" full-color | 800×480 | 20 RGB (10 top + 5 per side) | 198×134×35 | 875g (product page) / 930g (official datasheet — **discrepancy, flagged**) | IP67 |
| DDU 11 | 6.5" full-color | 800×480 | 18 RGB (8 top + 5 per side) | 203×128×38.5 | 649g | IP67 |

### Physical LED placement (from the actual DDU8 manual's own RaceCon device-mockup screenshots)

The shift-light LEDs are **physical LEDs embedded in the housing directly above the screen**, not on-screen graphics — confirmed by seeing the exact rendered unit in RaceCon's device view: a row of ~10 round LEDs sits in a strip across the top edge of the black housing, with the screen below it, and a "DDU 8 · Motorsport" + Bosch-logo badge strip below the screen. Starting with DDU10/11, Bosch added **additional LEDs on the left and right edges of the housing** (5+5), not just the top.

**Default/example color pattern** (from the DDU8 manual's shift-light configuration screenshot, RPM-threshold table): left-to-right the 10 LEDs are grouped roughly **green → green → green → green → yellow → orange → orange → red → red** (I counted this directly from the screenshot; exact per-color boundaries are user-configurable per RPM/gear, so this is Bosch's own example/default pattern, not a fixed spec — my exact count of the compressed screenshot image has some uncertainty, **flagged**).

### Page-layout model: there is NO single fixed "factory" RPM-bar/gear/alarm layout

This is an important and precise finding: **Bosch ships the DDU as a blank canvas.** RaceCon (the configuration tool) provides a **"Display Elements" toolbox** that teams drag onto up to 12 (DDU7/8/9/10) or 48 (DDU11, 12 pages × 4 switchable sets) pages. There is no default RPM-bar-at-top/gear-in-center template baked into the hardware — DTM/WEC/GT3 teams design their own page layouts per car/driver.

**Confirmed primitive catalog** (with visual appearance directly rendered from the manuals):

- **DDU 7/8/9 (older engine):** Large/Medium **Numeric** boxes, **Bargraph** (horizontal/vertical, "Solid" or "Stacked"-segment color), **Alarm** (text) / **Alarm Icon**, **Label**, **Picture**. **No needle-gauge widget exists on this generation** — confirmed by the DDU8 manual's own element list, which omits any gauge/dial primitive.
- **DDU 10/11 (newer "display element design generator," introduced with DDU10):** adds a full parallel "Classic" and "Modern" styled catalog — **Classic Box, Classic horizontal/vertical Bar, Classic Gauge Large/Small, Modern Box, Modern horizontal/vertical Bar, Modern Gauge Large/Small, Basic Box, Value/Text, Enumeration, Image, Alarm/Alarm Icon.**

I rendered the manual's own catalog illustrations directly and can describe them precisely:
- **"Classic Gauge"**: a simulated analogue dial — **bright chrome/brushed-metal bezel ring** (beveled, specular highlight), **radial blue gradient face** (dark navy outer → lighter center), **white tick marks** (bold major at each numeral, thin minor between), **numerals outside the tick marks**, and a **red, wedge-shaped needle** (wide at the hub, tapering to a point at the tip, no counterweight tail past the pivot). The center hosts a large flat lighter-blue disc reserved for an overlaid digital value. Conditional formatting can recolor the tick arc (e.g., for a redline band).
- **"Modern Gauge"**: **no bezel at all** — flat black background, a **thick cyan/blue radial progress-arc** (donut-style fill, not a needle) with a short white tick marking current value, small unlabeled tick dashes around the rim, and a **large digital numeral in the center** instead of a needle+dial reading.
- **"Classic/Modern Box" and "Bargraph"**: flat dark-navy-to-black gradient backgrounds, cyan/light-blue segmented fill bars (discrete rectangular LED-like blocks, not a smooth fill — the currently-filled segment nearest the value is rendered in a lighter/white shade), white channel-name label at top, large white numeral bottom-right.

### Alarms
Alarms are a dedicated element type (not just a colored box): **defined in one of 4 fixed screen areas**, available in "Classic" or "Modern" **style** (matching the box/gauge aesthetic), **non-transparent background**, **always rendered on top of every other element** (highest z-order), and if multiple alarms in the same area are active simultaneously **each is shown for ~1.5–2 seconds** in rotation. Alarms can show text, an icon, or a value, and support blink modes, minimum display time, and auto-reset.

### RaceCon / configuration tool
RaceCon is confirmed as the single tool across all DDU generations — Ethernet or MSA-Box II connection, drag-and-drop element placement, per-element Wizard dialogs for font size/alignment/border/background/foreground color, and (DDU10/11) an "ambient light sensor" for auto-brightness and a "state-of-the-art user interface menu" for in-car page/reset control without a laptop.

### Typography
Bosch's manual discloses that the **Graphic Engine uses the open-source FreeType library "for non-bitmap font rendering"** (explicit license text found in the DDU11 manual) — **no specific named commercial typeface is disclosed anywhere in the manuals**. Visually (from the rendered numeric-element screenshots), the digits are a **blocky, monospaced, tabular-figure "digital" style** — uniform stroke width, slightly rounded corners, reminiscent of a seven-segment display but not a true segmented glyph — used consistently across Numeric, Box, and Gauge elements.

Sources: bosch-motorsport.com/media/downloads/display_ddu_8.pdf (full manual, primary); bosch-motorsport.com/media/downloads/display_ddu_7.pdf and display_ddu_7_manual.pdf; bosch-motorsport.com/media/downloads/ddu_9_datasheet.pdf; xtreme-di.com Display_DDU_10_Datasheet PDF; bosch-motorsport.com/media/catalog_content/.../data_sheet_..._display_ddu_11.pdf and operation_manual_..._display_ddu_11.pdf (full manual, primary); bosch-motorsport.com/products/displays/display-ddu-10/.

## 4. Cross-brand: needle design

- **Stack (52/80mm aux + ST700):** thin, point-tapered needle, no counterweight tail past pivot, small unobtrusive hub cap; color pairs with face (white-on-black / orange-on-white).
- **VDO (Cockpit/Vision/Viewline):** broader, wedge-shaped needle (wider mid-section, tapering to a point), no counterweight tail past pivot; **large, glossy, domed black hub cap** is the most consistent VDO signature across both sub-lines; color pairs with face (white-on-black or red-on-white/black depending on sub-line).
- **Bosch (RaceCon "Classic Gauge" simulated needle only — DDU10/11):** red, wide-at-hub/tapering-to-point wedge needle, no counterweight tail. Not a physical needle — a rendered graphic. DDU7/8/9 have **no needle widget at all**.
- **Common thread:** none of the three brands' needles show a counterweight extending past the pivot in any sample I inspected — all are "one-directional" pointer shapes.

## 5. Cross-brand: bezel

- **Stack:** plain black bezel on small/auxiliary gauges (confirmed, no chrome option marketed); the large ST700 tach's hero photo shows a bright/chrome-look ring (unverified whether true chrome or glossy black under studio lighting); **the digital-dash family (ST8100/8130/8150) has no separate bezel at all** — the dial is inset flush into the same molded black composite panel.
- **VDO:** Cockpit/Vision = thin, flat, plain black ("peaked black") bezel, no chrome variant found. Viewline = thicker, rounded/domed black bezel as one option, with chrome and white-painted bezel variants also marketed (per VDO's own "black, white, and chrome" copy) — genuinely offers a chrome option, unlike Cockpit/Vision.
- **Bosch:** the physical unit housing has **no bezel concept at all** around the screen (it's a single flat TFT behind glass in a rectangular housing). On-screen, the RaceCon "Classic Gauge" widget **simulates** a chrome bezel purely as a rendered graphic; the "Modern Gauge" widget deliberately has **no bezel simulation** — flat black background only. This directly answers the brief's question of whether digital dashes simulate bezels: **yes, Bosch's DDU10/11 explicitly offer a chrome-bezel-simulating "Classic" gauge skin as a user choice, alongside a bezel-less "Modern" skin.**

## 6. Cross-brand: typography

- **Stack:** dot-matrix/segment LCD font (character display, not bitmap graphics) on the dash family; bold condensed sans-serif printed numerals on the analogue dial faces.
- **VDO:** bold, condensed, geometric grotesque sans-serif with tabular figures; no confirmed official name — community approximation is "Arial Black," based on the numeral "1" shape (unverified beyond forum consensus).
- **Bosch:** FreeType-rendered (open-source rendering library, confirmed in manual's license text; no named typeface disclosed); visually a blocky, monospaced, tabular "digital" numeral style across all display elements.

## 7. Cross-brand: gradients / glow / drop shadows / bloom

- **Stack:** flat, unlit product photography shows flat black faces with no gradient rendering (these are physical printed dial faces, not screens) — LCD screens show a flat yellow-green backlight wash, no glow/bloom effects visible in photos.
- **VDO:** flat matte or glossy physical dial faces; the one rendering nuance is the domed hub cap's specular highlight (a photographic/physical lighting effect, not a graphic design choice).
- **Bosch RaceCon widgets — the clearest confirmed use of gradients/glow in this entire research set:** the "Classic" style elements (Box, Bargraph, Gauge) all use a **visible radial/linear gradient** (dark navy-blue at the edges lightening toward the center or bottom), giving a deliberate soft-glow/backlit look; the "Modern" style elements use flatter, more saturated cyan/blue fills with less gradient but still show soft edge blending on the progress arcs. I saw **no drop-shadow or bloom effects** (no blurred halo around bright elements) in any of the rendered screenshots — flagged as "absence confirmed within the samples inspected," not an exhaustive claim across every RaceCon theme.
