## 1. Stack ST8100/ST700/ST8130 — actual verified screen layout

Confirmed via the 2004 manual's own diagrams (reproduced faithfully across every ST8100/ST8130 unit still sold) and current photography in Stack's 2011 catalog:

- **Housing shape:** a single molded carbon-composite panel, asymmetric rounded "shield/wedge" silhouette (not a rectangle or circle) — wider at the bottom-left, tapering to a curved top edge.
- **Overall module size:** **190mm × 97mm (7.48 in × 3.82 in)** — confirmed both in the manual's dashboard cut-out template and by Summit Racing/Pegasus/Demon Tweeks listings.
- **Top ⅔ of the panel:** analogue needle tachometer, semicircular scale (~230–270°), numerals 1–8, 1–10, etc. depending on RPM range variant (7 dial-face range options are sold), major tick at each numeral with several minor ticks between.
- **Two built-in warning lights** flank the tachometer near its upper corners (confirmed explicitly in the manual text: *"The Display Module has two built-in warning lights"*): one is the **amber Alarm light** (shown "lit" as a sun-burst icon in the manual, left side), the other is the **Gear-shift warning light** (right side). Both are simple round telltale lamps set into the black fascia, not a bar or arc.
- **Bottom ⅓ of the panel:** a rectangular **2-line, ~20-character dot-matrix LCD** (transflective, backlit — Stack's copy: *"Contrast improves when under bright illumination — clearly visible in bright sunlight"*). It is a genuine character/segment LCD, not a bitmap graphic panel — **no pixel "resolution" spec exists for it** because it isn't a raster display (this is a real difference vs. the Bosch DDU family below).
- **LCD backlight color:** yellow-green/amber (confirmed in multiple official product photos), with dark segmented-look digits.
- **Right of the LCD:** the "STACK / STACK / STACK" triple-stacked wordmark logo (echo/perspective effect), rendered in red on the physical product and in black/grey on print collateral.
- **Bezel:** no separate ring bezel — the tach dial and LCD are inset flush into the same molded **black composite panel** (unlike the standalone 80mm gauges, see below, which do have a distinct bezel ring).
- **Needle color:** varies by SKU — white needle observed on 0–10 RPM range units, **orange needle** observed on the ST8130 street-dash variant. Not a single fixed color across the family.
- **Dial-face options table** (from the catalog) lists 12 RPM-range options per model plus **"Inverted Dial Face"** variants as a cost option — I could not verify exactly what "inverted" changes (mirrored numeral direction vs. mirrored layout) — **flagged as unverified**.
- **Redline marking:** I could **not find any colored redline arc/zone printed on the tach face** in either the manual's line diagrams or the product photography I could inspect — flagged as unverified/possibly absent on this family (contrast with ST200 below, which is marketed with redline capability via its Pro-Control alarm feature, not a printed zone).

Sources: pegasusautoracing.com/pdfs/ST8100.pdf; images.carid.com/stack/items/pdf/stack-product-catalog.pdf; stackltd.com/st8100.html; stackltd.com/streetdash1.html; summitracing.com (ST8100/ST8130 listings); merlinmotorsport.co.uk (ST8100 listing, page blocked for direct fetch, used search snippet only).

---

## 2. Classic analogue gauge face conventions — Stack (52mm/80mm aux gauges, ST200, ST700 tach) vs VDO (Cockpit/Vision/Viewline)

I obtained and visually inspected actual product photography for both brands (not just marketing copy).

### Stack

- **Tick treatment:** major tick at every numeral, ~1 minor tick between majors on 52mm gauges (e.g., 0–7 Oil Pressure); ~4–5 minor ticks per major on the larger 80mm ST700 tachometer.
- **Numeral placement:** inside the tick ring (numerals sit inboard, ticks radiate outward to the rim) — upright, not rotated to follow the arc.
- **Face color:** black is standard across all ranges; **white and silver are optional** dial-face finishes on "selected gauges" (2011 catalog: *"White & Silver dial face options on selected gauges"*).
- **Needle color pairing:** **white needle on black face; orange needle on white/silver face** — confirmed both in text and in photos.
- **Needle shape:** thin, tapering to a point at the tip; no visible counterweight tail extending past the pivot in any Stack photo I inspected.
- **Hub/pivot cap:** small dark circular cap, unobtrusive (much smaller than VDO's, see below).
- **Bezel:** **plain black** ring on the 52mm/small auxiliary gauges (confirmed across Pro-Control, Electric, and Mechanical ranges — all listed only in "BLACK"). The larger 80mm ST700 tachometer's official hero photo shows a **bright/reflective chrome-look bezel** — but catalog thumbnails of what appears to be the same model show a plain black bezel. **I could not fully resolve this discrepancy** — it may be gloss-black plastic photographed under specular studio lighting rather than true chrome plate. Flagged as unverified.
- **Sweep angle:** explicitly stated — **270° sweep** for Pro-Control/stepper-motor and mechanical (Bourdon-tube) gauges; **90° sweep** for the cheaper "Electric Analogue" air-core range.
- **Alarm rendering (Pro-Control series):** a genuinely distinctive Stack feature — **the entire dial face backlight changes color** when a min/max alarm threshold is exceeded (7 selectable colors: white, red, yellow, green, blue, purple, turquoise), rather than a separate warning lamp.
- **Brand mark:** small "STACK/STACK/STACK" triple-stack logo printed near the 6 o'clock position on most dial faces.
- Numbers on ST200 specifically (from spec/retail pages, not photographed directly): 80mm diameter, IP67 sealed, stepper-motor movement; I could **not** obtain a clean, high-resolution photo of the ST200 dial itself (only the 52mm Pro-Control and 80mm ST700 families) — its tick/numeral geometry is presumed similar to the ST700 family shown above based on shared design language, but this is an **inference, not a direct observation, and should be flagged as such**.

### VDO

I inspected four real product photos directly (VDO Cockpit/Vision 80mm tachometer; two VDO Viewline units).

**VDO Cockpit / Vision (classic, e.g. 80mm tachometer, RPM×1000 0–10):**
- Face: matte **black**.
- Bezel: **plain, thin, flat black** ring (Vehiclecontrols.com's own copy calls it a **"peaked black" bezel** — no chrome option in this classic line).
- Numerals: **white**, bold condensed sans-serif, placed **inside** the tick ring, upright.
- Ticks: bold major tick at each numeral (0–10), with what appears to be **4 minor ticks per major interval** (i.e., graduated every ~200 rpm on the example photographed) — counted directly from product photography.
- Needle: **red**, thin, slight taper to a point, no counterweight tail past the pivot; VDO's own retailer copy independently confirms **"fire red/orange" pointers** on Cockpit-series gauges.
- Hub/pivot cap: a comparatively **large, glossy black domed cap** at the center — proportionally bigger than Stack's equivalent, and a recurring VDO signature.
- "RPM x 1000" and "VDO" wordmark printed in white in the same condensed font family, "VDO" logotype at the 6 o'clock position.
- Lighting: VDO's own copy distinguishes **Vision as "backlit with light coming through the numbers, fiber-optic needle"** vs **Cockpit as "side-lit"** — I could not independently visually verify this lighting-method distinction, only relay the manufacturer/retailer claim (flagged as sourced-but-unverified by direct inspection).

**VDO Viewline (modern):**
- Bezel: markedly **thicker, rounded/domed black bezel** with a soft "donut" cross-section — a visibly chunkier, more three-dimensional profile than the flat Cockpit/Vision bezel. A composite catalog thumbnail also shows **chrome/silver-bezel Viewline variants** alongside black-bezel ones, matching VDO's own marketing copy: *"three attractive designs in black, white, and chrome."*
- Two color schemes confirmed directly from product photos:
  - **"Onyx"** = black face + **white** needle + white numerals/ticks.
  - **"Ivory"** = white/cream face + **red** needle + black numerals/ticks.
  (Needle color pairs with face color, same pattern logic as Stack, but the specific colors used differ.)
- Hub/pivot cap: **very large, glossy, domed black cap** with a visible specular highlight — an even more pronounced version of the Cockpit/Vision hub, and the strongest single "VDO-look" identifier across both sub-lines.
- **Distinctive Viewline-only features not present on classic Cockpit/Vision:** an integrated **amber/yellow LCD sub-display window** (small rounded-rectangle segment-LCD, e.g. a 6-digit odometer) set into the lower half of the dial face, and a **red warning-triangle icon** printed directly on the face below the hub that illuminates for alarms.
- Ticks: major tick at each numeral, ~1 minor tick between majors (half-graduations) on the units photographed.
- "VDO" wordmark at 6 o'clock, same condensed white/black lettering depending on face color.

**Typeface:** No official VDO typeface name could be confirmed from any source. The one concrete data point I found is a **VW/Porsche forum consensus (914World.com, VWVortex.com) that "Arial Black" is the closest common font match**, specifically citing the shape of VDO's numeral "1" (a small flag/tail at the top-left) as the distinguishing tell. This is a **community approximation, not a manufacturer-confirmed fact** — flagged accordingly. Visually (from the photos I inspected) the numerals are a bold, geometric, condensed grotesque sans-serif with tabular (uniform-width) figures and minimal stroke contrast — consistent with, but not proof of, the Arial-Black-family claim.

Sources: races-shop.com (VDO Cockpit/Vision 80mm tacho + image); merlinmotorsport.co.uk VDO listing + image; vehiclecontrols.com/OurProducts/VDOInstruments/Cockpit.aspx; vehiclecontrols.com/shopping/shop700/images/A2C53194774-S.jpg (Viewline Onyx); .../A2C53210844-S.jpg (Viewline Ivory); gaugesvdo.com Viewline category page; vwvortex.com "VDO Vision vs Cockpit" thread; 914world.com gauge-font thread.

---

## 3. Bosch Motorsport DDU — display layout, alarms, shift lights (verified via official manuals, not marketing pages)

I obtained and fully extracted (text + rendered screenshot images) the **official DDU8 manual (162 pp.)** and **DDU11 manual (204 pp.)**, plus official datasheets for DDU7, DDU9, DDU10, DDU11.

### Hardware specs (all confirmed from primary datasheets)

| Model | Screen | Resolution | Shift/warning LEDs | Size (mm) | Weight | IP rating |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DDU 7 | 5.7" trans-reflective color | 640×480 | 10 RGB (top row) | 148×126×32 | 440g | IP54 |
| DDU 8 | 5" full-color TFT | 800×480 | 10 RGB (top row) | 161×111×31(49) | 675g | (not stated) |
| DDU 9 | 5.7" trans-reflective color | 640×480 | 10 RGB (top row) | 151×126×33.5 | 540g | IP54 |
| DDU 10 | 7" full-color | 800×480 | 20 RGB (10 top + 5 per side) | 198×134×35 | 875g (product page) / 930g (official datasheet — **discrepancy, flagged**) | IP67 |
| DDU 11 | 6.5" full-color | 800×480 | 18 RGB (8 top + 5 per side) | 203×128×38.5 | 649g | IP67 |

### Physical LED placement (from the actual DDU8 manual's own RaceCon device-mockup screenshots)

The shift-light LEDs are **physical LEDs embedded in the housing directly above the screen**, not on-screen graphics — confirmed by seeing the exact rendered unit in RaceCon's device view: a row of ~10 round LEDs sits in a strip across the top edge of the black housing, with the screen below it, and a "DDU 8 · Motorsport" + Bosch-logo badge strip below the screen. Starting with DDU10/11, Bosch added **additional LEDs on the left and right edges of the housing** (5+5), not just the top.

**Default/example color pattern** (from the DDU8 manual's shift-light configuration screenshot, RPM-threshold table): left-to-right the 10 LEDs are grouped roughly **green → green → green → green → yellow → orange → orange → red → red** (I counted this directly from the screenshot; exact per-color boundaries are user-configurable per RPM/gear, so this is Bosch's own example/default pattern, not a fixed spec — my exact count of the compressed screenshot image has some uncertainty, **flagged**).

### Page-layout model: there is NO single fixed "factory" RPM-bar/gear/alarm layout

This is an important and precise finding: **Bosch ships the DDU as a blank canvas.** RaceCon (the configuration tool) provides a **"Display Elements" toolbox** that teams drag onto up to 12 (DDU7/8/9/10) or 48 (DDU11, 12 pages × 4 switchable sets) pages. There is no default RPM-bar-at-top/gear-in-center template baked into the hardware — DTM/WEC/GT3 teams design their own page layouts per car/driver.

**Confirmed primitive catalog** (with visual appearance directly rendered from the manuals):

- **DDU 7/8/9 (older engine):** Large/Medium **Numeric** boxes, **Bargraph** (horizontal/vertical, "Solid" or "Stacked"-segment color), **Alarm** (text) / **Alarm Icon**, **Label**, **Picture**. **No needle-gauge widget exists on this generation** — confirmed by the DDU8 manual's own element list, which omits any gauge/dial primitive.
- **DDU 10/11 (newer "display element design generator," introduced with DDU10):** adds a full parallel "Classic" and "Modern" styled catalog — **Classic Box, Classic horizontal/vertical Bar, Classic Gauge Large/Small, Modern Box, Modern horizontal/vertical Bar, Modern Gauge Large/Small, Basic Box, Value/Text, Enumeration, Image, Alarm/Alarm Icon.**

I rendered the manual's own catalog illustrations directly and can describe them precisely:
- **"Classic Gauge"**: a simulated analogue dial — **bright chrome/brushed-metal bezel ring** (beveled, specular highlight), **radial blue gradient face** (dark navy outer → lighter center), **white tick marks** (bold major at each numeral, thin minor between), **numerals outside the tick marks**, and a **red, wedge-shaped needle** (wide at the hub, tapering to a point at the tip, no counterweight tail past the pivot). The center hosts a large flat lighter-blue disc reserved for an overlaid digital value. Conditional formatting can recolor the tick arc (e.g., for a redline band).
- **"Modern Gauge"**: **no bezel at all** — flat black background, a **thick cyan/blue radial progress-arc** (donut-style fill, not a needle) with a short white tick marking current value, small unlabeled tick dashes around the rim, and a **large digital numeral in the center** instead of a needle+dial reading.
- **"Classic/Modern Box" and "Bargraph"**: flat dark-navy-to-black gradient backgrounds, cyan/light-blue segmented fill bars (discrete rectangular LED-like blocks, not a smooth fill — the currently-filled segment nearest the value is rendered in a lighter/white shade), white channel-name label at top, large white numeral bottom-right.

### Alarms
Alarms are a dedicated element type (not just a colored box): **defined in one of 4 fixed screen areas**, available in "Classic" or "Modern" **style** (matching the box/gauge aesthetic), **non-transparent background**, **always rendered on top of every other element** (highest z-order), and if multiple alarms in the same area are active simultaneously **each is shown for ~1.5–2 seconds** in rotation. Alarms can show text, an icon, or a value, and support blink modes, minimum display time, and auto-reset.

### RaceCon / configuration tool
RaceCon is confirmed as the single tool across all DDU generations — Ethernet or MSA-Box II connection, drag-and-drop element placement, per-element Wizard dialogs for font size/alignment/border/background/foreground color, and (DDU10/11) an "ambient light sensor" for auto-brightness and a "state-of-the-art user interface menu" for in-car page/reset control without a laptop.

### Typography
Bosch's manual discloses that the **Graphic Engine uses the open-source FreeType library "for non-bitmap font rendering"** (explicit license text found in the DDU11 manual) — **no specific named commercial typeface is disclosed anywhere in the manuals**. Visually (from the rendered numeric-element screenshots), the digits are a **blocky, monospaced, tabular-figure "digital" style** — uniform stroke width, slightly rounded corners, reminiscent of a seven-segment display but not a true segmented glyph — used consistently across Numeric, Box, and Gauge elements.

Sources: bosch-motorsport.com/media/downloads/display_ddu_8.pdf (full manual, primary); bosch-motorsport.com/media/downloads/display_ddu_7.pdf and display_ddu_7_manual.pdf; bosch-motorsport.com/media/downloads/ddu_9_datasheet.pdf; xtreme-di.com Display_DDU_10_Datasheet PDF; bosch-motorsport.com/media/catalog_content/.../data_sheet_..._display_ddu_11.pdf and operation_manual_..._display_ddu_11.pdf (full manual, primary); bosch-motorsport.com/products/displays/display-ddu-10/.

---

## 4. Cross-brand: needle design

- **Stack (52/80mm aux + ST700):** thin, point-tapered needle, no counterweight tail past pivot, small unobtrusive hub cap; color pairs with face (white-on-black / orange-on-white).
- **VDO (Cockpit/Vision/Viewline):** broader, wedge-shaped needle (wider mid-section, tapering to a point), no counterweight tail past pivot; **large, glossy, domed black hub cap** is the most consistent VDO signature across both sub-lines; color pairs with face (white-on-black or red-on-white/black depending on sub-line).
- **Bosch (RaceCon "Classic Gauge" simulated needle only — DDU10/11):** red, wide-at-hub/tapering-to-point wedge needle, no counterweight tail. Not a physical needle — a rendered graphic. DDU7/8/9 have **no needle widget at all**.
- **Common thread:** none of the three brands' needles show a counterweight extending past the pivot in any sample I inspected — all are "one-directional" pointer shapes.

## 5. Cross-brand: bezel

- **Stack:** plain black bezel on small/auxiliary gauges (confirmed, no chrome option marketed); the large ST700 tach's hero photo shows a bright/chrome-look ring (unverified whether true chrome or glossy black under studio lighting); **the digital-dash family (ST8100/8130/8150) has no separate bezel at all** — the dial is inset flush into the same molded black composite panel.
- **VDO:** Cockpit/Vision = thin, flat, plain black ("peaked black") bezel, no chrome variant found. Viewline = thicker, rounded/domed black bezel as one option, with chrome and white-painted bezel variants also marketed (per VDO's own "black, white, and chrome" copy) — genuinely offers a chrome option, unlike Cockpit/Vision.
- **Bosch:** the physical unit housing has **no bezel concept at all** around the screen (it's a single flat TFT behind glass in a rectangular housing). On-screen, the RaceCon "Classic Gauge" widget **simulates** a chrome bezel purely as a rendered graphic; the "Modern Gauge" widget deliberately has **no bezel simulation** — flat black background only. This directly answers the brief's question of whether digital dashes simulate bezels: **yes, Bosch's DDU10/11 explicitly offer a chrome-bezel-simulating "Classic" gauge skin as a user choice, alongside a bezel-less "Modern" skin.**

## 6. Cross-brand: typography

- **Stack:** dot-matrix/segment LCD font (character display, not bitmap graphics) on the dash family; bold condensed sans-serif printed numerals on the analogue dial faces.
- **VDO:** bold, condensed, geometric grotesque sans-serif with tabular figures; no confirmed official name — community approximation is "Arial Black," based on the numeral "1" shape (unverified beyond forum consensus).
- **Bosch:** FreeType-rendered (open-source rendering library, confirmed in manual's license text; no named typeface disclosed); visually a blocky, monospaced, tabular "digital" numeral style across all display elements.

## 7. Cross-brand: gradients / glow / drop shadows / bloom

- **Stack:** flat, unlit product photography shows flat black faces with no gradient rendering (these are physical printed dial faces, not screens) — LCD screens show a flat yellow-green backlight wash, no glow/bloom effects visible in photos.
- **VDO:** flat matte or glossy physical dial faces; the one rendering nuance is the domed hub cap's specular highlight (a photographic/physical lighting effect, not a graphic design choice).
- **Bosch RaceCon widgets — the clearest confirmed use of gradients/glow in this entire research set:** the "Classic" style elements (Box, Bargraph, Gauge) all use a **visible radial/linear gradient** (dark navy-blue at the edges lightening toward the center or bottom), giving a deliberate soft-glow/backlit look; the "Modern" style elements use flatter, more saturated cyan/blue fills with less gradient but still show soft edge blending on the progress arcs. I saw **no drop-shadow or bloom effects** (no blurred halo around bright elements) in any of the rendered screenshots — flagged as "absence confirmed within the samples inspected," not an exhaustive claim across every RaceCon theme.

---

## Explicit list of things I could NOT verify

1. Whether the Stack ST700's chrome-look bezel is genuinely chrome-plated or glossy black under studio lighting (conflicting evidence between hero photo and catalog thumbnails of the same model).
2. Exact tick-subdivision count and dial geometry for the **ST200** specifically — I could not obtain a clean, high-resolution photo of an ST200 dial face itself; my description of Stack's small-gauge conventions is generalized from the 52mm Pro-Control range and 80mm ST700, not the ST200 directly.
3. VDO's actual production typeface name — only a forum/community approximation ("Arial Black") exists; no manufacturer confirmation found.
4. VDO's claimed Vision (through-dial/fiber-optic) vs Cockpit (side-lit) lighting-method distinction — this is retailer/manufacturer copy I could not independently confirm by inspection.
5. DDU10 weight: 875g (gomuchfaster.com product page) vs 930g (Bosch's own datasheet PDF) — unresolved discrepancy; the datasheet figure should be treated as authoritative.
6. Exact per-color LED boundary count in the DDU8 shift-light "default" pattern (I counted ~4 green/1 yellow/2 orange/2 red from a compressed screenshot — approximate, not a spec value, since the whole point of the feature is per-team configurability).
7. Whether Stack's "Inverted Dial Face" option means mirrored numeral direction, mirrored panel layout, or something else — undocumented in the sources I could reach.
8. Whether a printed redline zone/arc exists on the ST8100/ST700/ST8130 analogue tach face — not found in any diagram or photo I could inspect.
9. My WebSearch quota was exhausted partway through (after ~14 searches), so remaining research relied on WebFetch/curl on already-known or guessed URLs — some leads (e.g., a native-resolution ST200 photo, the VDO Viewline marine PDF brochure which 404'd) could not be pursued further.

---

## Sources actually used

**Stack:** pegasusautoracing.com/pdfs/ST8100.pdf (full manual, primary) · images.carid.com/stack/items/pdf/stack-product-catalog.pdf (2011 catalog, primary, all 7 pages inspected) · stackltd.com/st8100.html · stackltd.com/st200.html · stackltd.com/streetdash1.html · summitracing.com (ST8100-038/-C/-I/-B/-E-EC, ST8130-F/-A-EC/-P-EC/-08, ST200-010W/-04105W/-08W listings) · manualslib.com/manual/2203216/Stack-St8100.html (blocked, snippet only) · merlinmotorsport.co.uk (ST8100 listing, blocked for direct fetch) · demon-tweeks.com (blocked, snippet only) · en.oreca-store.com (blocked, snippet only) · performanceparts.com (ST200-0615W, ST200C-012) · ebay.com (ST200 listing) · rallystore.net · behrents.com · pegasusautoracing.com/pdfs/ST700.pdf (referenced, not deep-read) · manualslib.com/manual/1275068/Stack-St700.html.

**VDO:** races-shop.com/vdo-cockpit-vision-gauges/45503-... (+ product image) · merlinmotorsport.co.uk VDO Cockpit/Vision category (+ image) · vehiclecontrols.com/OurProducts/VDOInstruments/Cockpit.aspx · vehiclecontrols.com/shopping/shop700/Viewline2.png, .../images/A2C53194774-S.jpg, .../images/A2C53210844-S.jpg · gaugesvdo.com/products/c1219-vdo-viewline-marine-gauges/ · gaugesvdo.com/products/c935-vdo-viewline/ · aftermarketnews.com VDO Cockpit International GEN II article · vwvortex.com/threads/vdo-vision-vs-vdo-cockpit-boost-gauge.672840/ · vwvortex.com "Show Me Gauge Fonts That Look Dope" thread · 914world.com gauge-font thread · vdo.com marine Viewline brochure PDF (404, unusable) · acdcmarineinc.com Viewline product (blocked/empty response).

**Bosch:** bosch-motorsport.com/media/downloads/display_ddu_8.pdf (full 162-page manual, primary, text + rendered screenshots) · bosch-motorsport.com/media/downloads/display_ddu_7.pdf and display_ddu_7_manual.pdf · bosch-motorsport.com/media/downloads/ddu_9_datasheet.pdf · xtreme-di.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Display_DDU_10_Datasheet_51_en_29594642827.pdf · bosch-motorsport.com/media/catalog_content/downloads_catalog/pdf_catalog/data_sheet_323420299_display_ddu_11.pdf and operation_manual_323436043_display_ddu_11.pdf (full 204-page manual, primary, text + rendered screenshots) · bosch-motorsport.com/products/displays/display-ddu-10/ · bosch-motorsport.com/products/displays/ · manualslib.com DDU7/8/10 manual pages (blocked, snippets only) · xtramotorsport.com DDU10/DDU11 product pages (mostly blocked) · gomuchfaster.com DDU8/DDU10 listings · saxon-motorsport.co.uk, symprojects.com, poweron.shop, webshop.swindonpowertrain.com (DDU listings, snippet-level only).

Terminado. El panel está corriendo en **http://127.0.0.1:8036**.

## Cuatro pestañas

**Tablero** — tacómetro, refrigerante y carga como instrumentos analógicos reales: barrido de 270° arrancando abajo a la izquierda como los BMW, marcas mayores y menores, zona roja, y readout digital debajo del arco. Batería y aire van en barras segmentadas, como el indicador de temperatura del E36. Abajo, una fila de testigos que solo se encienden con el motor girando — un auto parado no debería estar gritando alarmas.

**Diagnóstico** — memoria de fallas decodificada, sonda DS2 para el EGS, y **comparación de snapshots que corre sola**: elegís dos y te dice qué contador subió. Ese es el método para probar que el código 73 vuelve a ocurrir justo cuando la caja falla, sin depender de la tasa de muestreo.

**Capturas** — métricas derivadas de cada sesión (ralentí medio 903 rpm, estabilidad ±30, tasa real **0,73 Hz** — el problema de muestreo ahora está medido y a la vista), un cursor único que recorre los cinco canales a la vez, y superposición de dos sesiones para comparar.

**Scanner** — el explorador de RAM, que es lo que puede desbloquear el diagnóstico. Acumula por byte cuántas veces cambió y entre qué valores osciló, y lista los candidatos ordenados por recorrido. Con el motor en marcha: Vigilar, pisar el acelerador, y el byte con mayor rango es el TPS.

## Tus cuatro decisiones, implementadas

**Escritura:** borrar códigos sí, con confirmación, y **siempre guarda un snapshot automático antes** — los contadores son la única evidencia y no se recuperan. Actuadores y escritura de RAM/EEPROM bloqueados **en el servidor**, no escondidos en la UI.

**Red:** `--lan` liga a 0.0.0.0 y genera un token comparado en tiempo constante.

**Datos:** archivos sueltos, sin base.

## Qué verifiqué de verdad

- Auth: sin token 403, token malo 403, token bueno 200, POST sin token 403
- Path traversal a `/etc/passwd` → rechazado
- **Guard de escritura probado con un ECU falso**: `0x02`, `0x1A` y `0x04` nunca llegan al bus; `0x00`, `0x01`, `0x07` sí pasan
- Acumulación de cambios de RAM probada en aislamiento: lecturas repetidas no cuentan, un cambio real da rango correcto
- Hot-plug del cable probado con un finder simulado
- Sintaxis Python y JS, las cuatro pestañas renderizadas

Agregué un **`--demo`** con datos sintéticos plausibles, que es como pude verificar todo esto sin el auto. También sirve para mostrar el panel sin tenerlo al lado.

## Tres cosas honestas

**Arreglé un defecto que te habría mordido:** arrancaba sin cable y desactivaba el modo vivo para siempre. Ahora reintenta y **conecta solo cuando lo enchufes**.

**Borré un snapshot de prueba** que había creado para verificar la comparación. Era dato inventado y no podía quedar mezclado con tus lecturas reales.

**Los dos agentes de investigación nunca volvieron** — construí con lo que ya sabíamos. Si aparecen, veo si traen algo que valga incorporar.

Nada de esto toca el diagnóstico real: el código 36 sigue presente, el 73 esporádico, y el EGS sin leer hasta que corras la sonda DS2 con el contacto puesto.

## 1. What exactly does it emulate, and how does a client connect?

It emulates the **ELM327 AT command set** + the **OBD-II service/PID layer** (SAE J1979 / ISO 15031) sitting on top of **ISO-TP (ISO 15765-2, 11-bit CAN)** and **KWP2000 (ISO 14230)** transports, with optional **UDS (ISO 14229-1)** diagnostic-session/security-access/routine-control behavior. It does **not** emulate a real CAN bus electrically — it's a byte-stream emulator that answers whatever an ELM327 adapter would answer, over one of these transports:

| Interface | Flag | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pseudo-terminal (pty) | *(default on Linux/macOS)* | `pty.openpty()` → prints a path like `/dev/pts/3`; this is the default, no flag needed |
| TCP/IP socket | `-n <port>` | Plain TCP server (`socket.socket(... SOCK_STREAM)`), for WiFi-ELM327-style clients (Torque, OBD Auto Doctor WiFi mode, raw `telnet`) |
| Serial COM port | `-p <PORT>` | Opens a real/virtual COM port via **pySerial**; on Windows this is meant to pair with **com0com** (null-modem emulator) |
| Arbitrary device node | `-P <DEVICE_PORT>` | `os.open(device, os.O_RDWR|os.O_NOCTTY|os.O_SYNC)` — used for Bluetooth RFCOMM devices (`/dev/rfcomm0`) |
| Bluetooth | via `-P` | Documented recipe: `rfcomm watch /dev/rfcomm0 1 python3 -m elm -P /dev/rfcomm0 -l -s car` |

Source (`elm/elm.py`) confirms the pty mechanics exactly:
```python
if os.name == 'nt':
    self.slave_fd = None
    return None
else:
    if not self.device_port and not self.serial_port:
        self.master_fd, self.slave_fd = pty.openpty()
        tty.setraw(self.slave_fd)
        self.slave_name = os.ttyname(self.slave_fd)
```

**Connecting a client (python-OBD):**
```shell
# terminal 1
python3 -m elm -s car
# → prints something like: /dev/pts/3
```
```python
# terminal 2 / your dashboard code
import obd
connection = obd.OBD("/dev/pts/3")   # or a real COM port on Windows
```

**Important caveat found in python-OBD's own docs** ([python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Connections](https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Connections/)): `obd.OBD(portstr=...)` is documented only as *"The UNIX device file or Windows COM Port for your adapter"* — there is **no documented `socket://` / TCP URL support**. So for **python-OBD specifically**, use the default pty/serial mode, not `-n`. The `-n` TCP mode is for other tools (OBD Auto Doctor's WiFi option, Torque, raw `telnet localhost 35000`) or your own socket client — not a native python-OBD target.

Also confirmed: **Ircama also publishes his own fork of python-OBD** at [github.com/Ircama/python-OBD](https://github.com/Ircama/python-OBD) — but its README states it's forked from the older `peterh/pyobd` / `Pbartek/pyobd-pi` lineage, installs as package `obd`, and does **not** mention ELM327-emulator, sockets, or TCP anywhere. Just use the standard `pip install obd` (python-OBD) — no special fork is required.

## 3. Scenarios — the ObdMessage dictionary structure

A **scenario** is just a named `dict` of PID-name → definition-dict, nested one level under a module-level `ObdMessage = {...}` dict in `elm/obd_message.py`. I parsed this file directly with Python (`exec()`'d it into an isolated namespace) to get ground truth rather than trusting a text summary:

```
ObdMessage = {
  'AT'        : { ... 68 entries ... }   # AT/ST commands
  'engineoff' : { ... 4 entries ... }    # ignition-off simulation
  'default'   : { ... 53 entries ... }   # generic baseline PIDs
  'car'       : { ... 246 entries ... }  # Toyota Auris Hybrid (CAN 500kbps)
  'mt05'      : { ... 25 entries ... }   # Delphi MT05 motorcycle/ATV ECU
}
```
**There is no `'test'` scenario** — that part of the brief's premise doesn't hold.

**How scenario selection actually merges dictionaries** (`elm/elm.py::set_sorted_obd_msg`), verbatim:
```python
if 'default' in self.ObdMessage and 'AT' in self.ObdMessage:
    self.sortedOBDMsg = {
        **self.ObdMessage['default'],   # highest priority
        **self.ObdMessage['AT'],
        **self.ObdMessage[self.scenario]
        # lowest priority ('Priority' to be checked)
    }
else:
    self.sortedOBDMsg = {**self.ObdMessage[self.scenario]}
self.sortedOBDMsg = sorted(
    self.sortedOBDMsg.items(),
    key=lambda x: x[1]['Priority'] if 'Priority' in x[1] else 10)
```
So running `scenario car` actually gets you `default` ∪ `AT` ∪ `car`, with `car`'s own definitions of any duplicate key (e.g. `RPM`) winning because Python dict-unpacking lets the last dict's keys overwrite earlier ones. Separately, **every entry's regex `Request` pattern is then tried in order of a numeric `'Priority'` field** (1 = highest priority / tried first, default 10 if unset) — this is how ambiguous/overlapping regexes get disambiguated (e.g. `engineoff`'s catch-all `NO_DATA` pattern `^[0-9][0-9][0-9A-F]+$` has `Priority: 6` so specific matches are tried before it).

### Concrete ObdMessage entry, field by field

Exact `RPM` entry under `'default'` (dynamic, sweeping):
```python
'RPM': {
    'Request': '^010C[0123456]?$',
    'Descr': 'Engine RPM',
    'ResponseFooter': lambda self, cmd, pid, uc_val: (
        PA(self.sequence(pid, base=2400, max=200, factor=80, n_bytes=2))
        + ' ' + HD(ECU_R_ADDR_H) + SZ('04') + DT('41 0C '
        + self.sequence(pid, base=2400, max=200, factor=80, n_bytes=2))
    )
}
```
Same PID under `'car'` (static rotating list of 14 real-looking frames instead):
```python
'RPM': {
    'Request': '^010C[0123456]?$',
    'Descr': 'Engine RPM',
    'Header': '7E0',
    'Response': [
        '<header>7E8</header><size>04</size><data>41 0C 14 5F</data>',
        '<header>7E8</header><size>04</size><data>41 0C 00 00</data>',
        '<header>7E8</header><size>04</size><data>41 0C 41 C2</data>',
        # ... 11 more frames, roughly 0–4200 rpm
    ]
}
```

**Field meanings** (cross-referenced against `elm/elm.py`'s request-matching loop, which does `uc_val = {k.upper(): v for k, v in val.items()}` then checks `'REQUEST'`, `'HEADER'`, `'ACTION'`, `'DESCR'`, `'EXEC'`, `'INFO'`/`'WARNING'`/`'LOG'`, `'RESPONSE'`/`'RESPONSEHEADER'`/`'RESPONSEFOOTER'`, `'PRIORITY'`, `'TASK'`):

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Request` | regex the incoming (unspaced, uppercased) command must match |
| `Descr` | human description (logged at DEBUG) |
| `Response` | static answer string, **or a list/tuple** of alternative answer strings (cycled/randomized via `choice`) |
| `ResponseHeader` / `ResponseFooter` | `lambda self, cmd, pid, uc_val: ...` computed at request time, prepended/appended to `Response` |
| `Header` | required CAN/K-line header (e.g. `"7E0"`) — request only matches if it equals the client's currently-set `ATSH` header (multi-ECU gate, see §7) |
| `Action` | `'skip'` → entry is ignored entirely (falls through to next candidate) |
| `Exec` | a Python statement string, executed via `exec()` against the request |
| `Log` / `Info` / `Warning` | Python expression strings fed to `logging.debug/info/warning` |
| `Priority` | match-order weight, 1 (tried first) .. 10 (default, tried last) |
| `Task` | name of a plugin module in `elm/plugins/` (see §6) that generates the answer programmatically instead of a static `Response` |

There is **no literal `'Pid'` or `'Cmd'` key** in the real dictionary — the dict key itself (e.g. `'RPM'`) *is* the PID label; I did not find a separate `'Pid'`/`'Cmd'` field anywhere in the 396-entry union I inspected, so that part of the brief's guess doesn't match the real schema.

### Response templating tags

`handle_response()` in `elm/elm.py` literally parses the response string **as XML** — `fromstring('<xml>' + resp + '</xml>')` — then walks child tags:

```python
elif i.tag.lower() == 'writeln':  answ += (i.text or "") + nl
elif i.tag.lower() == 'space':    answ += (i.text or "") + sp
elif i.tag.lower() in ('eval','exec'):
    ... evalmsg = eval(msg)              # tries eval() first
    ... exec(msg, globals())             # falls back to exec()
elif i.tag.lower() == 'flow':      answ += self.uds_answer(..., is_flow_control='30')
elif i.tag.lower() == 'answer':    answ += self.uds_answer(...)
elif i.tag.lower() in ('pos_answer','neg_answer'): ...   # builds UDS SID+0x40 / 0x7F NRC
elif i.tag.lower() == 'header':    size = next(s); data = next(s)  # <header><size><data>
```
This explains the classic `ELM_PIDS_A` "SEARCHING..." trick precisely:
```python
'ResponseHeader': lambda self, cmd, pid, uc_val: \
    "<string>SEARCHING...</string>" \
    "<exec>time.sleep(1.5)</exec>" + ST('') \
        if self.counters[pid] == 1 else ''
```
Because `<exec>` (unlike `<eval>`) flushes whatever's been accumulated so far straight to the device *before* running the code, the client actually sees `SEARCHING...` appear, then a real 1.5s pause, then the PID data — mimicking a genuine ELM327's bus-search delay on first query.

### Writing and loading a custom scenario

A custom scenario is just a `.py` file in your **current working directory** defining its own `ObdMessage = {'my_scenario': {...}}` dict (same shape as above). Load it with the `merge` REPL command — exact implementation:
```python
def do_merge(self, arg):
    if len(arg.split()) == 1 and arg.split()[0] in [x[:-3] for x in glob.glob('*.py')]:
        exec('from ' + arg + ' import ObdMessage', globals())
        self.emulator.ObdMessage.update(ObdMessage)
```
So:
```shell
$ python3 -m elm
> merge mycar        # looks for ./mycar.py, imports its ObdMessage, .update()s it in
> scenario mycar
```
There is no separate `-e "extra dictionary"` CLI flag in the current source (I looked — the argparse block above is exhaustive); `merge`/`scenario` at the REPL, or `-s scenario` at launch for one of the names already present in `ObdMessage`, are the only load paths. Programmatically you can also just do `emulator.ObdMessage.update(my_dict)` via the Python API.

## 4. Replay of a real car — the `obd_dictionary` companion tool (this is the important part for you)

**Correction to the premise:** `obd_dictionary` lives at [`github.com/Ircama/ELM327-emulator/tree/master/obd_dictionary`](https://github.com/Ircama/ELM327-emulator/tree/master/obd_dictionary) — a subpackage of the same repo (`obd_dictionary/__init__.py`, 512 lines, `obd_dictionary/__main__.py`), not its own repo.

**The exact "record once, replay forever" workflow:**

```shell
# Step 1 — with a REAL ELM327 dongle plugged into the real car:
python3 -m obd_dictionary -i /dev/ttyUSB0 -o mycar.py -n mycar -p 20

# Step 2 — offline forever after, no car needed:
python3 -m elm          # console
merge mycar
scenario mycar
```
or non-interactively:
```shell
python3 -m elm -s mycar    # if mycar.py is importable / merged some other way
```

To **replace the built-in dictionary entirely** (so `-s default` becomes your car):
```shell
python3 -m obd_dictionary -i /dev/ttyUSB0 -o obd_message.py -n default -t elm/obd_message.py
```

**Mechanics, verified against the actual source** (`obd_dictionary/__init__.py`):

1. Connects via **python-OBD** exactly like your dashboard would:
   ```python
   connection = obd.OBD(portstr=args.elm327, baudrate=args.baudrate,
                         timeout=args.timeout, protocol=args.protocol,
                         check_voltage=args.no_check_voltage, fast=args.fast)
   ```
2. Iterates `connection.supported_commands` (python-OBD's auto-detected PID set) across `-p N` **probe cycles**, storing every raw response:
   ```python
   OBDData = [dict() for x in range(args.probes)]
   for i in range(args.probes):
       for cmd in connection.supported_commands:
           OBDData[i][cmd] = connection.query(cmd)
           time.sleep(args.delay_commands)
       time.sleep(args.delay)
   ```
3. For each PID, it collects the **set of distinct raw frames** seen across all probes (duplicates removed via `list(set(list_resp))`) and prints either a single `'Response': HD(...)+SZ(...)+DT(...)` string, or — if the value actually changed between probes (e.g. you ran `-p 10` while the real engine's RPM was actually moving) — a **list** of those distinct frames:
   ```python
   f_resp = ('[\n' + ',\n'.join(list_resp) + '\n]') if len(list_resp) > 1 else list_resp[0]
   ```
   and even appends the decoded physical value as a comment (`# 1234.5 rpm`) for readability.
   
   **Important nuance to be precise about**: this is *not* a timestamped chronological trace — there's no timing/ordering preserved between the captured points. What you get is "the distinct raw values observed for PID X across N probe cycles," stored as a list that the emulator's `choice` mechanism (default: `sequential`) then cycles through **once per query of that specific PID**, in the fixed order captured. It *looks* like realistic variation to a client polling PIDs repeatedly, but it is not literally replaying your drive's timeline second-by-second.

4. **`-c CSV_FILE`** imports manufacturer-specific PIDs in **Torque's CSV PID format** (8 comma-separated fields: `Name, ShortName, Request(hex), Equation, Min, Max, Unit, ECU-header-hex`), turning each row into a `CUSTOM_<NAME>` `OBDCommand` that gets probed and captured alongside standard PIDs — this is how the built-in `'car'` scenario's ~190 `CUSTOM_*` Toyota-hybrid entries (`CUSTOM_SOC`, `CUSTOM_H_BATT`, etc.) were almost certainly produced.

5. **Safety-relevant caveat I found in the source**: a hard-coded `blacklisted_pids` tuple is excluded from probing **by default** (needs `-b/--blacklist` to override), and it's not just read-only PIDs:
   ```python
   blacklisted_pids = (
       'CLEAR_DTC',
       'CUSTOM_SFS5', # "Set Battery Cooling Fan Speed 5..."
       'CUSTOM_TRAC_DIS', # "Disable Traction Control..."
       'CUSTOM_RB_ENA', # "Reverse Beep Enable..."
       'CUSTOM_SBB_ENA_P', # "Seat Belt Beep Enable Passenger Only..."
       # ... more actuator/write commands
   )
   ```
   In other words: the tool deliberately avoids sending **actuator-test/write commands** to your real car during a scan, because they'd actually change real vehicle behavior (erase real DTCs, disable traction control, etc.). Good sign of a well-thought-out tool; also a reminder to be careful if you ever pass `-b`.

6. **`-t [FILE]`**: with no filename, also probes 5 built-in ELM_* meta-commands (`ELM_IGNITION`, `ELM_DESCR`, `ELM_ID`, `ELM_DP`, `ELM_DPN`); with a filename, it *additionally* brace-matches and copies the `'AT'` scenario block verbatim out of that file into your new output — this is how `-t elm/obd_message.py` makes a self-contained replacement dictionary that still answers all the standard `AT*`/`ST*` commands.

7. Output format is literal Python source, always starting with the same boilerplate (confirmed exact string in source):
   ```python
   header = """
   def SZ(size):
       return ('<size>' + size + '</size>')
   def HD(header):
       return ('<header>' + header + '</header>')
   def DT(data):
       return ('<data>' + data + '</data>')
   def ST(writeln):
       return ('<writeln>' + writeln + '</writeln>')
   ELM_R_OK = ST("OK")
   ELM_R_UNKNOWN = ST("?")
   ELM_FOOTER = '[0123456]?$'
   """
   ```
   followed by the `ECU_ADDR_*` constant table, then `ObdMessage = {'<name>': { ...one dict entry per probed PID... }}`.

**Dry-run / sanity-check mode**, useful before you commit to a full probe:
```shell
python3 -m obd_dictionary -i /dev/ttyUSB0 -B 38400 -T 30 -r
```

**On log/trace replay and "make values change over time":** there is **no separate "replay a candump/pcap-style timestamped logfile" feature** and no literal `-l logfile` replay flag (`-l` on the main `elm` command means `--newline`, unrelated). Dynamic/time-varying behavior instead comes from three mechanisms, all confirmed in source:
- **`self.sequence(pid, base, max, factor, n_bytes)`** — a genuine formula-driven sweep, exact code:
  ```python
  def sequence(self, pid, base, max, factor, n_bytes):
      c = self.counters[pid] if pid in self.counters else 0
      p = int(factor * abs(max - (c + max) % (max * 2))) + base
      s = ("%.X" % p).zfill(n_bytes * 2)
      return " ".join(s[i:i+2] for i in range(0, len(s), 2))
  ```
  This produces a **triangle wave** (rises then falls) bounded in `[base, base+factor*max]`, advancing one step per query of that PID — this is the literal "simulate RPM sweeping" mechanism, used by `'default'`'s RPM/SPEED.
- **Rotating list + `choice`** — as described in §3/§4 above (what `obd_dictionary` produces, and what `'car'`'s RPM/SPEED lists use).
- **The `Task` plugin system** — arbitrary stateful Python (§6).

## 5. The `'car'` scenario in depth

Confirmed by directly executing the module and inspecting `ObdMessage['car']` (246 keys): it's an emulation of a **Toyota Auris Hybrid**, explicitly commented in source as *"Pids of a Toyota Auris Hybrid car (ISO 15765-4 CAN 11 bit ID 500 kbaud protocol)"*.

- **Standard PIDs**: Mode 01 (all the usual — `RPM`, `SPEED`, `COOLANT_TEMP`, `THROTTLE_POS`, `MAF`, `O2_*`, `CATALYST_TEMP_*`, `FUEL_TYPE`, `ODOMETER` (added in v3.0.5), etc.), Mode 02 freeze-frame equivalents (the `DTC_*`-prefixed keys — 40 of them, one per Mode-01 PID), Mode 06 on-board monitoring (`MIDS_*`, `MONITOR_*`), Mode 09 vehicle info.
- **Mode 03 / Mode 07 (DTCs)**:
  ```python
  'GET_DTC': {'Request': '^03[0123456]?$', 'Header': '7E0',
              'Response': '<header>7E8</header><size>02</size><data>43 00</data>'}
  'GET_CURRENT_DTC': {'Request': '^07[0123456]?$', 'Header': '7E0',
              'Response': '<header>7E8</header><size>02</size><data>47 00</data>'}
  'CLEAR_DTC': {'Request': '^14[0123456]?$', 'Header': '7E0',
              'Response': '<neg_answer>11</neg_answer>'}   # rejects the clear (NRC 0x11)
  ```
  i.e. it reports **zero stored/pending DTCs** and, interestingly, **refuses** a Mode 04 clear-DTC request with a negative UDS answer rather than accepting it.
- **Mode 09 VIN**:

## 6. The Task / plugin system

Plugin files live in `elm/plugins/`, filenames must start with `task_`, and reference a PID entry via `'Task': 'task_modulename'`. Verified base classes in `elm/elm.py`:

```python
class Tasks:
    class RETURN:
        TERMINATE = False
        CONTINUE  = True
        ERROR       = (None, TERMINATE, None)
        INCOMPLETE  = (None, CONTINUE, None)
        def PASSTHROUGH(cmd): return None, Tasks.RETURN.TERMINATE, cmd
        def TASK_CONTINUE(cmd): return None, Tasks.RETURN.CONTINUE, cmd
        def ANSWER(answer): return answer, Tasks.RETURN.TERMINATE, None

    def __init__(self, emulator, pid, header, ecu, request, attrib, do_write=False):
        self.shared = ... # per-ECU shared namespace (task_shared_ns[ecu])
        self.pid, self.header, self.request, self.attrib = pid, header, request, attrib
        self.frame, self.length = None, None            # ISO-TP multiframe counters
        self.flow_control, self.flow_control_end = 0, 0x20
        self.logging = emulator.logger
        self.time_started = time.time()

    def HD(self, header): return '<header>' + header + '</header>'
    def SZ(self, size):   return '<size>' + size + '</size>'
    def DT(self, data):   return '<data>' + data + '</data>'
    def PA(self, pos_answer): return '<pos_answer>' + pos_answer + '</pos_answer>'
    def NA(self, neg_answer): return '<neg_answer>' + neg_answer + '</neg_answer>'
    def task_get_request(self): return self.request
    def task_request_matched(self, request):
        return re.match(self.attrib['REQUEST'], request) if self.attrib else None

    def start(self, cmd, length=None, frame=None):
        return self.run(cmd, length, frame)      # default: just calls run()
    def stop(self, cmd, length=None, frame=None):
        return Tasks.RETURN.ERROR                 # default: error on interruption
    def run(self, cmd, length=None, frame=None):
        return Tasks.RETURN.PASSTHROUGH(cmd)       # default: passthrough

class EcuTasks(Tasks):        # per-ECU preprocessor, filename task_ecu_<CANID>.py
    def run(self, cmd, length=None, frame=None):
        return EcuTasks.RETURN.TASK_CONTINUE(cmd)
```
`start()`/`run()`/`stop()` each return a **3-tuple**: `(xml_answer_or_None, terminate_bool, request_to_reprocess_or_None)`.

**Minimal real example** (`elm/plugins/task_request_seed.py`, UDS Mode 27 security-access seed, full file):
```python
from elm import Tasks
import time

EXECUTION_TIME = 0.5
SEED = 'A641B5E9'

class Task(Tasks):
    def run(self, cmd, *_):
        if time.time() < self.time_started + EXECUTION_TIME:
            return (self.NA('78'), Tasks.RETURN.CONTINUE,
                    None if self.task_request_matched(cmd) else cmd)
        else:
            seed_bytes = " ".join(SEED[i:i+2] for i in range(0, len(SEED), 2))
            return (self.PA(seed_bytes), Tasks.RETURN.TERMINATE,
                    None if self.task_request_matched(cmd) else cmd)
```
This is the canonical **state machine pattern** used across every UDS plugin in the repo (`task_hardware_reset.py`, `task_erase_memory.py`, `task_erase_mem_result.py`, `task_mt05_*`, all identical in shape): return NRC `0x78` ("requestCorrectlyReceived-ResponsePending") repeatedly while the client keeps re-polling the same request and `EXECUTION_TIME` hasn't elapsed yet, then flip to a positive answer and `TERMINATE`. That's a faithful simulation of a real ECU doing a slow flash-erase/reset/routine and making the tester wait.

**Shared state across requests**: `self.ns` is the per-task-instance namespace; `self.shared` is the **per-ECU namespace** shared by *all* tasks/requests addressed to that ECU (`emulator.task_shared_ns[ecu]`), which is how a security-access sequence in one Task can flip a flag that a different Task checks later:
```python
class Task(Tasks):
    def run(self, cmd, *_):
        if self.shared.auth_successful:
            return self.PA(''), Tasks.RETURN.TERMINATE, None
        else:
            return self.NA('33'), Tasks.RETURN.TERMINATE, None   # securityAccessDenied
```
**ISO-TP multi-frame aggregation** is itself implemented as a special internal task, `IsoTpMultiframe(Tasks)`, whose `run()` accumulates First-Frame/Consecutive-Frame fragments (tracked via `frame`/`length`) and auto-emits `<flow>20 00</flow>` flow-control frames, only calling your PID's real handler once the full multi-frame request is assembled — verified in `elm/elm.py`:
```python
if self.flow_control:
    self.flow_control -= 1
else:
    resp = self.emulator.handle_response(
        '<flow>' + hex(self.flow_control_end)[2:].upper() + ' 00</flow>', ...)
    self.flow_control = self.flow_control_end - 1
if self.length * 2 <= len(self.req):
    return Tasks.RETURN.PASSTHROUGH(self.req[:self.length * 2])
return Tasks.RETURN.INCOMPLETE
```

## 7. Multi-ECU / headers / UDS / ISO-TP multi-frame

**Yes**, and the exact gating mechanism is in `elm/elm.py::handle_request`:

Setting the header (client sends `ATSH7E2`):
```python
'AT_SET_HEADER': {
    'Request': '^ATSH[0-9A-F]+$',
    'Exec': 'self.counters["cmd_set_header"] = re.sub(r"^0*([0-9A-F]+)$", r"\1", cmd[4:])',
    'Response': '<writeln>OK</writeln>'
}
```
Matching a PID entry against the currently active header:
```python
if 'REQUEST' in uc_val and re.match(uc_val['REQUEST'], cmd):
    if ('HEADER' in uc_val and header and
            uc_val['HEADER'].upper() != self.counters["cmd_set_header"]):
        continue   # this ECU doesn't answer — wrong header selected
    ...
```
So a PID entry with `'Header': ECU_ADDR_H` (`"7E2"`, HV ECU) only answers while the client has done `ATSH7E2`; a PID with `'Header': ECU_ADDR_E` (`"7E0"`, engine) only answers under `ATSH7E0` (the default, per `reset()`: `self.counters['cmd_set_header'] = ECU_ADDR_E.upper()`); entries with **no** `Header` field answer regardless. This is exactly how the `'car'` scenario fans a single serial/pty/TCP stream out to multiple simulated ECUs (`7E0`/`7E8` engine, `7E5` Continental powertrain, and constants exist in source for `7E1/7E9` transmission, `7E2/7EA` HV, `7E3/7EB` battery, `7C0/7C8` ICE, `7C4/7CC` A/C, `7B0/7B8` skid control, `747/74F` and `7D2/7DA`).

**ISO-TP multi-frame / KWP2000** answer construction is real, in `uds_answer()`:
```python
if length > 7:  # multiframe output
    answer = answer_header + sp + "10" + sp + "%02X" % length + sp   # First Frame
    ...
    while remaining_length > 0:
        answer += answer_header + sp + "%02X" % (frame_count + 0x20) + sp   # Consecutive Frames (0x21, 0x22, ...)
        ...
```
and flow-control frames are auto-emitted by `IsoTpMultiframe` as shown in §6. The `mt05` scenario is the concrete manufacturer-specific UDS demo: `UDS_RMBA` (Mode 23, Read Memory By Address) and `UDS_WRITE_MEM_ADDR` (Mode 0x3D) are backed by `task_mt05_read_mem_addr.py`/`task_mt05_write_mem_addr.py`, which read/write a byte range out of a `mmap`-backed file (`mmap-input.bin` / `mmap-output.bin`, per `task_ecu_11F1.py`'s ECU-task setup, `MEM_RANGE = 0x3fffff`) — i.e. it can genuinely simulate a flashable ECU memory image, not just canned answers.

**CAN-level (not OBD-PID-level) alternatives**, if you ever need to go below the OBD abstraction and manipulate raw BMW CAN frames/DBC signals directly:
- **SocketCAN `candump`/`canplayer`** (Linux, `can-utils`) — canonical record/replay pair: `candump -l can0` writes a timestamped log, `canplayer -I logfile` replays it onto a real or virtual (`vcan0`) interface, **with real timing preserved** — this is the true "chronological trace replay" the brief was asking about, which ELM327-emulator itself does not do.
- **[python-can](https://python-can.readthedocs.io/en/stable/interfaces/virtual.html)** — a Python CAN abstraction with a built-in `virtual` backend for same-process bus simulation (`can.interface.Bus('test', interface='virtual')`), plus real `Logger`/`Player` classes for `.asc`/`.blf`/`.trc`/`.log` files, and backends for real SocketCAN/vcan on Linux. Documented limitation: the virtual backend only works within a single Python process (no rate limiting/arbitration under load) — cross-process needs SocketCAN/vcan or the Multicast IP interface instead.
- **SavvyCAN** (Collin Kidder) — Qt GUI, DBC-aware, can load a captured log and replay it back onto a SocketCAN-compatible interface with controllable timing — good for visual/manual replay and DBC reverse-engineering work.

**How these compare for your use case:** ELM327-emulator operates at the *OBD-II PID/UDS semantic layer* (it answers `010C` with an RPM value) — it's the right tool if your dashboard talks python-OBD/ELM327 AT commands. The python-can/candump/SavvyCAN family operates at the *raw CAN frame layer* (arbitration ID + 8 bytes) — the right tool if your dashboard reads BMW-proprietary CAN IDs directly via a DBC rather than going through an ELM327-style adapter abstraction. These are genuinely complementary, not really substitutes for each other.

## For your BMW E36 specifically

One thing worth flagging that isn't in the brief but matters a lot for you: the built-in `'car'` scenario is explicitly a **Toyota Auris Hybrid on ISO 15765‑4 CAN, 500 kbps** — a much newer electrical architecture than an E36. Depending on your car's actual model year:

- **US OBD‑II E36s (roughly 1996–1999)** talk standard SAE J1979 Mode‑01 PIDs, but over **ISO 9141‑2 / KWP2000 K‑line**, not CAN. The good news: OBD‑II *PID request/response byte semantics* (`010C` → RPM, etc.) are the same regardless of the underlying wire protocol, so python-OBD + ELM327-emulator's `'default'` scenario (which has no CAN-specific header requirements) is a reasonable generic starting point, and the emulator does implement the `ATSP`/K‑line-family AT commands (`AT_PROTO`, `^ATSP[0-9A-C]$`) if any client software inspects the reported protocol number.
- **Pre‑1996 E36s are OBD1, not OBD‑II at all** — no standard PIDs, no ELM327 compatibility, a completely different (largely undocumented/proprietary BMW) diagnostic protocol. ELM327-emulator/python-OBD won't help there regardless of scenario.
- Either way, the `'car'` scenario's specific CUSTOM_ Toyota-hybrid PIDs (battery SOC, inverter temps, etc.) are meaningless for your car — don't use it as a template for realism, just as a *syntax* reference.
- Given all this, your highest-leverage path is almost certainly: get an ELM327/OBDLink dongle on your actual E36 once (even briefly), run `obd_dictionary -i <port> -p 20 -n e36 -o e36_scenario.py` while idling/revving so RPM/SPEED/COOLANT_TEMP actually vary across probes, then develop your dashboard forever after against `merge e36_scenario` / `scenario e36` with zero car dependency — which is precisely the workflow this whole project was built for.

The training walkthrough shows layering one of these bitmaps via Z-order, then painting a solid black **Ellipse** (no border) on top to mask the bitmap's unwanted inner face texture before re-drawing ticks on top of that mask — a manual mask-and-layer technique, quoted: *"we create an oval that will cover the rings, allowing us to put our own over the top... The Z-Order needs to be correct so that the inner rings are covered but the dial numbers are not."*

From actual rendered examples (C125 manual, real unit photos): dial faces appear in **both a light/silver skin** (white face, black ticks/numerals, red arc wedge for the redline zone only, black needle with red tip) **and a dark skin** (black/navy face, white ticks, a filled colour arc — amber/orange from 0 up to the current value in one photographed C187 example, white for the remainder, with small red tick marks right at the redline value). One photographed example had **no needle at all** — the "dial" was a pure filled radial ring (a circular progress-bar look), confirming the round gauge can render as a needle instrument or as a needle-less filled arc.

**Bar graph (tachometer):** Two shapes observed — straight **linear** bar and curved **sweep/arc** bar — both rendered as a **continuous colour fill** from zero to the current value (not discrete rectangular blocks) in every worked example I opened, bounded by scale numerals above the track. Fill colour is a project choice (seen in orange-red on one unit, bright cyan on another). A thin perpendicular line across the bar marks the **user-configurable, optionally gear-dependent shift point** (manual: *"A fully programmable shift point can be displayed, which can also be gear dependent"*). Small red tick marks (not necessarily a filled zone) denote the redline value on the sweep-bar examples. Dash Manager's underlying Bar 1/Bar 2 dialog (screenshot obtained) works on **boundary points** (Left / Intermediate 1 / Intermediate 2 / Right) each assigned one of 3 colours, plus a **"Show intermediate tick marks"** checkbox and a **"Change whole bar colour"** checkbox (flips the *entire* bar to a warning colour rather than just colouring a zone) — this is a continuous-fill-with-colour-zones model, not true discrete segmentation. Release-notes search snippets additionally describe a **segmented Fill Style** ("fill only entire segments when the channel reaches the end value for that segment") as a distinct, selectable mode in Display Creator specifically — **not independently screenshot-verified** this session. Numeric RPM readout sits in a **separate field beside/below** the gauge cluster, not overlaid on the bar itself; a large gear-number readout typically occupies the visual centre of the cluster.

## 3. Fonts/typography and label conventions

**Exact font family names: NOT FOUND / NOT VERIFIED.** No manual, datasheet, or training page I reached names a specific typeface, and I did not get a screenshot of a Text/Channel-Value font-properties panel.

Observed conventions from rendered real examples:
- Numerals are **bold, large, blocky, slightly tech-styled** — manual placeholder examples deliberately show max-width dummy digits (`9:99.99`, `9999999999999`) to indicate the field must reserve space for full digit counts.
- **Alignment is not universal.** In the clearest photographed C187 factory page, numeric values are **left-aligned** flush with their label's left edge (`ENGINE OIL TMP / 110`, `GBOX OIL TMP / 92`, `DIFF OIL TMP / 113` all start at the same left X). A different, smaller/table-style fixed layout (bordered "spreadsheet" rows: `ENG TEMP | 97.0`) showed the value **right-aligned** in its cell instead. Both conventions exist across MoTeC's own stock layouts — I cannot report a single fixed rule.
- Labels are consistently **UPPERCASE, short abbreviations** ("ENG TEMP," "OIL PRESS," "GBOX OIL TMP," "DIFF OIL TMP," "WATER TMP," "MAX SPEED," "REFERENCE LAP," "GAIN/LOSS"), smaller point size than the value, positioned directly above it, and usually rendered in an accent colour (orange/amber, cyan, or red) distinct from the value's high-contrast white/black.
- **Units are not appended inline** to the large numerals in any stock example I saw (e.g. plain "482" for oil pressure, no "kPa" suffix on-screen); unit selection is a separate software setting (Dash Manager "Units" dropdown, e.g. "volt (V)"). Time values use colon+decimal formatting ("2:24.50").
- Mode/page label ("RACE," "PAGE") sits top-left, bold, sometimes italic, uppercase.

## 4. Alarm rendering behaviour

Directly quoted from the C125 User Manual and cross-confirmed by a real-unit product photo:

- **Active/unacknowledged alarm:** a full-width bar along the **bottom edge of the screen**, overwriting whatever numeric content was there, in **bright/vivid red** with bold white/cream **uppercase, centred** text (photographed real example: `ENGINE HOT`). Manual: *"When an alarm is activated, a message is shown along the bottom of the display until it is acknowledged... The message can be defined as required and can include the current sensor reading or the sensor reading when the alarm was triggered."*
- **States** (verbatim): "Active and unacknowledged," "Inactive and unacknowledged" (condition cleared but not yet acked — keeps displaying), "Active and acknowledged" (true but suppressed from view), "Inactive."
- **Acknowledgement:** physical Acknowledge Button, or automatic timeout; a configurable "do not display this message again until … seconds have elapsed" suppression window follows acknowledgement.
- **Priority:** only the highest-priority unacknowledged alarm shows at a time; as each is acked, the next-highest appears.
- **Alarm Status Panel** (off by default, toggled via the Acknowledge button when no message is showing): shows up to **6** active-and-acknowledged alarms in a **dark maroon/brick-red** bar — visibly less saturated than the bright-red unacknowledged bar — bold white uppercase text, laid out as 1 full-width bar, 2 halves, or a 2×2 (or denser) grid depending on count. This panel is hidden whenever a new unacknowledged alarm needs the space.
- **Escalation/gating logic:** up to 6 chained comparisons per alarm; auto-increment/decrement of the trigger threshold on repeat triggers (with a cap and an optional reset-after-time); can be gated on other channels (example given: engine-temp alarm suppressed unless ground speed has been >50 km/h for 30s, to avoid false triggers from pit-stop heat soak); alarms can be scoped to specific display-mode pages (Warm-up/Practice/Race).
- **Inside Display Creator specifically:** "Alarm 1" auto-imports from the Dash Manager alarm setup; unlimited additional alarms can be added, each with its own multi-condition logic, on/off delays, and a fully custom on-screen appearance (edited like any other page object, not a fixed template).
- Manual explicitly recommends pairing the on-screen message with a physical warning light, since the screen alone may not grab attention fast enough.

## 5. Shift lights

- **C125:** 10 full-colour RGB LEDs built into the top bezel arc, individually programmable colour/function/intensity — called "**10 stage shift lights**" in the manual (`Functions > Shift Light Module`).
- **C127:** **16** full-colour RGB LEDs (datasheet, both revisions).
- **Setup is a documented two-stage workflow** (training deck, quoted): (1) `Functions > Shift Lights` — pick the driving channel (typically RPM, though boost/G-force are usable), and *"remember to put the RPM signal lower than the actual RPM you wish to shift at... the driver will always need to see the light before he knows to change gear"*; set **Hysteresis** to prevent flicker right at the threshold; optionally make it **Gear Dependent** (requires a Gear channel). (2) `Functions > Shift Light Module` — assign physical LED stage/colour/pattern.
- **Real-world colour pattern observed** (photo of an actual C125 with all 10 LEDs lit): symmetric **red–red–amber–green–green–green–green–amber–red–red**, i.e., green in the centre, amber next, red at both extreme ends — read as a "safe (centre) → caution → shift-now (edges)" convention. This is *inferred from one photographed example, not a quoted spec sentence* — mark as inferred, not documented default.
- A separate marketing photo (D175) showed the same 10-LED strip lit in a **full rainbow** (red-pink-magenta-cyan-blue-green-yellow-orange-red-red) — best read as a "look how many RGB colours we support" capability demo, not a functional convention.
- **Shift vs. warning distinction** (clearest documented answer, from the external SLM/SLM-C module, which uses the same Functions menu logic as the built-in C125/C127 LEDs): patterns are **priority-ordered in a list**, top = highest priority. Quoted: *"if a pattern has a high priority, e.g. Warning Lights, it cannot be affected by another pattern condition lower in the list becoming true."* So Warning and Shift are not architecturally different signal types — both are "patterns" on the same LED strip — but a Warning pattern is simply placed **above** the Shift pattern in priority order, so it visually pre-empts/overrides the shift indication whenever both are true. SLM also supports flashing and two-colour toggling per LED.

## 7. Gradients, glow, bezels, skeuomorphism

**Present, and taught as the normal workflow — not absent:**

- **Bezels are bitmap, not vector.** Display Creator's asset library includes image categories **Gear, Icon, Lighting, Needle, Panels, Sweep, Dial** — the "Dial" category specifically holds photorealistic brushed-chrome/silver ring textures up to 1004×1004px, applied by import + Z-order layering, with vector Ellipses used only as masks to hide unwanted parts of the bitmap. This is an explicitly skeuomorphic, photographic-bezel workflow taught in MoTeC's own official training material, not a hack.
- **Needles** can be a flat vector "Built-In Dial Pointer" (Length/Width/Offset params) **or** a bitmap from the "Needle" library **or** fully custom-imported artwork — both flat and skeuomorphic needle styles are natively supported.
- **Glow is explicitly taught**, but implemented as an **opacity-blended bitmap**, not a shader: quoted instruction — *"we want to decrease the opacity so that you get more of a glowing effect."* I.e., a pre-made glow/bloom image is layered and set to partial transparency near a light source; there is no real-time blur/bloom rendering.
- **Gradients:** the Ellipse/Rectangle Fill panel shows a "Fill Style" dropdown (only "Solid" seen active) sitting next to a second colour swatch and a bidirectional-arrow icon, strongly suggesting a two-colour gradient option is present in that dropdown — **not textually confirmed**, moderate-to-high confidence only.
- **Both light and dark factory skins exist.** Rendered examples show a light/silver gauge face with black text and a chrome-look bezel *and* a black/navy dark-theme page with white/coloured text, both shipped as stock MoTeC layouts — there is no single mandated "dark background" house style at the hardware/firmware level.
- In practice, MoTeC's own training walks a user through building a **skeuomorphic** chrome-bezelled dial as the primary worked example — but several factory-stock pages (the all-black "Four Line Style" table page; the numeric-block-heavy C185/C187 pages) achieve density through **flat colour-blocked numeric tables with no gauge skeuomorphism at all**. Both aesthetics are officially supported and demonstrated; I found no single documented "house style" ruling one out.

# Automotive telltale standards — findings

## Method note

I worked from primary artwork and regulation text, not descriptions. Concretely: the UN R121 regulation PDF (rendered its Table 1 symbol plates at 450 dpi and read them), the ISO 2575:2004 and :2021 preview PDFs (clauses 1–5 and Annexes A–B are in the free preview), 49 CFR 571.101 from govinfo, and the ISO 7000 registered-symbol SVGs from Wikimedia Commons — whose vector geometry I compared against the R121 plates and found matching. Coordinates below are read out of those SVG paths, so they are exact, not eyeballed.

**Caveat that matters for redrawing:** ISO 2575:2021 §4.10 says *"Artwork in this document might differ from the artwork shown in IEC 60417, ISO 7000 or the ISO Online Browsing Platform (OBP) database... In this case, the artwork in this document shall be used."* The Commons SVGs are community traces of the ISO 7000 registrations. I verified each against the official R121 plate and they agree, but they are not themselves normative.

---

## 1. Glyph geometry

### Coordinate system

ISO 2575 §4.12: *"Symbols in the annexes... are presented at 32 % of original size. The grid marks '∟' denote the corners of the original 75 mm square."*

So every symbol is designed inside a **75 mm square**. The SVGs use a **200 × 200 unit box** for that square (corner L-marks sit at the box corners), giving **1 unit = 0.375 mm**. All coordinates below are in that 200-unit box, y down. UN R121 footnote 2 makes this binding: *"The symbols included in this Regulation are substantially identical to symbols described in ISO 2575:2004. Proportional dimensional characteristics specified in ISO 2575:2004 shall be maintained."*

Relative line weights in the originals: heavy strokes 10–11 units, medium 8, light outline circles 5.

---

### Coolant temperature — ISO 7000-0246 · R121 item 11 · **RED**

Official title: *"Engine coolant temperature — To indicate that the engine coolant may be overheating or fails outside of specified parameters. To identify the engine coolant temperature gauge."*

| Element | Geometry |
|---|---|
| Thermometer stem | Capsule: x 92.396→107.604 (w **15.208**), y 21.053→128.613, corner radius 7.604 (= half-width, so a fully rounded top cap). Centred on x=100. |
| Bulb | Circle, centre (100, **125.92**), r **13.217**. Bulb Ø = 1.74 × stem width. |
| Graduations | **Exactly 3**, on the **right side only**. Stroke width 11, drawn from x=100 to x=142.77, at y = **46.891 / 70.673 / 94.454** (even spacing 23.78). Visible length past the stem edge ≈ 35.2. |
| Upper wave | y ≈ 112.6–135.3. **Interrupted by the bulb** — a left segment (x ≈ 11–72) and a right segment (x ≈ 128–189), each ~1.5 cycles. The cut is made with clearance arcs of r 25.576 about the bulb. |
| Lower wave | y ≈ 144.9–162.3. **Continuous**, x ≈ 36.8–169, **4 full cycles** (period ≈ 33). |

**Direct answers:** **two** wave lines, not one and not three. The upper one is broken by the bulb — the bulb *sits in* it. The lower one is unbroken and has **four crests**. The upper wave is **wider** than the lower (it extends further left and right). Both waves are **filled ribbons ~11–12 units thick**, not strokes — the top and bottom edges are parallel offset curves.

### Battery / charging — ISO 7000-0247 · R121 item 12 · **RED**

Official title: *"Battery charging condition."*

| Element | Geometry |
|---|---|
| Case | Rect x 20.763, y 61.377, w **158.47**, h **88.983**, stroke 10, unfilled. Aspect **1.78 : 1**. |
| Terminals | Two **solid filled** blocks, each 25.636 × 16.737, sitting on the case top edge (y 44.64→61.377). Left at x 41.525, right at x 132.84. Inset **20.76** from each end of the case — symmetric. Terminal width = 0.162 × case width. |
| Signs | Both stroke 8, both bars **31.568** long, both centred at **y = 96.362** — which is *above* the case's vertical centre (105.87). |

**⚠️ Orientation gotcha — the ISO original puts MINUS on the LEFT and PLUS on the RIGHT.** Minus: x 36.726→68.294. Plus: horizontal x 131.71→163.278, vertical at x 147.49, y 80.582→112.15. I confirmed this twice — in the ISO 7000-0247 vector and independently in the rendered R121 Table 1 plate. A great many aftermarket and icon-font "battery warning" glyphs mirror this.

### Oil pressure — ISO 7000-0248 · R121 item 10 · **RED**

Official title: *"Engine oil."* Drawn as one even-odd **filled** path plus a separate drop; no stroke.

| Element | Geometry |
|---|---|
| Can body | Flat bottom y=133.09 from x 42.04 to 129.69. Vertical left wall at x 42.04. Right wall is a long diagonal from (129.69, 133.09) rising to (171.5, 82.6), ending in a **pointed pouring lip** with a small zig-zag notch at x 171–190, y 69–85. |
| Filler cap | Solid step on the top edge: x 62.34→94.86, y 61.53→71.53 with a raised plate above — the classic "T". |
| Tapered tube | Upper **left**. Outline from (11.95, 58.87) → (4.14, 88.01) → (42.04, 102.08), **hollow** (has an internal counter-path), i.e. drawn as a tube, not a solid wedge. |
| Drip | **Single teardrop on the RIGHT**, x ≈ 183–191, y ≈ 98–119 — directly below the pointed lip. |

**On "which way does the spout point":** the unambiguous, verifiable facts are that the **long hollow tapered tube points up and to the LEFT**, and the **single oil drop hangs at the lower RIGHT, below the can's pointed lip**. Whether one calls the left tube "the spout" and the right point "the lip", or vice versa, is a naming question the artwork doesn't settle — but the geometry is fixed and that's what you need to redraw it. Do not mirror it.

### Check engine / MIL — ISO 7000-**0640** · R121 item 30 · **YELLOW**

This is the one people most often get wrong. Official title: *"Engine — To indicate a possible malfunction of the engine or emission system."* R121 item 30 is *"Engine on-board diagnostics or engine malfunction"*, colour **Yellow**. **Never red under R121.**

Beware of the near-neighbour: **ISO 7000-1371** is *"Engine failure; engine malfunction"* and is a completely different glyph (a rounded flask/cylinder outline with an exclamation mark inside). It is **not** the check-engine light.

0640 geometry — engine block in **side view, front to the left**, drawn as an **outline, stroke 8, fill none**, with every corner filleted at **r = 7**:

- **Top deck:** a raised plateau **57.01** wide at y ≈ 63 (x ≈ 57.4→114.4). It steps down on the right to a shelf **20.46** long at y ≈ 80.2, then steps down again to y ≈ 91.1 at x ≈ 152.
- **Right end (bell housing):** a convex bulge. The far right edge is a **19.30-long straight vertical** run with curved/tapered transitions at both ends, extreme x ≈ 178. Two rectangular notches — one upper, one lower — separate the bulge from the block.
- **Bottom:** a **69.47**-long flat sump running leftward, then a **45° chamfer** up-left (18.226 in each axis), then 14.04 flat into the left wall.
- **Cam/rocker cover:** a separate **solid filled** "T": top plate x 55.34→118.83 (w **63.5**) × h 8 at y 43.03–51.03, with a narrower neck x 74.09→100.59 (w **26.5**) × h 12 descending onto the block deck. Solid, in contrast to the outlined block.
- **Left stub:** a separate **solid filled** shape — a vertical bar x 8.12→16.39 spanning y 66.21→132.72 with chamfered ends, joined to the block by a short horizontal arm x 16.39→30.32, y 95.47→103.47 (h 8). Reads as the accessory/belt drive. A sideways ⊢.

### Brake system — ISO 7000-0239 · R121 item 25 · **RED**

Official title: *"Brake failure; brake system malfunction."* ISO note: *"telltale shall be red; in the case where a single tell-tale indicates more than one brake system condition, this symbol"* shall be used.

The "flanked by parentheses" construction is precise and shared with ABS and parking brake:

| Element | Geometry |
|---|---|
| Circle | centre (100,100), **r 55.836**, stroke **5** (thin) |
| Arcs | **r 71.091**, stroke **10** (thick), **90° each**, centred on the horizontal axis — right arc runs −45°→+45°, left arc mirrored. Right arc: (150.27, 49.731) → (171.09, 100) → (150.27, 150.27). |
| Radial gap | circle outer edge 58.34, arc inner edge 66.09 → **clear gap 7.75** |
| Exclamation bar | capsule x 94.915→105.084 (w **10.169**), y 58.898→124.470 (h **65.572**), fully rounded ends r 5.0847 |
| Dot | circle centre (100, **137.71**), r **5.0847** (= half the bar width). Gap bar-to-dot **8.16**. |

Key ratios: arc r / circle r = **1.273**; bar height / circle r = 1.174; bar width / circle Ø = 0.091. The bar+gap+dot stack is vertically centred on the circle.

**Parking brake — ISO 7000-0238 · R121 item 28 · RED.** Same bracket construction, *different proportions*: circle **r 63**, arcs **r 77.5** → ratio **1.230** (a proportionally larger circle than 0239). Letter **P** in place of the "!", spanning y 63.54–137.29.

### ABS — ISO 7000-1407 · R121 item 26 · **YELLOW**

Official title: *"Anti-lock brake system, failure."* ISO note: *"telltale shall be yellow; the letters 'ABS' may match the typestyle used throughout the instrument panel."*

- Circle centre (99.986, 100), **r 55.431**, stroke 5.
- Arcs **r 70.711**, stroke 10, 90° each — ratio **1.276**, i.e. essentially identical to 0239. Right arc: (149.99, 50) → (170.71, 100) → (149.99, 150).

### Airbag and seat belt (brief)

- **Airbag — ISO 7000-2108 · R121 item 22 · Yellow and/or Red.** Side view, occupant **facing left**, seated with legs down-left, diagonal belt across the torso, and a **large solid circle** (the inflated bag) at upper-left in front of the head/chest. R121 footnote 7: if a single telltale indicates an airbag malfunction, *this* symbol must be used (not the side-airbag one).
- **Seat belt — ISO 7000-0249 · R121 item 21 · RED.** *"To indicate the status of a three-point seat belt (belt with single shoulder harness)."* Front view: rounded head, bell-shaped torso, diagonal shoulder strap, curved lap belt, seat below. R121 shows **two permitted variants** side by side ("or") — one with a solid seat, one with an outlined seat frame.
