## 2. Colour coding — the actual rule

**ISO 2575 §5.1** is the source rule. Identical verbatim in the 2004 and 2021 editions:

> — **red:** danger to persons or very serious damage to equipment, immediate or imminent;
> — **yellow or amber:** caution, outside normal operating limits, vehicle system malfunction, damage to vehicle likely, or other condition which may produce hazard in the longer term;
> — **green:** safe, normal operating condition (where blue or yellow is not required).

**§5.2** pins specific colours: blue = high/main beam; green = turn signals (and low beam, added in 2021); yellow/amber = ABS failure; red = hazard warning. **§5.3:** if colour is used on heating/cooling symbols, red = hot, blue = cold. **§5.4:** white where none of the above applies.

**ECE R121 §5.4.1:** *"Light of each tell-tale listed in Table 1 shall be of the colour shown in column 5."* **§5.4.2** says any telltale *not* in Table 1 *"shall follow the guidelines specified in paragraph 5 of standard ISO 2575:2004."* **§5.4.4:** *"The dark part of any symbol may be replaced by its outline."*

**R121 Table 1 colours** (read off the regulation):

| Item | Telltale | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 3 / 3a | Headlamp driving/main beam | **Blue** |
| 2 | Headlamp passing beam | Green |
| 5 | Direction indicator | Green |
| 6 | Hazard warning | **Red** |
| 7 / 8 | Front fog / rear fog | Green / **Yellow** |
| 9 | Fuel level | **Yellow** |
| 10 | Engine oil pressure | **Red** |
| 11 | Engine coolant temperature | **Red** |
| 12 | Electrical charging condition | **Red** |
| 21 | Seat belt | **Red** |
| 22/23 | Airbag / side airbag malfunction | Yellow and/or Red |
| 24 | Passenger air bag off | Yellow |
| 25 / 28 | Brake system malfunction / parking brake | *"See Regulation Nos. 13-H and 13 as appropriate"* |
| 26 | ABS malfunction | **Yellow** |
| 30 | Engine OBD / engine malfunction | **Yellow** |
| 31 | Diesel pre-heat | Yellow |
| 37 | Brake lining wear-out | Yellow |
| 43 | ESC (incl. malfunction) | per R13/R13-H |

R121 footnote 5 is worth knowing: *"Combination of the engine oil pressure symbol and the engine coolant temperature symbol in a single tell-tale is permitted."*

**The severity logic, stated plainly.** UN R13-H §5.2.21.1.1–.2 gives the cleanest articulation:

> **5.2.21.1.1** A **red** warning signal, indicating failures ... which preclude achievement of the prescribed service braking performance and/or which preclude the functioning of at least one of two independent service braking circuits;
> **5.2.21.1.2** Where applicable, a **yellow** warning signal indicating an electrically detected defect within the vehicle braking equipment, which is not indicated by the red warning signal...

That is the whole hierarchy in one sentence pair: **red = the primary function is lost. Amber = an enhancement/assist layer over an intact primary function is lost.** R13-H §5.2.21.3.3 also requires the brake warning signal be **constant, not flashing**.

**⚠️ Major US/ECE divergence — do not assume FMVSS mirrors ECE.** FMVSS 101 Table 1 (49 CFR 571.101, 2023 edition) specifies **no colour at all** for engine oil pressure, engine coolant temperature, electrical charge, or fuel level — column 6 is blank for all four. It also permits **words instead of symbols** ("Oil", "Temp", "Fuel", "Volts or Charge or Amp"), gives **no symbol** for brake system malfunction (only the word "Brake"), and allows the high-beam telltale to be **"Blue or Green"**. Where FMVSS *does* specify:

- **Red:** brake system malfunction, brake pressure, low brake fluid, parking brake applied, brake lining wear-out
- **Yellow:** ABS malfunction, variable brake proportioning malfunction, regenerative brake malfunction, ESC malfunction, ESC OFF
- **Green:** turn signals · **Blue or Green:** high beam

This explains why a US-market E36 has "BRAKE FLUID", "PARK BRAKE", "CHECK ENGINE" and "ABS" as *printed text panels* rather than pictograms — that's the US regulatory route, not a BMW styling choice.

## 3. Priority and grouping in real clusters

### There is no standard that dictates physical ordering or grouping. None.

Both FMVSS 101 and ECE R121 were read in full and searched for any provision on relative position, rows, left/right, or severity ordering. Every location requirement is of the form "must be visible" or "the identifier must be adjacent to what it identifies":

- **R121 §5.1.2:** *"The tell-tales and indicators shall be located so that they are visible and recognisable to a driver during night and day... Tell-tales and indicators need not be visible or recognisable when not activated."*
- **FMVSS 101 S5.1.2:** *"...must be located so that, when activated, they are visible to a driver under the conditions of S5.6.1 and S5.6.2."* The only conditions defined (S5.6.1/.2) are that the driver has adapted to ambient light and is belted. **FMVSS 101 never says "normal seated position" and never invokes an eye ellipse.**
- R121 §2.6 defines *"adjacent"* as *"no control, tell-tale, indicator or other potential source of distraction appears between the identifying symbol and the tell-tale... which that symbol identifies."*

**The single hard placement rule in either regime** is for the passenger-airbag-off telltale (R121 §5.1.4, FMVSS 208 S19.2.2(d)): forward of and above the design H-point of both front seats in their forwardmost position.

R121 §3.2.4 requires approval submissions to include *"Drawings and/or photographs showing the layout of controls and location of tell-tales and indicators"* — layout is **documented and approved, but not prescribed**.

### Where a documented priority scheme *does* exist: shared displays

This is the answer to "is there a documented convention on ordering by severity" — yes, but it governs shared pixels, not physical position.

**FMVSS 101:**
- **S5.5.2** — brake system malfunction (where red is required), air bag malfunction, low tire pressure, ESC malfunction, passenger air bag off, high beam, turn signal, and seat belt **must not be shown in the same common space**.
- **S5.5.5** — any of those, if designed to display in a common space, **must displace any other symbol or message** while its condition exists.
- **S5.5.4** — when two or more telltales are active, messages must be *"repeated automatically in sequence"* or driver-selectable.
- **S5.5.6(b)** — high beams, turn signal, low tire pressure, passenger air bag off, **and any telltale required to be red must not be cancelable** while the condition exists.
- **S5.3.3(b)** — dimming for *"brakes, highbeams, turn signals, and safety belts may not be adjustable under any driving condition to a level that is invisible."*

**ECE R121 §5.5.1** mirrors this with a narrower privileged set — **brake system malfunction, headlamp driving beam, direction indicator, seat belt**: not co-located (5.5.1.3), must displace others (5.5.1.4), not cancellable (5.5.1.5).

**⚠️ Genuinely surprising provision worth flagging: R121 §5.5.1.6** — *"Unless prescribed in a specific Regulation, the colour requirements regarding tell-tales do not apply when tell-tales appear in a common space."* In a shared digital display, ECE colour mandates lapse.

### ISO standards — what they actually cover

| Standard | What it does |
|---|---|
| ISO 2575 | Symbol library + colour guidance (§5). **No layout.** |
| ISO 4040:2009 *"Location of hand controls, indicators and tell-tales"* | Despite the title, its zone system assigns **hand controls** to reach zones. For indicators/telltales it addresses visibility, not zoning. *(Moderate confidence — abstract only, standard is paywalled.)* |
| ISO 15008 | Legibility of in-vehicle visual presentation: character height, contrast, luminance. Not a priority scheme. R121 §5.3 and ISO 2575 §4.7 both reference it for pixel-matrix rendering. |
| **ISO/TS 16951:2021** | *"Procedures for determining priority of on-board messages presented to drivers."* This is the standard for message prioritisation. *(Title sourced; body paywalled.)* |
| SAE J2402 | Symbols only, harmonised with ISO 2575. No location content. |

### "Red central, amber peripheral" — **not documented**

No authoritative source was found for this as a codified OEM convention — no published research, no OEM style guide. Consumer sources discuss colour-coded urgency but not spatial placement. **Present it as an emergent design heuristic, not a requirement.** It falls out of (a) colour semantics from ISO 2575, (b) the eye-ellipse/field-of-view constraint that anything safety-critical sits inside the steering-wheel aperture, and (c) the common-space displacement rules — not from any rule that says so.

One real OEM data point, from BMW factory service data for the E36: *"The various lamps are positioned at the top center and along the bottom of the cluster display. They are controlled internally by the cluster or externally by other sensors and modules **where required by legislation**."* Note that the stated driver of the split is legislation, not colour.

**Outstanding gap:** NHTSA's *Human Factors Design Guidance for Driver-Vehicle Interfaces* (DOT HS 812 360, Dec 2016) is the most likely home of published telltale prioritisation guidance. Both nhtsa.gov and rosap.ntl.bts.gov returned 403 to automated fetches. Worth a manual download.

## 4. BMW E36

### Dial layout — left to right: FUEL (small) · SPEEDOMETER (large) · TACHOMETER (large) · COOLANT TEMP (small)

Sourced from the BMW factory Owner's Manual, P/N 01 41 9 790 377, © 07/98 (figure 360us319, US 1999 MY, non-M3). **Speedometer is left of the tachometer.** Four discrete circular bezels — the small gauges flank the large ones, they are not inset into them and not full-size.

The two large dials each carry an inset element in their lower portion:
- **Speedometer** → the rectangular **LCD window**
- **Tachometer** → the small arc gauge (economy/MPG on US cars; **oil temperature** on the Euro M3, replacing the *Verbrauchsanzeige*)

**On the oil-temp-vs-oil-pressure dispute for the Euro M3, I can now settle it.** The BMW E36 ECE Electrical Troubleshooting Manual (BMW AG, "E36 ECE 1998", 05/99) instrument-cluster section 6211.0 lists connector **X16 pin 13 = "Oil temperature gauge ← Oil temperature sensor"**, and its component index has **"Oil temperature sensor, B6238 ... 6211.0-02"**. The cluster has a factory oil **temperature** input. One 318ti.org forum thread claiming oil *pressure* is wrong.

### Needles, not segments — three independent confirmations

**Both the coolant temperature gauge and the fuel gauge are continuous analog needle gauges. Neither is segmented.**

1. **Factory manual text** uses needle language explicitly. Fuel: *"If the tilt of the vehicle varies... this may cause the **needle** to fluctuate slightly."* Coolant: *"it is not unusual for the **needle** to rise as far as the edge of the red sector."* The economy gauge is also a needle: *"When the vehicle is stationary, the **needle** returns to zero."*
2. **BMW ETM schematic 6211.0-02** (which I rendered) draws the temperature gauge, tachometer, speedometer and fuel gauge as **round dials with pointer needles**.
3. **Sender types are analog-resistive.** Coolant: B6232 *"Remote thermometer sensor"*, drawn as an NTC thermistor (ϑ) into cluster pin 12. Fuel: *"Immersion tube sensor"* B10/B6, a resistive float sender.

### Scale markings

- **Coolant gauge:** no numbers, no C/H lettering. A **blue sector** (cold), an unmarked normal band, a **red sector** (hot), with a thermometer pictogram in the dial centre. Manual: *"Blue — The engine is still cold... Between the blue and red sectors — Normal operating range... Red — Indicator lamp comes on, the warning 'COOLANT TEMPERATURE' appears in Check Control: engine overheated."*
- **Fuel gauge:** marked **R — 1/2 — F**, fuel-pump pictogram in the centre, black reserve block at the left end of the arc, and (US only) "UNLEADED GASOLINE ONLY" printed on the lower dial face. Low-fuel warning at ≈ 2.1 US gal / 8 L.
- **Tachometer:** 0–7 ×1000, labelled "1/min x1000", with a **red overspeed sector**. ⚠️ The exact rpm where the red sector begins is **per-engine** and not readable from the manual raster — treat printed redline as unverified per variant. Note also that vendor listings quoting "8000 RPM" for an M3 face are quoting the *scale maximum*, while "7000/7400" quote the *start of the red sector*; don't conflate them.
- **Speedometer (US late non-M3):** dual scale, **MPH 20→140 primary, km/h 20→240 secondary**. ⚠️ Per-model **European** speedo maxima come only from aftermarket gauge-face vendors who generalise across model ranges — do not put them in a build guide.

### LCD / odometer

A **single rectangular LCD window inset into the bottom of the speedometer dial**:
- **left:** 6-digit odometer · **right:** trip odometer (0.1 resolution, rolls at 999.9)
- **below, spanning the window:** the **Service Interval Display (SIA)** with printed legends "OIL SERVICE" (left) and "INSPECTION" (right). The SIA is **discrete illuminated lamps, not LCD segments** — green lamps that decrement, plus a yellow (due) and a red (overdue).

Trip reset button: small round button outside the lower-right edge of the fuel gauge bezel. **No gear-position indicator anywhere in the cluster** — the only auto-trans item is a yellow "shift electronics" fault lamp. **No outside-temperature display in the cluster** — that lives in the centre-dash unit.

### Check Control is NOT a panel in the cluster

This is the most commonly misunderstood part. Three physically separate things:

1. **The CC text display** lives in the **LCD matrix of the centre-dash unit** — either the "Check Control with outside temperature display and digital clock" (multifunction clock) or the fuller On-Board Computer. It has its own CHECK key.
2. **A single Check Control warning lamp in the instrument cluster.** Confirmed in the ETM: connector **X17 pin 26 = "Central indicator lamp/check control ← On-board computer"**. Manual: *"Texts with messages and warnings are used to alert the driver to defective systems. In addition, there is a warning lamp in the instrument panel."* It flashes for Priority 1 and stops after 20 s or a CHECK keypress.
3. **The CCM module** behind the dash.

**It is optional**, and only available when the car has the Multi-Function Clock or the OBC. Lighting circuits are **warm-monitored only** — a fault is only detected when the circuit is energised.

Messages, verbatim from the factory manual:
- **Priority 1** (flashing lamp + flashing symbol): *Brake lamp electrical system*, *Brake lamps defective*
- **Priority 2** (appear at ignition position 2, symbols persist): *Brake lamp defective* (single bulb), *Low beams defective*, *Backup lamps defective*, *License plate lamp*, *Washer fluid low*, *Check Control inactive*
- **Priority 3** (status, typically after parking): *Check coolant level* — and *"not displayed while driving"*
- Driven in from the cluster: **COOLANT TEMPERATURE** when the needle enters the red sector
- Self-test: CHECK key at position 2 with no faults → **"CHECK CONTROL OK"**

### Telltale inventory and positions

From the US factory manual figure (positions), cross-checked against the ECE ETM connector pin lists (which give the full superset including Euro-only lamps).

**Top-centre pod, between speedo and tach**, left to right: **battery/charge (red) · high beam (blue) · oil pressure (red)**

**Upper flanks:** left turn arrow (green) between fuel gauge and speedo; right turn arrow (green) between tach and coolant gauge

**Between the big dials, lower:** ASC+T (yellow)

**Bottom strip, full width below all four dials**, left to right as drawn: fog lamps (green) · **"CHECK ENGINE"** text panel · automatic transmission / shift electronics (yellow) · seat belt (red) · **"ABS"** text panel (yellow) · brake warning (red) with printed **"BRAKE FLUID"** and **"PARK BRAKE"** legends · airbag/SRS (red). Low-fuel warning is a pictogram *inside* the fuel dial, not a strip position.

**ETM connector list — the authoritative superset** (BMW E36 ECE ETM 6211.0a/b/c):

*X16 (26-pin white):* 1 high beam · 3/4 turn right/left · 5 EGS fault + ATF temperature · 8 DDE fault (diesel) · 9 preheating (diesel) · 10 rollover protection (convertible) · 13 oil temperature gauge · 14 airbag · 17 handbrake · 18 brake fluid · 19 brake pad wear · 26 **catalytic converter overtemperature**

*X17 (26-pin blue):* 1 trailer turn / oil level (M3) · 5–6 battery charge indicator (terminal 15 + terminal 61 from alternator) · 8 front fog · 11/21 ABS · 12 upshift (M3) / ASC · **14 seat belt — "USA, Canada and Gulf countries"** · 19 oil pressure · 20 SMG fault (M3) · 26 check control

*X271 (12-pin black):* 1 fuel level sender · 5 rear fog

Two things fall out of this that the US manual can't tell you:
- **The seat belt telltale is market-specific** — ECE-market E36s don't have one wired.
- **There is no MIL/check-engine pin in the ECE cluster harness at all** (X16 pins 6, 7, 15, 16, 25 are "not used"). The petrol check-engine lamp is a US/OBD-II feature. The ECE cluster gets a *catalytic converter overtemperature* lamp instead.

**EML:** not present in the US non-M3 lamp list. Whether US-market M3s carry an EML lamp is **unverified** — flag rather than guess.

### Bus architecture

**The E36 cluster is a standalone, hardwired gauge cluster. No I-bus, no K-bus, no CAN.** BMW's bus rollout begins with the E38. Gauges are driven by discrete signals: RPM on cluster wire #20, vehicle speed on X17 pin 2, fuel level as an analog voltage (≈0.2 V empty → 3.53 V full), coolant via a two-wire NTC. What *is* present is a **K-line (ISO 9141 / KWP) diagnostic path** — which is exactly what this project already talks to. The OBC↔cluster link is a dedicated point-to-point serial connection, not a vehicle-wide bus (*protocol details unverified*).

## 5. Bulb check / self-test

### The telltale standards *permit* it; they never *require* it

- **FMVSS 101 S5.3.1(e):** *"A telltale must not emit light except when identifying the malfunction or vehicle condition it is designed to indicate, **or during a bulb check**."*
- **ECE R121 §5.3.5:** *"A tell-tale shall not emit light except when identifying the malfunction or vehicle condition for whose indication it is designed **or during a bulb check**."*

Both are worded as *exceptions to a prohibition*. Neither specifies a duration.

### The mandate lives in the individual system standards

**US:**
- **FMVSS 105 S5.3.2(a):** *"all indicator lamps shall be activated as a check of lamp function either when the ignition (start) switch is turned to the 'on' (run) position when the engine is not running, or when the ignition (start) switch is in a position between 'on' (run) and 'start' that is designated by the manufacturer as a check position."* S5.3.3(b) adds: deactivated at the end of the check unless a malfunction exists.
- **FMVSS 135 S5.5.2** — same, but uniquely also permits *"a single manual action by the driver, such as momentary activation of a test button."*
- **FMVSS 126 S5.3.4** (ESC) and **FMVSS 138 S4.3.3(a)** (TPMS) — same construction. FMVSS 126 S5.3.6 exempts telltales shown in a common space.

**UNECE — UN R13-H §5.2.21.4** (identical text at UN R13 §5.2.1.29.5):

> *"The warning signal(s) mentioned above shall light up when the electrical equipment of the vehicle (and the braking system) is energised. With the vehicle stationary, the braking system shall verify that none of the specified failures or defects are present before extinguishing the signals. Specified failures or defects which should activate the warning signals..., but which are not detected under static conditions, shall be stored upon detection and be displayed at start-up and at all times when the ignition (start) switch is in the 'On' (run) position, as long as the failure or defect persists."*

**ABS specifically — R13-H Annex 6 §4.1.1** explains a behaviour worth mimicking: sensor anomalies undetectable at standstill *"shall be detected not later than when the vehicle speed exceed 10 km/h... verification may be delayed but detected not later than when the vehicle speed exceeds 15 km/h."* That is why an ABS lamp can extinguish at key-on and then re-light once rolling.

### ⚠️ Correction: FMVSS 208 does **not** mandate an airbag illuminate-then-extinguish sequence

The complete text of 49 CFR 571.208 was retrieved and searched. **S4.5.2 in its entirety** requires only that the system *"have a monitoring system with a readiness indicator. The indicator shall monitor its own readiness and shall be clearly visible from the driver's designated seating position."* No sequence, no duration, no bulb-check requirement.

**The widely-repeated "1 to 8 seconds" figure is a misattribution.** The real number is **4 to 8 seconds**, it is in **S7.3**, and it belongs to the **seat belt warning** — not the airbag lamp, and not a bulb check: *"Activates a continuous or intermittent audible signal for a period of not less than 4 seconds and not more than 8 seconds and that activates a continuous or flashing warning light... for not less than 60 seconds."*

The only airbag-adjacent bulb-check language in FMVSS 208 is **S19.2.2(h)**, and it is permissive and applies to the *passenger air bag off* telltale: *"The telltale must not emit light except when any passenger air bag is turned off or during a bulb check upon vehicle starting."*

**Unverified:** whether ECE R94 mandates an airbag telltale self-check. R121 lists the airbag telltales and their colour but prescribes no check sequence; R94 itself was not retrieved. Don't state it.

### No regulation anywhere specifies a bulb-check duration

**The commonly cited "2–4 seconds" has no regulatory basis and no authoritative source was found for it.** The regulations say "activated as a check of lamp function" and, at most, "deactivated at the end of the check"; UN R13/R13-H specify a *completion condition* (the system has verified no faults), not a clock. Two hard, sourced BMW figures both contradict "2–4 s": the E36 SRS lamp runs **5 s**, and the E36 brake-pad-wear lamp runs **30 s**. Cite measured examples, not the folklore number.

### Which lamps don't bulb-check, and the actual mechanism

UN R48 defines two structurally different telltale types:
- ***"Operating tell-tale"*** — *"indicating that a device has been switched ON and is operating correctly or not."*
- ***"Closed-circuit tell-tale"*** — *"indicating that a device has been switched ON, but not indicating whether it is operating correctly or not."*

R48 assigns **circuit-closed** telltales to main beam (6.1.8), front fog (6.3.8), hazard (6.6.8), front position lamps (6.9.8) and rear fog (6.11.8). A circuit-closed telltale is by definition wired to report *switch state*; it has no fault state to self-test, and lighting it at key-on would violate FMVSS 101 S5.3.1(e) / R121 §5.3.5.

**Turn signals are the exception** — R48 6.5.8 requires an *operating* telltale that, on lamp failure, *"is either extinguished, or remains alight without flashing, or shows a marked change of frequency"* (the classic hyperflash). But that is monitored **continuously while in use**, never at key-on.

### E36-specific behaviour

**There is no automatic whole-cluster bulb sweep at key-on.** The factory service data documents none; lamps illuminate individually per their sensor/module state. Several *appear* to bulb-check as a **circuit side effect** rather than by design — the charge lamp lights because alternator field current flows through it, the oil pressure lamp lights because the pressure switch is closed at zero pressure. *(That mechanism explanation is inference from the circuits, not a manual quote.)*

**There IS a deliberate self-test, and it is on key position 1 (terminal R), not position 2.** From BMW's "Instrument Cluster Testing" for 1992–96 E36:

> *"There is a self test that can be carried out on the cluster by pressing the trip odometer reset button and switching the ignition to KL R. All gauges move from the zero position to the maximum display and back again. **The warning lamps are illuminated as a bulb check.** In addition, vehicle specific data is displayed in the LCD matrix as follows: BMW PART NUMBER (6 digits), CODE NUMBER (5 digits), K NUMBER (4 digits), CHASSIS NUMBER (5 digits), SOFTWARE VERSION (3 digits), REVISION INDEX (2 digits). The self test is canceled by switching the ignition off or to KL 15."*

Note the terminal designations — entered at **KL R**, *cancelled* by going to **KL 15**. For 1997–98 E36, E36/5 318ti and Z3 this became a 15-function test menu whose **TEST NO. 01** is the same gauge sweep + lamp test.

**Timed self-tests with real numbers:**
- **SRS: 5 seconds.** *"Each time the ignition is switched 'On', the Supplemental Restraint System (SRS) does a self-test. This is indicated by illumination of the SRS Warning Lamp for five seconds, after which the lamp extinguishes (standby mode) if no faults are detected."* The **lamp circuit itself is one of the monitored items** (checked for open/short). Fault tiering: "minor" faults light it ~2 minutes then extinguish; "non-critical" light it continuously with the system still operational; "critical" light it continuously and disable the system. Controller is the ZAE, introduced MY1994.
- **Brake pad wear: 30 seconds.** *"Once the circuit is rectified the brake pad wear indicator will shut off after first 30 seconds of switching the ignition on"* / *"after the 30 second start-up bulb check."* BMW's own manual calls this a bulb check — useful as a counterexample to the 2–4 s folklore. The US owner's manual describes it differently again: *"Lights up when starter is actuated and goes out when the engine is started."*

## Explicitly uncertain — do not state as fact

1. **"2–4 seconds is typical bulb-check duration"** — no source found, and contradicted by the two sourced BMW figures.
2. **"Red central, amber peripheral" as a documented convention** — no authoritative source found.
3. **ECE R94 mandating an airbag self-check** — R94 not retrieved.
4. **Pre-facelift (1992–95) E36 cluster layout** — all cluster-figure evidence is from a 1999 MY US manual. The four-dial order is almost certainly unchanged, but no factory diagram for the early car was obtained.
5. **Whether any E36 shipped without a tachometer** — no evidence either way (absence of evidence only).
6. **Per-model European speedometer maxima and per-engine printed redlines** — vendor data only.
7. **Whether US-market E36 M3s carry an EML lamp.**
8. **Exact within-strip ordering** of the brake-pad-wear, Check Control and rollover-protection lamps in the E36 bottom row.
9. **ISO 4040 and ISO/TS 16951 body text** — paywalled; scopes are from abstracts.
10. **SAE J1053** — appears to be a fastener standard ("Steel Stamped Nuts of One Pitch Thread Design"), not telltale-related. Drop it unless independently verified.

# Automotive telltale standards — findings

## Method note

I worked from primary artwork and regulation text, not descriptions. Concretely: the UN R121 regulation PDF (rendered its Table 1 symbol plates at 450 dpi and read them), the ISO 2575:2004 and :2021 preview PDFs (clauses 1–5 and Annexes A–B are in the free preview), 49 CFR 571.101 from govinfo, and the ISO 7000 registered-symbol SVGs from Wikimedia Commons — whose vector geometry I compared against the R121 plates and found matching. Coordinates below are read out of those SVG paths, so they are exact, not eyeballed.

**Caveat that matters for redrawing:** ISO 2575:2021 §4.10 says *"Artwork in this document might differ from the artwork shown in IEC 60417, ISO 7000 or the ISO Online Browsing Platform (OBP) database... In this case, the artwork in this document shall be used."* The Commons SVGs are community traces of the ISO 7000 registrations. I verified each against the official R121 plate and they agree, but they are not themselves normative.

## 1. Glyph geometry

### Coordinate system

ISO 2575 §4.12: *"Symbols in the annexes... are presented at 32 % of original size. The grid marks '∟' denote the corners of the original 75 mm square."*

So every symbol is designed inside a **75 mm square**. The SVGs use a **200 × 200 unit box** for that square (corner L-marks sit at the box corners), giving **1 unit = 0.375 mm**. All coordinates below are in that 200-unit box, y down. UN R121 footnote 2 makes this binding: *"The symbols included in this Regulation are substantially identical to symbols described in ISO 2575:2004. Proportional dimensional characteristics specified in ISO 2575:2004 shall be maintained."*

Relative line weights in the originals: heavy strokes 10–11 units, medium 8, light outline circles 5.

## 2. Colour coding — the actual rule

**ISO 2575 §5.1** is the source rule. Identical verbatim in the 2004 and 2021 editions:

> — **red:** danger to persons or very serious damage to equipment, immediate or imminent;
> — **yellow or amber:** caution, outside normal operating limits, vehicle system malfunction, damage to vehicle likely, or other condition which may produce hazard in the longer term;
> — **green:** safe, normal operating condition (where blue or yellow is not required).

**§5.2** pins specific colours: blue = high/main beam; green = turn signals (and low beam, added in 2021); yellow/amber = ABS failure; red = hazard warning. **§5.3:** if colour is used on heating/cooling symbols, red = hot, blue = cold. **§5.4:** white where none of the above applies.

**ECE R121 §5.4.1:** *"Light of each tell-tale listed in Table 1 shall be of the colour shown in column 5."* **§5.4.2** says any telltale *not* in Table 1 *"shall follow the guidelines specified in paragraph 5 of standard ISO 2575:2004."* **§5.4.4:** *"The dark part of any symbol may be replaced by its outline."*

**R121 Table 1 colours** (read off the regulation):

| Item | Telltale | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 3 / 3a | Headlamp driving/main beam | **Blue** |
| 2 | Headlamp passing beam | Green |
| 5 | Direction indicator | Green |
| 6 | Hazard warning | **Red** |
| 7 / 8 | Front fog / rear fog | Green / **Yellow** |
| 9 | Fuel level | **Yellow** |
| 10 | Engine oil pressure | **Red** |
| 11 | Engine coolant temperature | **Red** |
| 12 | Electrical charging condition | **Red** |
| 21 | Seat belt | **Red** |
| 22/23 | Airbag / side airbag malfunction | Yellow and/or Red |
| 24 | Passenger air bag off | Yellow |
| 25 / 28 | Brake system malfunction / parking brake | *"See Regulation Nos. 13-H and 13 as appropriate"* |
| 26 | ABS malfunction | **Yellow** |
| 30 | Engine OBD / engine malfunction | **Yellow** |
| 31 | Diesel pre-heat | Yellow |
| 37 | Brake lining wear-out | Yellow |
| 43 | ESC (incl. malfunction) | per R13/R13-H |

R121 footnote 5 is worth knowing: *"Combination of the engine oil pressure symbol and the engine coolant temperature symbol in a single tell-tale is permitted."*

**The severity logic, stated plainly.** UN R13-H §5.2.21.1.1–.2 gives the cleanest articulation:

> **5.2.21.1.1** A **red** warning signal, indicating failures ... which preclude achievement of the prescribed service braking performance and/or which preclude the functioning of at least one of two independent service braking circuits;
> **5.2.21.1.2** Where applicable, a **yellow** warning signal indicating an electrically detected defect within the vehicle braking equipment, which is not indicated by the red warning signal...

That is the whole hierarchy in one sentence pair: **red = the primary function is lost. Amber = an enhancement/assist layer over an intact primary function is lost.** R13-H §5.2.21.3.3 also requires the brake warning signal be **constant, not flashing**.

**⚠️ Major US/ECE divergence — do not assume FMVSS mirrors ECE.** FMVSS 101 Table 1 (49 CFR 571.101, 2023 edition) specifies **no colour at all** for engine oil pressure, engine coolant temperature, electrical charge, or fuel level — column 6 is blank for all four. It also permits **words instead of symbols** ("Oil", "Temp", "Fuel", "Volts or Charge or Amp"), gives **no symbol** for brake system malfunction (only the word "Brake"), and allows the high-beam telltale to be **"Blue or Green"**. Where FMVSS *does* specify:

- **Red:** brake system malfunction, brake pressure, low brake fluid, parking brake applied, brake lining wear-out
- **Yellow:** ABS malfunction, variable brake proportioning malfunction, regenerative brake malfunction, ESC malfunction, ESC OFF
- **Green:** turn signals · **Blue or Green:** high beam

This explains why a US-market E36 has "BRAKE FLUID", "PARK BRAKE", "CHECK ENGINE" and "ABS" as *printed text panels* rather than pictograms — that's the US regulatory route, not a BMW styling choice.

## 3. Priority and grouping in real clusters

### There is no standard that dictates physical ordering or grouping. None.

Both FMVSS 101 and ECE R121 were read in full and searched for any provision on relative position, rows, left/right, or severity ordering. Every location requirement is of the form "must be visible" or "the identifier must be adjacent to what it identifies":

- **R121 §5.1.2:** *"The tell-tales and indicators shall be located so that they are visible and recognisable to a driver during night and day... Tell-tales and indicators need not be visible or recognisable when not activated."*
- **FMVSS 101 S5.1.2:** *"...must be located so that, when activated, they are visible to a driver under the conditions of S5.6.1 and S5.6.2."* The only conditions defined (S5.6.1/.2) are that the driver has adapted to ambient light and is belted. **FMVSS 101 never says "normal seated position" and never invokes an eye ellipse.**
- R121 §2.6 defines *"adjacent"* as *"no control, tell-tale, indicator or other potential source of distraction appears between the identifying symbol and the tell-tale... which that symbol identifies."*

**The single hard placement rule in either regime** is for the passenger-airbag-off telltale (R121 §5.1.4, FMVSS 208 S19.2.2(d)): forward of and above the design H-point of both front seats in their forwardmost position.

R121 §3.2.4 requires approval submissions to include *"Drawings and/or photographs showing the layout of controls and location of tell-tales and indicators"* — layout is **documented and approved, but not prescribed**.

### Where a documented priority scheme *does* exist: shared displays

This is the answer to "is there a documented convention on ordering by severity" — yes, but it governs shared pixels, not physical position.

**FMVSS 101:**
- **S5.5.2** — brake system malfunction (where red is required), air bag malfunction, low tire pressure, ESC malfunction, passenger air bag off, high beam, turn signal, and seat belt **must not be shown in the same common space**.
- **S5.5.5** — any of those, if designed to display in a common space, **must displace any other symbol or message** while its condition exists.
- **S5.5.4** — when two or more telltales are active, messages must be *"repeated automatically in sequence"* or driver-selectable.
- **S5.5.6(b)** — high beams, turn signal, low tire pressure, passenger air bag off, **and any telltale required to be red must not be cancelable** while the condition exists.
- **S5.3.3(b)** — dimming for *"brakes, highbeams, turn signals, and safety belts may not be adjustable under any driving condition to a level that is invisible."*

**ECE R121 §5.5.1** mirrors this with a narrower privileged set — **brake system malfunction, headlamp driving beam, direction indicator, seat belt**: not co-located (5.5.1.3), must displace others (5.5.1.4), not cancellable (5.5.1.5).

**⚠️ Genuinely surprising provision worth flagging: R121 §5.5.1.6** — *"Unless prescribed in a specific Regulation, the colour requirements regarding tell-tales do not apply when tell-tales appear in a common space."* In a shared digital display, ECE colour mandates lapse.

### ISO standards — what they actually cover

| Standard | What it does |
|---|---|
| ISO 2575 | Symbol library + colour guidance (§5). **No layout.** |
| ISO 4040:2009 *"Location of hand controls, indicators and tell-tales"* | Despite the title, its zone system assigns **hand controls** to reach zones. For indicators/telltales it addresses visibility, not zoning. *(Moderate confidence — abstract only, standard is paywalled.)* |
| ISO 15008 | Legibility of in-vehicle visual presentation: character height, contrast, luminance. Not a priority scheme. R121 §5.3 and ISO 2575 §4.7 both reference it for pixel-matrix rendering. |
| **ISO/TS 16951:2021** | *"Procedures for determining priority of on-board messages presented to drivers."* This is the standard for message prioritisation. *(Title sourced; body paywalled.)* |
| SAE J2402 | Symbols only, harmonised with ISO 2575. No location content. |

### "Red central, amber peripheral" — **not documented**

No authoritative source was found for this as a codified OEM convention — no published research, no OEM style guide. Consumer sources discuss colour-coded urgency but not spatial placement. **Present it as an emergent design heuristic, not a requirement.** It falls out of (a) colour semantics from ISO 2575, (b) the eye-ellipse/field-of-view constraint that anything safety-critical sits inside the steering-wheel aperture, and (c) the common-space displacement rules — not from any rule that says so.

One real OEM data point, from BMW factory service data for the E36: *"The various lamps are positioned at the top center and along the bottom of the cluster display. They are controlled internally by the cluster or externally by other sensors and modules **where required by legislation**."* Note that the stated driver of the split is legislation, not colour.

**Outstanding gap:** NHTSA's *Human Factors Design Guidance for Driver-Vehicle Interfaces* (DOT HS 812 360, Dec 2016) is the most likely home of published telltale prioritisation guidance. Both nhtsa.gov and rosap.ntl.bts.gov returned 403 to automated fetches. Worth a manual download.

## 4. BMW E36

### Dial layout — left to right: FUEL (small) · SPEEDOMETER (large) · TACHOMETER (large) · COOLANT TEMP (small)

Sourced from the BMW factory Owner's Manual, P/N 01 41 9 790 377, © 07/98 (figure 360us319, US 1999 MY, non-M3). **Speedometer is left of the tachometer.** Four discrete circular bezels — the small gauges flank the large ones, they are not inset into them and not full-size.

The two large dials each carry an inset element in their lower portion:
- **Speedometer** → the rectangular **LCD window**
- **Tachometer** → the small arc gauge (economy/MPG on US cars; **oil temperature** on the Euro M3, replacing the *Verbrauchsanzeige*)

**On the oil-temp-vs-oil-pressure dispute for the Euro M3, I can now settle it.** The BMW E36 ECE Electrical Troubleshooting Manual (BMW AG, "E36 ECE 1998", 05/99) instrument-cluster section 6211.0 lists connector **X16 pin 13 = "Oil temperature gauge ← Oil temperature sensor"**, and its component index has **"Oil temperature sensor, B6238 ... 6211.0-02"**. The cluster has a factory oil **temperature** input. One 318ti.org forum thread claiming oil *pressure* is wrong.

### Needles, not segments — three independent confirmations

**Both the coolant temperature gauge and the fuel gauge are continuous analog needle gauges. Neither is segmented.**

1. **Factory manual text** uses needle language explicitly. Fuel: *"If the tilt of the vehicle varies... this may cause the **needle** to fluctuate slightly."* Coolant: *"it is not unusual for the **needle** to rise as far as the edge of the red sector."* The economy gauge is also a needle: *"When the vehicle is stationary, the **needle** returns to zero."*
2. **BMW ETM schematic 6211.0-02** (which I rendered) draws the temperature gauge, tachometer, speedometer and fuel gauge as **round dials with pointer needles**.
3. **Sender types are analog-resistive.** Coolant: B6232 *"Remote thermometer sensor"*, drawn as an NTC thermistor (ϑ) into cluster pin 12. Fuel: *"Immersion tube sensor"* B10/B6, a resistive float sender.

### Scale markings

- **Coolant gauge:** no numbers, no C/H lettering. A **blue sector** (cold), an unmarked normal band, a **red sector** (hot), with a thermometer pictogram in the dial centre. Manual: *"Blue — The engine is still cold... Between the blue and red sectors — Normal operating range... Red — Indicator lamp comes on, the warning 'COOLANT TEMPERATURE' appears in Check Control: engine overheated."*
- **Fuel gauge:** marked **R — 1/2 — F**, fuel-pump pictogram in the centre, black reserve block at the left end of the arc, and (US only) "UNLEADED GASOLINE ONLY" printed on the lower dial face. Low-fuel warning at ≈ 2.1 US gal / 8 L.
- **Tachometer:** 0–7 ×1000, labelled "1/min x1000", with a **red overspeed sector**. ⚠️ The exact rpm where the red sector begins is **per-engine** and not readable from the manual raster — treat printed redline as unverified per variant. Note also that vendor listings quoting "8000 RPM" for an M3 face are quoting the *scale maximum*, while "7000/7400" quote the *start of the red sector*; don't conflate them.
- **Speedometer (US late non-M3):** dual scale, **MPH 20→140 primary, km/h 20→240 secondary**. ⚠️ Per-model **European** speedo maxima come only from aftermarket gauge-face vendors who generalise across model ranges — do not put them in a build guide.

### LCD / odometer

A **single rectangular LCD window inset into the bottom of the speedometer dial**:
- **left:** 6-digit odometer · **right:** trip odometer (0.1 resolution, rolls at 999.9)
- **below, spanning the window:** the **Service Interval Display (SIA)** with printed legends "OIL SERVICE" (left) and "INSPECTION" (right). The SIA is **discrete illuminated lamps, not LCD segments** — green lamps that decrement, plus a yellow (due) and a red (overdue).

Trip reset button: small round button outside the lower-right edge of the fuel gauge bezel. **No gear-position indicator anywhere in the cluster** — the only auto-trans item is a yellow "shift electronics" fault lamp. **No outside-temperature display in the cluster** — that lives in the centre-dash unit.

### Check Control is NOT a panel in the cluster

This is the most commonly misunderstood part. Three physically separate things:

1. **The CC text display** lives in the **LCD matrix of the centre-dash unit** — either the "Check Control with outside temperature display and digital clock" (multifunction clock) or the fuller On-Board Computer. It has its own CHECK key.
2. **A single Check Control warning lamp in the instrument cluster.** Confirmed in the ETM: connector **X17 pin 26 = "Central indicator lamp/check control ← On-board computer"**. Manual: *"Texts with messages and warnings are used to alert the driver to defective systems. In addition, there is a warning lamp in the instrument panel."* It flashes for Priority 1 and stops after 20 s or a CHECK keypress.
3. **The CCM module** behind the dash.

**It is optional**, and only available when the car has the Multi-Function Clock or the OBC. Lighting circuits are **warm-monitored only** — a fault is only detected when the circuit is energised.

Messages, verbatim from the factory manual:
- **Priority 1** (flashing lamp + flashing symbol): *Brake lamp electrical system*, *Brake lamps defective*
- **Priority 2** (appear at ignition position 2, symbols persist): *Brake lamp defective* (single bulb), *Low beams defective*, *Backup lamps defective*, *License plate lamp*, *Washer fluid low*, *Check Control inactive*
- **Priority 3** (status, typically after parking): *Check coolant level* — and *"not displayed while driving"*
- Driven in from the cluster: **COOLANT TEMPERATURE** when the needle enters the red sector
- Self-test: CHECK key at position 2 with no faults → **"CHECK CONTROL OK"**

### Telltale inventory and positions

From the US factory manual figure (positions), cross-checked against the ECE ETM connector pin lists (which give the full superset including Euro-only lamps).

**Top-centre pod, between speedo and tach**, left to right: **battery/charge (red) · high beam (blue) · oil pressure (red)**

**Upper flanks:** left turn arrow (green) between fuel gauge and speedo; right turn arrow (green) between tach and coolant gauge

**Between the big dials, lower:** ASC+T (yellow)

**Bottom strip, full width below all four dials**, left to right as drawn: fog lamps (green) · **"CHECK ENGINE"** text panel · automatic transmission / shift electronics (yellow) · seat belt (red) · **"ABS"** text panel (yellow) · brake warning (red) with printed **"BRAKE FLUID"** and **"PARK BRAKE"** legends · airbag/SRS (red). Low-fuel warning is a pictogram *inside* the fuel dial, not a strip position.

**ETM connector list — the authoritative superset** (BMW E36 ECE ETM 6211.0a/b/c):

*X16 (26-pin white):* 1 high beam · 3/4 turn right/left · 5 EGS fault + ATF temperature · 8 DDE fault (diesel) · 9 preheating (diesel) · 10 rollover protection (convertible) · 13 oil temperature gauge · 14 airbag · 17 handbrake · 18 brake fluid · 19 brake pad wear · 26 **catalytic converter overtemperature**

*X17 (26-pin blue):* 1 trailer turn / oil level (M3) · 5–6 battery charge indicator (terminal 15 + terminal 61 from alternator) · 8 front fog · 11/21 ABS · 12 upshift (M3) / ASC · **14 seat belt — "USA, Canada and Gulf countries"** · 19 oil pressure · 20 SMG fault (M3) · 26 check control

*X271 (12-pin black):* 1 fuel level sender · 5 rear fog

Two things fall out of this that the US manual can't tell you:
- **The seat belt telltale is market-specific** — ECE-market E36s don't have one wired.
- **There is no MIL/check-engine pin in the ECE cluster harness at all** (X16 pins 6, 7, 15, 16, 25 are "not used"). The petrol check-engine lamp is a US/OBD-II feature. The ECE cluster gets a *catalytic converter overtemperature* lamp instead.

**EML:** not present in the US non-M3 lamp list. Whether US-market M3s carry an EML lamp is **unverified** — flag rather than guess.

### Bus architecture

**The E36 cluster is a standalone, hardwired gauge cluster. No I-bus, no K-bus, no CAN.** BMW's bus rollout begins with the E38. Gauges are driven by discrete signals: RPM on cluster wire #20, vehicle speed on X17 pin 2, fuel level as an analog voltage (≈0.2 V empty → 3.53 V full), coolant via a two-wire NTC. What *is* present is a **K-line (ISO 9141 / KWP) diagnostic path** — which is exactly what this project already talks to. The OBC↔cluster link is a dedicated point-to-point serial connection, not a vehicle-wide bus (*protocol details unverified*).

## 5. Bulb check / self-test

### The telltale standards *permit* it; they never *require* it

- **FMVSS 101 S5.3.1(e):** *"A telltale must not emit light except when identifying the malfunction or vehicle condition it is designed to indicate, **or during a bulb check**."*
- **ECE R121 §5.3.5:** *"A tell-tale shall not emit light except when identifying the malfunction or vehicle condition for whose indication it is designed **or during a bulb check**."*

Both are worded as *exceptions to a prohibition*. Neither specifies a duration.

### The mandate lives in the individual system standards

**US:**
- **FMVSS 105 S5.3.2(a):** *"all indicator lamps shall be activated as a check of lamp function either when the ignition (start) switch is turned to the 'on' (run) position when the engine is not running, or when the ignition (start) switch is in a position between 'on' (run) and 'start' that is designated by the manufacturer as a check position."* S5.3.3(b) adds: deactivated at the end of the check unless a malfunction exists.
- **FMVSS 135 S5.5.2** — same, but uniquely also permits *"a single manual action by the driver, such as momentary activation of a test button."*
- **FMVSS 126 S5.3.4** (ESC) and **FMVSS 138 S4.3.3(a)** (TPMS) — same construction. FMVSS 126 S5.3.6 exempts telltales shown in a common space.

**UNECE — UN R13-H §5.2.21.4** (identical text at UN R13 §5.2.1.29.5):

> *"The warning signal(s) mentioned above shall light up when the electrical equipment of the vehicle (and the braking system) is energised. With the vehicle stationary, the braking system shall verify that none of the specified failures or defects are present before extinguishing the signals. Specified failures or defects which should activate the warning signals..., but which are not detected under static conditions, shall be stored upon detection and be displayed at start-up and at all times when the ignition (start) switch is in the 'On' (run) position, as long as the failure or defect persists."*

**ABS specifically — R13-H Annex 6 §4.1.1** explains a behaviour worth mimicking: sensor anomalies undetectable at standstill *"shall be detected not later than when the vehicle speed exceed 10 km/h... verification may be delayed but detected not later than when the vehicle speed exceeds 15 km/h."* That is why an ABS lamp can extinguish at key-on and then re-light once rolling.

### ⚠️ Correction: FMVSS 208 does **not** mandate an airbag illuminate-then-extinguish sequence

The complete text of 49 CFR 571.208 was retrieved and searched. **S4.5.2 in its entirety** requires only that the system *"have a monitoring system with a readiness indicator. The indicator shall monitor its own readiness and shall be clearly visible from the driver's designated seating position."* No sequence, no duration, no bulb-check requirement.

**The widely-repeated "1 to 8 seconds" figure is a misattribution.** The real number is **4 to 8 seconds**, it is in **S7.3**, and it belongs to the **seat belt warning** — not the airbag lamp, and not a bulb check: *"Activates a continuous or intermittent audible signal for a period of not less than 4 seconds and not more than 8 seconds and that activates a continuous or flashing warning light... for not less than 60 seconds."*

The only airbag-adjacent bulb-check language in FMVSS 208 is **S19.2.2(h)**, and it is permissive and applies to the *passenger air bag off* telltale: *"The telltale must not emit light except when any passenger air bag is turned off or during a bulb check upon vehicle starting."*

**Unverified:** whether ECE R94 mandates an airbag telltale self-check. R121 lists the airbag telltales and their colour but prescribes no check sequence; R94 itself was not retrieved. Don't state it.

### No regulation anywhere specifies a bulb-check duration

**The commonly cited "2–4 seconds" has no regulatory basis and no authoritative source was found for it.** The regulations say "activated as a check of lamp function" and, at most, "deactivated at the end of the check"; UN R13/R13-H specify a *completion condition* (the system has verified no faults), not a clock. Two hard, sourced BMW figures both contradict "2–4 s": the E36 SRS lamp runs **5 s**, and the E36 brake-pad-wear lamp runs **30 s**. Cite measured examples, not the folklore number.

### Which lamps don't bulb-check, and the actual mechanism

UN R48 defines two structurally different telltale types:
- ***"Operating tell-tale"*** — *"indicating that a device has been switched ON and is operating correctly or not."*
- ***"Closed-circuit tell-tale"*** — *"indicating that a device has been switched ON, but not indicating whether it is operating correctly or not."*

R48 assigns **circuit-closed** telltales to main beam (6.1.8), front fog (6.3.8), hazard (6.6.8), front position lamps (6.9.8) and rear fog (6.11.8). A circuit-closed telltale is by definition wired to report *switch state*; it has no fault state to self-test, and lighting it at key-on would violate FMVSS 101 S5.3.1(e) / R121 §5.3.5.

**Turn signals are the exception** — R48 6.5.8 requires an *operating* telltale that, on lamp failure, *"is either extinguished, or remains alight without flashing, or shows a marked change of frequency"* (the classic hyperflash). But that is monitored **continuously while in use**, never at key-on.

### E36-specific behaviour

**There is no automatic whole-cluster bulb sweep at key-on.** The factory service data documents none; lamps illuminate individually per their sensor/module state. Several *appear* to bulb-check as a **circuit side effect** rather than by design — the charge lamp lights because alternator field current flows through it, the oil pressure lamp lights because the pressure switch is closed at zero pressure. *(That mechanism explanation is inference from the circuits, not a manual quote.)*

**There IS a deliberate self-test, and it is on key position 1 (terminal R), not position 2.** From BMW's "Instrument Cluster Testing" for 1992–96 E36:

> *"There is a self test that can be carried out on the cluster by pressing the trip odometer reset button and switching the ignition to KL R. All gauges move from the zero position to the maximum display and back again. **The warning lamps are illuminated as a bulb check.** In addition, vehicle specific data is displayed in the LCD matrix as follows: BMW PART NUMBER (6 digits), CODE NUMBER (5 digits), K NUMBER (4 digits), CHASSIS NUMBER (5 digits), SOFTWARE VERSION (3 digits), REVISION INDEX (2 digits). The self test is canceled by switching the ignition off or to KL 15."*

Note the terminal designations — entered at **KL R**, *cancelled* by going to **KL 15**. For 1997–98 E36, E36/5 318ti and Z3 this became a 15-function test menu whose **TEST NO. 01** is the same gauge sweep + lamp test.

**Timed self-tests with real numbers:**
- **SRS: 5 seconds.** *"Each time the ignition is switched 'On', the Supplemental Restraint System (SRS) does a self-test. This is indicated by illumination of the SRS Warning Lamp for five seconds, after which the lamp extinguishes (standby mode) if no faults are detected."* The **lamp circuit itself is one of the monitored items** (checked for open/short). Fault tiering: "minor" faults light it ~2 minutes then extinguish; "non-critical" light it continuously with the system still operational; "critical" light it continuously and disable the system. Controller is the ZAE, introduced MY1994.
- **Brake pad wear: 30 seconds.** *"Once the circuit is rectified the brake pad wear indicator will shut off after first 30 seconds of switching the ignition on"* / *"after the 30 second start-up bulb check."* BMW's own manual calls this a bulb check — useful as a counterexample to the 2–4 s folklore. The US owner's manual describes it differently again: *"Lights up when starter is actuated and goes out when the engine is started."*

---

## Explicitly uncertain — do not state as fact

1. **"2–4 seconds is typical bulb-check duration"** — no source found, and contradicted by the two sourced BMW figures.
2. **"Red central, amber peripheral" as a documented convention** — no authoritative source found.
3. **ECE R94 mandating an airbag self-check** — R94 not retrieved.
4. **Pre-facelift (1992–95) E36 cluster layout** — all cluster-figure evidence is from a 1999 MY US manual. The four-dial order is almost certainly unchanged, but no factory diagram for the early car was obtained.
5. **Whether any E36 shipped without a tachometer** — no evidence either way (absence of evidence only).
6. **Per-model European speedometer maxima and per-engine printed redlines** — vendor data only.
7. **Whether US-market E36 M3s carry an EML lamp.**
8. **Exact within-strip ordering** of the brake-pad-wear, Check Control and rollover-protection lamps in the E36 bottom row.
9. **ISO 4040 and ISO/TS 16951 body text** — paywalled; scopes are from abstracts.
10. **SAE J1053** — appears to be a fastener standard ("Steel Stamped Nuts of One Pitch Thread Design"), not telltale-related. Drop it unless independently verified.

## 1. Display Creator object/primitive vocabulary

Confirmed by a direct screenshot of the "Pages" tab toolbar (Display & Data Training 2015 deck, p.83/88). Top-level project tabs: **Settings | Communications | Channels & Functions | Alarms | Pages | Images | Simulate**. Within the Pages canvas, the drawing-tool icons, left to right, are:

1. **Select/Pointer**
2. **Page** (screen icon — new page)
3. **Group** (folder icon) — confirmed by text: *"it is often a good idea to use groups to collect together parts of the project... it also allows you to hide a group and all of the elements within for testing purposes."*
4. **Switch** — confirmed by text: *"Switches allow you to switch between multiple objects with the use of conditions."* Each Switch holds ordered Switch Groups, each with its own Condition(s); one group may have no condition (becomes the default/fallback); group order = priority order.
5. **Rectangle**
6. **Ellipse/Oval**
7. **Image** (bitmap import)
8. **Animation** (filmstrip icon) — confirmed by text: *"Animation: Create animations from a number of images."*
9. **Text** ("T") — static label
10. A second text-like icon (wavy-line glyph) — almost certainly **Channel Value** (dynamic numeric field bound to a channel), used and aligned distinctly from static Text per the manual's alignment walkthrough
11. **Bar Graph** (icon literally drawn as a small horizontal bar divided into discrete green blocks)
12. A second, vertical-orientation bar icon (vertical bar graph variant)
13. **Dial Gauge** (speedometer icon — confirmed via on-screen callout "Select New Dial Gauge")
14. **Sweep/Arc Gauge** (curved-arc icon, matching the "Sweep" image-library category)
15. One unidentified icon (dashed box with a small mark) — **not verified**, possibly Table or LED indicator

Non-visual **Functions** (from the "Additional Features" page, quoted): *"Timers/Counters... Animation... Simulation... Bit Decode: Decodes a bit stream... Backlight Control... Splash Screen: Set an image to be displayed when the device powers up... Input Signals... Beacons/Lap Timing... M800 CAN Input."*

**Object property panels directly observed:**
- **Ellipse/Rectangle:** Size & Position (Left/Top/Diameter or W×H) → Border (Show Border checkbox, Border Width, Border Colour) → Fill (Show Fill checkbox, **Fill Style dropdown** [only "Solid" seen selected, but a second colour swatch + bidirectional-arrow icon sits next to it, strongly suggesting a **Gradient** option exists — not 100% textually confirmed]).
- **Dial Gauge → "Configure Gauge" dialog:** a **"Ticks"** tab (visually confirmed) — Input Channel; Values: First Angle/Last Angle (default **‑120° to +120°**, a 240° sweep), First Value/Last Value, Major Divisions (count), Minor Divisions (checkbox + count); Text: Decimal Places, First/Last displayed text; plus a right-hand editable table mapping **Tick Value → Tick Text** per major division independently (e.g., raw channel 0–9000 RPM shown with tick text "0"–"9"). A **"Segments"** tab is referenced in Display Creator release-notes search snippets (colour zones, fill-style: proportional vs. "only fill entire segment when reached") but I did not get a direct screenshot of it this session — **partially verified**.
- **Dial Pointer (needle):** Length / Width / Offset numeric fields; Appearance → Element = **"Built-In Dial Pointer"** (vector) or **"Image"** (bitmap, selectable from a "Needle" library category or user-imported).
- Per release-notes snippets (not primary-source verified): dial gauges can have **multiple dial needles**, each with its own visibility Condition; a **"Physics"** setting gives needles/bars simulated inertia by default, disable via "Do not apply physics."
- **Channels:** created ahead of time in a Channels tab, or inline while building an element; linked to a DBC signal (the DBC is generated by Dash Manager and imported). **Enumerators** map raw integer/state values to text (e.g., gear channel −1→"R", 0→"N"), with a dedicated "Gear Display" data type.
- **Z-order** (drag up/down a layer list) and **Alignment** (multi-select, right-click → Alignment → Top/etc., first-selected = reference) are both explicit, discrete UI operations.

---

## 2. Round gauge + bar graph tick/redline rendering

**Round gauge (dial):** Ticks are **procedurally drawn**, not baked into a bitmap — Major/Minor division counts are numeric fields in the Configure Gauge dialog, confirmed by direct screenshot. Default sweep is **‑120° to +120°** (0° = top-centre, positive = clockwise toward bottom-centre, negative = anti-clockwise toward bottom-centre) — quoted from the training deck: *"0 degrees is top centre. Positive is clockwise to bottom centre and negative is anti-clockwise to bottom centre. The Minor and Major divisions set the number of tick marks on the dial."*

The decorative **bezel/"Surround," by contrast, is bitmap-based, not vector** — Display Creator ships a **"Dial"** image-library category of photorealistic brushed-chrome/silver ring textures (named e.g. `MoTeC-DL-09.png` at 1004×1004px down to `MoTeC-DL-12.png` at 511×511px). The training walkthrough shows layering one of these bitmaps via Z-order, then painting a solid black **Ellipse** (no border) on top to mask the bitmap's unwanted inner face texture before re-drawing ticks on top of that mask — a manual mask-and-layer technique, quoted: *"we create an oval that will cover the rings, allowing us to put our own over the top... The Z-Order needs to be correct so that the inner rings are covered but the dial numbers are not."*

From actual rendered examples (C125 manual, real unit photos): dial faces appear in **both a light/silver skin** (white face, black ticks/numerals, red arc wedge for the redline zone only, black needle with red tip) **and a dark skin** (black/navy face, white ticks, a filled colour arc — amber/orange from 0 up to the current value in one photographed C187 example, white for the remainder, with small red tick marks right at the redline value). One photographed example had **no needle at all** — the "dial" was a pure filled radial ring (a circular progress-bar look), confirming the round gauge can render as a needle instrument or as a needle-less filled arc.

**Bar graph (tachometer):** Two shapes observed — straight **linear** bar and curved **sweep/arc** bar — both rendered as a **continuous colour fill** from zero to the current value (not discrete rectangular blocks) in every worked example I opened, bounded by scale numerals above the track. Fill colour is a project choice (seen in orange-red on one unit, bright cyan on another). A thin perpendicular line across the bar marks the **user-configurable, optionally gear-dependent shift point** (manual: *"A fully programmable shift point can be displayed, which can also be gear dependent"*). Small red tick marks (not necessarily a filled zone) denote the redline value on the sweep-bar examples. Dash Manager's underlying Bar 1/Bar 2 dialog (screenshot obtained) works on **boundary points** (Left / Intermediate 1 / Intermediate 2 / Right) each assigned one of 3 colours, plus a **"Show intermediate tick marks"** checkbox and a **"Change whole bar colour"** checkbox (flips the *entire* bar to a warning colour rather than just colouring a zone) — this is a continuous-fill-with-colour-zones model, not true discrete segmentation. Release-notes search snippets additionally describe a **segmented Fill Style** ("fill only entire segments when the channel reaches the end value for that segment") as a distinct, selectable mode in Display Creator specifically — **not independently screenshot-verified** this session. Numeric RPM readout sits in a **separate field beside/below** the gauge cluster, not overlaid on the bar itself; a large gear-number readout typically occupies the visual centre of the cluster.

---

## 3. Fonts/typography and label conventions

**Exact font family names: NOT FOUND / NOT VERIFIED.** No manual, datasheet, or training page I reached names a specific typeface, and I did not get a screenshot of a Text/Channel-Value font-properties panel.

Observed conventions from rendered real examples:
- Numerals are **bold, large, blocky, slightly tech-styled** — manual placeholder examples deliberately show max-width dummy digits (`9:99.99`, `9999999999999`) to indicate the field must reserve space for full digit counts.
- **Alignment is not universal.** In the clearest photographed C187 factory page, numeric values are **left-aligned** flush with their label's left edge (`ENGINE OIL TMP / 110`, `GBOX OIL TMP / 92`, `DIFF OIL TMP / 113` all start at the same left X). A different, smaller/table-style fixed layout (bordered "spreadsheet" rows: `ENG TEMP | 97.0`) showed the value **right-aligned** in its cell instead. Both conventions exist across MoTeC's own stock layouts — I cannot report a single fixed rule.
- Labels are consistently **UPPERCASE, short abbreviations** ("ENG TEMP," "OIL PRESS," "GBOX OIL TMP," "DIFF OIL TMP," "WATER TMP," "MAX SPEED," "REFERENCE LAP," "GAIN/LOSS"), smaller point size than the value, positioned directly above it, and usually rendered in an accent colour (orange/amber, cyan, or red) distinct from the value's high-contrast white/black.
- **Units are not appended inline** to the large numerals in any stock example I saw (e.g. plain "482" for oil pressure, no "kPa" suffix on-screen); unit selection is a separate software setting (Dash Manager "Units" dropdown, e.g. "volt (V)"). Time values use colon+decimal formatting ("2:24.50").
- Mode/page label ("RACE," "PAGE") sits top-left, bold, sometimes italic, uppercase.

---

## 4. Alarm rendering behaviour

Directly quoted from the C125 User Manual and cross-confirmed by a real-unit product photo:

- **Active/unacknowledged alarm:** a full-width bar along the **bottom edge of the screen**, overwriting whatever numeric content was there, in **bright/vivid red** with bold white/cream **uppercase, centred** text (photographed real example: `ENGINE HOT`). Manual: *"When an alarm is activated, a message is shown along the bottom of the display until it is acknowledged... The message can be defined as required and can include the current sensor reading or the sensor reading when the alarm was triggered."*
- **States** (verbatim): "Active and unacknowledged," "Inactive and unacknowledged" (condition cleared but not yet acked — keeps displaying), "Active and acknowledged" (true but suppressed from view), "Inactive."
- **Acknowledgement:** physical Acknowledge Button, or automatic timeout; a configurable "do not display this message again until … seconds have elapsed" suppression window follows acknowledgement.
- **Priority:** only the highest-priority unacknowledged alarm shows at a time; as each is acked, the next-highest appears.
- **Alarm Status Panel** (off by default, toggled via the Acknowledge button when no message is showing): shows up to **6** active-and-acknowledged alarms in a **dark maroon/brick-red** bar — visibly less saturated than the bright-red unacknowledged bar — bold white uppercase text, laid out as 1 full-width bar, 2 halves, or a 2×2 (or denser) grid depending on count. This panel is hidden whenever a new unacknowledged alarm needs the space.
- **Escalation/gating logic:** up to 6 chained comparisons per alarm; auto-increment/decrement of the trigger threshold on repeat triggers (with a cap and an optional reset-after-time); can be gated on other channels (example given: engine-temp alarm suppressed unless ground speed has been >50 km/h for 30s, to avoid false triggers from pit-stop heat soak); alarms can be scoped to specific display-mode pages (Warm-up/Practice/Race).
- **Inside Display Creator specifically:** "Alarm 1" auto-imports from the Dash Manager alarm setup; unlimited additional alarms can be added, each with its own multi-condition logic, on/off delays, and a fully custom on-screen appearance (edited like any other page object, not a fixed template).
- Manual explicitly recommends pairing the on-screen message with a physical warning light, since the screen alone may not grab attention fast enough.

---

## 5. Shift lights

- **C125:** 10 full-colour RGB LEDs built into the top bezel arc, individually programmable colour/function/intensity — called "**10 stage shift lights**" in the manual (`Functions > Shift Light Module`).
- **C127:** **16** full-colour RGB LEDs (datasheet, both revisions).
- **Setup is a documented two-stage workflow** (training deck, quoted): (1) `Functions > Shift Lights` — pick the driving channel (typically RPM, though boost/G-force are usable), and *"remember to put the RPM signal lower than the actual RPM you wish to shift at... the driver will always need to see the light before he knows to change gear"*; set **Hysteresis** to prevent flicker right at the threshold; optionally make it **Gear Dependent** (requires a Gear channel). (2) `Functions > Shift Light Module` — assign physical LED stage/colour/pattern.
- **Real-world colour pattern observed** (photo of an actual C125 with all 10 LEDs lit): symmetric **red–red–amber–green–green–green–green–amber–red–red**, i.e., green in the centre, amber next, red at both extreme ends — read as a "safe (centre) → caution → shift-now (edges)" convention. This is *inferred from one photographed example, not a quoted spec sentence* — mark as inferred, not documented default.
- A separate marketing photo (D175) showed the same 10-LED strip lit in a **full rainbow** (red-pink-magenta-cyan-blue-green-yellow-orange-red-red) — best read as a "look how many RGB colours we support" capability demo, not a functional convention.
- **Shift vs. warning distinction** (clearest documented answer, from the external SLM/SLM-C module, which uses the same Functions menu logic as the built-in C125/C127 LEDs): patterns are **priority-ordered in a list**, top = highest priority. Quoted: *"if a pattern has a high priority, e.g. Warning Lights, it cannot be affected by another pattern condition lower in the list becoming true."* So Warning and Shift are not architecturally different signal types — both are "patterns" on the same LED strip — but a Warning pattern is simply placed **above** the Shift pattern in priority order, so it visually pre-empts/overrides the shift indication whenever both are true. SLM also supports flashing and two-colour toggling per LED.

---

## 6. C125/C127 hardware specs (design-constraining)

**C125** (datasheet + manual, quoted):
- Display: *"Colour TFT LCD, anti-reflective"*, *"Resolution: 800 x 480, anti-aliased graphics"*, ~125 mm (5") diagonal, "ultra bright" / sunlight-readable.
- 10 full-colour RGB LEDs; 12 customisable fixed-layout options + optional Display Creator; 48 scrollable message lines; 3 display-mode pages; adjustable backlight.
- Power 6–32 V DC; reverse-battery and transient protection.
- Optional 120 MB logging upgrade, up to 500 samples/sec.

**C127** (two full datasheet revisions extracted directly, Part 18036 & Part 18048 — quoted):
- *"Type: Colour TFT LCD, anti-reflective"*; *"Resolution: 800 x 480, anti-aliased graphics"*; *"High resolution 178 mm (7" approx) colour LCD display"*; *"High brightness for sunlight readability."*
- *"16 full colour (RGB) LEDs; colour, function and intensity are fully programmable."*
- 48 scrollable message lines; 3 programmable modes.
- Newer revision (2018) adds a **composite video input** ("live on-screen footage, for example from a rear view camera (requires Display Creator)").
- Power 6–32 V DC, **0.8 A typical at 14 V**; operating temp internal **‑20°C to 80°C**, with an explicitly documented thermal-derating behaviour: *"above 60°C maximum backlight brightness progressively reduced"* — i.e., brightness is throttled by firmware under heat.
- **IP67**, dependent on connector-cavity sealing; physical size 196.2 × 122.5 × 24.9 mm; weight 615–630 g; 34-pin connector (+ mini-USB on the newer revision).

**Brightness in nits/cd/m²: NOT FOUND anywhere I reached.** MoTeC's public materials describe brightness only qualitatively ("ultra bright," "high brightness for sunlight readability," "high contrast") — I found no numeric candela figure for any C-series model.

**C1212, C185, C187 — search-snippet only, NOT independently PDF-verified this session (lower confidence):** same 800×480 anti-aliased anti-reflective TFT family; C1212 ≈311mm/12"; C185≈125mm/5", C187≈178mm/7"; C18x series ships with **250 MB logging standard** (vs. C125/C127's logging as a paid upgrade), USB-upgradeable to 500 MB.

**D-Series contrast** (training-deck slide, quoted): *"D Series (D153/D175)... Display only... No logging hardware... Switch and dial inputs... CAN communications"* vs. *"C Series (C125/7 and C185/7)... Display Loggers... 120MB to 500MB memory... Replaces CDL3/SDL3/ADL3."* This confirms C-series is MoTeC's positioned successor to the old ADL/SDL/CDL line, but I did **not** get further into the ADL/SDL/CDL screens' own visual conventions (e.g., dot-matrix vs. early colour rendering) — mark as not reached.

---

## 7. Gradients, glow, bezels, skeuomorphism

**Present, and taught as the normal workflow — not absent:**

- **Bezels are bitmap, not vector.** Display Creator's asset library includes image categories **Gear, Icon, Lighting, Needle, Panels, Sweep, Dial** — the "Dial" category specifically holds photorealistic brushed-chrome/silver ring textures up to 1004×1004px, applied by import + Z-order layering, with vector Ellipses used only as masks to hide unwanted parts of the bitmap. This is an explicitly skeuomorphic, photographic-bezel workflow taught in MoTeC's own official training material, not a hack.

# Finding meaning in unknown bytes by watching them change: tool survey

## 0. Read this first — your specific answer may already be published

RomRaider ships a **BMW DS2 logger definition for MS41/MS42/MS43** with real RAM addresses. If your E36 is an M52 on MS41.1:

| | Address | Type | Expression | Units |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TPS** | `0xE8D7` | uint8 | `x*100/255` | % |
| **Vehicle speed** | `0xDA63` | uint8 | `x` | km/h (1:1) |

Cross-check anchors from the same file: RPM `0xDA2A` uint16 `x`; MAF `0xDA34` uint16 `x*0.25` kg/h; IAT `0xDA50` uint8 `x*0.747-48`; ECT `0xDA5A` uint8 `x*0.747-48`; Load `0xFAFC` uint16 `x*0.0212` mg/stroke; IPW `0xEF7E` uint16 `x*0.00534` ms.

Source: https://github.com/0x000NULL/tuning/blob/main/BMW/MS41%20Logger%20Definitions.xml (89 `ecuparam`s, ECU IDs `1405854, 1406464, SHINDE1, 1429373, 1429861, 1432401, 1437806, 1440176`).

**Caveat worth resolving before you build anything:** coolant, IAT, RPM and vehicle speed all cluster in `0xDA2A–0xDA63`, a ~57-byte span. But TPS is at `0xE8D7` and Load at `0xFAFC` — thousands of bytes away. A single 252-byte window cannot contain both your known injection-load byte and TPS if these addresses are right. Dump your window's base address and check it against the table. Either your window isn't the `0xDA00` block, or your "injection load" is a different quantity. Companion defs: https://github.com/Rustle333/Siemens-MS43, https://github.com/Rustle333/MSS52.

That said — the tooling research below is what you asked for, and you still want the discovery UI, both to verify these and because published defs are per-ECU-ID and yours may not match.
