## 1. Cheat Engine — the exact scan vocabulary

### Scan types (verbatim UI names)

Available on both First and Next Scan:
- **Exact Value**
- **Bigger than...**
- **Smaller than...**
- **Value between...** — "Finds all values within the specified interval (inclusive)"
- **Unknown initial value** — the entry point when you know nothing

Next Scan only (these compare against the *previous* scan's stored value per address):
- **Increased value** / **Increased value by...**
- **Decreased value** / **Decreased value by...**
- **Changed value**
- **Unchanged value**
- **Value between... at least xx%**
- **Increased by... at least xx%** / **Decreased by... at least xx%**

Plus two orthogonal modifiers that sit next to the dropdown:
- **Compare to first/saved scan** vs **Compare to previous scan** — changes the reference frame of every relative operator
- **Not** — inverts the selected scan type

Value types: **Binary** (with `?`/`*` bit wildcards), **Byte**, **2 Bytes**, **4 Bytes**, **8 Bytes**, **Float**, **Double**, **String**, **Array of byte** (`??`/`**` wildcards), **All** (unions Byte/2/4/8/Float/Double when you don't know the type).

Scan options: **Fast Scan (aligned scan)** with configurable alignment, **Last digits**, readonly checkbox, memory range start/stop, **Enable Speedhack**, **Unrandomizer**.

Buttons: **First Scan**, **Next Scan**, **Undo scan**, **New scan**. Undo is one level and it matters — a mis-timed scan kills the true candidate and undo is the only recovery.

URLs: https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File:Scan_types · https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File:Value_types · https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File:Memory_scan_settings

### The percentage scan — the most underrated feature, and directly your TPS answer

https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File:Percentage_scans_and_compare_to_saved_results

The workflow: unknown-initial-value scan establishes a baseline = 100%. Later, select **Compare to first scan**, **Value between...**, tick the **between %** checkbox, enter e.g. 95–97%.

Why this matters to you: *you cannot know TPS's raw value, but you can know its physical percentage.* Hold the throttle at what you judge to be half travel and search for "between 45% and 55% of the value seen at WOT." The docs are explicit that this is scale-invariant — "it doesn't matter if the values are multiplied, you will find them easily using this method." It was designed for health bars you can only see graphically; a throttle pedal is the same problem.

### Address list / watch table

https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File%3AAddressCheat_List

Columns: **Active** (freeze checkbox) | **Description** | **Address** | **Type** | **Value**.

Freeze has three modes, not one: normal (`=`), increase-only (`+`), decrease-only (`−`), restoring "every few milliseconds (the interval can be changed in the settings)."

Hotkeys: `Enter` modify value, `Ctrl+Enter` edit description, `Ctrl+Alt+Enter` change address, `Space` toggle freeze, numpad `+`/`−` for directional freeze. Entries drag to reorder and nest under **Create Header** groups.

Right-click: **Browse this memory region**, **Find out what accesses this address**, **Find out what writes to this address**, **Pointer scan for this address**, **Recalculate new addresses**.

The two "find out what..." items are debugger breakpoint features. **They have no analogue for you** — you have a serial peephole, not a debugger. Skip them; everything else transfers.

### scanmem / GameConqueror (open-source Linux equivalent)

https://github.com/scanmem/scanmem · https://www.mankier.com/1/scanmem

The CLI operator syntax is more compact than CE's dropdown and maps better to a keyboard-driven web UI:

| Input | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | current value is exactly n |
| `n..m` | range, inclusive |
| `>` | increased (bare) / greater than n (with arg) |
| `<` | decreased / less than n |
| `+` `[n]` | increased by n |
| `-` `[n]` | decreased by n |
| `=` `[n]` | unchanged / equal to n |
| `!=` `[n]` | changed / not equal to n |
| `snapshot` | "Match any value. This is useful when an initial value or range is not known" |

Commands: `pid`, `list [max]`, `set [match-id=]value[/delay]`, `delete`, `reset`, `watch match-id` ("Monitor the value of match-id, and print its value as it changes"), `lregions`, `dregion`, `option`, `update`.

`watch` is worth noting — a single-address live tail, separate from the match list. GameConqueror is the GTK front-end: scan entry + type dropdown + results list on top, a lock/description/address/type/value cheat table underneath.

### BizHawk RAM Search — the one built for slow, frame-stepped observation

https://tasvideos.org/EmulatorResources/RamSearch

This is the closest fit to 1 Hz sampling, because TAS workflows are inherently frame-by-frame and deliberate.

**Compare To** (four options): **Previous Value** · **Specific Value** · **Specific Address** · **Number of Changes**

**Compare operators**: Less Than, Greater Than, Less than or equal, Greater than or equal, Equal to, Not Equal to, **Different By []** ("Keeps values that are less then or greater than the compare value by the amount typed into the edit box"), **Modulo [] Is**.

**The "Number of Changes" column is the single best idea in this whole survey for your use case.** Per the docs: *"RAM search keeps track of values every frame. Each time they change, the change counter increases."* The canonical trick: move right for exactly 6 frames, then search **Changes = 6** to find the position variable.

At 1 Hz over 252 bytes this is nearly free and devastatingly effective. Blip the throttle exactly 4 times over 60 samples; TPS-related bytes have a change count in a narrow band, while RPM (changes constantly) and coolant temp (changes rarely) are excluded by the same filter. It also survives your slow link in a way that per-sample increased/decreased does not, because it's an aggregate over the whole window rather than a comparison of two adjacent samples.

Also: **Preview** — visualize what a search *will* remove before committing. Given that a mis-timed Next Scan at 1 Hz is expensive, preview-before-commit is worth building.

## 2. CAN reverse-engineering tools — byte-change visualisation

### 2a. cabana (deanlee's actively-maintained fork) — steal this wholesale

https://github.com/deanlee/openpilot-cabana

This fork has evolved well past comma.ai's original and contains a **literal Cheat Engine clone**. Headline features, verbatim:

- **Live bit heatmap** — "bit flips flash on change and fade out, instantly revealing active signals"
- **Pattern coloring** — "bytes auto-colored by trend: increasing, decreasing, toggling, or noisy"
- **Find Similar Bits** — "discover related signals across messages and buses"
- **Find Signal** — "search all messages by value range or threshold"
- **Bit muting** — "suppress known bits to isolate undocumented signals"
- **Sparklines** — "inline signal previews in the message list"

Colour table:

| Colour | Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Green | Increasing | "byte value is steadily climbing (e.g., a counter)" |
| Red | Decreasing | "byte value is steadily dropping" |
| Amber | Toggle | "bits flipping back and forth between states (e.g., flags)" |
| Purple | Noisy | "High-entropy data with no discernible trend (e.g., CRC/Encryption)" |
| Grey | Static | "data is currently inactive or hasn't changed recently" |

**I pulled the actual classifier out of the source** — `src/core/streams/message_state.cc`. It is ~20 lines and directly portable to JS:

```c
constexpr float TOGGLE_EMA_ALPHA       = 0.15f;  // ~6-sample half-life
constexpr int8_t TREND_STREAK_MAX      = 8;      // saturating limit
constexpr int8_t TREND_STREAK_THRESHOLD= 4;      // consecutive same-direction changes
constexpr float NOISE_EMA_THRESHOLD    = 0.55f;  // above this = noisy

// on every byte change:
a.toggle_ema += TOGGLE_EMA_ALPHA;
a.last_change_ts = current_ts;
const int delta = new_byte - old_byte;
const bool is_toggle = (delta == -a.last_delta) && (abs(a.trend_streak) < TREND_STREAK_THRESHOLD);
if (is_toggle)      a.trend_streak = 0;
else if (delta > 0) a.trend_streak = (a.trend_streak > 0) ? min(a.trend_streak+1, MAX) : 1;
else if (delta < 0) a.trend_streak = (a.trend_streak < 0) ? max(a.trend_streak-1,-MAX) : -1;

if      (abs(a.trend_streak) >= TREND_STREAK_THRESHOLD) pattern = trend_streak>0 ? Increasing : Decreasing;
else if (is_toggle)                                     pattern = Toggle;
else if (a.toggle_ema > NOISE_EMA_THRESHOLD)            pattern = RandomlyNoisy;
```

Plus an idle decay path: if a byte doesn't change and `toggle_ema <= NOISE_EMA_THRESHOLD`, `trend_streak /= 2` each tick until it hits 0 and the classification clears.

**The fade function** (`colorFromDataPattern`) is adaptive to message rate — important for you, because at 1 Hz a fixed fade would be invisible:

```c
double decay_limit = 1.5;
if (freq > 0) decay_limit = clamp(2.0 / freq, 0.4, 2.5);
if (elapsed >= decay_limit) return TRANSPARENT;
float t = elapsed / decay_limit;
float intensity = (1-t) * (1-t);          // quadratic ease-out
uint32_t alpha = 230.0f * intensity;
```

At 1 Hz that clamps to a 2.0 s decay — a byte that changed stays visibly lit for two full samples. Palette: Increasing `#2ecc71`, Decreasing `#e74c3c`, Toggle `#f1c40f`, Noisy `#9b59b6` (light theme; darker variants for dark).

**Bit muting** (`muteActiveBits`) — a two-second lookback that ORs every recently-changed bit into a suppression mask:

```c
static constexpr double kMuteActivityWindowSec = 2.0;
const double cutoff = ts - kMuteActivityWindowSec;
for each byte i, for each bit b:
    if (bit_change_ts_[i][b] > cutoff) active_bits |= (0x80 >> b);
suppressed_mask[i] |= active_bits;
```

The interaction: do the thing you *don't* care about, click Mute, those bits go grey permanently. Then do the thing you *do* care about and only new bits light up. This is "hide static bytes" inverted, and it's better — static bytes are boring but *constantly-noisy* bytes are the actual problem.

**Find Signal** — `src/tools/findsignal.cc`. Cheat Engine, verbatim, for CAN. The buttons literally read **First Scan** / **Next Scan** / **Undo** / **New Scan**, and the status line reads *"%1 candidate(s) remaining. Right-click to create signal, double-click to open message."*

Compare modes (indices 0–7 absolute, 8–13 relative — relative only meaningful on Next Scan):

```
Any Value | = Exact Value | ≠ Not Equal | > Greater Than | ≥ Greater or Equal
< Less Than | ≤ Less or Equal | Between A…B
↕ Changed | = Unchanged | ↑ Increased | ↓ Decreased | ↑ Increased By | ↓ Decreased By
```

Candidate enumeration is dumb brute force, and that's the point:

```cpp
for (int size = min_size; size <= max_size; ++size)
  for (int start = 0; start <= total_bits - size; ++start) {
      s.sig.start_bit = start; s.sig.size = size;
      s.value = s.sig.toPhysical(dat, len);
      initial_signals.push_back(s);
  }
```

Inputs: Bus, Address (comma-separated hex, blank = all), **Scan At** (seconds, with a **Now** button), **Size** min–max spinners, **Little endian** checkbox, **Signed** checkbox, **Factor**, **Offset**.

Result columns: **Message | Signal (start|size) | Prev Value | Value | Δ** — with Δ coloured green `#22c55e` when positive, red `#ef4444` when negative. Signal column renders as `12|8 [LU]` (start|size, endianness letter, sign letter).

Two details worth copying exactly: (1) the candidate parameters lock after First Scan and only unlock on New Scan, so you can't corrupt a narrowing run; (2) history is a stack of candidate lists, so Undo is O(1) and unlimited, not one-level like Cheat Engine's.

**Find Similar Bits** — `src/tools/findsimilarbits.cc`. Pick a reference `(message, byte index, bit index)`, then for every other `(address, byte, bit)` in the capture, count mismatches against the reference bit's live value:

```cpp
mismatched[i*8 + j] += equal ? (bit != bit_to_find) : (bit == bit_to_find);
...
if (float perc = (mismatched[i] / (double)cnt) * 100; perc < 50)
    result.push_back({address, i/8, i%8, mismatched[i], cnt, perc});
sort(result, {}, &mismatched_struct::perc);
```

Result columns: `address | byte idx | bit idx | mismatches | total msgs | % mismatched`, ascending. UI has an **Equal: Yes/No** dropdown (find agreement or find anti-correlation) and a **Min msg count** guard defaulted to 100. The `< 50%` cut is just "better than a coin flip."

This is binary correlation ranking against a known reference, in 30 lines. For you, the reference is a *derived* bit — "is the throttle open?" — computed from any known channel or supplied by hand.

**Endianness by drag direction** — `binary_view.cc` has a `Settings::DragDirection` enum: `MsbFirst`, `LsbFirst`, `AlwaysLE`, `AlwaysBE`. Under the first two, dragging left-to-right vs right-to-left across bits *sets the endianness of the signal you just created*. Very slick, zero extra UI.

### 2b. SavvyCAN

Docs: https://www.savvycan.com/docs/

**Sniffer Window** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/sniffer.html) — bytes that decrease render red, bytes that increase render green. Refresh 200 ms. IDs unseen for 5 s turn red then vanish.

Four options that are each a distinct good idea:
- **Never Expire IDs** — keeps a stable row set so things don't jump around
- **Notch** — "will remember all the bits that were set in the last 200ms window and will not color the output if those bits are toggled in the future." Click repeatedly to accumulate. **Unnotch** resets. Same concept as cabana's bit muting, arrived at independently.
- **Mute notched bits** — stronger: notched bytes "ignore any notched bits and not even change the display to update if only notched bits were changed"
- **Fade inactive bytes** — bytes that stop updating "gradually fade toward white, ensuring only data which is actively changing will be very visible"
- **View Bits** — per-bit blocks: black = set/unchanged, white = unset/unchanged, red = freshly unset, green = freshly set

**Flow View** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/flowview.html) — an 8×8 bit grid plus a byte-value graph, with **playback**. "Bits which are white are currently 0 or off. Bits which are black are 1 or on." Green = newly on this frame, red = newly off. **Auto Reference** compares against the previous frame; static reference compares against a pinned frame (e.g. the first).

The graph "plots all eight data bytes. The '+' in the center marks the 'current' time. You can thus see both into the future and the past (relative to the current frame)." Playback controls: step back / stop / step forward, play backward / pause / play forward, adjustable speed, Loop Playback, **Live Mode**, **Synchronize windows**, and **seek to specific values** (enter a target byte value, playback auto-stops on match).

**A past-and-future window centred on "now" is the right shape for 1 Hz.** You have very few samples; showing ±30 s around the cursor costs nothing and lets the eye do the correlation.

**Range State Window** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/rangestate.html) — the "Fuzzy Scope" you were thinking of. It "searches for signals that seem to vary somewhat coherently" and openly admits it "will generate a lot of false positives but it will still provide some decent ideas for where to look for signals."

Parameters: **ID Filter list**, **Sensitivity** ("a subjective measurement"), **Min Signal Size** (down to 1 bit), **Max Signal Size**, **Granularity** (bit jump width — set 8 to only consider byte-aligned starts), **Signal Mode** (big endian / little endian / both), **Signed Mode** (unsigned / signed / both). Button: **Recalculate Candidate Signals**. Output list "Candidate Signals" with ID, start bit, length, signed/unsigned, endianness.

The interaction that matters: **arrow-key through the candidate list and each one previews as a graph.** You are not reading numbers, you are flipping through plots looking for a shape you recognise. At 252 bytes × 3 widths × 2 endian × 2 sign ≈ 3000 candidates, arrow-key-through-plots is genuinely viable at ~2/second.

**Frame Details** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/framedetails.html) — per byte: which bits changed, value ranges encountered, histograms both graphical and textual, "the number of times a specific value occurred." Top-right: "A histogram of all the bits and the number of times each bit was set" — useful to "quickly visually see where data has changed." Bottom-right: "Each individual byte as its value varies over time." There's a logarithmic toggle for the bit counts, which matters because flip counts span orders of magnitude.

**File Comparison** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/filecomparison.html) — the differential-analysis workflow, and it maps perfectly onto your problem. Capture a baseline with the feature *off* ("vehicle idling without gear shifts"), capture with the feature *on* ("shifting gears several times"), diff. Output tree: IDs only in file of interest / IDs only in reference / IDs in both, the last with sub-nodes showing "bits set only on one side and not the other" and "values only found on one side or the other." The doc's own framing: *"Somewhere in the differences should be the gear selection you couldn't find. The list ought to be much more narrow than just 'shooting in the dark.'"*

**Manual signal graphing** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/graphsetup.html) — the no-DBC ad-hoc definition form, which is exactly the minimum field set you need: **Name**, **ID**, **Data Len** (bits), **Little Endian** checkbox, start bit picked by clicking an 8×8 grid ("Click on the start bit and the rest of the bits will automatically be selected"), **Signed**, **Mask**, **Bias**, **Scale**, **Stride**, **Color**.

**Signal Editor** (https://github.com/collin80/SavvyCAN/blob/master/help/signaleditor.md) — full DBC field set: Signal Name, Bit Length, Start Bit, Byte Order (checked = little endian), Type (unsigned int / signed int / single float / double float / string), **Scale**, **Bias**, Min Value ("purely informational"), Max Value, Units Name, Receiving Node, multiplexing, **Value Tables** (text substitution, e.g. `0x10 = "PARK"`), Comments. Bitfield grid: start bit is black with diagonal stripes, other bits in the signal are green with stripes the other way, bits claimed by other signals get their own colours.

## 3. ECU tuning / RAM watch tools

### RomRaider

The Logger DTD (https://github.com/RomRaider/RomRaider/blob/master/definitions/logger.dtd) is the smallest schema that covers everything you need:

```dtd
<!ELEMENT address ( #PCDATA ) >
<!ATTLIST address length CDATA #IMPLIED >          <!-- default 1 -->
<!ATTLIST address bit ( 0..31 ) #IMPLIED >         <!-- default -1 = no bit extract -->

<!ELEMENT conversion ( replace* ) >
<!ATTLIST conversion expr        CDATA #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST conversion format      ( 0 | 0.0 | 0.00 | ... ) #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST conversion storagetype ( int8|int16|uint8|uint16|int32|uint32|float ) #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion endian      CDATA #IMPLIED >  <!-- default BIG -->
<!ATTLIST conversion units       CDATA #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST conversion gauge_min   CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion gauge_max   CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion gauge_step  CDATA #IMPLIED >
```

**The most important structural decision: one parameter has N conversions.** Units is not a label, it's a selector — the user picks °C vs °F at runtime and each carries its own expression, format, and gauge range. For a discovery tool this generalises beautifully: one address, several *competing hypotheses* about what it means, switchable live.

**Default gauge ranges keyed on the units string** (`ConverterMaxMinDefaults.java`) — steal this table verbatim, it makes a newly-defined parameter render sensibly with zero configuration:

```
"%"    0→100 step 10      "c"    -20→200 step 20     "rpm"   0→8000 step 1000
"km/h" 0→300 step 20      "mph"  0→200  step 20      "v"     0→5    step 0.5
"bar"  -1.5→3 step 0.5    "psi"  -20→40 step 5       "g/s"   0→400  step 20
"degrees" -15→60 step 5   "ms"   0→100  step 10      "lambda" 0.5→1.5 step 0.1
fallback: 0→100 step 10
```

Type "km/h" into a units box and get a 0–300 axis for free. That's a plausibility check disguised as a convenience.

**`parameter` vs `ecuparam`** (https://www.romraider.com/RomRaider/LoggerXMLReferenceGuide): `<parameter>` is a documented, manufacturer-standard PID with one address valid across all ECUs, gated by **capability bits** (`ecubyteindex` + `ecubit` index into a bitmask the ECU returns at init — if the bit is 0, RomRaider *hides the parameter entirely*). `<ecuparam>` is a reverse-engineered RAM address that differs per calibration ID, carrying `<ecu id="...">` children each with their own `<address>`. Conventionally named with a `*` suffix in the UI to mark "this is RE'd, not documented."

`group`/`subgroup`/`groupsize` batch several ecuparams into **one memory read** — release notes: *"Group individual DS2 ECU queries into a single memory read start address."* That is literally your 252-byte block.

**Derived parameters** via `<depends>`/`<ref>` — computed channels with no address, letting a user test hypotheses without code:

```xml
<parameter id="P200" name="Engine Load (Calculated)">
    <depends><ref parameter="P8"/><ref parameter="P12"/></depends>
    <conversions>
        <conversion units="g/rev" expr="(P12*60)/P8" format="0.00"/>
    </conversions>
</parameter>
```

Note `[P7:psi]` syntax — reference another parameter *in a specific unit*.

Expression language is **JEP** with one custom function: `BitWise(mask, x, op)` where op 1=AND, 2=OR, and mask must be decimal. Real MS41 usage: `BitWise(8,x,1)/8` extracts bit 3 as 0/1; `!BitWise(32,x,1)/32` is an inverted bit 5.

`<replace value="8" with="Closed Loop"/>` is the discrete lookup escape hatch, applied *after* conversion — for enum-ish bytes this beats a formula.

**Live data table columns: `Logger Data | Min Value | Current Value | Max Value | Units`**, with min/max session-accumulated. Free range discovery on every byte simultaneously. A byte that has covered 0–255 in one drive is not coolant temp.

Profiles (`profile.dtd`) are three independent per-parameter checkboxes — `livedata`, `graph`, `dash` — plus a remembered `units` choice.

ROM-side (`ecu_defs.dtd`) adds the thing the logger format lacks: **two formulas, forward and inverse** — `to_real` and `to_byte` — plus `coarseincrement`/`fineincrement`, where fineincrement should equal one raw LSB expressed in engineering units. Any editable field needs both directions. There's also `scale@logparam IDREF`, which links a ROM table to a live logger parameter.

### TunerPro RT

**ADX (the datastream format) is your real analogue, not XDF.** TunerPro separates bin definition (XDF) from live-stream definition (ADX).

ADX Value fields (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DADefValue.htm): Title, **Unique ID** (max 15 chars), Data Type + Stock Units (optional, only used to auto-link to an XDF item), **Units Override**, **Packet Offset** presented as *side-by-side hex and decimal input boxes*, **Data Source Size** in bits, **Signed**, **LSB First**, **Range Low / Range High**, **Alarm High / Low with enables** (value renders red bold when breached).

Output formats include **Percentage of Defined Range** = `(current − min) / (max − min)`. Truncation, never rounding.

**ADX Lookup Tables** (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DADefLookup.htm) — a first-class calibration primitive with four modes and **a Table Graph tab where you drag points with the mouse**:

| Mode | entries `[2.0→4.0], [4.0→8.0]`, inputs 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.5 |
|---|---|
| **Interpolate** | 5.0 / 6.0 / 7.0 |
| **Closest** | 4.0 / 8.0 / 8.0 |
| **Previous** | 4.0 / 4.0 / 4.0 |
| **Next** | 8.0 / 8.0 / 8.0 |

This is exactly the right UI for "I have 40 samples of raw byte vs. a known ground truth, fit me a curve" — much better than making the user guess `a*x+b`.

The general conversion engine (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/genconv.htm) allows `* / + - %` and bitwise `| & ^`; any alpha character is an **argument**, and each argument binds independently to one of three sources: **This Item's Raw Data**, **Other XDF Item Output** (the *converted* output), or **Raw Value at Address** (arbitrary address + size in bits + endianness flag). Examples straight from the docs: `(1.35 * X) - 40`, `0.351567 * (X - Y)`, `(0.351567 * X) - Y`.

**ADX Bitmask**: offset, size, LSB First, **Operation = AND or XOR** against an operand, then **Display on TRUE** / **Display on FALSE** strings. A mask plus an operator, not a bit index.

**Data Acquisition Tracing** (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DATracing.htm) is the standout feature: link the XDF to the ADX and, while streaming, **the live value highlights the currently-active cell in the ROM table.**

XDF item fields (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/XDFConstantEditor.htm): Address (offset by header Base Offset), **Size in bits** (not bytes), **Signed**, **LSB First** ("checked for Intel, unchecked for Motorola"), Output Type (Floating Point / Integer / Hex Digits / String), Significant Digits, Category A/B, Use Low/High Range (input is *truncated* to range), **Visibility Level** for progressive disclosure.

There is **no published XDF spec document**. The authoritative decoder is RomRaider's `XDFConversionLayer.java`:

```
mmedtypeflags:  0x01 signed | 0x02 LSB first (clear ⇒ big-endian) | 0x04 swap X/Y
mmedmajorstridebits / mmedminorstridebits: row/col strides in BITS, negative legal
```

Other parsers: https://github.com/bri3d/a2l2xdf, https://github.com/willemml/xdftuneparser-rs.

### WinOLS — map-finding heuristics

Vendor: https://www.evc.de/en/product/ols/software/ — *"Program code, empty areas, maps etc. are automatically detected. An overview window shows what can be found where in the file. Program code and empty areas are automatically displayed in pale."*

Reported detection criteria (https://ecufiles.io/technik/winols-map-erkennung):

1. **Statistical distribution analysis** to separate code from data — machine code has a distinct byte histogram
2. **Axis monotonicity** — runs of strictly increasing values, ~8–32 elements, in plausible ranges, flag a candidate axis
3. **Smoothness / second derivative** — maps have low second derivatives; code has high ones throughout
4. **Value-range plausibility** per candidate data type; reject all-`0xFF` / all-`0x00`
5. **Known-ECU database matching**
6. **Cross-version differencing** — the most reliable: two calibrations of the same ECU *"differ almost exclusively in the map regions"*

Visual framing (https://www.fileservice24.at/en/blog/winols-guide-finding-maps): code is *"chaotic, high-frequency noise with no discernible pattern"*; maps are *"smooth, structured shapes: gentle curves, clean staircases, ramps that rise and plateau, or flat lines."*

**Two interaction ideas worth taking:**
- **Adjustable display width + one-byte alignment nudge.** `M`/`W` increase/decrease columns, `Ctrl+arrow` shifts alignment by one byte. You don't know the stride of your RAM layout — make width a slider, not a config field, and watch for the width at which structure appears.
- **A free-floating preview window slaved to the current selection**, rendering it live as a 2D/3D plot. Drag the selection edges, watch the shape. Shape coherence *is* the confirmation.

Manual definition: click-drag from left of the data, drag edges to fine-tune, press **K** to convert the selection into a map. Properties: Name, Units, **Data Type** (e.g. *"16 bit high low"* — endianness baked into the type name), **Factor**, **Offset**. Right-click → "copy map properties", untick *"data source plus address"*, Ctrl+V onto the next map. Typical factors in the wild: `/4096` relative fill %, **`/327.68` throttle %** (16-bit full-scale 0–100), `×40` RPM, `/128` lambda.

### ECUFlash

Near-isomorphic to RomRaider — the Subaru defs are literally stamped *"generated by RR2EcuFlash"*.

```xml
<scaling name="Advance(degrees)2" units="Advance (degrees)"
         toexpr="(x*.001525879)-40" frexpr="(x+40)/.001525879"
         format="%.2f" min="0" max="50.00" inc=".5"
         storagetype="uint16" endian="big" />

<table name="Fuel Map 1" type="3D" swapxy="true" scaling="AFR" address="118A3">
    <table name="Load" address="2eb42" type="X Axis" elements="10" scaling="Load"/>
    <table name="RPM"  address="2ec62" type="Y Axis" elements="15" scaling="RPM"/>
</table>
```

Mapping: `toexpr`/`frexpr` ⇄ RomRaider `expression`/`to_byte`; `inc` ⇄ `fineincrement`; `format="%.2f"` (printf) ⇄ `"0.00"` (DecimalFormat). `storagetype` adds **`bloblist`** — the enum editor, a list of `<data name="..." value="..."/>` pairs.

### Firmware hex-diff tooling

**TunerPro Comparison Tool** (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DiffTool.htm) is the best-documented model: pick 2 of 5 loaded bins, enter a **start/end address range**, checkbox **"limit to items defined in the XDF"**. Output is one row per differing byte, with **undefined bytes rendered in blue** — i.e. the diff visually flags *changes you have no definition for*, which is precisely the discovery signal. Click to locate in list, double-click to open the editor.

Others: **OpenRemap** (https://github.com/v-arapidis/openremap-core) diffs two binaries into a `.remap` recipe capturing every changed byte **plus 32 bytes of context anchors** so patches survive firmware revisions. **VBinDiff** (https://www.cjmweb.net/vbindiff/) — two-pane synchronised hex with differences highlighted, trivially copyable interaction. **ImHex** (https://imhex.werwolv.net/) — file diffing plus entropy/digram/byte-distribution visualisers, the closest open-source analogue to WinOLS's code-vs-data overview.

## 4. Correlation-based discovery — the academic pipelines

### READ (Marchetti & Stabili, IEEE TIFS 2018)

https://weblab.ing.unimore.it/people/stabili/papers/2018_READ.pdf

The canonical bit-flip tokenizer. Two phases, not three.

```
bitFlip[i]  = (# times bit i differs from bit i in previous message) / N
magnitude[i]= ceil(log10(bitFlip[i]))          # ceiling, not floor
```

Ceiling is confirmed by the paper's own worked example — a 4-bit counter with rates `[0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0]` yields magnitudes `[0,0,0,0]` only under ceiling. Buckets are decades: rate ∈ (0.1,1] → 0; (0.01,0.1] → −1; etc.

**Phase 1 — boundaries at magnitude drops.** Within one signal, flip rate decreases monotonically from LSB toward MSB. A *drop* scanning left-to-right means you crossed from one signal's LSB into the next signal's MSB:

```
ixS = 0; prev = magnitude[0]
for ix in 1..DLC-1:
    if magnitude[ix] < prev: ref.append((ixS, ix-1)); ixS = ix
    prev = magnitude[ix]
ref.append((ixS, DLC-1))
```

**Phase 2 — labels.** COUNTER: LSB magnitude is 0 (flip probability 1.0) *and* rates double at each step toward the LSB. CRC: all bits magnitude 0 *and* rates distributed normally about 0.5, tested `0.5−σ ≤ μ ≤ 0.5+σ`. PHYS: everything else.

Empirically stable around 100k messages.

### LibreCAN (Pesé et al., ACM CCS 2019)

https://mpese.com/publication/pese-2019-librecan/ACM_CCS_LibreCAN_Paper.pdf

Three phases (0, 1, 2). **IMU data is used in Phase 1 alongside OBD-II PIDs, not in a later phase.** Phase 2 is body/comfort events and uses no IMU.

**Phase 0** is a strictly better READ. Four stages: (0) partition bits into `UNUSED` / `CONST` / `POSS` — this fixes READ silently dropping the high-order constant bits of a physical signal; (1) **replace READ's decade drop with a percentage drop** — boundary when flip rate falls by more than `Tp0,2` fraction from the previous bit; (2) if distinct value count < `Tp0,3`, relabel `MULTI` (categorical); (3) counter test, remainder → `PHYS`.

**The percentage drop is the single most portable improvement in the literature** — it removes the arbitrary decade quantization.

**Phase 1 — matching against ground truth.** 15 OBD-II PIDs + 9 phone channels (3-axis accel, 3-axis gyro, barometric pressure, altitude, bearing) = 24 references, correlated against every Phase-0 signal.

Metric: **normalized cross-correlation**, not DTW. Both sets **resampled to 1 Hz** first — "essential… so that both signals are temporally aligned." (Note: your data is *natively* 1 Hz. You are already at their working resolution.)

Cut-off is adaptive rather than a fixed threshold — Algorithm 2, `Top_X`:

```
running_avg = c[0]; out = [c[0]]; count = 1; running_sum = c[0]
for val in c[1:]:
    if val < (1 - Tp1) * running_avg: break
    out.append(val); running_sum += val; count += 1
    running_avg = running_sum / count
```

`Tp1 = 0.05`. This returns "the leading cluster" whatever the absolute correlation level — much better UI behaviour than a hard `r ≥ 0.8` line.

Scale/offset: `d = m·r + t` by least-squares linear regression on the matched pair.

**Stated limitation, and it is exactly your problem.** Appendix A lists what cross-correlation cannot separate: torque ∝ RPM below ~2000–3000 rpm; **engine load ∝ torque**; torque ∝ boost ∝ MAP; **accelerator pedal position ∝ throttle position**.

**Phase 2 — body events by reference-state diffing.** Build a reference state from idle data, keep IDs with low bit-flip rate, then three filters: drop IDs whose payload never changes during the event; diff against reference, dropping `(ID, payload)` pairs already seen at idle; drop IDs already claimed as powertrain.

Accuracy 90–95%, **precision only 8.5–15%**, recall 46–58% — *deliberately*: "we preferred those parameters that resulted in a high FP rate instead of a high FN rate." Net effect is a >10× reduction in candidates. **This is the correct posture for a human-in-the-loop UI**: shrink the haystack hard, accept false positives, let the human adjudicate.

### ACTT (Verma, Bridges, Hollifield, CSCI 2018) — the one to actually implement

https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.07897

CAN-D explicitly reuses ACTT for its Step 4, and it's the cleanest formulation of "correlate unknowns against a known reference, recover the linear map."

**Tokenization is deliberately dumb.** No flip-rate cascade. Categorize bits into `B0` (always 0), `B1` (always 1), `B_used` (varies). **A valid token is any contiguous run of bits containing no constant bit.** Constants are hard walls; every sub-range inside a run is a candidate.

**Fit and score:**

```
minimize over (a,b):  || a·x̃ + b − y ||²
R² = 1 − S_res / S_tot
accept if R² ≥ α          # α = 0.50 in their experiments
```

**Conflict resolution — the part everyone forgets.** Overlapping accepted tokens (bits 2–8 fits reference A at R²=0.98; bits 1–4 fits reference B at R²=0.95) are resolved by **weighted interval scheduling**, maximizing `Σ R²_T · width_T`, solved exactly by DP in O(n log n) after sorting by end bit.

Without this your UI shows "byte 42 is speed" and "bytes 41–42 are speed" as two separate findings and the user loses trust.

### CAN-D (Verma et al., ORNL)

https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05993

**Step 1 — 15 features per bit pair.** Five *local* features, all flip probabilities:

```
P(F_i), P(F_i | F_{i+1}), P(F_{i+1} | F_i), P(¬F_i | ¬F_{i+1}), P(¬F_{i+1} | ¬F_i)
```

Feature vector = 5 for bit i ⊕ 5 for bit i+1 ⊕ 5 elementwise differences ∈ ℝ¹⁵. Output is a per-bit boundary *probability*, not a hard decision.

**The conditional-flip features are the genuinely new idea and they're cheap.** `P(F_i | F_{i+1})` near 1 means bit i almost always flips when its neighbour does — the signature of two bits inside one integer. That works even when the marginal flip rates have saturated, which is exactly the failure mode you'll hit at 1 Hz.

**Step 2 — endianness as constrained optimization.** Per-byte-boundary state `v(j) ∈ {C, J_B, J_L}` (cut, big-endian join, little-endian join) with constraints (`v(0) ≠ J_L`, `v(7) ≠ J_B`, `v(j)=J_B ⟹ v(j+1) ≠ J_L and v(j+2) ≠ J_L`, …) leaving **577 valid configurations**, grid-searched.

**Step 3 — signedness.** The subagent could not extract the actual rule from the PDF and explicitly flagged its reconstruction as low-confidence. Pull the IEEE version if you need it. A practical test that does work: a signed field crossing zero shows the high bits flipping together, and its *unsigned* reading shows a discontinuity from ~2ⁿ−1 to ~0. Score both interpretations by R² and keep the winner.

**Step 4** delegates to ACTT.

### CANMatch (Buscemi et al., IEEE TVT 2021)

https://orbilu.uni.lu/bitstream/10993/48502/1/FINAL%20VERSION.pdf

Phase 3 is the part worth stealing:

1. **Interpolate every series to n = 60 points** (1 point/sec)
2. **Min-max scale each to [0,1]** — removes all format dependence, compares *shape* only
3. Score by **RMSE**, threshold **θ = 0.01**. They evaluated area-between-curves, RMSE, and DTW and chose RMSE; DTW was slow and unnecessary because these signals have no temporal skew
4. **Scale/offset by linear regression** of raw token values against already-decoded reference values — slope → factor, intercept → offset
5. **Speed disambiguation:** multiple speed-like signals in one frame → wheel speeds; a lone one → vehicle speed

Also a useful correction to READ and LibreCAN: for little-endian, reverse bits *within each byte* while preserving byte order — "endianness is a property of the order of the bytes, not the bits."

**Note the contrast with ACTT:** ACTT regresses raw-against-reference and scores R² ≥ 0.50 on unnormalized data; CANMatch min-max normalizes *both* and scores RMSE ≤ 0.01. **Normalizing first makes the score scale-free and is the better default for a UI ranking list** — keep the regression afterwards purely to recover a and b.

### ByCAN (arXiv 2408.09265)

https://arxiv.org/html/2408.09265v1

Cluster **bytes** before clustering **bits** (DBSCAN at both levels), with a hard **max 2-byte cluster length** justified by: **98.25% of signals in industry DBCs are ≤ 16 bits**.

The labeling parameter is the nice trick:

```
u_mn = |distinct values| / 2^(n−m+1)      # distinct / representable
θ_mn = flip_rate × u_mn
```
```
θ = 0, flip = 0        → Unused
0 < θ ≤ ε₀             → Switch (categorical/flag)
θ ≥ ε₀, flip < 0.99    → Dynamic (physical)
θ ≥ ε₀, flip ≥ 0.99    → Verification (counter/checksum)
```

`ε₀` itself found by DBSCAN over the (θ, flip) population — no hand-set threshold. **`θ = flip_rate × distinct_ratio` is a better one-number type discriminator than flip rate alone** and is trivial to implement.

Slicing accuracy 80.21% vs CAN-D 63.88% vs READ 51.99%. Data needs: **~1,000 frames for slicing, ~10,000 for labeling.** At 1 Hz that's ~17 minutes and ~3 hours respectively — budget your capture sessions accordingly and show the user a sample-count confidence indicator.

### Setterstrom & Straub 2026 — event-windowed correlation

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.16722

Deliberately skips tokenization: chops payloads into **fixed 16-bit hypothesis channels** and does semantic correlation only. Five layers: IMU + CAN capture → **event detection** (accel / decel / steering, in bounded windows) → **rate-of-change correlation within event windows** → ranked association → GUI verification.

Achieved r: accelerator 0.455–0.832, brake 0.744–0.945, steering 0.567–0.863 across six vehicles. Validated against openDBC — on a 2016 Sierra it flagged ID 241 for brake and openDBC confirms BrakePedalPosition at bit 15 of message 241, **despite the fixed 16-bit window not aligning to the true 8-bit field.**

Two transferable ideas, both high-value for you:
1. **Correlate on the rate of change, not the raw value** — this kills the "everything correlates with everything" problem caused by slow-moving confounders
2. **Correlate only inside event windows the human deliberately created**, not over the whole trace

And one reassurance: a misaligned but *overlapping* window still correlates well enough to localize. Your UI doesn't need perfect boundaries before it can rank.

### CANvas (Kulandaivel et al., USENIX Security 2019)

https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity19/presentation/kulandaivel

Network mapper — which ECU sends each ID, which receive it, how many exist. Pairwise clock-offset tracking (σ(Δ) < 1 ms ⇒ same ECU), plus forced ECU isolation via bus-off injection. **Explicitly does no payload semantics.** Zero applicability to a flat RAM window; listed for completeness only.

### Practical (non-academic)

**CSS Electronics AI RE workflow** — https://www.csselectronics.com/pages/can-bus-reverse-engineering-ai-llm-claude, skills repo (MIT) at https://github.com/CSS-Electronics/can-bus-reverse-engineering-skills. The most UI-shaped source. Four stages:

1. **Bit-activity heatmap** — counters and checksum bytes are *flagged and excluded before anything else runs*
2. **Correlation against reference** — **windowed Spearman rank correlation, median-pooled across overlapping windows**. Spearman rather than Pearson because it survives monotone-but-nonlinear maps and outliers. Test both signednesses; slide the reference over a small lag range; mask "signal unavailable" sentinel outliers
3. **Bitsearch** — exhaustive grid over start bit × length × endianness × signedness, scored by R². Tie-break: **prefer shorter fields**, since longer ones swallow neighbours
4. **Scale & offset** — slope as the **median slope over many point pairs** (robust, not OLS); then round to OEM-plausible values (0.1, not 0.0999281) if the fit doesn't degrade; then enforce physical anchors (must read zero when stationary) by re-fitting

Reference-quality tiers: CAN-based best, dashboard-video OCR next, human-generated worst — the last needs deliberate 0/25/50/75/100% hold sweeps. ~90%+ success, 5–10 min per signal.

**canair** — https://philipkocanda.github.io/canair/bring-your-own-car/06-analyze/

```
canair hunt uds MyECU:2101 --against ESC:22C101:REAL_SPEED_KMH
canair hunt uds MyECU:2101 --against-file gps_speed.csv
```

Sweeps every byte offset × {u8, i16, f32} × endianness × linear `y = scale·x + offset`, against either an on-bus signal or an external two-column CSV joined by nearest timestamp.

- **Pearson r for continuous; Cramér's V or mutual information for categorical/flag channels.** Worth copying — a bitfield correlated by Pearson is nonsense
- `--control` regresses out a nuisance signal to surface correlations hidden behind a dominant driver
- Evidence standard: r near 1.0 **and** a physically plausible fitted equation (slope ≈ 1.0 for speed-to-speed)
- **Physical plausibility bands** when no reference exists — does the scaled value land in a named range (12 V rail, HV pack)?
- UI keys: `e` annotates a capture ("Heating started"), `s` jumps to named moments, `V` shows only changed parameters, `p` toggles signals

**The `e`-key event annotation is the cheapest high-value feature in any tool surveyed**, and it is exactly the user-supplied event track you asked about.

- **Data Inspector** — show the selected bytes simultaneously as every type, signed and unsigned, both endiannesses

**Cheat Engine's own memory viewer**, reached via right-click → **Browse this memory region**, keeps the hex dump and the watch table as separate but linked panes. That separation is right: the dump is for discovery, the table is for accumulated knowledge.

## 6. Concrete design for 252 bytes at 1 Hz

### The arithmetic is in your favour, and it changes everything

252 bytes × widths {1, 2, 4} × 2 endianness × 2 signedness ≈ **3,000 hypotheses**. At 1 Hz that's 3,000 evaluations per second — nothing, in a browser, in JS.

**So don't build a tokenizer.** READ, LibreCAN Stage 1, ByCAN and CANMatch all exist because CAN payloads are 64 bits and bit-packed and you must guess boundaries before you can do anything. You have a flat byte-addressed RAM map on a 1990s Motronic — it is 8- and 16-bit scalars on byte boundaries, near-certainly. Enumerate every hypothesis exhaustively, every sample, forever. Skip candidates that span a byte you've classified UNUSED or CONST (ACTT's rule: constants are hard walls).

### The 1 Hz problem, stated plainly

**Most of the tokenization literature will underperform on your data, and you should design around that rather than port it.** READ's decade cascade assumes consecutive samples differ by a small fraction of range, which holds at 10–100 Hz. At 1 Hz, RPM moves hundreds between samples and the low 6–8 bits of a 16-bit field are effectively random — all sitting at flip rate ≈ 0.5, magnitude 0. The cascade flattens and you get one giant token or garbage boundaries.

Consequences: prefer LibreCAN's percentage drop or CANMatch's absolute τ = 0.3 over READ's `ceil(log10)`; lean on CAN-D's *conditional* flip features which survive saturation; and lean hardest on **reference correlation**, which doesn't depend on the cascade at all. With 5 known anchors you're better positioned than any blind tokenizer.

One addition none of the papers need: at 1 Hz a *fast* physical signal masquerades as a checksum on flip rate alone. Disambiguate with **lag-1 autocorrelation of the byte value** — physical channels retain structure, checksums don't.

### The build, in order of value per unit of effort

**1. Live hex grid, 252 cells, colour-by-pattern with fade.** Port cabana's classifier verbatim (§2a) — it's 20 lines and the constants are published. At 1 Hz set `decay_limit = 2.0 s` so a changed byte stays lit for two full samples. Width adjustable (WinOLS `M`/`W`) with a one-byte alignment nudge. Grey out UNUSED/CONST automatically; that alone will probably eliminate half your 252 bytes on the first idle capture.

**2. Min / Current / Max columns, session-accumulated** (RomRaider). Free range discovery on all 252 bytes at once. A byte that covered 0–255 is not coolant temp; a byte that never left 0–200 might be TPS.

**3. "Number of Changes" per byte, with a reset button** (BizHawk + Mesen's counter reset). Blip the throttle exactly 4 times in a 60-sample window, filter `changes ≈ 4`. This is the single highest-value primitive at 1 Hz because it's an aggregate — immune to the sample-timing jitter that wrecks per-sample Increased/Decreased.

**4. Cheat Engine scan panel.** Copy cabana's `findsignal.cc` exactly: First Scan / Next Scan / Undo / New Scan, an unlimited undo stack (a history of candidate lists, not one level), parameters locked after First Scan, and a live "N candidates remaining" line. Compare modes: `Any Value | = | ≠ | > | ≥ | < | ≤ | Between A…B | ↕ Changed | = Unchanged | ↑ Increased | ↓ Decreased | ↑ Increased By | ↓ Decreased By`, plus a **Compare to: previous / first / saved snapshot** selector.

**Add the percentage scan** (§1). It is how you find TPS without knowing its scaling.

**Add Preview** (BizHawk) — at 1 Hz a mis-timed Next Scan is expensive; show what will be removed before committing.

**5. An event track, with a keyboard shortcut.** This is the highest-leverage feature in the entire survey and almost nobody has it. One key marks the current sample: `throttle floored`, `throttle closed`, `stopped`, `coasting`. Then score candidates **inside those windows only** (Setterstrom & Straub), on **rate of change** rather than raw value. This dissolves most of the physical-coupling ambiguity that LibreCAN flags as its hard limit.

**6. Correlation ranking against your 5 knowns + the event track.** Per candidate:

```
join on timestamp (both already 1 Hz — no resampling needed)
optionally differentiate both
min-max normalize both to [0,1]                    # CANMatch: scale-free
r_s = Spearman(c, d)                               # CSS: survives nonlinearity
best_lag = argmax over lag ∈ [-3s, +3s]

Then **de-overlap with ACTT's weighted interval scheduling** so you never show "byte 42 is speed" and "bytes 41–42 are speed" as two findings.

**7. Arrow-key candidate browser with live plot preview** (SavvyCAN Range State). You are not reading correlation coefficients, you are flipping through plots looking for a shape you recognise. At ~2 candidates/second this beats any ranking metric for the final call.

**8. Baseline-vs-event diff** (SavvyCAN File Comparison, LibreCAN Phase 2, WinOLS cross-version). Capture idle-with-no-throttle as a reference; capture with the action. **9. Watch table with confidence tiers.** Columns: freeze/pin | description | address | type | current | min | max | units. Conversion { units*, expr*, format*, storagetype?, endian?=big,

### Finding TPS specifically

You already have injection load — and LibreCAN's Appendix A says **engine load ∝ torque ∝ throttle**, so TPS *will* correlate strongly with what you have. That's how you find it, and also why correlation alone won't confirm it. Discriminators:

- TPS is **bounded and clips hard at both ends** (0% and 100%); load does not clip the same way
- On **closed-throttle overrun**, TPS drops to its floor immediately while load lags and fuel cuts
- **Drive a deliberate staircase**: hold 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100% for ~10 s each. A true TPS byte becomes a clean five-step function; load stays noisy. **This makes TPS findable by shape alone, no reference needed** — and it's also what feeds the percentage scan and the lookup-table fitter
- Expect a single byte, monotone, non-negative, 0–255 or 0–200. If MS41 is right it's `x*100/255`, i.e. full-scale 255

### Finding road speed specifically

Nothing you have correlates with it directly. Three attacks, best first:

**Gear-ratio heuristic — build this, it's the strongest signal available and it's in none of the papers.** For each candidate `c`, compute `c / RPM` across the drive and test whether the ratio is **piecewise constant with a small number of discrete levels**. That is the definitive signature of road speed on a manual E36 and nothing else in the ECU has it. Cluster the ratio series (1-D DBSCAN, or just count histogram modes); a candidate yielding 4–5 tight modes plus a scatter class for neutral/clutch-in is your speed byte. Far more decisive than any correlation coefficient.

**GPS ground truth.** canair's `--against-file` model: log phone GPS speed at 1 Hz during the same drive, join by nearest timestamp, correlate. Turns the problem into a solved one, and gives you the scale for free (if MS41 is right, slope should come out ≈ 1.0 against km/h).

**Stop/start events.** Mark "stopped" moments with the event key. Road speed is the only channel that is *exactly* zero at every stop and nonzero between them — RPM idles nonzero, load idles nonzero.

If several speed-like bytes appear adjacent in the map, CANMatch's rule applies: adjacent cluster ⇒ per-wheel speeds; solitary ⇒ vehicle speed. An E36 with ABS may well show both.

# Finding meaning in unknown bytes by watching them change: tool survey

## 0. Read this first — your specific answer may already be published

RomRaider ships a **BMW DS2 logger definition for MS41/MS42/MS43** with real RAM addresses. If your E36 is an M52 on MS41.1:

| | Address | Type | Expression | Units |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TPS** | `0xE8D7` | uint8 | `x*100/255` | % |
| **Vehicle speed** | `0xDA63` | uint8 | `x` | km/h (1:1) |

Cross-check anchors from the same file: RPM `0xDA2A` uint16 `x`; MAF `0xDA34` uint16 `x*0.25` kg/h; IAT `0xDA50` uint8 `x*0.747-48`; ECT `0xDA5A` uint8 `x*0.747-48`; Load `0xFAFC` uint16 `x*0.0212` mg/stroke; IPW `0xEF7E` uint16 `x*0.00534` ms.

Source: https://github.com/0x000NULL/tuning/blob/main/BMW/MS41%20Logger%20Definitions.xml (89 `ecuparam`s, ECU IDs `1405854, 1406464, SHINDE1, 1429373, 1429861, 1432401, 1437806, 1440176`).

**Caveat worth resolving before you build anything:** coolant, IAT, RPM and vehicle speed all cluster in `0xDA2A–0xDA63`, a ~57-byte span. But TPS is at `0xE8D7` and Load at `0xFAFC` — thousands of bytes away. A single 252-byte window cannot contain both your known injection-load byte and TPS if these addresses are right. Dump your window's base address and check it against the table. Either your window isn't the `0xDA00` block, or your "injection load" is a different quantity. Companion defs: https://github.com/Rustle333/Siemens-MS43, https://github.com/Rustle333/MSS52.

That said — the tooling research below is what you asked for, and you still want the discovery UI, both to verify these and because published defs are per-ECU-ID and yours may not match.

---

## 1. Cheat Engine — the exact scan vocabulary

### Scan types (verbatim UI names)

Available on both First and Next Scan:
- **Exact Value**
- **Bigger than...**
- **Smaller than...**
- **Value between...** — "Finds all values within the specified interval (inclusive)"
- **Unknown initial value** — the entry point when you know nothing

Next Scan only (these compare against the *previous* scan's stored value per address):
- **Increased value** / **Increased value by...**
- **Decreased value** / **Decreased value by...**
- **Changed value**
- **Unchanged value**
- **Value between... at least xx%**
- **Increased by... at least xx%** / **Decreased by... at least xx%**

Plus two orthogonal modifiers that sit next to the dropdown:
- **Compare to first/saved scan** vs **Compare to previous scan** — changes the reference frame of every relative operator
- **Not** — inverts the selected scan type

Value types: **Binary** (with `?`/`*` bit wildcards), **Byte**, **2 Bytes**, **4 Bytes**, **8 Bytes**, **Float**, **Double**, **String**, **Array of byte** (`??`/`**` wildcards), **All** (unions Byte/2/4/8/Float/Double when you don't know the type).

Scan options: **Fast Scan (aligned scan)** with configurable alignment, **Last digits**, readonly checkbox, memory range start/stop, **Enable Speedhack**, **Unrandomizer**.

Buttons: **First Scan**, **Next Scan**, **Undo scan**, **New scan**. Undo is one level and it matters — a mis-timed scan kills the true candidate and undo is the only recovery.

URLs: https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File:Scan_types · https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File:Value_types · https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File:Memory_scan_settings

### The percentage scan — the most underrated feature, and directly your TPS answer

https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File:Percentage_scans_and_compare_to_saved_results

The workflow: unknown-initial-value scan establishes a baseline = 100%. Later, select **Compare to first scan**, **Value between...**, tick the **between %** checkbox, enter e.g. 95–97%.

Why this matters to you: *you cannot know TPS's raw value, but you can know its physical percentage.* Hold the throttle at what you judge to be half travel and search for "between 45% and 55% of the value seen at WOT." The docs are explicit that this is scale-invariant — "it doesn't matter if the values are multiplied, you will find them easily using this method." It was designed for health bars you can only see graphically; a throttle pedal is the same problem.

### Address list / watch table

https://wiki.cheatengine.org/index.php?title=Help_File%3AAddressCheat_List

Columns: **Active** (freeze checkbox) | **Description** | **Address** | **Type** | **Value**.

Freeze has three modes, not one: normal (`=`), increase-only (`+`), decrease-only (`−`), restoring "every few milliseconds (the interval can be changed in the settings)."

Hotkeys: `Enter` modify value, `Ctrl+Enter` edit description, `Ctrl+Alt+Enter` change address, `Space` toggle freeze, numpad `+`/`−` for directional freeze. Entries drag to reorder and nest under **Create Header** groups.

Right-click: **Browse this memory region**, **Find out what accesses this address**, **Find out what writes to this address**, **Pointer scan for this address**, **Recalculate new addresses**.

The two "find out what..." items are debugger breakpoint features. **They have no analogue for you** — you have a serial peephole, not a debugger. Skip them; everything else transfers.

### scanmem / GameConqueror (open-source Linux equivalent)

https://github.com/scanmem/scanmem · https://www.mankier.com/1/scanmem

The CLI operator syntax is more compact than CE's dropdown and maps better to a keyboard-driven web UI:

| Input | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | current value is exactly n |
| `n..m` | range, inclusive |
| `>` | increased (bare) / greater than n (with arg) |
| `<` | decreased / less than n |
| `+` `[n]` | increased by n |
| `-` `[n]` | decreased by n |
| `=` `[n]` | unchanged / equal to n |
| `!=` `[n]` | changed / not equal to n |
| `snapshot` | "Match any value. This is useful when an initial value or range is not known" |

Commands: `pid`, `list [max]`, `set [match-id=]value[/delay]`, `delete`, `reset`, `watch match-id` ("Monitor the value of match-id, and print its value as it changes"), `lregions`, `dregion`, `option`, `update`.

`watch` is worth noting — a single-address live tail, separate from the match list. GameConqueror is the GTK front-end: scan entry + type dropdown + results list on top, a lock/description/address/type/value cheat table underneath.

### BizHawk RAM Search — the one built for slow, frame-stepped observation

https://tasvideos.org/EmulatorResources/RamSearch

This is the closest fit to 1 Hz sampling, because TAS workflows are inherently frame-by-frame and deliberate.

**Compare To** (four options): **Previous Value** · **Specific Value** · **Specific Address** · **Number of Changes**

**Compare operators**: Less Than, Greater Than, Less than or equal, Greater than or equal, Equal to, Not Equal to, **Different By []** ("Keeps values that are less then or greater than the compare value by the amount typed into the edit box"), **Modulo [] Is**.

**The "Number of Changes" column is the single best idea in this whole survey for your use case.** Per the docs: *"RAM search keeps track of values every frame. Each time they change, the change counter increases."* The canonical trick: move right for exactly 6 frames, then search **Changes = 6** to find the position variable.

At 1 Hz over 252 bytes this is nearly free and devastatingly effective. Blip the throttle exactly 4 times over 60 samples; TPS-related bytes have a change count in a narrow band, while RPM (changes constantly) and coolant temp (changes rarely) are excluded by the same filter. It also survives your slow link in a way that per-sample increased/decreased does not, because it's an aggregate over the whole window rather than a comparison of two adjacent samples.

Also: **Preview** — visualize what a search *will* remove before committing. Given that a mis-timed Next Scan at 1 Hz is expensive, preview-before-commit is worth building.

## 2. CAN reverse-engineering tools — byte-change visualisation

### 2a. cabana (deanlee's actively-maintained fork) — steal this wholesale

https://github.com/deanlee/openpilot-cabana

This fork has evolved well past comma.ai's original and contains a **literal Cheat Engine clone**. Headline features, verbatim:

- **Live bit heatmap** — "bit flips flash on change and fade out, instantly revealing active signals"
- **Pattern coloring** — "bytes auto-colored by trend: increasing, decreasing, toggling, or noisy"
- **Find Similar Bits** — "discover related signals across messages and buses"
- **Find Signal** — "search all messages by value range or threshold"
- **Bit muting** — "suppress known bits to isolate undocumented signals"
- **Sparklines** — "inline signal previews in the message list"

Colour table:

| Colour | Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Green | Increasing | "byte value is steadily climbing (e.g., a counter)" |
| Red | Decreasing | "byte value is steadily dropping" |
| Amber | Toggle | "bits flipping back and forth between states (e.g., flags)" |
| Purple | Noisy | "High-entropy data with no discernible trend (e.g., CRC/Encryption)" |
| Grey | Static | "data is currently inactive or hasn't changed recently" |

**I pulled the actual classifier out of the source** — `src/core/streams/message_state.cc`. It is ~20 lines and directly portable to JS:

```c
constexpr float TOGGLE_EMA_ALPHA       = 0.15f;  // ~6-sample half-life
constexpr int8_t TREND_STREAK_MAX      = 8;      // saturating limit
constexpr int8_t TREND_STREAK_THRESHOLD= 4;      // consecutive same-direction changes
constexpr float NOISE_EMA_THRESHOLD    = 0.55f;  // above this = noisy

// on every byte change:
a.toggle_ema += TOGGLE_EMA_ALPHA;
a.last_change_ts = current_ts;
const int delta = new_byte - old_byte;
const bool is_toggle = (delta == -a.last_delta) && (abs(a.trend_streak) < TREND_STREAK_THRESHOLD);
if (is_toggle)      a.trend_streak = 0;
else if (delta > 0) a.trend_streak = (a.trend_streak > 0) ? min(a.trend_streak+1, MAX) : 1;
else if (delta < 0) a.trend_streak = (a.trend_streak < 0) ? max(a.trend_streak-1,-MAX) : -1;

if      (abs(a.trend_streak) >= TREND_STREAK_THRESHOLD) pattern = trend_streak>0 ? Increasing : Decreasing;
else if (is_toggle)                                     pattern = Toggle;
else if (a.toggle_ema > NOISE_EMA_THRESHOLD)            pattern = RandomlyNoisy;
```

Plus an idle decay path: if a byte doesn't change and `toggle_ema <= NOISE_EMA_THRESHOLD`, `trend_streak /= 2` each tick until it hits 0 and the classification clears.

**The fade function** (`colorFromDataPattern`) is adaptive to message rate — important for you, because at 1 Hz a fixed fade would be invisible:

```c
double decay_limit = 1.5;
if (freq > 0) decay_limit = clamp(2.0 / freq, 0.4, 2.5);
if (elapsed >= decay_limit) return TRANSPARENT;
float t = elapsed / decay_limit;
float intensity = (1-t) * (1-t);          // quadratic ease-out
uint32_t alpha = 230.0f * intensity;
```

At 1 Hz that clamps to a 2.0 s decay — a byte that changed stays visibly lit for two full samples. Palette: Increasing `#2ecc71`, Decreasing `#e74c3c`, Toggle `#f1c40f`, Noisy `#9b59b6` (light theme; darker variants for dark).

**Bit muting** (`muteActiveBits`) — a two-second lookback that ORs every recently-changed bit into a suppression mask:

```c
static constexpr double kMuteActivityWindowSec = 2.0;
const double cutoff = ts - kMuteActivityWindowSec;
for each byte i, for each bit b:
    if (bit_change_ts_[i][b] > cutoff) active_bits |= (0x80 >> b);
suppressed_mask[i] |= active_bits;
```

The interaction: do the thing you *don't* care about, click Mute, those bits go grey permanently. Then do the thing you *do* care about and only new bits light up. This is "hide static bytes" inverted, and it's better — static bytes are boring but *constantly-noisy* bytes are the actual problem.

**Find Signal** — `src/tools/findsignal.cc`. Cheat Engine, verbatim, for CAN. The buttons literally read **First Scan** / **Next Scan** / **Undo** / **New Scan**, and the status line reads *"%1 candidate(s) remaining. Right-click to create signal, double-click to open message."*

Compare modes (indices 0–7 absolute, 8–13 relative — relative only meaningful on Next Scan):

```
Any Value | = Exact Value | ≠ Not Equal | > Greater Than | ≥ Greater or Equal
< Less Than | ≤ Less or Equal | Between A…B
↕ Changed | = Unchanged | ↑ Increased | ↓ Decreased | ↑ Increased By | ↓ Decreased By
```

Candidate enumeration is dumb brute force, and that's the point:

```cpp
for (int size = min_size; size <= max_size; ++size)
  for (int start = 0; start <= total_bits - size; ++start) {
      s.sig.start_bit = start; s.sig.size = size;
      s.value = s.sig.toPhysical(dat, len);
      initial_signals.push_back(s);
  }
```

Inputs: Bus, Address (comma-separated hex, blank = all), **Scan At** (seconds, with a **Now** button), **Size** min–max spinners, **Little endian** checkbox, **Signed** checkbox, **Factor**, **Offset**.

Result columns: **Message | Signal (start|size) | Prev Value | Value | Δ** — with Δ coloured green `#22c55e` when positive, red `#ef4444` when negative. Signal column renders as `12|8 [LU]` (start|size, endianness letter, sign letter).

Two details worth copying exactly: (1) the candidate parameters lock after First Scan and only unlock on New Scan, so you can't corrupt a narrowing run; (2) history is a stack of candidate lists, so Undo is O(1) and unlimited, not one-level like Cheat Engine's.

**Find Similar Bits** — `src/tools/findsimilarbits.cc`. Pick a reference `(message, byte index, bit index)`, then for every other `(address, byte, bit)` in the capture, count mismatches against the reference bit's live value:

```cpp
mismatched[i*8 + j] += equal ? (bit != bit_to_find) : (bit == bit_to_find);
...
if (float perc = (mismatched[i] / (double)cnt) * 100; perc < 50)
    result.push_back({address, i/8, i%8, mismatched[i], cnt, perc});
sort(result, {}, &mismatched_struct::perc);
```

Result columns: `address | byte idx | bit idx | mismatches | total msgs | % mismatched`, ascending. UI has an **Equal: Yes/No** dropdown (find agreement or find anti-correlation) and a **Min msg count** guard defaulted to 100. The `< 50%` cut is just "better than a coin flip."

This is binary correlation ranking against a known reference, in 30 lines. For you, the reference is a *derived* bit — "is the throttle open?" — computed from any known channel or supplied by hand.

**Endianness by drag direction** — `binary_view.cc` has a `Settings::DragDirection` enum: `MsbFirst`, `LsbFirst`, `AlwaysLE`, `AlwaysBE`. Under the first two, dragging left-to-right vs right-to-left across bits *sets the endianness of the signal you just created*. Very slick, zero extra UI.

### 2b. SavvyCAN

Docs: https://www.savvycan.com/docs/

**Sniffer Window** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/sniffer.html) — bytes that decrease render red, bytes that increase render green. Refresh 200 ms. IDs unseen for 5 s turn red then vanish.

Four options that are each a distinct good idea:
- **Never Expire IDs** — keeps a stable row set so things don't jump around
- **Notch** — "will remember all the bits that were set in the last 200ms window and will not color the output if those bits are toggled in the future." Click repeatedly to accumulate. **Unnotch** resets. Same concept as cabana's bit muting, arrived at independently.
- **Mute notched bits** — stronger: notched bytes "ignore any notched bits and not even change the display to update if only notched bits were changed"
- **Fade inactive bytes** — bytes that stop updating "gradually fade toward white, ensuring only data which is actively changing will be very visible"
- **View Bits** — per-bit blocks: black = set/unchanged, white = unset/unchanged, red = freshly unset, green = freshly set

**Flow View** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/flowview.html) — an 8×8 bit grid plus a byte-value graph, with **playback**. "Bits which are white are currently 0 or off. Bits which are black are 1 or on." Green = newly on this frame, red = newly off. **Auto Reference** compares against the previous frame; static reference compares against a pinned frame (e.g. the first).

The graph "plots all eight data bytes. The '+' in the center marks the 'current' time. You can thus see both into the future and the past (relative to the current frame)." Playback controls: step back / stop / step forward, play backward / pause / play forward, adjustable speed, Loop Playback, **Live Mode**, **Synchronize windows**, and **seek to specific values** (enter a target byte value, playback auto-stops on match).

**A past-and-future window centred on "now" is the right shape for 1 Hz.** You have very few samples; showing ±30 s around the cursor costs nothing and lets the eye do the correlation.

**Range State Window** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/rangestate.html) — the "Fuzzy Scope" you were thinking of. It "searches for signals that seem to vary somewhat coherently" and openly admits it "will generate a lot of false positives but it will still provide some decent ideas for where to look for signals."

Parameters: **ID Filter list**, **Sensitivity** ("a subjective measurement"), **Min Signal Size** (down to 1 bit), **Max Signal Size**, **Granularity** (bit jump width — set 8 to only consider byte-aligned starts), **Signal Mode** (big endian / little endian / both), **Signed Mode** (unsigned / signed / both). Button: **Recalculate Candidate Signals**. Output list "Candidate Signals" with ID, start bit, length, signed/unsigned, endianness.

The interaction that matters: **arrow-key through the candidate list and each one previews as a graph.** You are not reading numbers, you are flipping through plots looking for a shape you recognise. At 252 bytes × 3 widths × 2 endian × 2 sign ≈ 3000 candidates, arrow-key-through-plots is genuinely viable at ~2/second.

**Frame Details** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/framedetails.html) — per byte: which bits changed, value ranges encountered, histograms both graphical and textual, "the number of times a specific value occurred." Top-right: "A histogram of all the bits and the number of times each bit was set" — useful to "quickly visually see where data has changed." Bottom-right: "Each individual byte as its value varies over time." There's a logarithmic toggle for the bit counts, which matters because flip counts span orders of magnitude.

**File Comparison** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/filecomparison.html) — the differential-analysis workflow, and it maps perfectly onto your problem. Capture a baseline with the feature *off* ("vehicle idling without gear shifts"), capture with the feature *on* ("shifting gears several times"), diff. Output tree: IDs only in file of interest / IDs only in reference / IDs in both, the last with sub-nodes showing "bits set only on one side and not the other" and "values only found on one side or the other." The doc's own framing: *"Somewhere in the differences should be the gear selection you couldn't find. The list ought to be much more narrow than just 'shooting in the dark.'"*

**Manual signal graphing** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/graphsetup.html) — the no-DBC ad-hoc definition form, which is exactly the minimum field set you need: **Name**, **ID**, **Data Len** (bits), **Little Endian** checkbox, start bit picked by clicking an 8×8 grid ("Click on the start bit and the rest of the bits will automatically be selected"), **Signed**, **Mask**, **Bias**, **Scale**, **Stride**, **Color**.

**Signal Editor** (https://github.com/collin80/SavvyCAN/blob/master/help/signaleditor.md) — full DBC field set: Signal Name, Bit Length, Start Bit, Byte Order (checked = little endian), Type (unsigned int / signed int / single float / double float / string), **Scale**, **Bias**, Min Value ("purely informational"), Max Value, Units Name, Receiving Node, multiplexing, **Value Tables** (text substitution, e.g. `0x10 = "PARK"`), Comments. Bitfield grid: start bit is black with diagonal stripes, other bits in the signal are green with stripes the other way, bits claimed by other signals get their own colours.
