## 3. ECU tuning / RAM watch tools

### RomRaider

The Logger DTD (https://github.com/RomRaider/RomRaider/blob/master/definitions/logger.dtd) is the smallest schema that covers everything you need:

```dtd
<!ELEMENT address ( #PCDATA ) >
<!ATTLIST address length CDATA #IMPLIED >          <!-- default 1 -->
<!ATTLIST address bit ( 0..31 ) #IMPLIED >         <!-- default -1 = no bit extract -->

<!ELEMENT conversion ( replace* ) >
<!ATTLIST conversion expr        CDATA #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST conversion format      ( 0 | 0.0 | 0.00 | ... ) #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST conversion storagetype ( int8|int16|uint8|uint16|int32|uint32|float ) #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion endian      CDATA #IMPLIED >  <!-- default BIG -->
<!ATTLIST conversion units       CDATA #REQUIRED >
<!ATTLIST conversion gauge_min   CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion gauge_max   CDATA #IMPLIED >
<!ATTLIST conversion gauge_step  CDATA #IMPLIED >
```

**The most important structural decision: one parameter has N conversions.** Units is not a label, it's a selector — the user picks °C vs °F at runtime and each carries its own expression, format, and gauge range. For a discovery tool this generalises beautifully: one address, several *competing hypotheses* about what it means, switchable live.

**Default gauge ranges keyed on the units string** (`ConverterMaxMinDefaults.java`) — steal this table verbatim, it makes a newly-defined parameter render sensibly with zero configuration:

```
"%"    0→100 step 10      "c"    -20→200 step 20     "rpm"   0→8000 step 1000
"km/h" 0→300 step 20      "mph"  0→200  step 20      "v"     0→5    step 0.5
"bar"  -1.5→3 step 0.5    "psi"  -20→40 step 5       "g/s"   0→400  step 20
"degrees" -15→60 step 5   "ms"   0→100  step 10      "lambda" 0.5→1.5 step 0.1
fallback: 0→100 step 10
```

Type "km/h" into a units box and get a 0–300 axis for free. That's a plausibility check disguised as a convenience.

**`parameter` vs `ecuparam`** (https://www.romraider.com/RomRaider/LoggerXMLReferenceGuide): `<parameter>` is a documented, manufacturer-standard PID with one address valid across all ECUs, gated by **capability bits** (`ecubyteindex` + `ecubit` index into a bitmask the ECU returns at init — if the bit is 0, RomRaider *hides the parameter entirely*). `<ecuparam>` is a reverse-engineered RAM address that differs per calibration ID, carrying `<ecu id="...">` children each with their own `<address>`. Conventionally named with a `*` suffix in the UI to mark "this is RE'd, not documented."

`group`/`subgroup`/`groupsize` batch several ecuparams into **one memory read** — release notes: *"Group individual DS2 ECU queries into a single memory read start address."* That is literally your 252-byte block.

**Derived parameters** via `<depends>`/`<ref>` — computed channels with no address, letting a user test hypotheses without code:

```xml
<parameter id="P200" name="Engine Load (Calculated)">
    <depends><ref parameter="P8"/><ref parameter="P12"/></depends>
    <conversions>
        <conversion units="g/rev" expr="(P12*60)/P8" format="0.00"/>
    </conversions>
</parameter>
```

Note `[P7:psi]` syntax — reference another parameter *in a specific unit*.

Expression language is **JEP** with one custom function: `BitWise(mask, x, op)` where op 1=AND, 2=OR, and mask must be decimal. Real MS41 usage: `BitWise(8,x,1)/8` extracts bit 3 as 0/1; `!BitWise(32,x,1)/32` is an inverted bit 5.

`<replace value="8" with="Closed Loop"/>` is the discrete lookup escape hatch, applied *after* conversion — for enum-ish bytes this beats a formula.

**Live data table columns: `Logger Data | Min Value | Current Value | Max Value | Units`**, with min/max session-accumulated. Free range discovery on every byte simultaneously. A byte that has covered 0–255 in one drive is not coolant temp.

Profiles (`profile.dtd`) are three independent per-parameter checkboxes — `livedata`, `graph`, `dash` — plus a remembered `units` choice.

ROM-side (`ecu_defs.dtd`) adds the thing the logger format lacks: **two formulas, forward and inverse** — `to_real` and `to_byte` — plus `coarseincrement`/`fineincrement`, where fineincrement should equal one raw LSB expressed in engineering units. Any editable field needs both directions. There's also `scale@logparam IDREF`, which links a ROM table to a live logger parameter.

### TunerPro RT

**ADX (the datastream format) is your real analogue, not XDF.** TunerPro separates bin definition (XDF) from live-stream definition (ADX).

ADX Value fields (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DADefValue.htm): Title, **Unique ID** (max 15 chars), Data Type + Stock Units (optional, only used to auto-link to an XDF item), **Units Override**, **Packet Offset** presented as *side-by-side hex and decimal input boxes*, **Data Source Size** in bits, **Signed**, **LSB First**, **Range Low / Range High**, **Alarm High / Low with enables** (value renders red bold when breached).

Output formats include **Percentage of Defined Range** = `(current − min) / (max − min)`. Truncation, never rounding.

**ADX Lookup Tables** (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DADefLookup.htm) — a first-class calibration primitive with four modes and **a Table Graph tab where you drag points with the mouse**:

| Mode | entries `[2.0→4.0], [4.0→8.0]`, inputs 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.5 |
|---|---|
| **Interpolate** | 5.0 / 6.0 / 7.0 |
| **Closest** | 4.0 / 8.0 / 8.0 |
| **Previous** | 4.0 / 4.0 / 4.0 |
| **Next** | 8.0 / 8.0 / 8.0 |

This is exactly the right UI for "I have 40 samples of raw byte vs. a known ground truth, fit me a curve" — much better than making the user guess `a*x+b`.

The general conversion engine (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/genconv.htm) allows `* / + - %` and bitwise `| & ^`; any alpha character is an **argument**, and each argument binds independently to one of three sources: **This Item's Raw Data**, **Other XDF Item Output** (the *converted* output), or **Raw Value at Address** (arbitrary address + size in bits + endianness flag). Examples straight from the docs: `(1.35 * X) - 40`, `0.351567 * (X - Y)`, `(0.351567 * X) - Y`.

**ADX Bitmask**: offset, size, LSB First, **Operation = AND or XOR** against an operand, then **Display on TRUE** / **Display on FALSE** strings. A mask plus an operator, not a bit index.

**Data Acquisition Tracing** (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DATracing.htm) is the standout feature: link the XDF to the ADX and, while streaming, **the live value highlights the currently-active cell in the ROM table.**

XDF item fields (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/XDFConstantEditor.htm): Address (offset by header Base Offset), **Size in bits** (not bytes), **Signed**, **LSB First** ("checked for Intel, unchecked for Motorola"), Output Type (Floating Point / Integer / Hex Digits / String), Significant Digits, Category A/B, Use Low/High Range (input is *truncated* to range), **Visibility Level** for progressive disclosure.

There is **no published XDF spec document**. The authoritative decoder is RomRaider's `XDFConversionLayer.java`:

```
mmedtypeflags:  0x01 signed | 0x02 LSB first (clear ⇒ big-endian) | 0x04 swap X/Y
mmedmajorstridebits / mmedminorstridebits: row/col strides in BITS, negative legal
```

Other parsers: https://github.com/bri3d/a2l2xdf, https://github.com/willemml/xdftuneparser-rs.

### WinOLS — map-finding heuristics

Vendor: https://www.evc.de/en/product/ols/software/ — *"Program code, empty areas, maps etc. are automatically detected. An overview window shows what can be found where in the file. Program code and empty areas are automatically displayed in pale."*

Reported detection criteria (https://ecufiles.io/technik/winols-map-erkennung):

1. **Statistical distribution analysis** to separate code from data — machine code has a distinct byte histogram
2. **Axis monotonicity** — runs of strictly increasing values, ~8–32 elements, in plausible ranges, flag a candidate axis
3. **Smoothness / second derivative** — maps have low second derivatives; code has high ones throughout
4. **Value-range plausibility** per candidate data type; reject all-`0xFF` / all-`0x00`
5. **Known-ECU database matching**
6. **Cross-version differencing** — the most reliable: two calibrations of the same ECU *"differ almost exclusively in the map regions"*

Visual framing (https://www.fileservice24.at/en/blog/winols-guide-finding-maps): code is *"chaotic, high-frequency noise with no discernible pattern"*; maps are *"smooth, structured shapes: gentle curves, clean staircases, ramps that rise and plateau, or flat lines."*

**Two interaction ideas worth taking:**
- **Adjustable display width + one-byte alignment nudge.** `M`/`W` increase/decrease columns, `Ctrl+arrow` shifts alignment by one byte. You don't know the stride of your RAM layout — make width a slider, not a config field, and watch for the width at which structure appears.
- **A free-floating preview window slaved to the current selection**, rendering it live as a 2D/3D plot. Drag the selection edges, watch the shape. Shape coherence *is* the confirmation.

Manual definition: click-drag from left of the data, drag edges to fine-tune, press **K** to convert the selection into a map. Properties: Name, Units, **Data Type** (e.g. *"16 bit high low"* — endianness baked into the type name), **Factor**, **Offset**. Right-click → "copy map properties", untick *"data source plus address"*, Ctrl+V onto the next map. Typical factors in the wild: `/4096` relative fill %, **`/327.68` throttle %** (16-bit full-scale 0–100), `×40` RPM, `/128` lambda.

### ECUFlash

Near-isomorphic to RomRaider — the Subaru defs are literally stamped *"generated by RR2EcuFlash"*.

```xml
<scaling name="Advance(degrees)2" units="Advance (degrees)"
         toexpr="(x*.001525879)-40" frexpr="(x+40)/.001525879"
         format="%.2f" min="0" max="50.00" inc=".5"
         storagetype="uint16" endian="big" />

<table name="Fuel Map 1" type="3D" swapxy="true" scaling="AFR" address="118A3">
    <table name="Load" address="2eb42" type="X Axis" elements="10" scaling="Load"/>
    <table name="RPM"  address="2ec62" type="Y Axis" elements="15" scaling="RPM"/>
</table>
```

Mapping: `toexpr`/`frexpr` ⇄ RomRaider `expression`/`to_byte`; `inc` ⇄ `fineincrement`; `format="%.2f"` (printf) ⇄ `"0.00"` (DecimalFormat). `storagetype` adds **`bloblist`** — the enum editor, a list of `<data name="..." value="..."/>` pairs.

### Firmware hex-diff tooling

**TunerPro Comparison Tool** (http://tunerpro.net/WebHelp/source/DiffTool.htm) is the best-documented model: pick 2 of 5 loaded bins, enter a **start/end address range**, checkbox **"limit to items defined in the XDF"**. Output is one row per differing byte, with **undefined bytes rendered in blue** — i.e. the diff visually flags *changes you have no definition for*, which is precisely the discovery signal. Click to locate in list, double-click to open the editor.

Others: **OpenRemap** (https://github.com/v-arapidis/openremap-core) diffs two binaries into a `.remap` recipe capturing every changed byte **plus 32 bytes of context anchors** so patches survive firmware revisions. **VBinDiff** (https://www.cjmweb.net/vbindiff/) — two-pane synchronised hex with differences highlighted, trivially copyable interaction. **ImHex** (https://imhex.werwolv.net/) — file diffing plus entropy/digram/byte-distribution visualisers, the closest open-source analogue to WinOLS's code-vs-data overview.

## 4. Correlation-based discovery — the academic pipelines

### READ (Marchetti & Stabili, IEEE TIFS 2018)

https://weblab.ing.unimore.it/people/stabili/papers/2018_READ.pdf

The canonical bit-flip tokenizer. Two phases, not three.

```
bitFlip[i]  = (# times bit i differs from bit i in previous message) / N
magnitude[i]= ceil(log10(bitFlip[i]))          # ceiling, not floor
```

Ceiling is confirmed by the paper's own worked example — a 4-bit counter with rates `[0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0]` yields magnitudes `[0,0,0,0]` only under ceiling. Buckets are decades: rate ∈ (0.1,1] → 0; (0.01,0.1] → −1; etc.

**Phase 1 — boundaries at magnitude drops.** Within one signal, flip rate decreases monotonically from LSB toward MSB. A *drop* scanning left-to-right means you crossed from one signal's LSB into the next signal's MSB:

```
ixS = 0; prev = magnitude[0]
for ix in 1..DLC-1:
    if magnitude[ix] < prev: ref.append((ixS, ix-1)); ixS = ix
    prev = magnitude[ix]
ref.append((ixS, DLC-1))
```

**Phase 2 — labels.** COUNTER: LSB magnitude is 0 (flip probability 1.0) *and* rates double at each step toward the LSB. CRC: all bits magnitude 0 *and* rates distributed normally about 0.5, tested `0.5−σ ≤ μ ≤ 0.5+σ`. PHYS: everything else.

Empirically stable around 100k messages.

### LibreCAN (Pesé et al., ACM CCS 2019)

https://mpese.com/publication/pese-2019-librecan/ACM_CCS_LibreCAN_Paper.pdf

Three phases (0, 1, 2). **IMU data is used in Phase 1 alongside OBD-II PIDs, not in a later phase.** Phase 2 is body/comfort events and uses no IMU.

**Phase 0** is a strictly better READ. Four stages: (0) partition bits into `UNUSED` / `CONST` / `POSS` — this fixes READ silently dropping the high-order constant bits of a physical signal; (1) **replace READ's decade drop with a percentage drop** — boundary when flip rate falls by more than `Tp0,2` fraction from the previous bit; (2) if distinct value count < `Tp0,3`, relabel `MULTI` (categorical); (3) counter test, remainder → `PHYS`.

**The percentage drop is the single most portable improvement in the literature** — it removes the arbitrary decade quantization.

**Phase 1 — matching against ground truth.** 15 OBD-II PIDs + 9 phone channels (3-axis accel, 3-axis gyro, barometric pressure, altitude, bearing) = 24 references, correlated against every Phase-0 signal.

Metric: **normalized cross-correlation**, not DTW. Both sets **resampled to 1 Hz** first — "essential… so that both signals are temporally aligned." (Note: your data is *natively* 1 Hz. You are already at their working resolution.)

Cut-off is adaptive rather than a fixed threshold — Algorithm 2, `Top_X`:

```
running_avg = c[0]; out = [c[0]]; count = 1; running_sum = c[0]
for val in c[1:]:
    if val < (1 - Tp1) * running_avg: break
    out.append(val); running_sum += val; count += 1
    running_avg = running_sum / count
```

`Tp1 = 0.05`. This returns "the leading cluster" whatever the absolute correlation level — much better UI behaviour than a hard `r ≥ 0.8` line.

Scale/offset: `d = m·r + t` by least-squares linear regression on the matched pair.

**Stated limitation, and it is exactly your problem.** Appendix A lists what cross-correlation cannot separate: torque ∝ RPM below ~2000–3000 rpm; **engine load ∝ torque**; torque ∝ boost ∝ MAP; **accelerator pedal position ∝ throttle position**.

**Phase 2 — body events by reference-state diffing.** Build a reference state from idle data, keep IDs with low bit-flip rate, then three filters: drop IDs whose payload never changes during the event; diff against reference, dropping `(ID, payload)` pairs already seen at idle; drop IDs already claimed as powertrain.

Accuracy 90–95%, **precision only 8.5–15%**, recall 46–58% — *deliberately*: "we preferred those parameters that resulted in a high FP rate instead of a high FN rate." Net effect is a >10× reduction in candidates. **This is the correct posture for a human-in-the-loop UI**: shrink the haystack hard, accept false positives, let the human adjudicate.

### ACTT (Verma, Bridges, Hollifield, CSCI 2018) — the one to actually implement

https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.07897

CAN-D explicitly reuses ACTT for its Step 4, and it's the cleanest formulation of "correlate unknowns against a known reference, recover the linear map."

**Tokenization is deliberately dumb.** No flip-rate cascade. Categorize bits into `B0` (always 0), `B1` (always 1), `B_used` (varies). **A valid token is any contiguous run of bits containing no constant bit.** Constants are hard walls; every sub-range inside a run is a candidate.

**Fit and score:**

```
minimize over (a,b):  || a·x̃ + b − y ||²
R² = 1 − S_res / S_tot
accept if R² ≥ α          # α = 0.50 in their experiments
```

**Conflict resolution — the part everyone forgets.** Overlapping accepted tokens (bits 2–8 fits reference A at R²=0.98; bits 1–4 fits reference B at R²=0.95) are resolved by **weighted interval scheduling**, maximizing `Σ R²_T · width_T`, solved exactly by DP in O(n log n) after sorting by end bit.

Without this your UI shows "byte 42 is speed" and "bytes 41–42 are speed" as two separate findings and the user loses trust.

### CAN-D (Verma et al., ORNL)

https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05993

**Step 1 — 15 features per bit pair.** Five *local* features, all flip probabilities:

```
P(F_i), P(F_i | F_{i+1}), P(F_{i+1} | F_i), P(¬F_i | ¬F_{i+1}), P(¬F_{i+1} | ¬F_i)
```

Feature vector = 5 for bit i ⊕ 5 for bit i+1 ⊕ 5 elementwise differences ∈ ℝ¹⁵. Output is a per-bit boundary *probability*, not a hard decision.

**The conditional-flip features are the genuinely new idea and they're cheap.** `P(F_i | F_{i+1})` near 1 means bit i almost always flips when its neighbour does — the signature of two bits inside one integer. That works even when the marginal flip rates have saturated, which is exactly the failure mode you'll hit at 1 Hz.

**Step 2 — endianness as constrained optimization.** Per-byte-boundary state `v(j) ∈ {C, J_B, J_L}` (cut, big-endian join, little-endian join) with constraints (`v(0) ≠ J_L`, `v(7) ≠ J_B`, `v(j)=J_B ⟹ v(j+1) ≠ J_L and v(j+2) ≠ J_L`, …) leaving **577 valid configurations**, grid-searched.

**Step 3 — signedness.** The subagent could not extract the actual rule from the PDF and explicitly flagged its reconstruction as low-confidence. Pull the IEEE version if you need it. A practical test that does work: a signed field crossing zero shows the high bits flipping together, and its *unsigned* reading shows a discontinuity from ~2ⁿ−1 to ~0. Score both interpretations by R² and keep the winner.

**Step 4** delegates to ACTT.

### CANMatch (Buscemi et al., IEEE TVT 2021)

https://orbilu.uni.lu/bitstream/10993/48502/1/FINAL%20VERSION.pdf

Phase 3 is the part worth stealing:

1. **Interpolate every series to n = 60 points** (1 point/sec)
2. **Min-max scale each to [0,1]** — removes all format dependence, compares *shape* only
3. Score by **RMSE**, threshold **θ = 0.01**. They evaluated area-between-curves, RMSE, and DTW and chose RMSE; DTW was slow and unnecessary because these signals have no temporal skew
4. **Scale/offset by linear regression** of raw token values against already-decoded reference values — slope → factor, intercept → offset
5. **Speed disambiguation:** multiple speed-like signals in one frame → wheel speeds; a lone one → vehicle speed

Also a useful correction to READ and LibreCAN: for little-endian, reverse bits *within each byte* while preserving byte order — "endianness is a property of the order of the bytes, not the bits."

**Note the contrast with ACTT:** ACTT regresses raw-against-reference and scores R² ≥ 0.50 on unnormalized data; CANMatch min-max normalizes *both* and scores RMSE ≤ 0.01. **Normalizing first makes the score scale-free and is the better default for a UI ranking list** — keep the regression afterwards purely to recover a and b.

### ByCAN (arXiv 2408.09265)

https://arxiv.org/html/2408.09265v1

Cluster **bytes** before clustering **bits** (DBSCAN at both levels), with a hard **max 2-byte cluster length** justified by: **98.25% of signals in industry DBCs are ≤ 16 bits**.

The labeling parameter is the nice trick:

```
u_mn = |distinct values| / 2^(n−m+1)      # distinct / representable
θ_mn = flip_rate × u_mn
```
```
θ = 0, flip = 0        → Unused
0 < θ ≤ ε₀             → Switch (categorical/flag)
θ ≥ ε₀, flip < 0.99    → Dynamic (physical)
θ ≥ ε₀, flip ≥ 0.99    → Verification (counter/checksum)
```

`ε₀` itself found by DBSCAN over the (θ, flip) population — no hand-set threshold. **`θ = flip_rate × distinct_ratio` is a better one-number type discriminator than flip rate alone** and is trivial to implement.

Slicing accuracy 80.21% vs CAN-D 63.88% vs READ 51.99%. Data needs: **~1,000 frames for slicing, ~10,000 for labeling.** At 1 Hz that's ~17 minutes and ~3 hours respectively — budget your capture sessions accordingly and show the user a sample-count confidence indicator.

### Setterstrom & Straub 2026 — event-windowed correlation

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.16722

Deliberately skips tokenization: chops payloads into **fixed 16-bit hypothesis channels** and does semantic correlation only. Five layers: IMU + CAN capture → **event detection** (accel / decel / steering, in bounded windows) → **rate-of-change correlation within event windows** → ranked association → GUI verification.

Achieved r: accelerator 0.455–0.832, brake 0.744–0.945, steering 0.567–0.863 across six vehicles. Validated against openDBC — on a 2016 Sierra it flagged ID 241 for brake and openDBC confirms BrakePedalPosition at bit 15 of message 241, **despite the fixed 16-bit window not aligning to the true 8-bit field.**

Two transferable ideas, both high-value for you:
1. **Correlate on the rate of change, not the raw value** — this kills the "everything correlates with everything" problem caused by slow-moving confounders
2. **Correlate only inside event windows the human deliberately created**, not over the whole trace

And one reassurance: a misaligned but *overlapping* window still correlates well enough to localize. Your UI doesn't need perfect boundaries before it can rank.

### CANvas (Kulandaivel et al., USENIX Security 2019)

https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity19/presentation/kulandaivel

Network mapper — which ECU sends each ID, which receive it, how many exist. Pairwise clock-offset tracking (σ(Δ) < 1 ms ⇒ same ECU), plus forced ECU isolation via bus-off injection. **Explicitly does no payload semantics.** Zero applicability to a flat RAM window; listed for completeness only.

### Practical (non-academic)

**CSS Electronics AI RE workflow** — https://www.csselectronics.com/pages/can-bus-reverse-engineering-ai-llm-claude, skills repo (MIT) at https://github.com/CSS-Electronics/can-bus-reverse-engineering-skills. The most UI-shaped source. Four stages:

1. **Bit-activity heatmap** — counters and checksum bytes are *flagged and excluded before anything else runs*
2. **Correlation against reference** — **windowed Spearman rank correlation, median-pooled across overlapping windows**. Spearman rather than Pearson because it survives monotone-but-nonlinear maps and outliers. Test both signednesses; slide the reference over a small lag range; mask "signal unavailable" sentinel outliers
3. **Bitsearch** — exhaustive grid over start bit × length × endianness × signedness, scored by R². Tie-break: **prefer shorter fields**, since longer ones swallow neighbours
4. **Scale & offset** — slope as the **median slope over many point pairs** (robust, not OLS); then round to OEM-plausible values (0.1, not 0.0999281) if the fit doesn't degrade; then enforce physical anchors (must read zero when stationary) by re-fitting

Reference-quality tiers: CAN-based best, dashboard-video OCR next, human-generated worst — the last needs deliberate 0/25/50/75/100% hold sweeps. ~90%+ success, 5–10 min per signal.

**canair** — https://philipkocanda.github.io/canair/bring-your-own-car/06-analyze/

```
canair hunt uds MyECU:2101 --against ESC:22C101:REAL_SPEED_KMH
canair hunt uds MyECU:2101 --against-file gps_speed.csv
```

Sweeps every byte offset × {u8, i16, f32} × endianness × linear `y = scale·x + offset`, against either an on-bus signal or an external two-column CSV joined by nearest timestamp.

- **Pearson r for continuous; Cramér's V or mutual information for categorical/flag channels.** Worth copying — a bitfield correlated by Pearson is nonsense
- `--control` regresses out a nuisance signal to surface correlations hidden behind a dominant driver
- Evidence standard: r near 1.0 **and** a physically plausible fitted equation (slope ≈ 1.0 for speed-to-speed)
- **Physical plausibility bands** when no reference exists — does the scaled value land in a named range (12 V rail, HV pack)?
- UI keys: `e` annotates a capture ("Heating started"), `s` jumps to named moments, `V` shows only changed parameters, `p` toggles signals

**The `e`-key event annotation is the cheapest high-value feature in any tool surveyed**, and it is exactly the user-supplied event track you asked about.

## 5. Hex dump UI conventions

**FCEUX Hex Editor** (https://fceux.com/web/help/HexEditor.html) — the classic live-RAM view. Colours: black standard, **green bookmarked**, **blue frozen**, **red modified**. **Highlight Activity** "can draw your attention to bytes that changed their value since the last frame" — with the honest caveat that "this feature does not track the actual changes of RAM. It works by simply comparing current values to previously displayed values." At 1 Hz that limitation is irrelevant; you *only* have displayed values.

**Mesen Memory Tools** (https://www.mesen.ca/docs/debugging/memorytools.html):
- **View → Memory Access Highlighting** — reads blue, writes red, executions green, with **configurable fade-out periods**
- **View → De-emphasize** — render unused / read / written / executed bytes in grey. Inverse of highlighting, and often the more useful direction
- **Memory Access Counters** with **Sort By** and a reset button — the aggregate view, and the reset is what makes it a scoped experiment
- Frozen values render magenta

**ImHex** (https://docs.werwolv.net/imhex/views/hex-editor):
- Footer toggles: **Upper case hex characters**, **Gray out zeros**, **Display ASCII column**, **Display advanced decoding column**, **Mini Map**
- **Mini Map** next to the scrollbar, one line per row, coloured by entropy — "the bluer the color, the higher the entropy". Right-click for alternative visualizers
- Cell visualizer dropdown (hex / decimal / float / colour) + **a slider for big/little endian interpretation** + column count + **Segment Separator** every N bytes + address radix
- **Data Inspector** — show the selected bytes simultaneously as every type, signed and unsigned, both endiannesses

**Cheat Engine's own memory viewer**, reached via right-click → **Browse this memory region**, keeps the hex dump and the watch table as separate but linked panes. That separation is right: the dump is for discovery, the table is for accumulated knowledge.

---

## 6. Concrete design for 252 bytes at 1 Hz

### The arithmetic is in your favour, and it changes everything

252 bytes × widths {1, 2, 4} × 2 endianness × 2 signedness ≈ **3,000 hypotheses**. At 1 Hz that's 3,000 evaluations per second — nothing, in a browser, in JS.

**So don't build a tokenizer.** READ, LibreCAN Stage 1, ByCAN and CANMatch all exist because CAN payloads are 64 bits and bit-packed and you must guess boundaries before you can do anything. You have a flat byte-addressed RAM map on a 1990s Motronic — it is 8- and 16-bit scalars on byte boundaries, near-certainly. Enumerate every hypothesis exhaustively, every sample, forever. Skip candidates that span a byte you've classified UNUSED or CONST (ACTT's rule: constants are hard walls).

### The 1 Hz problem, stated plainly

**Most of the tokenization literature will underperform on your data, and you should design around that rather than port it.** READ's decade cascade assumes consecutive samples differ by a small fraction of range, which holds at 10–100 Hz. At 1 Hz, RPM moves hundreds between samples and the low 6–8 bits of a 16-bit field are effectively random — all sitting at flip rate ≈ 0.5, magnitude 0. The cascade flattens and you get one giant token or garbage boundaries.

Consequences: prefer LibreCAN's percentage drop or CANMatch's absolute τ = 0.3 over READ's `ceil(log10)`; lean on CAN-D's *conditional* flip features which survive saturation; and lean hardest on **reference correlation**, which doesn't depend on the cascade at all. With 5 known anchors you're better positioned than any blind tokenizer.

One addition none of the papers need: at 1 Hz a *fast* physical signal masquerades as a checksum on flip rate alone. Disambiguate with **lag-1 autocorrelation of the byte value** — physical channels retain structure, checksums don't.

### The build, in order of value per unit of effort

**1. Live hex grid, 252 cells, colour-by-pattern with fade.** Port cabana's classifier verbatim (§2a) — it's 20 lines and the constants are published. At 1 Hz set `decay_limit = 2.0 s` so a changed byte stays lit for two full samples. Width adjustable (WinOLS `M`/`W`) with a one-byte alignment nudge. Grey out UNUSED/CONST automatically; that alone will probably eliminate half your 252 bytes on the first idle capture.

**2. Min / Current / Max columns, session-accumulated** (RomRaider). Free range discovery on all 252 bytes at once. A byte that covered 0–255 is not coolant temp; a byte that never left 0–200 might be TPS.

**3. "Number of Changes" per byte, with a reset button** (BizHawk + Mesen's counter reset). Blip the throttle exactly 4 times in a 60-sample window, filter `changes ≈ 4`. This is the single highest-value primitive at 1 Hz because it's an aggregate — immune to the sample-timing jitter that wrecks per-sample Increased/Decreased.

**4. Cheat Engine scan panel.** Copy cabana's `findsignal.cc` exactly: First Scan / Next Scan / Undo / New Scan, an unlimited undo stack (a history of candidate lists, not one level), parameters locked after First Scan, and a live "N candidates remaining" line. Compare modes: `Any Value | = | ≠ | > | ≥ | < | ≤ | Between A…B | ↕ Changed | = Unchanged | ↑ Increased | ↓ Decreased | ↑ Increased By | ↓ Decreased By`, plus a **Compare to: previous / first / saved snapshot** selector.

**Add the percentage scan** (§1). It is how you find TPS without knowing its scaling.

**Add Preview** (BizHawk) — at 1 Hz a mis-timed Next Scan is expensive; show what will be removed before committing.

**5. An event track, with a keyboard shortcut.** This is the highest-leverage feature in the entire survey and almost nobody has it. One key marks the current sample: `throttle floored`, `throttle closed`, `stopped`, `coasting`. Then score candidates **inside those windows only** (Setterstrom & Straub), on **rate of change** rather than raw value. This dissolves most of the physical-coupling ambiguity that LibreCAN flags as its hard limit.

**6. Correlation ranking against your 5 knowns + the event track.** Per candidate:

```
join on timestamp (both already 1 Hz — no resampling needed)
optionally differentiate both
min-max normalize both to [0,1]                    # CANMatch: scale-free
r_s = Spearman(c, d)                               # CSS: survives nonlinearity
best_lag = argmax over lag ∈ [-3s, +3s]
a, b, R² = linreg(c_raw, d_raw)                    # raw, to recover real scale/offset
```

Rank by R². Then apply **LibreCAN's adaptive `Top_X` cut, `Tp1 = 0.05`**, not a fixed threshold — show the leading cluster, whatever its absolute level. For flag/categorical candidates use **Cramér's V or mutual information**, never Pearson.

Then **de-overlap with ACTT's weighted interval scheduling** so you never show "byte 42 is speed" and "bytes 41–42 are speed" as two findings.

**7. Arrow-key candidate browser with live plot preview** (SavvyCAN Range State). You are not reading correlation coefficients, you are flipping through plots looking for a shape you recognise. At ~2 candidates/second this beats any ranking metric for the final call.

**8. Baseline-vs-event diff** (SavvyCAN File Comparison, LibreCAN Phase 2, WinOLS cross-version). Capture idle-with-no-throttle as a reference; capture with the action. Then show, per byte, **values present in one capture and not the other**. Render bytes with no definition in a distinct colour (TunerPro's blue-for-undefined) — the undefined changes *are* the discovery signal.

**9. Watch table with confidence tiers.** Columns: freeze/pin | description | address | type | current | min | max | units. Add a **confidence field** — `confirmed / probable / guess / unknown` — repurposing RomRaider's `userlevel` and TunerPro's `vislevel`, and colour the hex grid by it. Adopt RomRaider's `*`-suffix convention for RE'd-vs-documented.

**10. Definition schema.** RomRaider's, minus the parts you don't need:

```
Parameter  { id, name, desc, address, length=1, bit=-1, confidence }
Conversion { units*, expr*, format*, storagetype?, endian?=big,
             gauge_min?, gauge_max?, gauge_step?, replace[] }
```

**N conversions per parameter** — competing hypotheses about the same address, switchable live. Gauge defaults keyed on the units string (§3). `expr` in a small JEP-like language with `BitWise(mask, x, op)`. `<replace>` for enums. Derived channels via `depends`/`ref` so a user can test "byte 47 × 0.5 − byte 12" without touching code.

**11. Interactive lookup-table fitter** (TunerPro ADX). Plot raw byte vs. ground truth, drag points, pick Interpolate / Closest / Previous / Next. Far better than asking a user to guess `a*x+b`. Follow with the CSS cleanup: **median-of-pairwise-slopes** rather than OLS, round to plausible OEM constants (0.1, 0.25, 1/8, 0.375, 1.28) if R² barely moves, then anchor-enforce (speed = 0 when stationary).

### Finding TPS specifically

You already have injection load — and LibreCAN's Appendix A says **engine load ∝ torque ∝ throttle**, so TPS *will* correlate strongly with what you have. That's how you find it, and also why correlation alone won't confirm it. Discriminators:

- TPS is **bounded and clips hard at both ends** (0% and 100%); load does not clip the same way
- On **closed-throttle overrun**, TPS drops to its floor immediately while load lags and fuel cuts
- **Drive a deliberate staircase**: hold 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100% for ~10 s each. A true TPS byte becomes a clean five-step function; load stays noisy. **This makes TPS findable by shape alone, no reference needed** — and it's also what feeds the percentage scan and the lookup-table fitter
- Expect a single byte, monotone, non-negative, 0–255 or 0–200. If MS41 is right it's `x*100/255`, i.e. full-scale 255

### Finding road speed specifically

Nothing you have correlates with it directly. Three attacks, best first:

**Gear-ratio heuristic — build this, it's the strongest signal available and it's in none of the papers.** For each candidate `c`, compute `c / RPM` across the drive and test whether the ratio is **piecewise constant with a small number of discrete levels**. That is the definitive signature of road speed on a manual E36 and nothing else in the ECU has it. Cluster the ratio series (1-D DBSCAN, or just count histogram modes); a candidate yielding 4–5 tight modes plus a scatter class for neutral/clutch-in is your speed byte. Far more decisive than any correlation coefficient.

**GPS ground truth.** canair's `--against-file` model: log phone GPS speed at 1 Hz during the same drive, join by nearest timestamp, correlate. Turns the problem into a solved one, and gives you the scale for free (if MS41 is right, slope should come out ≈ 1.0 against km/h).

**Stop/start events.** Mark "stopped" moments with the event key. Road speed is the only channel that is *exactly* zero at every stop and nonzero between them — RPM idles nonzero, load idles nonzero.

If several speed-like bytes appear adjacent in the map, CANMatch's rule applies: adjacent cluster ⇒ per-wheel speeds; solitary ⇒ vehicle speed. An E36 with ABS may well show both.

### Threshold quick-reference

| Constant | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| cabana toggle EMA alpha | 0.15 | cabana source |
| cabana trend streak threshold / max | 4 / 8 | cabana source |
| cabana noise EMA threshold | 0.55 | cabana source |
| cabana fade decay | `clamp(2/freq, 0.4, 2.5)` s, quadratic ease-out | cabana source |
| cabana bit-mute window | 2.0 s | cabana source |
| SavvyCAN sniffer refresh / notch window | 200 ms | SavvyCAN docs |
| READ magnitude | `ceil(log10(bfr))` | READ |
| LibreCAN pct-drop `Tp0,2` | 0.01 (raise for small spaces) | LibreCAN |
| LibreCAN adaptive cut `Tp1` | 0.05 | LibreCAN |
| LibreCAN idle BFR `Tp2,0` | 0.02–0.03 | LibreCAN |
| ACTT R² accept `α` | 0.50 | ACTT |
| CANMatch BFR drop `τ` | 0.3 | CANMatch |
| CANMatch normalized-RMSE `θ` | 0.01 | CANMatch |
| CANMatch resample | 60 pts @ 1 Hz | CANMatch |
| ByCAN max cluster width | 2 bytes (98.25% of signals ≤ 16 bits) | ByCAN |
| ByCAN verification flip rate | ≥ 0.99 | ByCAN |
| Samples needed | ~1k slice / ~10k label (17 min / 3 hr @ 1 Hz) | ByCAN |

---

## 7. Caveats

- The CAN-literature agent flagged that PDFs were read through a text-extraction proxy, so equations and constants are reconstructions rather than literal transcriptions. Verify anything you hard-code against the linked PDF. **CAN-D's Step 3 signedness rule specifically could not be extracted** and the plausible-looking version the agent produced was self-rated low-confidence / possibly synthesized. Pull the IEEE version if you need it.
- READ's `ceil` vs `floor` on the log10: one extraction pass said floor, but the paper's own worked example only works with ceiling, and LibreCAN independently describes it as `⌈log₁₀⌉`. Use ceiling.
- `CANHunter` and `CSER` returned nothing. The agent believes those may be misremembered names for ACTT/CAN-D (same ORNL group) and CANMatch, but the search budget capped mid-task so treat them as "not found" rather than confirmed nonexistent.
- The WinOLS map-detection criteria come from third-party writeups, not vendor documentation — EVC doesn't publish the algorithm.
- `romraider.com` and `tunerpro.net` return 403 to automated fetchers but serve fine to curl with a browser UA, if you script any of this.
- My web-search budget hit its cap during this session; later lookups used direct URL fetches only. ---

# What actually separates professional instrumentation from amateur dashboards

## The headline correction

The intuitive thesis — *professionals use flat design, amateurs use skeuomorphism* — **is false**, and worth killing early.

- **Bosch Motorsport** (DTM/WEC/GT3) ships a stock `Classic Gauge` widget on DDU10/11 with a **brushed-chrome bezel ring with specular highlight, a radial navy→cyan gradient face, and a red wedge needle**. I verified this by rendering p.51 of the official DDU11 manual.
- **MoTeC's own 2015 dealer training deck** teaches building a chrome-bezelled dial as its primary worked example, using photorealistic ring bitmaps from Display Creator's `Dial` image library (up to 1004×1004px), plus glow via *"decrease the opacity so that you get more of a glowing effect."*
- **AiM** ships `Analog 1 / Analog 1 white / Analog 2` page templates — literal round dials with radial ticks and a red needle on a pivot hub.

The real dividing line is not ornament. It is **four things**:

1. **Geometric hierarchy is encoded in length, not colour or weight.** Amateur gauges differentiate major/minor ticks by making them a lighter grey. Professional ones use a *documented length ratio* and hold stroke weight nearly constant.
2. **The pointer never occludes what you need to read.** This is a hard rule in every standard and the single most common amateur failure.
3. **Alarm state is a system-level concept with one consistent rendering**, hysteresis, priority ordering, and acknowledgement — not a per-widget colour change.
4. **Every visual effect is load-bearing.** Bosch's gradient is a fill indicator. MoTeC's glow is a simulated backlight on a specific object. Neither applies bloom to *values*.

---

## 1. Tick mark treatment

**The converged geometry.** Two independent authorities agree almost exactly:

| | Major | Intermediate | Minor | Ratio (maj:int:min) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MIL-STD-1472F/G, Fig. 3/26 (**length**, visual angle) | 7.86 mrad (27′) | 5.82 mrad (20′) | 3.49 mrad (12′) | **2.25 : 1.67 : 1** |
| Grether & Baker 1972 via Sanders & McCormick Fig. 5-4 (**length**, at 710 mm) | 0.22 in (5.6 mm) | 0.16 in (4.1 mm) | 0.09 in (2.3 mm) | **2.44 : 1.78 : 1** |

So: **major ≈ 2.2–2.5× minor length; intermediate ≈ 1.6–1.8× minor.** A 2.0× ratio (what most amateur gauges use, if they vary length at all) is slightly under-differentiated.

**Stroke weight is the surprise.** Under normal illumination, Grether & Baker specify **all three tick sizes at identical width** (0.0125 in). Hierarchy is length-only. Only under low illumination do widths diverge, and only mildly (0.035 / 0.030 / 0.025 in = 1.4 : 1.2 : 1). MIL-STD-1472 notes explicitly: *"the width of the minor graduation mark can be used for major and intermediate graduation marks as well. Use of this strategy allows the width of the pointer tip to be the same as all of the graduation marks."*

**Counting rules (MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.3.1.5, verbatim):**
- *"Scale graduations shall progress by 1, 2, or 5 units or decimal multiples thereof."*
- *"No more than three sizes of marks (minor, intermediate, and major) shall be used on any scale."*
- Two-level marking: **no more than 4 minor marks** between numbered markers.
- Three-level marking: **no more than 9 minor marks**.
- *"Intermediate marks shall only be used when there are more than four minor marks."* — i.e. you don't earn a third tier until you have five or more subdivisions.

Sanders & McCormick add that progression **by 1s is easiest, 5s satisfactory, 2s moderately so; avoid 3s and 8s.**

**Direction and rail.** MIL-STD figures show ticks on a **common base line, extending different lengths from it** — no arc/rail line drawn joining them. Ticks point **inward from the outer edge** in the accuracy-optimised layout (Fig. 4 top). Bosch's `Classic Gauge` and `Modern Gauge` both do exactly this: ticks hang inward from the outer edge, no rail. AiM's arc tach and Bosch's `Modern horizontal Bar` put ticks **outside/above the bar**, pointing at it.

**In the wild:** Bosch's gauges use **two-level marking, 1 minor per major** (majors at 0–10, one tick between each) — consistent with the "≤4 minors ⇒ no intermediate tier" rule. VDO Cockpit 80mm tachos observed at 4 minors per major (200 rpm graduations). Stack 52mm aux gauges: 1 minor per major; Stack 80mm ST700 tach: 4–5 minors per major.

**Where TunerStudio fails:** ticks are **not authorable at all**. Developer Phil Tobin, replying to a user asking for majors at 0/25/50/75/100 with minors between: *"They are auto generated based on min/max and size."* Manual tick placement was a promised, unshipped feature.

---

## 2. Numeral placement

This has an unambiguous documented answer, and it's the rule most amateur gauges break.

**MIL-STD-1472F §5.2.3.2.3.6:** *"When reading time and accuracy are critical, scale markings and the location of associated numbers shall be arranged to prevent pointers from covering any portion of the scale marks or numerals... If readout accuracy is not critical (i.e., gross relationship between the pointer and number is all that is required), an arrangement of numerals inside the scale annulus may be used."*

Figure 4 labels these two layouts explicitly:
- Numerals **outside** the tick ring → *"FOR MAXIMUM READING ACCURACY"*
- Numerals **inside** the tick ring → *"ALTERNATE FORMAT FOR GROSS READING OF NUMBERS"*

**§5.2.3.2.4.4:** *"Numerals shall be placed on the side of the graduation marks away from the pointer."*

**Orientation (§5.2.3.2.2, and 1472G):** *"On fixed scales, numerals shall be vertically oriented"* — **upright, never rotated to the radius**. (Rotation is required only on *moving* scales, where numerals rotate to be upright as they pass the index.) Every professional dash I examined obeys this: AiM, MoTeC, Bosch Classic *and* Modern gauges all use upright numerals.

**The one documented exception**, from MIL-STD-1472G Fig. 26: *"When dial face is deeply inset within instrument case and visibility of numbers is more important than scale pointer-mark association, pointer may be located inside the graduations along with numbers at major markings. Pointer width shall be narrowed at point in which it passes numbers."* — Note the compensating requirement. If you put numerals inside, you must thin the needle where it crosses them.

**Which values get numerals:** *"whole numbers shall be used for major graduation marks"*; *"A display scale shall start at zero."* Fig. 26 adds: *"For short, finite scale, every 5th graduation is marked, using only two-level marking."*

**Observed:** Bosch `Classic Gauge` puts numerals inside the ticks (gross-reading layout, consistent with it being a supplementary gauge with a digital value in the centre); Bosch `Modern Gauge` puts them outside. VDO Cockpit: inside, upright. Stack: inside, upright.

---

## 3. Redline / warning zone rendering

**The aviation ancestry is the actual standard**, and it makes a distinction most car dashboards blur. From **14 CFR 25.1549**:

- **Red radial line** = *"Each maximum and, if applicable, minimum safe operating limit"* — a **limit is a line, not a band**.
- **Red arc** = a *restricted range* (e.g. excessive vibration stresses).
- **Green arc** = *"Each normal operating range... not extending beyond the maximum and minimum safe limits."*
- **Yellow arc** = *"Each takeoff and precautionary range."*

MIL-STD-1472F §5.2.3.1.10 permits red/yellow/green zone coding on scale faces, and adds a robustness requirement: *"Zone scales may be shape coded when the indicator must be viewed in blackout conditions or where the illuminant color will cause difficulty in color band discrimination."* — redundant coding, not colour alone.

**What the products actually do:**

| System | Redline rendering |
|---|---|
| **AiM** | No printed redline zone. The **shift-LED bar *is* the redline mechanism**, via per-LED RPM thresholds. |
| **Bosch DDU** | Conditional formatting recolours the **tick arc**; segmented bars recolour by zone. |
| **MoTeC** | Dash Manager bars work on **boundary points** (Left / Intermediate 1 / Intermediate 2 / Right), each assigned one of 3 colours, plus *"Show intermediate tick marks"* and a **`Change whole bar colour`** checkbox — flips the entire bar rather than only the exceeded portion. Round gauges: small red ticks at the redline value, or a red arc wedge. |
| **Stack ST8100 family** | **No printed redline arc found** on the analogue tach face in either the manual diagrams or product photography. Warning is delegated to a discrete amber lamp. |
| **Stack Pro-Control gauges** | The **entire dial face backlight changes colour** on threshold breach (7 selectable colours). |
| **TunerStudio** | Coloured arc segment on the face **plus** danger colour applied to gauge background — but *"only the portion of the bar exceeding that threshold changes color. The rest remains in the normal color."* Whole-gauge alerting requires manually building a boolean channel and layering a second element. |

The MoTeC `Change whole bar colour` option and Stack's whole-face backlight change are the professional answer to the exact problem TunerStudio users had to file a feature request about: **at a glance you want a binary in/out-of-bounds read, not a proportional colour sliver.**

---

## 4. Needle design

MIL-STD-1472F/G §5.2.3.1.7 is fully prescriptive:

- **Taper:** *"The pointer tip shall be tapered at a 20 degree angle (40 degree included angle), terminating in a flat tip equal in width to the minor scale graduations."* Note: a **flat tip matched to minor tick width**, not a sharp point and not a rounded cap.
- **Length:** *"shall extend to, but not overlap, the shortest scale graduation marks."* Figure 4 quantifies the gap: *"THE POINTER IS AN EQUAL DISTANCE — NOMINAL 0.8–1.6 mm (0.031–0.061 in.) — FROM ALL SCALE MARKS, NEVER OVERLAPPING ANY MARK OR NUMERAL."*
- **Colour:** *"Pointer color from the tip to the center of the dial shall be the same as the color of the marks. The tail of the pointer shall be the same color as the dial face, unless the tail is used as an indicator itself or unless the pointer is used for horizontal alignment."*

That last clause is the counter-intuitive one: **the counterweight tail should be invisible.** It exists mechanically, not visually. And this is borne out in hardware — across Stack, VDO, and Bosch's rendered needle, **not one sample showed a counterweight extending past the pivot.** All are one-directional pointer shapes.

- **Mounting:** *"as close as possible to the face of the dial to minimize parallax"* — and marks *"on or close to the plane of the pointer tip."*

**Hub treatment.** VDO's signature is a **large, glossy, domed black hub cap with a specular highlight**, consistently across Cockpit/Vision and Viewline — the strongest single VDO identifier. Stack uses a much smaller, unobtrusive dark cap. Bosch's `Classic Gauge Large` has **no hub cap at all** — the needle stops well short of centre, leaving a lighter disc reserved for an overlaid digital value.

**Needle colour pairs with face colour:** Stack = white needle on black face, orange on white/silver. VDO Cockpit/Vision = red needle on black. VDO Viewline "Onyx" = white on black, "Ivory" = red on white.

**The Bosch `Modern Gauge` abandons the needle entirely** — a thick cyan arc fills from zero to value, and the *current value is marked by a short white radial tick at the leading edge of the fill*, with a large digital numeral in the centre. This is the most sophisticated pattern I found (see §7).

## 5. Bezel treatment

**Physical hardware:** essentially no bezels. AiM housings are flat anodised aluminium or glass-fibre nylon, matte, screen glass flush. Bosch DDU is a flat TFT behind glass in a rectangular housing. Stack's ST8100 dial and LCD are **inset flush into a single moulded black composite panel** with no ring at all. VDO Cockpit/Vision uses a thin, flat *"peaked black"* bezel — no chrome option in the classic line; Viewline adds thicker rounded black plus chrome and white variants.

**On-screen, the professional tools split into two explicit modes**, and this is the most useful framing I found:

- Bosch DDU10/11 offers **`Classic`** (chrome bezel, gradient face, red wedge needle) and **`Modern`** (no bezel, flat black, arc fill, centre numeral) as **parallel, equally-supported catalogues** of the same primitives (Box, horizontal/vertical Bar, Gauge Large/Small).
- MoTeC supports both: skeuomorphic chrome-bezel dials via bitmap layering, *and* flat colour-blocked numeric table pages with no gauge skeuomorphism (the "Four Line Style" page).

**Bosch DDU7/8/9 have no needle-gauge widget at all** — only Numeric, Bargraph, Alarm/Alarm Icon, Label, Picture. The dial only arrived with the DDU10 generation.

**One genuinely functional reason to recess**, from MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.1.3.3: *"When the detection of faint signals is required and when the ambient illuminance may be above 2.7 lux, displays shall be hooded, shielded, or recessed."* A recess is a real optical device against glare. Simulating an inset shadow in software delivers none of that benefit and costs contrast.

## 6. Layout density and grid

**800 × 480 is the de facto race-dash resolution.** This is a striking convergence:

| Device | Size | Resolution | LEDs |
|---|---|---|---|
| AiM MXS 1.2 | 5″ | 800×480 | 10 shift + 6 alarm |
| AiM MXP | 6″ | 800×480 | 10 shift + 5 alarm |
| AiM MXG 1.2 | 7″ | 800×480 | 10 shift + 8 alarm |
| MoTeC C125 | 5″ (125 mm) | 800×480 | 10 RGB |
| MoTeC C127 | 7″ (178 mm) | 800×480 | 16 RGB |
| Bosch DDU 8 | 5″ | 800×480 | 10 RGB (top) |
| Bosch DDU 11 | 6.5″ | 800×480 | 18 (8 top + 5/side) |
| Bosch DDU 10 | 7″ | 800×480 | 20 (10 top + 5/side) |
| Bosch DDU 7 / 9 | 5.7″ trans-reflective | 640×480 | 10 RGB |

AiM does **not scale resolution with screen size** — only physical DPI. Note MoTeC's spec sheet lists *"Colour TFT LCD, anti-reflective"* and *"800 x 480 resolution, anti-aliased graphics"* as **first-class spec-table line items**. Anti-glare treatment and anti-aliasing are engineering claims, not styling.

**The standard page composition** (AiM Driver page, confirmed across many rendered examples):
- **Top:** RPM bar/arc spanning full width, shift-LED row directly above it
- **Centre:** **gear number, consistently the single largest glyph — 1.5–3× the cap-height of everything else**
- **Around/below:** a 2×2 to 3×2 grid of secondary fields (speed, water temp, oil pressure, battery, lap time), each a Channel + Label + Unit triplet with independent show/hide toggles
- **Bottom:** a full-width `INFO LINE` text banner plus small status icons

Primary/secondary hierarchy is conveyed by **vertical position and size, not colour**. Colour is reserved for semantic status.

**Alignment is not universally settled.** MoTeC's own stock layouts contradict each other: the C187 factory page **left-aligns** values flush with their label's left edge, while the bordered "spreadsheet" table page **right-aligns** values in their cells. There is no single MoTeC rule.

**MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.2.3.5 gives a hard hierarchy rule worth adopting:** *"No more than three size levels shall be used. The major dimensions of the larger size shall be not less than 150 percent of the major dimension of the smaller."*

**Page count:** AiM up to 8 pages, template-based (you pick from a thumbnail gallery and remap channels — **not a blank canvas**). MoTeC C125: 12 customisable fixed layouts, or full freeform via the paid Display Creator upgrade. Bosch: fully blank canvas, 12 pages (DDU7/8/9/10) or 48 (DDU11 = 12 pages × 4 switchable sets) — **no default factory template at all**; teams design their own per car and per driver.

## 7. Glow, bloom, and gradients

**Professional systems use gradients. They do not use bloom on values.** The distinction is that every effect maps to a physical referent:

| Effect | Professional use | Amateur tell |
|---|---|---|
| **Gradient** | Bosch `Modern Bar`: each filled segment has an internal gradient; the arc has a subtle inner-edge lightening. AiM's arc tach: the colour fill *is* the indicator. | Decorative radial gradient on a static gauge face; glossy "glass" highlight arcs. |
| **Glow** | MoTeC teaches it as a **reduced-opacity bitmap layered near a light source** — simulating a real backlight, on a specific object. | `text-shadow`/`drop-shadow` applied globally to numerals, needles, and traces. |
| **Drop shadow** | Essentially absent. RaceCapture ships `round_gauge_270_shadow.png` composited every frame — and it is one of the things that marks it as hobbyist. | Shadow on the needle, on values, on tiles. |
| **Bloom/halo** | **None found in any AiM, MoTeC, or Bosch rendering.** | Halos on lit LEDs and active segments. |

The governing rule, MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.2.3.1: ***"Coding shall not be used if it reduces legibility or transmission time."***

Two more constraints that bite directly:
- §5.2.2.3.3: *"No more than two levels of brightness shall be used and each level shall be separated... by not less than a 2:1 ratio."* A glow gradient creates a continuum of brightness levels, destroying the coding channel.
- §5.2.3.1.8: *"A luminance contrast not less than 3.0 shall be provided between the scale face and the markings and pointer."* Table XII requires **≥5:1 between lighter and darker surfaces within the task**. Every glow halo raises the local background luminance around the very element it surrounds, which reduces that ratio.

**Physics reinforces this.** In sunlight, reflected ambient light adds a constant luminance floor to *both* the lit and unlit states. A dark UI's contrast advantage collapses; only peak luminance (AiM: 700 cd/m²) and low reflectance (MoTeC: *"anti-reflective"*) help. A software glow adds emitted light *around* a glyph — precisely where you need the floor lowest.

**The one hard-won detail worth stealing:** Bosch's `Modern` bars render **discrete segments with the leading segment in a brighter, near-white shade**. This is not decoration — it simultaneously provides the filled-bar magnitude read *and* a distinct pointer position, resolving a tradeoff Paul Green identified in 1984 (see §10).

## 8. Typography

**Named typefaces actually in use:**

| System | Typeface | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **AiM RaceStudio 3** | **`MicrogrammaDBolExt`** — Microgramma D Bold Extended | Novarese & Butti, Nebiolo, **1952**; caps-only; predecessor of Eurostile (1962). Squarish superellipse counters. Used for **both** Digit Font and Label Font. |
| **MoTeC** | Not disclosed. But ships **three icon fonts: `MoTeC01`, `MoTeC02`, `MoTeC03`** | See below — this is the important finding. |
| **Bosch DDU** | Not disclosed; **FreeType** for *"non-bitmap font rendering"* (license text in DDU11 manual) | Visually blocky, monospaced, tabular figures. |
| **RaceCapture** | Bespoke `ASL_light.ttf` / `ASL_regular.ttf` + Roboto family | But bundles **six-plus families** including `enigmatic.ttf` and `forgotten_futurist-rg.ttf`. |
| **Smiths** | **None — hand-drawn.** | Restoration forums: originals were *"hand painted by a sign writer then reduced and transferred to a silk screen."* Don't chase a "Smiths font." |
| **VDO** | Not disclosed. Community approximation: Arial Black, per the numeral "1" shape. Treat as unverified. |

**MoTeC's telltale approach is the single best implementation idea in this research:** *"A great way to incorporate tell tales into your DC project is by using font based icons. By using a font, the icon (tell tale) remains a vector graphic and is therefore scaleable and remains crisp. It also means that you set the colour of the icon, perhaps using different colours to indicate various states."* Icons as a font, recoloured for state.

**Size relationships (measured):** AiM's Display config shows `Digit Font: MicrogrammaDBolExt` **size 42**, `Label Font: MicrogrammaDBolExt` **size 20** — **label ≈ 48% of value**. Units render as small tags adjacent to the value (superscript-like, upper-right), not as a separate row.

**Labels are uppercase, short, abbreviated:** `ENG TEMP`, `OIL PRESS`, `GBOX OIL TMP`, `DIFF OIL TMP`, `WATER TMP` (MoTeC); `R/P/M` stacked letter-per-line (AiM). Labels sit **above** values, smaller, usually in an accent colour distinct from the value's high-contrast white.

**MIL-STD-1472F §5.5.5 numbers** (all relative to character height):

- Stroke width, **dark on light: 1/6 to 1/7**
- Stroke width, **light on dark: 1/7 to 1/8** — *thinner*, to counter irradiation
- Stroke width, **transilluminated: 1/10**
- Numeral width: **3/5 of height**, except "4" = 4/5 and "1" = 1/5
- *"Where wide characters are required, e.g. ... for column alignment of numbers, the basic height-to-width ratio may be increased to as much as 1:1"* — the standards' endorsement of tabular figures
- Minimum character spacing = **one stroke width**; minimum line spacing = **half character height**
- Character height at 710 mm viewing: critical fixed-position markings (scale numerals) **2.5–5 mm** above 3.5 cd/m², **4–8 mm** at/below. Scale by D/710 mm.

**A caveat I should flag:** MIL-STD-1472F *and* G both carry a footnote that tick-mark **widths** become 4.36 mrad (15′) for light-on-dark — roughly 3.7× the dark-on-light value, and more than half the length of a major tick. That is dimensionally implausible and looks like a long-standing typo carried across revisions. The *direction* (light-on-dark ticks get thicker) is consistent with Grether & Baker's low-illumination case, but note it directly contradicts the standard's own guidance that light-on-dark *numerals* get **thinner**. Treat the direction as real and the magnitude as suspect.

## 9. Shift lights and alarm rendering

**Why shift lights are physical LEDs at the top edge, not a screen element.** MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.2.3.2(b): ***"Color shall not be used for gaining attention outside the optimum visual field."*** Colour is a foveal cue. Peripheral alerting needs luminance, motion, and flash. Wikipedia's shift-light entry gives the operational counterpart: they let a driver judge the shift point *"without having to glance down at the tachometer... keeping their focus near the track at all times."* An RPM bar that turns red is a foveal signal; an LED strip at the top of the housing is a peripheral one.

**Actual documented threshold tables:**

| System | Pattern | Steps |
|---|---|---|
| **AiM** (canonical example, identical across MXS Strada / MXP / MXL2 manuals) | 10 LEDs, **5 green : 2 yellow : 3 red** | 8200→10000 rpm, **200 rpm per LED**, 1800 rpm span |
| **Bosch DDU8** (manual's default pattern) | 10 LEDs, **4 green : 2 yellow : 2 orange : 2 red** | 6000, 6050, 6100, 6200, 6300, 6400, 6500, 6600, 6700, 6800 — **non-uniform**: 50 rpm for the first two steps, then 100 rpm |
| **Autosport Labs ShiftX3** (factory power-on default) | 3 LEDs green @3000 → 5 cyan @5000 → **7 red flashing @5 Hz** @7000 | Green → cyan → flashing red |

Three professional details amateur systems omit:

1. **Hysteresis on threshold crossings.** Bosch: *"The RPM hysteresis function avoids the high-frequent switchover of the measurement channel value."* MoTeC has the same field. Without it, LEDs chatter at the boundary.
2. **Gear-dependent thresholds.** AiM and Bosch both provide a full per-gear threshold table (Bosch's dialog has columns `Default, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8`).
3. **Lead compensation.** MoTeC's training deck: *"remember to put the RPM signal lower than the actual RPM you wish to shift at... the driver will always need to see the light before he knows to change gear."*

**Two sequencing modes** (AiM, verbatim): *"A LED stays on if its threshold is exceeded"* (cumulative VU-meter fill) or *"A LED stays on until another LED with higher threshold is turned on"* (chase, one lit at a time).

**How shift is disambiguated from alarm:**

- **AiM:** physically separate hardware. Shift LEDs are a row of 10 across the top; **alarm LEDs are 2–8 discrete LEDs in clusters flanking the screen** (MXL2 manual labels them *"Configurable Alarm LEDs 1-3"* left, *"4-6"* right). Different location, different purpose.
- **MoTeC:** same LED strip, but **patterns are priority-ordered in a list** — *"if a pattern has a high priority, e.g. Warning Lights, it cannot be affected by another pattern condition lower in the list becoming true."* A warning pattern placed above the shift pattern pre-empts it.
- **Bosch DDU10/11:** adds 5 LEDs on each side of the housing beyond the top row, giving a spatial split.

**Alarm rendering — the most transferable material:**

**MoTeC C125** (from the user manual):
- Active + unacknowledged → **full-width bar along the bottom edge, bright red, bold white uppercase centred text**, overwriting whatever was there (`ENGINE HOT`).
- Four states: *active/unacknowledged, inactive/unacknowledged* (condition cleared but still displaying), *active/acknowledged* (true but suppressed), *inactive*.
- **Only the highest-priority unacknowledged alarm shows at a time**; as each is acked the next appears.
- Acknowledged alarms move to an **Alarm Status Panel** — up to 6, in a **dark maroon** bar, visibly less saturated than the bright-red unacknowledged bar. Hidden whenever a new unacknowledged alarm needs the space.
- **Gating on other channels**, with a documented example: suppress the engine-temp alarm unless ground speed has been >50 km/h for 30 s — to avoid false triggers from pit-stop heat soak.
- The manual explicitly recommends pairing the on-screen message with a **physical warning light**.

**Bosch DDU:** alarms live in one of **4 fixed screen areas**, are **non-transparent**, **always rendered at the highest z-order**, and when several are simultaneously active in one area **each is shown for ~1.5–2 s in rotation**.

**MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.2.3.4 and §5.7.3.2.4 give the flash grammar:**
- **Warning: flashing red, 3.0–5.0 Hz, 50% duty cycle, synchronised across all warnings.**
- **Caution: yellow, flashing text ≤2.0 Hz at ~70% on. *"Caution signals shall be not more than half the intensity of the warning signal."*** and *"A minimum of two discriminatory characteristics shall be employed."*
- ***"Characters that must be read shall not flash; an adjacent flashing symbol or flashing background may be used to add emphasis to text."*** — the rule amateur dashboards break most often.
- *"Only a small area of a display shall flash at any time."*
- *"Event acknowledgment or flash suppression control shall be provided."*
- Colour meanings (§5.2.2.1.13): **flashing red** = emergency requiring action without delay; **red** = inoperative/no-go; **yellow** = marginal, caution, recheck; **green** = in tolerance; **white** = no right/wrong implication; **blue** = avoid.
- Warning/caution text height: **8.7–17.4 mrad (30–60′)** at the longest anticipated viewing distance.

## 10. Analogue vs digital: the human-factors argument

### The canonical decision table

**MIL-STD-1472F Table III, "Application of various types of mechanical displays"** is the authoritative source. Transcribed from the original:

| Use | Moving pointer (fixed scale) | Fixed pointer (moving scale) | Counters (digital) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quantitative information** | **FAIR** — *"May be difficult to read while pointer is in motion."* | **FAIR** | **GOOD** — *"Minimum time and error for exact numerical value; however, cannot be read when changing rapidly."* |
| **Qualitative information** | **GOOD** — *"Location of pointer easy. Numbers and scale need not be read. Position change easily detected."* | **POOR** — *"Difficult to judge direction and magnitude of deviation without reading numbers and scale."* | **POOR** — *"Numbers must be read. Position changes not easily detected."* |
| **Setting** | **GOOD** | FAIR | **GOOD** — *"Most accurate... Not readable during rapid setting."* |
| **Tracking** | **GOOD** — *"Pointer position readily controlled and monitored."* | FAIR | **POOR** — *"No gross position changes to aid monitoring."* |
| **General** | *"Requires largest exposed and illuminated area on panel."* | *"Saves panel space."* | *"Most economical of space and illumination."* |

### The four task types

Sanders & McCormick, *Human Factors in Engineering and Design*, Ch. 5, define the taxonomy that everything else hangs on:

1. **Quantitative reading** — *"read a precise numeric value"* → *"The pressure is 125 psi."*
2. **Qualitative reading** — *"read an approximate value or to discern a trend, rate of change, or change in direction"* → *"The pressure is rising."*
3. **Check reading** — *"determine if parameters are within some 'normal' bounds"* → *"All pressures are normal."*
4. **Situation awareness** — spatial/predictive.

Their worked example is, conveniently, **a car engine temperature gauge**:

> *"At the most elementary level, only check reading is necessary; that is, is the engine overheated or not? A warning light... would properly provide such information... So do we need an engine-temperature gauge in a car? The answer is yes. The reason is that we do need to make qualitative readings such as whether the temperature is rising or whether it is getting near the overheating point."*

### The empirical record

| Study | Finding |
|---|---|
| **Grether (1949)**, *J. Applied Psychology* 33, 363–72 | 97 USAF pilots + 79 college men, 12 settings on 9 altimeter designs. *"Instruments that combine the indications from two or more pointers or rotating subdials are conducive to large reading errors; indicators on which the digits are already combined in the proper sequence are more easily read."* Direct-reading counters won decisively for quantitative reading. |
| **Sleight (1948)**, *J. Applied Psychology* 32, 170–188 | 60 subjects, 5 dial shapes. Accuracy order: **open-window > round > semicircular > horizontal > vertical**. Error rates spanned **0.5% to 35.5%**. Errors were more frequent on mid-division than whole-number settings. |
| **Elkin (1959)**, WADC TR 58-472 (Sanders & McCormick Table 5-1) | Reading times by task, in index units: **Qualitative** — vertical 101 < circular 107 < open-window 115. **Quantitative** — open-window 102 < circular 113 < vertical 118. **The crossover is demonstrated directly**: the display that is fastest for one task is slowest for the other. |
| **Dashevsky (1964)**, *J. Applied Psychology* 48, 344–347 | Check-reading a 4×4 dial matrix was made **85% more efficient** by continuing the line formed by the aligned pointers across the entire panel face. The deviant dial then *"appeared as a break in a line"* — Gestalt figural continuity. **No significant difference between 9 and 12 o'clock null orientations.** |
| **Simmonds, Galer & Baines (1981)**, SAE 810826 | Compared digital speedometers against three dials and a curvilinear display. **Digital consistently better** for both reading accuracy and preference. |
| **Green (1984)**, SAE 840314, *"Driver understanding of fuel and engine gauges"* | For bar-type displays, **only one segment of the bar should be shown**; extending the bar to zero *"was confusing to some people."* But a single-segment bar is **inappropriate for a fuel gauge** (no empty indication), while a full bar suits speed *"because it would grow longer or shorter with changing values."* |
| **Cohen & Follert (1970)**, *Human Factors* 12(5), 481–483 | Interpolation of **fifths, and even tenths**, yields satisfactory accuracy — you do not need a tick per readable unit. |
| **Whitehurst (1982)**, *Human Factors* 24(3), 301–310 | Numeric progression and scale-unit length dominate speed/accuracy. Scales are read **fastest when pointers land precisely on markers**. |
| **François, Crave, Osiurak, Fort & Navarro (2017)**, *Applied Ergonomics*, doi:10.1016/j.apergo.2017.05.013 | Simulated truck driving. *"A digital speedometer would be more beneficial when obtaining absolute and relative readings, while an analogue speedometer would be more efficient and less distracting when detecting dynamic speed changes... The redundant speedometer combined the benefits of each type presented separately."* |
| **François, Fort, Crave, Osiurak & Navarro (2019)**, *Int. J. Industrial Ergonomics*, doi:10.1016/j.ergon.2019.06.004 | **The most directly applicable study.** 18 truck drivers, 8 gauge designs varying shape/orientation/indicator, across all three task types. *"Horizontal gauges and pointer indicators were more efficient and less demanding visually... circular and horizontal gauges were preferred by drivers. Specific gauge designs implied a gain in visual demand up to 250 ms."* |

### Design rules that fall out

- **MIL-STD-1472G:** *"Moving pointer, fixed scales shall be used in preference to fixed pointer, moving scales."* And: *"Where reading speed is important, circular scales shall be used in preference to horizontal scales, and horizontal scales... in preference to vertical scales."* (Note this conflicts with François 2019, which found horizontal more efficient than circular but circular *preferred*. Objective efficiency and subjective preference diverge.)
- **Scale indicators are for *"quantitative information combined with qualitative information (e.g. trend, direction-of-motion)"***; use a numeric readout where *"speed, accuracy of response"* demand it.
- **Redundancy wins.** François 2017 found the combined display captured both advantages. This is exactly what Bosch's `Modern Gauge` does: arc + leading-edge cursor + centre digital numeral. And Sanders & McCormick note precoded zones can serve all three tasks at once: *"quantitative displays with coded zones also can be used to reflect trends... Further, they can be used for quantitative reading if the scale values are included."*
- **Check-reading layout, MIL-STD-1472F §5.2.3.2.3.5:** arrange indicators *"in rows so that all pointers line up horizontally on the 9 o'clock position under normal operating conditions"* or in columns aligning at 12 o'clock. *"If a matrix of indicators is needed, preference shall be given to the 9 o'clock position."* Plus Dashevsky's connecting line for the 85% gain.
- **Circular scale geometry:** zero/minimum between **225° and 300°**, maximum between **60° and 135°**, symmetrically arranged; *"an obvious break of at least 10° of arc between the two ends of the scale"*; magnitude increases clockwise.

## 11. Specific findings against `e36obd/static/dashboard.html`

I read your existing dashboard so this lands concretely. Geometry: `GS = 300`, `c = 150`, `rOut = 136.5`, `rTick = 120`, `rNum = 85.5`, sweep `A0 = -135°`, `SWEEP = 270°`.

**Correct already:** 270° sweep starting at −135° is inside MIL-STD's zero-position window. Ticks point inward. Numerals upright, `text-anchor: middle`, at majors only. Redline drawn as a stroked arc at `rOut` — i.e. a coloured rail segment *outside* the ticks, which matches the aviation arc convention. `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on bar values. And the comment *"real clusters keep these in one strip, unlit unless active"* on `.telltales` is exactly right.

**Conflicts with the standards:**

| Location | Current | Standard |
|---|---|---|
| `.tick` / `.tick-maj` | Differ by **colour only** (`--ink-4` vs `--ink-2`) | Hierarchy should be **length**, at a common luminance. Colour-coding a tick tier spends a coding channel on something length already conveys. |
| Tick lengths `GS*0.048` / `GS*0.024` | **Exactly 2.0×** | 2.2–2.5×. And there is no intermediate tier — fine, but then ≤4 minors between majors. |
| Tick widths `1.8` / `1.0` | **1.8× ratio** | Grether & Baker: equal under normal illumination; MIL: 1.33×. 1.8× is heavier than either. |
| `rNum = 85.5`, ticks end at `105.6` | Numerals **inside** the tick ring, and the needle sweeps from centre outward **straight through them** | MIL-STD-1472F §5.2.3.2.4.4: *"Numerals shall be placed on the side of the graduation marks away from the pointer."* The needle will occlude numerals. Either move numerals outside `rTick`, or (per §Fig. 26) narrow the needle where it crosses them. |
| Needle tip at `GS*0.385 = 115.5`; minor ticks span `112.8→120` | Tip lands **inside the minor tick band** | *"extend to, but not overlap, the shortest scale graduation marks"* — should stop at ~112.8 with 0.8–1.6 mm clearance. |
| Needle tail at `-GS*0.075` | Visible **22.5-unit counterweight in the same colour** as the needle | *"The tail of the pointer shall be the same color as the dial face."* No physical gauge I examined (Stack, VDO, Bosch) shows a tail. |
| `stroke-linecap: round`, constant width `GS*0.017` | Rounded cap, **5× wider than the minor ticks**, no taper | 20° taper (40° included), **flat tip equal in width to the minor graduations**. |
| `.needle { filter: drop-shadow(0 0 5px …) }` | Glowing needle | No professional system does this. It also lowers face-to-pointer luminance contrast below the required 3.0. |
| `--glow`/`--glow-soft` on values, `box-shadow` on `.segs i.on`, `.led`, `.tt.lit` | Pervasive bloom | *"Coding shall not be used if it reduces legibility."* Max two brightness levels at ≥2:1. |
| `.gauge-zone { opacity: .55 }` | Redline at 55% opacity | A limit marking should be full-strength. Better: draw the limit as a **radial line** and the caution range as an **arc**, per 14 CFR 25.1549. |
| `.cap` at `9.5px` with `letter-spacing: .22em` | Heavy tracking on very small type | MIL: minimum character spacing = one stroke width. 0.22em at 9.5px is far above that and costs word-shape recognition. |
| All type `var(--mono)` | Single monospace family | Reasonable, but tabular figures are only needed on *values*. AiM's 42/20 pt ratio (label ≈48% of value) is a useful target; yours is 0.04/0.115 = 35%. |
| `.segs i.on` fills from zero | Full bar fill | Green (1984): a filled bar suits speed; for a *level* channel it is fine, but consider Bosch's pattern — **discrete segments with the leading segment in a brighter shade**, giving both magnitude and pointer position. |
