## 1. python-OBD — architecture worth stealing

Repo: https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD (★1,304, GPL-2.0, v0.7.3 / 2025-04-07)
Docs: https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/

### The layering (the maintainer's own diagram, in `obd/README.md`, not the top-level one)

https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/blob/master/obd/README.md

```
        API:  obd.py / asynchronous.py
                ↕
        OBDCommand.py  ←→  decoders.py  ←→  UnitsAndScaling.py
                ↕
        elm327.py      ←→  protocols/
                ↕
        pyserial → serial port
```

Serial transport → adapter/AT-command shim → protocol frame/message parser → per-PID decoder fn → typed response object. Each layer is independently unit-testable (their `tests/` has `test_protocol.py`, `test_protocol_can.py`, `test_decoders.py`, `test_uas.py`) — you can test decoders against synthetic bytearrays with no hardware.

### Things worth copying directly

**A command is a self-executing recipe object.** `OBDCommand` bundles request bytes + expected length + ECU filter + decoder, and implements `__call__(messages) -> OBDResponse`. So `OBD.query()` ends with literally `return cmd(messages)`.

```python
OBDCommand(name, desc, command, _bytes, decoder,
           ecu=ECU.ALL, fast=False, header=ECU_HEADER.ENGINE)
```

Equality/hashing is on `(header, command)` — **not** name. Two commands with the same raw request bytes are the same dict key regardless of what you named them. Bite-worthy if you define several custom BMW commands over the same title.

**Runtime-learned frame counts to truncate adapter timeouts** — the single biggest latency lever in the codebase:

```python
def __build_command_string(self, cmd):
    cmd_string = cmd.command
    if self.fast and cmd.fast and (cmd in self.__frame_counts):
        cmd_string += str(self.__frame_counts[cmd]).encode()   # "010C" -> "010C1"
    if self.fast and (cmd_string == self.__last_command):
        cmd_string = b""    # bare CR repeats last command
    return cmd_string
```

First query pays the full adapter timeout; afterwards it tells the adapter "stop listening after N frames." Directly analogous for you: cache per-title expected response lengths so your KWP71 read loop doesn't wait out a timeout every poll.

**Never raise, always return a typed null.**

```python
def is_null(self):
    return (not self.messages) or (self.value == None)
```

Every early-exit in `query()` (not connected / unsupported / no messages) returns a blank `OBDResponse()` rather than throwing. UI code becomes `r = q(cmd); if not r.is_null(): ...` with no try/except scaffolding. `response.time` is `time.time()` stamped at construction — use it to detect stale values.

**Header as a first-class per-command field with automatic switch-back.** `OBD.__set_header()` only emits `AT SH <hdr>` when the header differs from last time, and swaps back automatically. This is the hook for manufacturer-specific requests.

### `obd.Async` — the watch/callback model, and its limits

https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Async%20Connections/

```python
connection = obd.Async()
connection.watch(obd.commands.RPM, callback=new_rpm)
connection.start()
...
connection.stop()

with connection.paused() as was_running:   # stops, yields, restarts if it was running
    ...
```

Real implementation details that matter:

- **One daemon thread total**, round-robin over all watched commands *sequentially and synchronously*, then `time.sleep(delay_cmds)` (default 0.25s). Watch 20 PIDs at 50ms round-trip each and your true per-PID refresh is ~1.25s, not 0.25s.
- **No per-command rate or priority.** If you want RPM fast and VIN once, you build that yourself. Worth designing in from day one for your ADC sweep vs. slow-changing channels.
- **Callbacks run on the polling thread**, synchronously, in registration order. A slow callback blocks the whole loop — hand off to a queue.
- `watch()`/`unwatch()` **hard-refuse while running** (log a warning and no-op). Mutual exclusion is by convention, not a lock — the command dict is a plain `dict`.
- On disconnect the thread sets `__running = False` and returns silently; no exception.
- `Async.query()` never touches serial — it returns the last cached `OBDResponse` for watched commands, a fresh null otherwise.

### Supported-command probing

`__load_commands()` walks the bitmask chain `PIDS_A (0100) → PIDS_B (0120) → PIDS_C (0140)`, each returning a 32-bit mask whose top bit says "the next bitmask PID exists." Decoder is trivially `BitArray(messages[0].data[2:])`. Mode 1 support is mirrored into mode 2 (freeze frame) automatically. `supported_commands` is a public mutable `set` — the documented way to enable a custom command is `connection.supported_commands.add(cmd)` or `query(cmd, force=True)`.

Mode 06 is hard-gated to CAN protocols in `test_cmd()` (`protocol_id() in ["6","7","8","9"]`).

### `OBDStatus` — exact values (verified in `obd/utils.py`)

Plain class with string attributes, **not** an `Enum`:

```python
NOT_CONNECTED = "Not Connected"
ELM_CONNECTED = "ELM Connected"
OBD_CONNECTED = "OBD Connected"   # port has battery voltage, ignition off
CAR_CONNECTED = "Car Connected"   # 0100 answered
```

Docs footgun worth knowing: *"`status()` shall not be checked after the queries to verify that the connection is kept active."* It's a snapshot set at connect time and never updated.

### Pint units

`obd.Unit` **is** the process-wide `pint.UnitRegistry()` instance — reuse it rather than making a second registry, or quantities won't interoperate. Migration to Pint was **v0.6.0 (2016-07-27)**, not v0.7. `response.value.magnitude` is the documented escape hatch to a plain float.

The `UAS` table is a nice pattern: a scale/offset/unit triple keyed by a J1979 byte ID, with `uas(id_) = functools.partial(decode_uas, id_=id_)` so command tables read `OBDCommand("RPM", ..., uas(0x07), ...)`.

### Custom commands (your BMW hook)

https://python-obd.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Custom%20Commands/

```python
def rpm(messages):
    d = messages[0].data[2:]          # skip mode+PID bytes (v0.7.0 breaking change)
    return (bytes_to_int(d) / 4.0) * Unit.rpm

c = OBDCommand("RPM", "Engine RPM", b"010C", 4, rpm, ECU.ENGINE, True)
o.supported_commands.add(c)
```

Decoder contract guarantees: `messages` is non-empty when called; each `Message.data` is already padded/truncated to the declared byte count; `Message.hex()` / `.raw()` are available if you want the wire format.

DTC decoding: `parse_dtc()` maps the top 2 bits to `['P','C','B','U']`, next 2 to the first digit, rest as hex nibbles, then `DTC.get(code, "")` — **unknown/manufacturer codes still decode to a correct code string with a blank description**. `obd/codes.py` is ~130KB of generic descriptions and doesn't contain BMW codes; you'd keep your own table.

### Example dashboard — correction

**python-OBD has never shipped an `examples/` directory or a bundled Kivy/Tkinter dashboard.** Checked master and the oldest tags. What exists is a separate repo:

**`brendan-w/pihud`** — https://github.com/brendan-w/pihud (★48) — PyQt4 (not Kivy), gauges/bars/text widgets, multiple pages switchable via TAB or GPIO buttons, **declarative JSON config in `~/pihud.rc`**, and a **demo mode driving gauges with sine-wave data so you can build UI with no car attached**. That last bit is the pattern to copy.

Their own hardware-free test path is `obdsim` from `obdgpslogger` (http://icculus.org/obdgpslogger/obdsim.html) opening a pty — which is exactly why the debug traces in the docs show `/dev/pts/2`.

### Known gotchas (from real issues, not speculation)

| Issue | Finding |
|---|---|
| [#131](https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/131) | The `fast=True` bare-CR repeat trick breaks on clone chips — queries go null after the first two. `fast=False` fixes it. |
| [#282](https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/282) | Post-2022 clones emit non-UTF-8 garbage; an unmerged patch wraps the decode in try/except, claiming "5–10x compatibility." Not in v0.7.3. |
| [#136](https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/136) | `import obd` takes >10s on a Pi — eager construction of the DTC table + command tables + Pint registry at import. **Lazy-load big tables in your own code.** |
| [#232](https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/232) | Torque Pro is faster because it sets `ATAT2` (aggressive adaptive timing) and `ATH0`; python-OBD hardcodes `ATH1` and never touches adaptive timing. Sending `AT AT2` yourself is a real lever it doesn't pull. |
| [#177](https://github.com/brendan-w/python-OBD/issues/177) | Enabling debug logging *changed* connection success — timing-sensitive race on cheap hardware. |

## 2. ELM327-emulator — the offline dev story

Repo: https://github.com/Ircama/ELM327-emulator (★665, **CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 — not OSI open source, forbids commercial use**), PyPI 3.0.5 (2025-12-12), 18 releases.

Two premise corrections up front:

- **`obd_dictionary` is a subfolder of this repo**, not `github.com/Ircama/obd_dictionary` (that 404s): https://github.com/Ircama/ELM327-emulator/tree/master/obd_dictionary
- **There is no `'test'` scenario.** The built-ins are exactly `AT`, `engineoff`, `default`, `car`, `mt05`.
- **`pyprodtools` does not exist** on Ircama's account. Flagging rather than inventing.

### What it emulates and how you attach

ELM327 AT command set + OBD-II service/PID layer over ISO-TP (11-bit CAN) and KWP2000, with optional UDS session/security-access/routine-control behavior. Transports:

| Mode | Flag | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| pty (default, Linux/macOS) | — | `pty.openpty()`, prints `/dev/pts/N` |
| TCP socket | `-n 35000` | for WiFi-ELM327 apps / telnet |
| Serial COM | `-p COM3` | pairs with com0com on Windows |
| Device node | `-P /dev/rfcomm0` | Bluetooth: `rfcomm watch /dev/rfcomm0 1 python3 -m elm -P /dev/rfcomm0 -l -s car` |

```shell
python3 -m elm -s car        # prints /dev/pts/3
```
```python
import obd
connection = obd.OBD("/dev/pts/3")
```

**Caveat:** python-OBD's `portstr` is documented only as a UNIX device file or Windows COM port — there's no `socket://` support. Use pty/serial mode with python-OBD; `-n` is for other clients.

### Scenario structure (verified by `exec()`-ing `elm/obd_message.py` and introspecting)

```
ObdMessage = {
  'AT':        68 entries,
  'engineoff':  4,
  'default':   53,
  'car':      246,   # Toyota Auris Hybrid, ISO 15765-4 CAN 11-bit 500k
  'mt05':      25,   # Delphi MT05 motorcycle ECU
}
```

Scenario selection **merges**: `{**default, **AT, **selected}`, then sorts every entry by a numeric `'Priority'` (1 first, default 10) before regex-matching the incoming command.

Real fields (there is **no** `'Pid'` or `'Cmd'` key — the dict key *is* the label):

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Request` | regex the uppercased, unspaced command must match |
| `Response` | static string **or a list** of alternatives (cycled via `choice`) |
| `ResponseHeader` / `ResponseFooter` | `lambda self, cmd, pid, uc_val: ...` evaluated per request |
| `Header` | e.g. `'7E0'` — only matches if it equals the client's current `ATSH` header |
| `Action` | `'skip'` to disable an entry |
| `Exec` | Python statement `exec()`'d against the request |
| `Log`/`Info`/`Warning` | expression strings fed to the logger |
| `Priority` | match order, 1..10 |
| `Task` | plugin module name in `elm/plugins/` |

Responses are parsed **as XML** — `fromstring('<xml>' + resp + '</xml>')` — with tags `<header>/<size>/<data>`, `<writeln>`, `<string>`, `<space>`, `<eval>`, `<exec>`, `<flow>`, `<answer>`, `<pos_answer>`, `<neg_answer>`. The `SEARCHING...` trick works because `<exec>` flushes accumulated output to the device *before* running:

```python
'ResponseHeader': lambda self, cmd, pid, uc_val: \
    "<string>SEARCHING...</string><exec>time.sleep(1.5)</exec>" + ST('') \
        if self.counters[pid] == 1 else ''
```

### Time-varying values — three mechanisms

1. **`sequence()`** — a genuine triangle wave, one step per query of that PID:
```python
def sequence(self, pid, base, max, factor, n_bytes):
    c = self.counters[pid] if pid in self.counters else 0
    p = int(factor * abs(max - (c + max) % (max * 2))) + base
    ...
```
Used by `'default'`'s RPM (`base=2400, max=200, factor=80`). This is your "sweep RPM" primitive.

2. **Rotating lists + `choice [sequential|random] [weights]`** — what `'car'` uses (14 RPM frames ≈ 0–4200, 13 SPEED frames ≈ 0–114 km/h). Each PID advances on its *own* counter, so RPM and SPEED don't stay physically correlated.

3. **`Task` plugins** — arbitrary stateful Python.

### The record-once/replay-forever workflow — `obd_dictionary`

**This is the answer to your offline-dev question.**

```shell
# once, in the car, with a real ELM327:
python3 -m obd_dictionary -i /dev/ttyUSB0 -o e36.py -n e36 -p 20

# forever after, at the desk:
python3 -m elm
> merge e36
> scenario e36
```

Or replace the built-in dictionary wholesale so `-s default` becomes your car:
```shell
python3 -m obd_dictionary -i /dev/ttyUSB0 -o obd_message.py -n default -t elm/obd_message.py
```

Mechanics (from source): it connects via python-OBD, iterates `connection.supported_commands` for `-p N` probe cycles, collects the **set of distinct raw frames** per PID, and emits either a single `Response` or a list.

```python
OBDData = [dict() for x in range(args.probes)]
for i in range(args.probes):
    for cmd in connection.supported_commands:
        OBDData[i][cmd] = connection.query(cmd)
        time.sleep(args.delay_commands)
    time.sleep(args.delay)
...
f_resp = ('[\n' + ',\n'.join(list_resp) + '\n]') if len(list_resp) > 1 else list_resp[0]
```

**Be precise about what this is:** it is *not* a timestamped chronological trace. There's no timing or ordering preserved. You get "the distinct raw values seen for PID X across N probes," replayed in capture order by the `choice` cycler. It looks like realistic variation to a polling client, but it is not a second-by-second replay of your drive. If you want true chronological replay you need the CAN-level tools (§3.4).

Also in `obd_dictionary`:
- `-c CSV_FILE` imports **Torque-format custom PIDs** (`Name, ShortName, Request, Equation, Min, Max, Unit, ECU-header`) as `CUSTOM_<NAME>` commands — almost certainly how `'car'`'s ~190 Toyota `CUSTOM_*` entries were made.
- A hardcoded `blacklisted_pids` tuple excluded by default (needs `-b`) covering `CLEAR_DTC`, `CUSTOM_TRAC_DIS` (disable traction control), fan-speed setters, etc. — actuator/write commands it refuses to send to a real car. Good design; also a warning about `-b`.
- `-r` = dry run / connection test.

### REPL commands (28 `do_*` methods, extracted via `ast`)

`echo, quit, version, delay, wait, prompt, color, reset, loglevel, verify, write, test, port, timer, tasks, counters, pause, resume, edit, scenario, choice, merge, engineoff, default, commands, usage, history`

Notables: `test 010c` fires a request without a client; `edit <PID> <pos> <bytes>` patches an answer at runtime; `counters` shows per-PID hit counts; `merge <module>` imports `./<module>.py`'s `ObdMessage` and `.update()`s it in.

Batch mode: `echo -e 'scenario car\ntest 010c' | elm -b /tmp/output.txt`

### Multi-ECU and UDS

Header gating is exact and simple:

```python
if 'REQUEST' in uc_val and re.match(uc_val['REQUEST'], cmd):
    if ('HEADER' in uc_val and header and
            uc_val['HEADER'].upper() != self.counters["cmd_set_header"]):
        continue     # wrong ECU selected
```

Constants exist for `7E0/7E8` engine, `7E1/7E9` trans, `7E2/7EA` HV, `7E3/7EB` battery, `7E5` Continental, etc. ISO-TP multi-frame is real (`uds_answer()` emits `10 <len>` First Frame then `21, 22, ...` Consecutive Frames; `IsoTpMultiframe(Tasks)` reassembles inbound and auto-emits `<flow>20 00</flow>`).

The `mt05` scenario is the interesting one for you: `UDS_RMBA` (Mode 23 Read Memory By Address) and `UDS_WRITE_MEM_ADDR` (Mode 3D) are backed by plugins that read/write a byte range out of an **`mmap`-backed file** (`mmap-input.bin`, `MEM_RANGE = 0x3fffff`). **That is a working template for emulating a DME memory image** — which is exactly what you'd want to fake your `ADDR:LEN` RAM reads offline.

### Task plugin shape

Files in `elm/plugins/` named `task_*.py`. Every method returns a 3-tuple `(xml_answer_or_None, terminate_bool, request_to_reprocess_or_None)`.

```python
from elm import Tasks
import time
EXECUTION_TIME = 0.5
SEED = 'A641B5E9'

class Task(Tasks):
    def run(self, cmd, *_):
        if time.time() < self.time_started + EXECUTION_TIME:
            return (self.NA('78'), Tasks.RETURN.CONTINUE,      # 0x78 = response pending
                    None if self.task_request_matched(cmd) else cmd)
        seed = " ".join(SEED[i:i+2] for i in range(0, len(SEED), 2))
        return (self.PA(seed), Tasks.RETURN.TERMINATE,
                None if self.task_request_matched(cmd) else cmd)
```

`self.ns` is per-task state; `self.shared` is per-ECU state shared across all tasks addressed to that ECU (`emulator.task_shared_ns[ecu]`) — how a security-access flag set in one task is read by another.

#### Sniffer window — bit-change heatmap with "lock this byte"
https://www.savvycan.com/docs/sniffer.html · impl: `SnifferWindow`/`SnifferModel`/`SnifferItem`/`SnifferDelegate`

Described in its own docs as *"essentially a turbo charged graphical version of the linux can_utils program 'cansniffer'."* Refreshes on a **200ms timer**. IDs unseen for 5s turn **red** then disappear.

Color rules:
- Hex mode: **green** = byte incremented, **red** = byte decremented.
- **"View Bits"** mode: each bit is its own cell — **black** = stable 1, **white** = stable 0, **green** = fresh 0→1, **red** = fresh 1→0, **gray** = notched.

**Notching is your "lock this byte" filter.** *"If you push the notch button the system will remember all the bits that were set in the last 200ms window and will not color the output if those bits are toggled in the future."* Repeated clicks accumulate ignored bits; "Un-notch" resets. Notch cycle timer defaults to 750ms and is configurable. Checkboxes: **Never Expire IDs**, **Mute notched bits** (hide them entirely), **Fade inactive bytes** (fade toward white so only active bytes stand out), **View Bits**.

Workflow: notch away everything that's moving on its own (counters, background chatter), *then* do the thing you're trying to find. Only the new bits light up.

#### Flow View — frame-by-frame scrubber with a reference baseline
https://www.savvycan.com/docs/flowview.html

Pick one ID; see three synchronized views: 8 byte value boxes, an 8×8 bit grid (white=0, black=1, green=newly set, red=newly cleared), and a time-series graph of all 8 bytes. Playback control box: *"Go back one frame, Stop, Go forward one frame"* / *"Play backward, pause, Play forward"*, adjustable speed, Loop Playback.

**Reference Values** sit left of the bit grid. **"Auto Reference"** diffs against the previous frame; unchecked, it diffs against a **static reference you set** — i.e. "show me everything that differs from this known-good state." **"Data Seek Values"** (default -1) auto-stop playback when a byte hits a target value.

#### File Comparison — literal A/B "record while I do X"
https://www.savvycan.com/docs/filecomparison.html

Compares a **"File of interest"** against multiple reference files. Output has three sections:

1. **IDs found only in \<file of interest\>**
2. **IDs found only in reference frames**
3. **IDs found in both** — showing *"bits set only on one side and not the other"* and *"values only found on one side or the other"*

The docs describe the exact workflow you'd want: capture baseline while idling and *not* doing the thing, capture again while doing it repeatedly, diff. *"Somewhere in the differences should be the gear selection you couldn't find. The list ought to be much more narrow than just 'shooting in the dark'."*

#### Range State — auto-detected multi-byte candidates with endianness/sign guessing
https://www.savvycan.com/docs/rangestate.html

**This is the one that most directly maps to your problem.** Purpose: *"search for signals that look like they might be important… find signals that seem to vary somewhat coherently. It will generate a lot of false positives but it will still provide some decent ideas."*

Seven controls: **ID Filter list**, **Sensitivity**, **Min Signal Size** (down to 1 bit), **Max Signal Size**, **Granularity** (bit jump width — 8 searches byte boundaries only, 1 searches every bit position; *"some designers are more devious and place signals at uneven boundaries"*), **Signal Mode** (big-endian / little-endian / both), **Signed Mode** (unsigned / signed / both).

Click **"Recalculate Candidate Signals"** → a **"Candidate Signals"** list with ID, start bit, length, sign, endianness. Select one and it graphs below. The intended UX is genuinely good: *"hold down the arrow key and let it rapidly scroll. As it scrolls through the signals you can look at the graph and stop when you see a signal that catches your eye."*

The docs even name the heuristic: *"vehicle speed is pretty easy to recognize. You can't go from 0 to 100 in an instant so speed tends to have a lot of sweeping motions up and down."* That's exactly your coolant-warmup-monotonic-ramp reasoning, automated.

#### Frame Details — per-ID statistics and value histograms
https://www.savvycan.com/docs/framedetails.html

Per ID: frame count, payload length, **average / min / max inter-frame interval**. Per byte: which bits ever changed, observed value range, and a **histogram both graphically and textually** with *"the number of times a specific value occurred."* Two graphs on the right: top = *"a histogram of all the bits and the number of times each bit was set,"* bottom = *"each individual byte as its value varies over time."* All textual info exportable to a text file.

This is your value-range-histogram ask, and the bit-set-count histogram is a static (whole-capture) version of the bit-change heatmap.

#### Bisector — binary search over the capture
https://www.savvycan.com/docs/bisector.html

Split the frame list by ID Range, Frame Number, or Percentage; **"Calculate Split"** previews counts; then **"Save split frames to a new file"**. Iteratively halve until you isolate the frame responsible for a behavior. (*"Replace main list with split frames"* is documented as unimplemented — save and reload instead.)

#### Temporal window — bus activity density map
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/collin80/SavvyCAN/master/help/temporalwindow.md

Scatter of (time, frame ID) with color-coded density. *"Things that are sent rapidly are important. Steering data is usually sent rapidly, low level engine performance data is usually sent rapidly."* Also surfaces **ID clusters** (0x102/0x103/0x104 = one device sending long-form data).

#### Playback — replay a capture back onto a bus
https://www.savvycan.com/docs/playbackwindow.html

A **"Playback Sequence"** of captures, each with its own ID filter list and repeat count, optional **"Loop Sequence"**. **"Use original frame timing from captured frames"** preserves real timing (2–3ms jitter acknowledged); unchecked gives you a fixed tick + burst rate. There's a "wait for traffic before sending" checkbox so playback starts only once the bus wakes up.

#### Custom Sender — trigger rules and per-frame data modifiers
https://www.savvycan.com/docs/customsender.html

Grid of En / Bus / ID / Len / Data / **Trigger** / **Modifications** / Count. Trigger syntax is genuinely expressive:

```
id0x200 5ms 10x bus0,1000ms
```
= "when 0x200 arrives on bus 0, wait 5ms then send, max 10 times; also send every 1000ms forever." Conditions: `id<hex>`, `<n>ms`, `<n>x`, `bus<n>`, comma-separated for multiple triggers, space-separated for conditions within one trigger. Modifications are `D4=<expr>` with operands referencing other data bytes.

#### Others
- **Fuzzing** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/fuzzingwindow.html) — 8×8 grid where white=never set, black=always set, green=follows the fuzz pattern; Bit Scanning modes Sequential / Sweep / Random; ID Scanning Sequential/Random over a range or a filter list. The docs are refreshingly blunt: *"It just might put your vehicle into gear and cause you to drive over a box full of kittens."*
- **UDS Scanner** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/uds_scanner.html) — scans an ID range for UDS-ish nodes, with **"Allow adaptive reply offset"** for ECUs that don't reply at request+8, and a **"Read By ID"** brute-force over DID ranges. Conceptually identical to your `raw --title 0xNN` probing.
- **ISO-TP Decoder** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/isotp_decoder.html) — auto-detects ISO-TP-conformant traffic, deselect false-positive IDs, "Interpret Previously Captured Frames" to recompute, and it decodes UDS negative responses in English (*"0x7F 0x10 0x12 was interpreted as a UDS error response saying that the ECU does not support the requested sub-function"*).
- **Scripting** (https://www.savvycan.com/docs/scriptingwindow.html) — JavaScript, multiple scripts at once, "Public Variables" panel updating 4×/sec, `host`/`can`/`isotp`/`uds` objects, callbacks. Escape hatch for custom analysis.
- **Graphing / Graph Setup** — manual signal definition with an 8×8 start-bit grid, Data Len (odd lengths like 9/11/15 supported), Little Endian toggle, Signed, Mask, Bias, Scale, Stride, Associated Bus. Save/load graph definition sets. Double-clicking a plotted point scrolls the main frame list to the frame that produced it.

**Note on "bus load":** SavvyCAN shows **frames-per-second** (`ui->lbFPS`, averaged), not a true bus-load percentage — I checked `mainwindow.cpp`. For actual bus utilization use `canbusload` from can-utils.

#### Feeding your KWP71 data into SavvyCAN (macOS-friendly, actionable)

SavvyCAN's native format is trivial to synthesize. From `framefileio.cpp`:

```
Time Stamp,ID,Extended,Dir,Bus,LEN,D1,D2,D3,D4,D5,D6,D7,D8
39747828,000005EB,false,Rx,0,8,E8,45,85,4B,4A,28,36,69,
```
Timestamp in **microseconds**, ID as 8 hex digits, bytes as 2 hex digits, trailing comma. There's also an even simpler **"Generic ID/Data CSV"**: `<hexID>,<space-separated hex bytes>`. Load filters include Autodetect, GVRET, CRTD, BusMaster, Microchip, Vector trace, IXXAT MiniLog, CAN-DO, Vehicle Spy, Candump/Kayak, CANDump Lawicel, PCAN Viewer, Kvaser, CANalyzer ASC/BLF, CARBUS, Cabana CSV, Wireshark PCAP.

**So: write a ~30-line converter that emits each ADC sweep / RAM read as a synthetic "CAN frame"** — e.g. ID `0x100` = ADC channels 0–7, ID `0x101` = channels 8–15, ID `0x200+n` = RAM block n — and you inherit Sniffer bit heatmaps, Flow View scrubbing with static reference, Frame Details histograms, File Comparison A/B diffing, and Range State candidate scanning for free, on macOS, today. That is by far the highest leverage item in this entire report for your project.

### 3.2 Cabana — the actively maintained fork is `deanlee/openpilot-cabana`

**Important correction:** `commaai/openpilot/tools/cabana` **no longer exists** (404 on master). `commaai/cabana` (the old React web version) is **archived** since 2023-04. The living project is:

**https://github.com/deanlee/openpilot-cabana** — C++/Qt6, MIT, active June 2026. *"Originally developed as the CAN analysis tool for openpilot, Cabana is now maintained independently as a standalone general-purpose analyzer."*

Feature list, verbatim from the README:

- **Live bit heatmap** — bit flips flash on change and fade out, instantly revealing active signals
- **Pattern coloring** — bytes auto-colored by trend: increasing, decreasing, toggling, or noisy
- **Find Similar Bits** — discover related signals across messages and buses
- **Find Signal** — search all messages by value range or threshold
- **Bit muting** — suppress known bits to isolate undocumented signals
- **Sparklines** — inline signal previews in the message list
- **Signal charts** — drag-and-drop plotting, multi-column layout and tabs
- **Video sync** — multi-camera playback locked to the CAN timeline
- **Log stitching** — merge multiple log files into one continuous timeline
- **CAN FD** — frames up to 64 bytes
- **DBC editor** — full editing with undo/redo, value tables, CSV export

**Binary Activity Analysis** color table (verbatim):

| Color | Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Green | Increasing | byte value steadily climbing (e.g. a counter) |
| Red | Decreasing | steadily dropping |
| Amber | Toggle | bits flipping back and forth (flags) |
| Purple | Noisy | high-entropy, no trend (CRC/encryption) |
| Grey | Static | inactive / unchanged recently |

**That purple "noisy → probably CRC" classification is the single most useful auto-triage idea here** — it tells you which bytes to stop looking at.

Sources: openpilot routes, Vector `.asc`, `candump -l` `.log`, PEAK `.trc` (v1.x and v2.x), SocketCAN, comma Panda, ZMQ/msgq. Multiple files are **stitched and sorted by timestamp automatically**; each interface name (`can0`, `can1`) maps to a separate bus channel.

#### Find Signal — this is Cheat Engine for CAN, and it's the model for your RAM problem

https://deepwiki.com/deanlee/openpilot-cabana/8.1-find-signal-tool

*"Brute-force scanning of every possible bit position across all messages."* Parameters: bus + comma-separated hex addresses, **bit size range 1–64**, **endianness**, **signedness**, **factor and offset** (so you can search in physical units), comparison operator = **exact value / increased / decreased / changed**, and a **"Scan At" timestamp**.

The workflow is the memory-scanner workflow: initial scan produces a large candidate set → you change the real-world thing → filter by "increased"/"decreased"/"changed" → repeat until a handful remain. It maintains a **stack of refinement stages with undo** so you can back out of an over-constrained filter. Results table: Message | Signal (start bit + definition) | Prev Value | Value | **Δ** (green for increase, red for decrease).

**Apply this to your DME directly.** You have `raw` RAM reads with `ADDR:LEN`. Dump a wide address window repeatedly, then implement exactly this loop: snapshot → "throttle went up" → keep addresses that increased → snapshot → "throttle went back down" → keep addresses that decreased → converge. That's a much faster path to the RAM map than eyeballing CSV columns, and it's ~100 lines on top of what you already have.

#### Find Similar Bits
https://deepwiki.com/deanlee/openpilot-cabana/8.2-find-similar-bits-tool

Pick a reference bit; it linear-scans all cached events tracking the reference bit's last state, and for every bit on the target bus counts mismatches in **"Equal"** or **"Not Equal"** mode, filters by a minimum message count, and returns bits with **<50% mismatch**. Results: Address | Byte Index | Bit Index | Mismatches | Total | Percentage. Double-click navigates to that message. Use cases named: steering-direction bits that toggle at center crossing, status bits mirrored across ECUs, inverted signal pairs via "Not Equal."

#### Architecture (worth reading if you build your own tool)
https://deepwiki.com/commaai/openpilot/6.1-cabana

- `MainWindow` (dock layout, `QSettings` state restore) → `MessagesWidget` (left) / `DetailWidget` (tabbed, lazy-init) / `BinaryView` / `ChartsWidget` / `VideoWidget`+`CameraView`
- `AbstractStream` base with `ReplayStream` / `DeviceStream` / `PandaStream` / `SocketCanStream`; `MonotonicBuffer` for event allocation
- `BinaryView` is a table where **each cell is one bit**; `BinaryItemDelegate` draws signal backgrounds, bit values, and heatmap overlays. Two heatmap modes from the `DetailWidget` toolbar: **Live** (recent flips relative to `current_sec_`) and **All** (flips within the selected time range)
- Signals are created by **dragging across bits**; selection derives `start_bit`, `size`, `is_little_endian`
- Keyboard: **X / Backspace / Delete** remove signal, **E** toggle endianness, **S** toggle signedness, **P / G / C** chart actions
- All edits go through `UndoStack::instance()` (`AddSigCommand`, `RemoveSigCommand`, `EditMsgCommand`, `EditSigCommand`)
- `DBCManager` singleton maps multiple DBC files to buses, auto-loading via `car_fingerprint_to_dbc.json`
- Streams implement *"bit-level suppression of defined signals to highlight unknown data"* — i.e. bit muting is at the stream layer, not just the view

CLI: `cabana --demo`, `cabana --socketcan can0`, `cabana --panda`, `cabana --dbc file.dbc`, `cabana --data_dir <dir>`. Live streams are logged to `~/cabana_live_stream/` for later replay.

Practical caveat for you: Cabana's build is Linux-oriented (scons, Qt6, AUR/Ubuntu deps, prebuilt `cabana-linux-x86_64`). **On macOS, SavvyCAN is the practical choice.**

### 3.3 The CSS Electronics methodology + its automated implementation

This is the most rigorous published account of "how do you actually determine what an unknown field means," and it has a runnable reference implementation.

**Manual methodology:** https://www.csselectronics.com/pages/can-bus-sniffer-reverse-engineering

8 steps. The taxonomy up front is the useful part: classify your target as **stationary vs driving** and **discrete vs continuous**, because that determines the technique.

- Stationary/discrete → *"Stream raw CAN live while repeatedly manipulating the signal (open/close door, wipers on/off, turn gauge from 0 to max) — look for CAN IDs where the data bytes change in sync with each action."* Tool: bit-level sniffer view, or webCAN's **fade mode** which *"will grey out inactive data bytes."*
- Driving/continuous → *"Drive a representative trip while a passenger logs the dashboard value with timestamps… In parallel, record the full raw timestamped CAN trace for offline comparison."* Tool: range-state batch hypothesis testing.
- **Reference channel trick:** *"If your parameter has an OBD2 equivalent (RPM, speed), logging OBD2 data in parallel gives you an extra reference for faster analysis."*
- **Event marker injection:** *"set up custom transmit lists with 'event tags', i.e. CAN frames you inject into the bus (and thus your trace) to serve as event tags for subsequent analysis."* — Directly stealable: inject a marker row into your CSV when you press a key, so "I just floored it" is machine-findable later.
- Scale/offset: `physical = offset + scale * raw`; *"Plot the raw decimal signal vs. your timestamped reference and iterate scale, then offset, until the curves overlap. A trip with a smooth MIN-to-MAX transition makes this easier."*

**Automated implementation:** https://github.com/CSS-Electronics/can-bus-reverse-engineering-skills (★140, MIT) + writeup https://www.csselectronics.com/pages/can-bus-reverse-engineering-ai-llm-claude

Scripts: `detect_bus.py`, `capture.py`, `annotate.py`, `survey.py`, `correlate.py`, `bitsearch.py`, `calibrate.py`, `build_dbc.py`, `verify.py`, `decode_reference.py`, `vision_reference.py`, `merge_dbc.py`. The pipeline, from their own docstrings:

**`survey.py`** — bit-activity heatmap, deterministic replacement for eyeballing fade mode:
> *"For each CAN ID: frame count, mean cycle time + jitter, payload length, latest payload, and per-byte / per-bit activity… Each byte is classified static | counter | checksum | signal: rolling counters `[ctr@]` are excluded from later correlation; checksum-like bytes `[cks@]` are flagged as a hint only."*

It also proposes a **field map** for bit-packed frames using a genuinely clever heuristic:
> *"Within a packed region a field's bits run LSB (high flip-rate) → MSB (low flip-rate); a field BOUNDARY is where the flip-rate JUMPS back up — the next field's LSB toggling."*

**`correlate.py`** — ranks (ID, byte, width, endianness) against a reference:
> *"lag search — slides the reference ± a window to absorb reaction delay; rank-based — Spearman (monotonic, scale-free); outlier-aware — scored over overlapping windows, aggregated by median; coverage flag."*

**`bitsearch.py`** — the exhaustive permutation search, with an explicit ranking rubric:
> 1. lag-aligned linear-fit R²
> 2. **plausibility (reference-free)** — *"penalises a decoded series that wraps at a field/byte boundary or jumps like noise (catches wrong endianness/width)"*
> 3. windowed-Spearman magnitude
> 4. **parsimony at equal fit** — among nested candidates fitting equally well, keep the shortest, *"demotes an OVER-WIDE read that merely appended a separate CO-VARYING field"*
> 5. tidiness — byte-aligned/standard-width tie-break

Little-endian search covers every start × every length but *"restricted to candidates whose BOUNDARY bits actually change — so we don't grab a constant valid-flag / padding bit and report a half-scale field."* Big-endian search is restricted to byte-aligned widths.

**The reference-free plausibility prior** is the most portable idea in the whole document, because it needs no ground truth at all:
> *"the decoded raw series, in frame order, must be physically plausible — smooth (autocorrelated frame-to-frame) and wrap-free (no per-frame deltas near ±2^length, which betray a wrong start bit / length / endianness). A correct field scores high; a scrambled one scores low however well it happens to correlate."*

**Sentinel detection** (their `common.detect_extreme_outliers`) — four scale-free pillars: robust band (median ± k·MAD), **clear empty gap tested per side** (catches a signed `0x8000` most-negative sentinel too), **teleport** (a sentinel jumps in one frame; a real signal ramps), and episode counting rather than raw frame counting. Their note that *"a signal-unavailable RPM can read `0x3FFF` (a 14-bit all-ones inside a 16-bit read)"* is exactly the kind of thing that would silently wreck a least-squares fit on your ADC channels.

**Verification as a hard gate** — and the failure mode it catches is one you will hit:
> *"A candidate can correlate with the reference and even decode correctly at a few calibration points while being the WRONG encoding — a scrambled but deterministic function of the true field. The classic tell: it matches when the signal is parked but diverges in motion."*
> *"2–3 collinear points fit any line with R²≈1."*

**Sweep vs holds** — their two-excitation protocol maps perfectly onto your throttle-sweep and battery-voltage procedures:
> *"SWEEP (continuous) → identification + resolution… on a smooth ramp the true field scores ~1.0 while counters and unrelated traffic fall to ~0, whereas a few discrete holds let counters spuriously rank-match the monotone step pattern."*
> *"HOLDS (steady anchors) → calibration + absolute verify."*
> *"Identify on the sweep, calibrate on the holds."*

Claimed results: 90%+ success with a clean reference, 5–10 min/signal, ~95% time reduction vs manual.

Their signal-encoding reference (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CSS-Electronics/can-bus-reverse-engineering-skills/master/.claude/skills/cansub-reverse-engineering/references/signal-encoding.md) also has the correct cantools bit-numbering formulas and the priors: booleans 1–2 bits, continuous 1–2 bytes usually on a clean byte border, high-precision up to 4 bytes.

### 3.4 can-utils — the CLI ancestors of all of this

https://github.com/linux-can/can-utils

**`cansniffer`** — *"volatile CAN content visualizer."* Its interactive commands (extracted from source) are where SavvyCAN's notch button came from:

```
 b  - toggle binary / HEX-ASCII output
 c  - toggle color mode
 #  - notch currently marked/changed bits (can be used repeatedly)
 *  - clear notched marked
 rMYNAME / wMYNAME - read/write settings file (filter/notch)
 +1F5 / -42E       - add/remove single ID
 -500700           - remove SFF CAN-IDs 0x500-0x5FF (ID/bitmask)
```
Flags: `-c` (color changes), `-b`/`-B`/`-8` (binary modes), `-t <time>` ID display timeout, `-h <time>` hold marker on changes, `-l <time>` display loop time.

**`canplayer`** — replays a `candump -l` log **with original timing preserved**. This is the true chronological replay that ELM327-emulator doesn't do.
**`canbusload`** — actual bus utilization %.
**`candump -l`** — the log format cabana and SavvyCAN both read: `(1609779922.655421) vcan0 00000343#B204B9049C049C04`
Also: `cangen`, `cansend`, `cansequence`, `cangw`, the full `isotp*` family (`isotpdump`, `isotpsniffer`, `isotpperf`, `isotptun`), `asc2log`/`log2asc`/`log2long`, `slcand`/`slcanpty`.

**python-can** (https://github.com/hardbyte/python-can, ★1,578) ships `can.logger`, `can.player` (preserves timing by default; `--ignore-timestamps` to fire immediately), `can.bridge`, `can.logconvert`, and **`can.viewer`** — a curses live view whose shortcuts include **`h` to highlight changed bytes (in blue)**, SPACE to pause, `s` to sort. ### 3.7 ICSim — a practice car with randomized signal placement

https://github.com/zombieCraig/ICSim (★971, C/SDL2, from the Car Hacker's Handbook)

The training mode is the good part:

```bash

Linux-only (vcan), but if you want to **practice and validate a reverse-engineering workflow with known ground truth before pointing it at your DME**, this is the tool. ## 6. Synthesis — what I'd actually do with this, for the E36

1. **Write the SavvyCAN CSV exporter this week.** Emit your ADC sweeps and RAM reads as synthetic CAN frames in GVRET native format (`Time Stamp,ID,Extended,Dir,Bus,LEN,D1..D8`, µs timestamps). It's the cheapest possible way to get a mature bit-heatmap + histogram + A/B-diff + candidate-scan UI on macOS today, and it costs you ~30 lines. Group channels so each synthetic ID is a coherent 8-byte payload.

2. **Build the Cheat-Engine loop on your `raw` command.** Snapshot a RAM window → do the thing → filter to addresses that increased / decreased / changed / stayed → repeat. Cabana's Find Signal (with its refinement stack and undo) is the exact UX spec. This will find your ADC channel meanings and RAM addresses far faster than reading CSV columns, and it's the single highest-value piece of new code you could write.

3. **Steal the CSS reference-free plausibility prior.** You don't need ground truth to reject garbage: a correctly-sized, correctly-signed field produces a *smooth, wrap-free* series. Any candidate whose frame-to-frame deltas approach ±2^length is a wrong start bit / width / endianness. Combined with "reject bytes that are pure counters or high-entropy," that alone will cut your candidate set enormously before you correlate against anything.

4. **Adopt sweep-vs-holds explicitly.** Your README already does this instinctively (throttle sweeps, two-point battery calibration). Make it formal: *identify* on a smooth sweep (discriminating), *calibrate* on steady holds (low noise), and **validate the fitted line against the moving data** — 2–3 collinear points fit any line with R²≈1, which is exactly the trap your battery-voltage two-point calibration could fall into.

5. **Inject event markers into your CSV.** A keypress that writes a marker row means "I just floored it" becomes machine-findable instead of requiring you to remember wall-clock times. Cheap, and it makes every later analysis pass better.

6. **For offline dev, pick the right tool for the right layer.** ELM327-emulator is the wrong layer for KWP71 — but its `mt05` scenario (mmap-backed memory image serving Read/Write Memory By Address) is a working template for faking your DME's RAM over your own transport. Simpler still: your existing `session_*.csv` files replayed through a fake serial port. And borrow pihud's sine-wave demo mode so the UI is buildable with nothing plugged in.

7. **For the dashboard itself:** OnBoardPi's shape (Python service owning the serial link, WebSocket outward, TimescaleDB for history, web UI with `canvas-gauges` or `justgage`) plus AutoDash's rendering discipline (**decouple render rate from poll rate** — poll at whatever KWP71 allows, animate at 60fps by interpolating toward the latest value; worker thread owns the socket; keep the frontend stateless). Design the UI **schema-first** — a dropdown over "whatever channels I've mapped so far" rather than hardcoded gauges — because your channel map is going to keep changing for months.

8. **For the signal-definition file:** look at RealDash's XML format (https://github.com/janimm/RealDash-extras) before inventing your own, and at VisualME7Logger's ECU variable-definition format (https://github.com/sbloom82/VisualME7Logger) since it solves precisely your "RAM address → name + scaling" problem for a sibling Bosch ECU.</result>

# What actually separates professional instrumentation from amateur dashboards

## The headline correction

The intuitive thesis — *professionals use flat design, amateurs use skeuomorphism* — **is false**, and worth killing early.

- **Bosch Motorsport** (DTM/WEC/GT3) ships a stock `Classic Gauge` widget on DDU10/11 with a **brushed-chrome bezel ring with specular highlight, a radial navy→cyan gradient face, and a red wedge needle**. I verified this by rendering p.51 of the official DDU11 manual.
- **MoTeC's own 2015 dealer training deck** teaches building a chrome-bezelled dial as its primary worked example, using photorealistic ring bitmaps from Display Creator's `Dial` image library (up to 1004×1004px), plus glow via *"decrease the opacity so that you get more of a glowing effect."*
- **AiM** ships `Analog 1 / Analog 1 white / Analog 2` page templates — literal round dials with radial ticks and a red needle on a pivot hub.

The real dividing line is not ornament. It is **four things**:

1. **Geometric hierarchy is encoded in length, not colour or weight.** Amateur gauges differentiate major/minor ticks by making them a lighter grey. Professional ones use a *documented length ratio* and hold stroke weight nearly constant.
2. **The pointer never occludes what you need to read.** This is a hard rule in every standard and the single most common amateur failure.
3. **Alarm state is a system-level concept with one consistent rendering**, hysteresis, priority ordering, and acknowledgement — not a per-widget colour change.
4. **Every visual effect is load-bearing.** Bosch's gradient is a fill indicator. MoTeC's glow is a simulated backlight on a specific object. Neither applies bloom to *values*.

## 1. Tick mark treatment

**The converged geometry.** Two independent authorities agree almost exactly:

| | Major | Intermediate | Minor | Ratio (maj:int:min) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MIL-STD-1472F/G, Fig. 3/26 (**length**, visual angle) | 7.86 mrad (27′) | 5.82 mrad (20′) | 3.49 mrad (12′) | **2.25 : 1.67 : 1** |
| Grether & Baker 1972 via Sanders & McCormick Fig. 5-4 (**length**, at 710 mm) | 0.22 in (5.6 mm) | 0.16 in (4.1 mm) | 0.09 in (2.3 mm) | **2.44 : 1.78 : 1** |

So: **major ≈ 2.2–2.5× minor length; intermediate ≈ 1.6–1.8× minor.** A 2.0× ratio (what most amateur gauges use, if they vary length at all) is slightly under-differentiated.

**Stroke weight is the surprise.** Under normal illumination, Grether & Baker specify **all three tick sizes at identical width** (0.0125 in). Hierarchy is length-only. Only under low illumination do widths diverge, and only mildly (0.035 / 0.030 / 0.025 in = 1.4 : 1.2 : 1). MIL-STD-1472 notes explicitly: *"the width of the minor graduation mark can be used for major and intermediate graduation marks as well. Use of this strategy allows the width of the pointer tip to be the same as all of the graduation marks."*

**Counting rules (MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.3.1.5, verbatim):**
- *"Scale graduations shall progress by 1, 2, or 5 units or decimal multiples thereof."*
- *"No more than three sizes of marks (minor, intermediate, and major) shall be used on any scale."*
- Two-level marking: **no more than 4 minor marks** between numbered markers.
- Three-level marking: **no more than 9 minor marks**.
- *"Intermediate marks shall only be used when there are more than four minor marks."* — i.e. you don't earn a third tier until you have five or more subdivisions.

Sanders & McCormick add that progression **by 1s is easiest, 5s satisfactory, 2s moderately so; avoid 3s and 8s.**

**Direction and rail.** MIL-STD figures show ticks on a **common base line, extending different lengths from it** — no arc/rail line drawn joining them. Ticks point **inward from the outer edge** in the accuracy-optimised layout (Fig. 4 top). Bosch's `Classic Gauge` and `Modern Gauge` both do exactly this: ticks hang inward from the outer edge, no rail. AiM's arc tach and Bosch's `Modern horizontal Bar` put ticks **outside/above the bar**, pointing at it.

**In the wild:** Bosch's gauges use **two-level marking, 1 minor per major** (majors at 0–10, one tick between each) — consistent with the "≤4 minors ⇒ no intermediate tier" rule. VDO Cockpit 80mm tachos observed at 4 minors per major (200 rpm graduations). Stack 52mm aux gauges: 1 minor per major; Stack 80mm ST700 tach: 4–5 minors per major.

**Where TunerStudio fails:** ticks are **not authorable at all**. Developer Phil Tobin, replying to a user asking for majors at 0/25/50/75/100 with minors between: *"They are auto generated based on min/max and size."* Manual tick placement was a promised, unshipped feature.

## 2. Numeral placement

This has an unambiguous documented answer, and it's the rule most amateur gauges break.

**MIL-STD-1472F §5.2.3.2.3.6:** *"When reading time and accuracy are critical, scale markings and the location of associated numbers shall be arranged to prevent pointers from covering any portion of the scale marks or numerals... If readout accuracy is not critical (i.e., gross relationship between the pointer and number is all that is required), an arrangement of numerals inside the scale annulus may be used."*

Figure 4 labels these two layouts explicitly:
- Numerals **outside** the tick ring → *"FOR MAXIMUM READING ACCURACY"*
- Numerals **inside** the tick ring → *"ALTERNATE FORMAT FOR GROSS READING OF NUMBERS"*

**§5.2.3.2.4.4:** *"Numerals shall be placed on the side of the graduation marks away from the pointer."*

**Orientation (§5.2.3.2.2, and 1472G):** *"On fixed scales, numerals shall be vertically oriented"* — **upright, never rotated to the radius**. (Rotation is required only on *moving* scales, where numerals rotate to be upright as they pass the index.) Every professional dash I examined obeys this: AiM, MoTeC, Bosch Classic *and* Modern gauges all use upright numerals.

**The one documented exception**, from MIL-STD-1472G Fig. 26: *"When dial face is deeply inset within instrument case and visibility of numbers is more important than scale pointer-mark association, pointer may be located inside the graduations along with numbers at major markings. Pointer width shall be narrowed at point in which it passes numbers."* — Note the compensating requirement. If you put numerals inside, you must thin the needle where it crosses them.

**Which values get numerals:** *"whole numbers shall be used for major graduation marks"*; *"A display scale shall start at zero."* Fig. 26 adds: *"For short, finite scale, every 5th graduation is marked, using only two-level marking."*

**Observed:** Bosch `Classic Gauge` puts numerals inside the ticks (gross-reading layout, consistent with it being a supplementary gauge with a digital value in the centre); Bosch `Modern Gauge` puts them outside. VDO Cockpit: inside, upright. Stack: inside, upright.

## 3. Redline / warning zone rendering

**The aviation ancestry is the actual standard**, and it makes a distinction most car dashboards blur. From **14 CFR 25.1549**:

- **Red radial line** = *"Each maximum and, if applicable, minimum safe operating limit"* — a **limit is a line, not a band**.
- **Red arc** = a *restricted range* (e.g. excessive vibration stresses).
- **Green arc** = *"Each normal operating range... not extending beyond the maximum and minimum safe limits."*
- **Yellow arc** = *"Each takeoff and precautionary range."*

MIL-STD-1472F §5.2.3.1.10 permits red/yellow/green zone coding on scale faces, and adds a robustness requirement: *"Zone scales may be shape coded when the indicator must be viewed in blackout conditions or where the illuminant color will cause difficulty in color band discrimination."* — redundant coding, not colour alone.

**What the products actually do:**

| System | Redline rendering |
|---|---|
| **AiM** | No printed redline zone. The **shift-LED bar *is* the redline mechanism**, via per-LED RPM thresholds. |
| **Bosch DDU** | Conditional formatting recolours the **tick arc**; segmented bars recolour by zone. |
| **MoTeC** | Dash Manager bars work on **boundary points** (Left / Intermediate 1 / Intermediate 2 / Right), each assigned one of 3 colours, plus *"Show intermediate tick marks"* and a **`Change whole bar colour`** checkbox — flips the entire bar rather than only the exceeded portion. Round gauges: small red ticks at the redline value, or a red arc wedge. |
| **Stack ST8100 family** | **No printed redline arc found** on the analogue tach face in either the manual diagrams or product photography. Warning is delegated to a discrete amber lamp. |
| **Stack Pro-Control gauges** | The **entire dial face backlight changes colour** on threshold breach (7 selectable colours). |
| **TunerStudio** | Coloured arc segment on the face **plus** danger colour applied to gauge background — but *"only the portion of the bar exceeding that threshold changes color. The rest remains in the normal color."* Whole-gauge alerting requires manually building a boolean channel and layering a second element. |

The MoTeC `Change whole bar colour` option and Stack's whole-face backlight change are the professional answer to the exact problem TunerStudio users had to file a feature request about: **at a glance you want a binary in/out-of-bounds read, not a proportional colour sliver.**

## 4. Needle design

MIL-STD-1472F/G §5.2.3.1.7 is fully prescriptive:

- **Taper:** *"The pointer tip shall be tapered at a 20 degree angle (40 degree included angle), terminating in a flat tip equal in width to the minor scale graduations."* Note: a **flat tip matched to minor tick width**, not a sharp point and not a rounded cap.
- **Length:** *"shall extend to, but not overlap, the shortest scale graduation marks."* Figure 4 quantifies the gap: *"THE POINTER IS AN EQUAL DISTANCE — NOMINAL 0.8–1.6 mm (0.031–0.061 in.) — FROM ALL SCALE MARKS, NEVER OVERLAPPING ANY MARK OR NUMERAL."*
- **Colour:** *"Pointer color from the tip to the center of the dial shall be the same as the color of the marks. The tail of the pointer shall be the same color as the dial face, unless the tail is used as an indicator itself or unless the pointer is used for horizontal alignment."*

That last clause is the counter-intuitive one: **the counterweight tail should be invisible.** It exists mechanically, not visually. And this is borne out in hardware — across Stack, VDO, and Bosch's rendered needle, **not one sample showed a counterweight extending past the pivot.** All are one-directional pointer shapes.

- **Mounting:** *"as close as possible to the face of the dial to minimize parallax"* — and marks *"on or close to the plane of the pointer tip."*

**Hub treatment.** VDO's signature is a **large, glossy, domed black hub cap with a specular highlight**, consistently across Cockpit/Vision and Viewline — the strongest single VDO identifier. Stack uses a much smaller, unobtrusive dark cap. Bosch's `Classic Gauge Large` has **no hub cap at all** — the needle stops well short of centre, leaving a lighter disc reserved for an overlaid digital value.

**Needle colour pairs with face colour:** Stack = white needle on black face, orange on white/silver. VDO Cockpit/Vision = red needle on black. VDO Viewline "Onyx" = white on black, "Ivory" = red on white.

**The Bosch `Modern Gauge` abandons the needle entirely** — a thick cyan arc fills from zero to value, and the *current value is marked by a short white radial tick at the leading edge of the fill*, with a large digital numeral in the centre. This is the most sophisticated pattern I found (see §7).

## 5. Bezel treatment

**Physical hardware:** essentially no bezels. AiM housings are flat anodised aluminium or glass-fibre nylon, matte, screen glass flush. Bosch DDU is a flat TFT behind glass in a rectangular housing. Stack's ST8100 dial and LCD are **inset flush into a single moulded black composite panel** with no ring at all. VDO Cockpit/Vision uses a thin, flat *"peaked black"* bezel — no chrome option in the classic line; Viewline adds thicker rounded black plus chrome and white variants.

**On-screen, the professional tools split into two explicit modes**, and this is the most useful framing I found:

- Bosch DDU10/11 offers **`Classic`** (chrome bezel, gradient face, red wedge needle) and **`Modern`** (no bezel, flat black, arc fill, centre numeral) as **parallel, equally-supported catalogues** of the same primitives (Box, horizontal/vertical Bar, Gauge Large/Small).
- MoTeC supports both: skeuomorphic chrome-bezel dials via bitmap layering, *and* flat colour-blocked numeric table pages with no gauge skeuomorphism (the "Four Line Style" page).

**Bosch DDU7/8/9 have no needle-gauge widget at all** — only Numeric, Bargraph, Alarm/Alarm Icon, Label, Picture. The dial only arrived with the DDU10 generation.

**One genuinely functional reason to recess**, from MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.1.3.3: *"When the detection of faint signals is required and when the ambient illuminance may be above 2.7 lux, displays shall be hooded, shielded, or recessed."* A recess is a real optical device against glare. Simulating an inset shadow in software delivers none of that benefit and costs contrast.

## 6. Layout density and grid

**800 × 480 is the de facto race-dash resolution.** This is a striking convergence:

| Device | Size | Resolution | LEDs |
|---|---|---|---|
| AiM MXS 1.2 | 5″ | 800×480 | 10 shift + 6 alarm |
| AiM MXP | 6″ | 800×480 | 10 shift + 5 alarm |
| AiM MXG 1.2 | 7″ | 800×480 | 10 shift + 8 alarm |
| MoTeC C125 | 5″ (125 mm) | 800×480 | 10 RGB |
| MoTeC C127 | 7″ (178 mm) | 800×480 | 16 RGB |
| Bosch DDU 8 | 5″ | 800×480 | 10 RGB (top) |
| Bosch DDU 11 | 6.5″ | 800×480 | 18 (8 top + 5/side) |
| Bosch DDU 10 | 7″ | 800×480 | 20 (10 top + 5/side) |
| Bosch DDU 7 / 9 | 5.7″ trans-reflective | 640×480 | 10 RGB |

AiM does **not scale resolution with screen size** — only physical DPI. Note MoTeC's spec sheet lists *"Colour TFT LCD, anti-reflective"* and *"800 x 480 resolution, anti-aliased graphics"* as **first-class spec-table line items**. Anti-glare treatment and anti-aliasing are engineering claims, not styling.

**The standard page composition** (AiM Driver page, confirmed across many rendered examples):
- **Top:** RPM bar/arc spanning full width, shift-LED row directly above it
- **Centre:** **gear number, consistently the single largest glyph — 1.5–3× the cap-height of everything else**
- **Around/below:** a 2×2 to 3×2 grid of secondary fields (speed, water temp, oil pressure, battery, lap time), each a Channel + Label + Unit triplet with independent show/hide toggles
- **Bottom:** a full-width `INFO LINE` text banner plus small status icons

Primary/secondary hierarchy is conveyed by **vertical position and size, not colour**. Colour is reserved for semantic status.

**Alignment is not universally settled.** MoTeC's own stock layouts contradict each other: the C187 factory page **left-aligns** values flush with their label's left edge, while the bordered "spreadsheet" table page **right-aligns** values in their cells. There is no single MoTeC rule.

**MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.2.3.5 gives a hard hierarchy rule worth adopting:** *"No more than three size levels shall be used. The major dimensions of the larger size shall be not less than 150 percent of the major dimension of the smaller."*

**Page count:** AiM up to 8 pages, template-based (you pick from a thumbnail gallery and remap channels — **not a blank canvas**). MoTeC C125: 12 customisable fixed layouts, or full freeform via the paid Display Creator upgrade. Bosch: fully blank canvas, 12 pages (DDU7/8/9/10) or 48 (DDU11 = 12 pages × 4 switchable sets) — **no default factory template at all**; teams design their own per car and per driver.

## 7. Glow, bloom, and gradients

**Professional systems use gradients. They do not use bloom on values.** The distinction is that every effect maps to a physical referent:

| Effect | Professional use | Amateur tell |
|---|---|---|
| **Gradient** | Bosch `Modern Bar`: each filled segment has an internal gradient; the arc has a subtle inner-edge lightening. AiM's arc tach: the colour fill *is* the indicator. | Decorative radial gradient on a static gauge face; glossy "glass" highlight arcs. |
| **Glow** | MoTeC teaches it as a **reduced-opacity bitmap layered near a light source** — simulating a real backlight, on a specific object. | `text-shadow`/`drop-shadow` applied globally to numerals, needles, and traces. |
| **Drop shadow** | Essentially absent. RaceCapture ships `round_gauge_270_shadow.png` composited every frame — and it is one of the things that marks it as hobbyist. | Shadow on the needle, on values, on tiles. |
| **Bloom/halo** | **None found in any AiM, MoTeC, or Bosch rendering.** | Halos on lit LEDs and active segments. |

The governing rule, MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.2.3.1: ***"Coding shall not be used if it reduces legibility or transmission time."***

Two more constraints that bite directly:
- §5.2.2.3.3: *"No more than two levels of brightness shall be used and each level shall be separated... by not less than a 2:1 ratio."* A glow gradient creates a continuum of brightness levels, destroying the coding channel.
- §5.2.3.1.8: *"A luminance contrast not less than 3.0 shall be provided between the scale face and the markings and pointer."* Table XII requires **≥5:1 between lighter and darker surfaces within the task**. Every glow halo raises the local background luminance around the very element it surrounds, which reduces that ratio.

**Physics reinforces this.** In sunlight, reflected ambient light adds a constant luminance floor to *both* the lit and unlit states. A dark UI's contrast advantage collapses; only peak luminance (AiM: 700 cd/m²) and low reflectance (MoTeC: *"anti-reflective"*) help. A software glow adds emitted light *around* a glyph — precisely where you need the floor lowest.

**The one hard-won detail worth stealing:** Bosch's `Modern` bars render **discrete segments with the leading segment in a brighter, near-white shade**. This is not decoration — it simultaneously provides the filled-bar magnitude read *and* a distinct pointer position, resolving a tradeoff Paul Green identified in 1984 (see §10).

## 8. Typography

**Named typefaces actually in use:**

| System | Typeface | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **AiM RaceStudio 3** | **`MicrogrammaDBolExt`** — Microgramma D Bold Extended | Novarese & Butti, Nebiolo, **1952**; caps-only; predecessor of Eurostile (1962). Squarish superellipse counters. Used for **both** Digit Font and Label Font. |
| **MoTeC** | Not disclosed. But ships **three icon fonts: `MoTeC01`, `MoTeC02`, `MoTeC03`** | See below — this is the important finding. |
| **Bosch DDU** | Not disclosed; **FreeType** for *"non-bitmap font rendering"* (license text in DDU11 manual) | Visually blocky, monospaced, tabular figures. |
| **RaceCapture** | Bespoke `ASL_light.ttf` / `ASL_regular.ttf` + Roboto family | But bundles **six-plus families** including `enigmatic.ttf` and `forgotten_futurist-rg.ttf`. |
| **Smiths** | **None — hand-drawn.** | Restoration forums: originals were *"hand painted by a sign writer then reduced and transferred to a silk screen."* Don't chase a "Smiths font." |
| **VDO** | Not disclosed. Community approximation: Arial Black, per the numeral "1" shape. Treat as unverified. |

**MoTeC's telltale approach is the single best implementation idea in this research:** *"A great way to incorporate tell tales into your DC project is by using font based icons. By using a font, the icon (tell tale) remains a vector graphic and is therefore scaleable and remains crisp. It also means that you set the colour of the icon, perhaps using different colours to indicate various states."* Icons as a font, recoloured for state.

**Size relationships (measured):** AiM's Display config shows `Digit Font: MicrogrammaDBolExt` **size 42**, `Label Font: MicrogrammaDBolExt` **size 20** — **label ≈ 48% of value**. Units render as small tags adjacent to the value (superscript-like, upper-right), not as a separate row.

**Labels are uppercase, short, abbreviated:** `ENG TEMP`, `OIL PRESS`, `GBOX OIL TMP`, `DIFF OIL TMP`, `WATER TMP` (MoTeC); `R/P/M` stacked letter-per-line (AiM). Labels sit **above** values, smaller, usually in an accent colour distinct from the value's high-contrast white.

**MIL-STD-1472F §5.5.5 numbers** (all relative to character height):

- Stroke width, **dark on light: 1/6 to 1/7**
- Stroke width, **light on dark: 1/7 to 1/8** — *thinner*, to counter irradiation
- Stroke width, **transilluminated: 1/10**
- Numeral width: **3/5 of height**, except "4" = 4/5 and "1" = 1/5
- *"Where wide characters are required, e.g. ... for column alignment of numbers, the basic height-to-width ratio may be increased to as much as 1:1"* — the standards' endorsement of tabular figures
- Minimum character spacing = **one stroke width**; minimum line spacing = **half character height**
- Character height at 710 mm viewing: critical fixed-position markings (scale numerals) **2.5–5 mm** above 3.5 cd/m², **4–8 mm** at/below. Scale by D/710 mm.

**A caveat I should flag:** MIL-STD-1472F *and* G both carry a footnote that tick-mark **widths** become 4.36 mrad (15′) for light-on-dark — roughly 3.7× the dark-on-light value, and more than half the length of a major tick. That is dimensionally implausible and looks like a long-standing typo carried across revisions. The *direction* (light-on-dark ticks get thicker) is consistent with Grether & Baker's low-illumination case, but note it directly contradicts the standard's own guidance that light-on-dark *numerals* get **thinner**. Treat the direction as real and the magnitude as suspect.

## 9. Shift lights and alarm rendering

**Why shift lights are physical LEDs at the top edge, not a screen element.** MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.2.3.2(b): ***"Color shall not be used for gaining attention outside the optimum visual field."*** Colour is a foveal cue. Peripheral alerting needs luminance, motion, and flash. Wikipedia's shift-light entry gives the operational counterpart: they let a driver judge the shift point *"without having to glance down at the tachometer... keeping their focus near the track at all times."* An RPM bar that turns red is a foveal signal; an LED strip at the top of the housing is a peripheral one.

**Actual documented threshold tables:**

| System | Pattern | Steps |
|---|---|---|
| **AiM** (canonical example, identical across MXS Strada / MXP / MXL2 manuals) | 10 LEDs, **5 green : 2 yellow : 3 red** | 8200→10000 rpm, **200 rpm per LED**, 1800 rpm span |
| **Bosch DDU8** (manual's default pattern) | 10 LEDs, **4 green : 2 yellow : 2 orange : 2 red** | 6000, 6050, 6100, 6200, 6300, 6400, 6500, 6600, 6700, 6800 — **non-uniform**: 50 rpm for the first two steps, then 100 rpm |
| **Autosport Labs ShiftX3** (factory power-on default) | 3 LEDs green @3000 → 5 cyan @5000 → **7 red flashing @5 Hz** @7000 | Green → cyan → flashing red |

Three professional details amateur systems omit:

1. **Hysteresis on threshold crossings.** Bosch: *"The RPM hysteresis function avoids the high-frequent switchover of the measurement channel value."* MoTeC has the same field. Without it, LEDs chatter at the boundary.
2. **Gear-dependent thresholds.** AiM and Bosch both provide a full per-gear threshold table (Bosch's dialog has columns `Default, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8`).
3. **Lead compensation.** MoTeC's training deck: *"remember to put the RPM signal lower than the actual RPM you wish to shift at... the driver will always need to see the light before he knows to change gear."*

**Two sequencing modes** (AiM, verbatim): *"A LED stays on if its threshold is exceeded"* (cumulative VU-meter fill) or *"A LED stays on until another LED with higher threshold is turned on"* (chase, one lit at a time).

**How shift is disambiguated from alarm:**

- **AiM:** physically separate hardware. Shift LEDs are a row of 10 across the top; **alarm LEDs are 2–8 discrete LEDs in clusters flanking the screen** (MXL2 manual labels them *"Configurable Alarm LEDs 1-3"* left, *"4-6"* right). Different location, different purpose.
- **MoTeC:** same LED strip, but **patterns are priority-ordered in a list** — *"if a pattern has a high priority, e.g. Warning Lights, it cannot be affected by another pattern condition lower in the list becoming true."* A warning pattern placed above the shift pattern pre-empts it.
- **Bosch DDU10/11:** adds 5 LEDs on each side of the housing beyond the top row, giving a spatial split.

**Alarm rendering — the most transferable material:**

**MoTeC C125** (from the user manual):
- Active + unacknowledged → **full-width bar along the bottom edge, bright red, bold white uppercase centred text**, overwriting whatever was there (`ENGINE HOT`).
- Four states: *active/unacknowledged, inactive/unacknowledged* (condition cleared but still displaying), *active/acknowledged* (true but suppressed), *inactive*.
- **Only the highest-priority unacknowledged alarm shows at a time**; as each is acked the next appears.
- Acknowledged alarms move to an **Alarm Status Panel** — up to 6, in a **dark maroon** bar, visibly less saturated than the bright-red unacknowledged bar. Hidden whenever a new unacknowledged alarm needs the space.
- **Gating on other channels**, with a documented example: suppress the engine-temp alarm unless ground speed has been >50 km/h for 30 s — to avoid false triggers from pit-stop heat soak.
- The manual explicitly recommends pairing the on-screen message with a **physical warning light**.

**Bosch DDU:** alarms live in one of **4 fixed screen areas**, are **non-transparent**, **always rendered at the highest z-order**, and when several are simultaneously active in one area **each is shown for ~1.5–2 s in rotation**.

**MIL-STD-1472G §5.2.2.3.4 and §5.7.3.2.4 give the flash grammar:**
- **Warning: flashing red, 3.0–5.0 Hz, 50% duty cycle, synchronised across all warnings.**
- **Caution: yellow, flashing text ≤2.0 Hz at ~70% on. *"Caution signals shall be not more than half the intensity of the warning signal."*** and *"A minimum of two discriminatory characteristics shall be employed."*
- ***"Characters that must be read shall not flash; an adjacent flashing symbol or flashing background may be used to add emphasis to text."*** — the rule amateur dashboards break most often.
- *"Only a small area of a display shall flash at any time."*
- *"Event acknowledgment or flash suppression control shall be provided."*
- Colour meanings (§5.2.2.1.13): **flashing red** = emergency requiring action without delay; **red** = inoperative/no-go; **yellow** = marginal, caution, recheck; **green** = in tolerance; **white** = no right/wrong implication; **blue** = avoid.
- Warning/caution text height: **8.7–17.4 mrad (30–60′)** at the longest anticipated viewing distance.

## 10. Analogue vs digital: the human-factors argument

### The canonical decision table

**MIL-STD-1472F Table III, "Application of various types of mechanical displays"** is the authoritative source. Transcribed from the original:

| Use | Moving pointer (fixed scale) | Fixed pointer (moving scale) | Counters (digital) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quantitative information** | **FAIR** — *"May be difficult to read while pointer is in motion."* | **FAIR** | **GOOD** — *"Minimum time and error for exact numerical value; however, cannot be read when changing rapidly."* |
| **Qualitative information** | **GOOD** — *"Location of pointer easy. Numbers and scale need not be read. Position change easily detected."* | **POOR** — *"Difficult to judge direction and magnitude of deviation without reading numbers and scale."* | **POOR** — *"Numbers must be read. Position changes not easily detected."* |
| **Setting** | **GOOD** | FAIR | **GOOD** — *"Most accurate... Not readable during rapid setting."* |
| **Tracking** | **GOOD** — *"Pointer position readily controlled and monitored."* | FAIR | **POOR** — *"No gross position changes to aid monitoring."* |
| **General** | *"Requires largest exposed and illuminated area on panel."* | *"Saves panel space."* | *"Most economical of space and illumination."* |

### The four task types

Sanders & McCormick, *Human Factors in Engineering and Design*, Ch. 5, define the taxonomy that everything else hangs on:

1. **Quantitative reading** — *"read a precise numeric value"* → *"The pressure is 125 psi."*
2. **Qualitative reading** — *"read an approximate value or to discern a trend, rate of change, or change in direction"* → *"The pressure is rising."*
3. **Check reading** — *"determine if parameters are within some 'normal' bounds"* → *"All pressures are normal."*
4. **Situation awareness** — spatial/predictive.

Their worked example is, conveniently, **a car engine temperature gauge**:

> *"At the most elementary level, only check reading is necessary; that is, is the engine overheated or not? A warning light... would properly provide such information... So do we need an engine-temperature gauge in a car? The answer is yes. The reason is that we do need to make qualitative readings such as whether the temperature is rising or whether it is getting near the overheating point."*

### The empirical record

| Study | Finding |
|---|---|
| **Grether (1949)**, *J. Applied Psychology* 33, 363–72 | 97 USAF pilots + 79 college men, 12 settings on 9 altimeter designs. *"Instruments that combine the indications from two or more pointers or rotating subdials are conducive to large reading errors; indicators on which the digits are already combined in the proper sequence are more easily read."* Direct-reading counters won decisively for quantitative reading. |
| **Sleight (1948)**, *J. Applied Psychology* 32, 170–188 | 60 subjects, 5 dial shapes. Accuracy order: **open-window > round > semicircular > horizontal > vertical**. Error rates spanned **0.5% to 35.5%**. Errors were more frequent on mid-division than whole-number settings. |
| **Elkin (1959)**, WADC TR 58-472 (Sanders & McCormick Table 5-1) | Reading times by task, in index units: **Qualitative** — vertical 101 < circular 107 < open-window 115. **Quantitative** — open-window 102 < circular 113 < vertical 118. **The crossover is demonstrated directly**: the display that is fastest for one task is slowest for the other. |
| **Dashevsky (1964)**, *J. Applied Psychology* 48, 344–347 | Check-reading a 4×4 dial matrix was made **85% more efficient** by continuing the line formed by the aligned pointers across the entire panel face. The deviant dial then *"appeared as a break in a line"* — Gestalt figural continuity. **No significant difference between 9 and 12 o'clock null orientations.** |
| **Simmonds, Galer & Baines (1981)**, SAE 810826 | Compared digital speedometers against three dials and a curvilinear display. **Digital consistently better** for both reading accuracy and preference. |
| **Green (1984)**, SAE 840314, *"Driver understanding of fuel and engine gauges"* | For bar-type displays, **only one segment of the bar should be shown**; extending the bar to zero *"was confusing to some people."* But a single-segment bar is **inappropriate for a fuel gauge** (no empty indication), while a full bar suits speed *"because it would grow longer or shorter with changing values."* |
| **Cohen & Follert (1970)**, *Human Factors* 12(5), 481–483 | Interpolation of **fifths, and even tenths**, yields satisfactory accuracy — you do not need a tick per readable unit. |
| **Whitehurst (1982)**, *Human Factors* 24(3), 301–310 | Numeric progression and scale-unit length dominate speed/accuracy. Scales are read **fastest when pointers land precisely on markers**. |
| **François, Crave, Osiurak, Fort & Navarro (2017)**, *Applied Ergonomics*, doi:10.1016/j.apergo.2017.05.013 | Simulated truck driving. *"A digital speedometer would be more beneficial when obtaining absolute and relative readings, while an analogue speedometer would be more efficient and less distracting when detecting dynamic speed changes... The redundant speedometer combined the benefits of each type presented separately."* |
| **François, Fort, Crave, Osiurak & Navarro (2019)**, *Int. J. Industrial Ergonomics*, doi:10.1016/j.ergon.2019.06.004 | **The most directly applicable study.** 18 truck drivers, 8 gauge designs varying shape/orientation/indicator, across all three task types. *"Horizontal gauges and pointer indicators were more efficient and less demanding visually... circular and horizontal gauges were preferred by drivers. Specific gauge designs implied a gain in visual demand up to 250 ms."* |

### Design rules that fall out

- **MIL-STD-1472G:** *"Moving pointer, fixed scales shall be used in preference to fixed pointer, moving scales."* And: *"Where reading speed is important, circular scales shall be used in preference to horizontal scales, and horizontal scales... in preference to vertical scales."* (Note this conflicts with François 2019, which found horizontal more efficient than circular but circular *preferred*. Objective efficiency and subjective preference diverge.)
- **Scale indicators are for *"quantitative information combined with qualitative information (e.g. trend, direction-of-motion)"***; use a numeric readout where *"speed, accuracy of response"* demand it.
- **Redundancy wins.** François 2017 found the combined display captured both advantages. This is exactly what Bosch's `Modern Gauge` does: arc + leading-edge cursor + centre digital numeral. And Sanders & McCormick note precoded zones can serve all three tasks at once: *"quantitative displays with coded zones also can be used to reflect trends... Further, they can be used for quantitative reading if the scale values are included."*
- **Check-reading layout, MIL-STD-1472F §5.2.3.2.3.5:** arrange indicators *"in rows so that all pointers line up horizontally on the 9 o'clock position under normal operating conditions"* or in columns aligning at 12 o'clock. *"If a matrix of indicators is needed, preference shall be given to the 9 o'clock position."* Plus Dashevsky's connecting line for the 85% gain.
- **Circular scale geometry:** zero/minimum between **225° and 300°**, maximum between **60° and 135°**, symmetrically arranged; *"an obvious break of at least 10° of arc between the two ends of the scale"*; magnitude increases clockwise.
